title: What is a period
answer: A period (menstruation) is when blood and tissue leave your body through the vagina, usually for 2 to 7 days. It is a sign that you are growing up normally and that your body is healthy. All girls go through this change.

title: When girls start their period
answer: Girls can start their period any time from about age 8 to 18. Most girls start between 10 and 14. Every body has its own timing. If you are worried about your own timing, a nurse can talk with you.

title: How often periods come and irregular periods
answer: A period usually comes about every 28 days, but anything from 21 to 35 days can be normal. In the first year or two it can be irregular while your body adjusts. Stress, heavy exercise, poor eating or an emergency situation can also make periods irregular. If you have had sex and your period is late, pregnancy is possible, so think about a pregnancy test.
source: UNICEF/IMC Growing Healthy booklet 2015; REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018
reviewer_note: Last sentence added from CSE book (missed period may mean pregnancy).

title: How long a period lasts
answer: Bleeding usually lasts 2 to 7 days, but it can be different for different girls. If bleeding is very heavy, for example soaking a pad every hour, or lasts much longer than 7 days, please see a health worker.
reviewer_note: Second sentence (heavy bleeding advice) is general practice, not from the booklet. Please confirm.

title: Staying clean and bad smell during a period
answer: A bad smell comes from bacteria that grow when blood is warm and moist. Change your pad or cloth every 3 to 5 hours, or sooner if it is soaked. Wash your genital area with soap and water at least twice a day, wash your hands after using the toilet or changing your pad, and wipe from front to back. Do not use perfumes, herbs or ointments on your private parts.

title: Period pain and cramps
answer: Pain in the lower back or stomach during a period is common. To feel better you can move and stretch, do some exercise, put a hot compress on the painful area or have a warm bath. Ibuprofen may help if you have it. If the pain is very strong or stops you from doing your normal activities, see a health worker.
reviewer_note: Last sentence is general practice, not from the booklet. Please confirm.

title: Vaginal discharge
answer: Clear, cloudy white or yellowish discharge between periods is normal. Changes in your discharge, a new bad smell, itching or a burning feeling can be signs of infection. If you notice these, please see a health worker.

title: Pads, leaks, disposal and washing cloths
answer: Use only clean and dry pads or cloths and keep a spare with you, especially at school. If blood leaks through your clothes, which happens to almost every girl, tie a jacket or sweater around your waist and change as soon as you can. Wrap used pads in paper or plastic and put them in a bin. Never throw them in the toilet. Wash reusable cloths with clean water and soap and dry them in the sun, which helps kill germs.

title: Period myths
answer: You can bathe, swim and wash your hair during your period. Washing helps prevent infection. Eating sour or salty food or drinking cold drinks does not stop your period. You do not need to stop running or moving; movement may even ease cramps, but rest if your body asks for it. Menstrual blood is not dirty. Menstruation is a natural part of life.
source: UNICEF/IMC Growing Healthy booklet 2015; REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018

title: Tracking your period on a calendar
answer: Mark the first day of each period on a calendar, how many days it lasts and which days are heavy. After a few months you can predict when the next one will come. A cycle is usually 21 to 35 days, counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. Cycles can be irregular in the first years.
reviewer_note: Booklet says to count 21-35 days 'from the end of each period'. Standard practice counts from the first day. Please confirm wording.

title: What is puberty
answer: Puberty is the time when your body changes from a child's body to an adult's body. Your body, your feelings and your social life all change. It is normal and healthy. It does not start at the same age for everyone, and girls usually start earlier than boys.

title: Body changes in girls and boys
answer: Both girls and boys grow taller, grow hair on the body, in the armpits and on the genitals, get oilier skin with pimples, sweat more and have bigger genitals. Girls also develop breasts, get wider hips and start their periods. Boys also get broader shoulders, more muscle, facial hair, a deeper voice, first ejaculation and wet dreams.

title: Wet dreams and sudden erections
answer: A wet dream is when a boy ejaculates while he sleeps. Sudden erections are also common in teenage boys, even many times a day. Both are normal and harmless, and part of growing up. Erections go away by themselves. They do not mean a boy needs to have sex.

title: Masturbation
answer: Many boys and girls masturbate during puberty or sometimes earlier. It does not cause physical or emotional harm, and it does not make you blind or weak. It is a private matter and should be done in private. If you feel worried or guilty about it, you can talk to a nurse or a trusted adult.
source: REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018; UNESCO ITGSE
reviewer_note: Last sentence added for support. Please confirm tone.

title: Mood changes and feelings in puberty
answer: During puberty your moods can change quickly, you may feel confused, worry about being normal, start to feel attraction to others and want to fit in with friends. All of this is common. Talking to a trusted friend, family member, teacher or nurse can help.
source: REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018; UNICEF/IMC Growing Healthy booklet 2015

title: Body hygiene in puberty
answer: In puberty your sweat and oil glands become more active, so wash your body and genital area often with soap and water. Wash your hands after using the toilet. Do not use perfumes, herbs or ointments on your private parts.
source: REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018; UNICEF/IMC Growing Healthy booklet 2015

title: Hymen and virginity myths
answer: The hymen can stretch or tear from sport, exercise or other activities, not only from sex. Some girls are born with a loose or very small hymen. So the hymen is not a reliable sign of virginity. Herbs or other things cannot restore virginity. A person can decide to wait for sex at any time, even after having had sex.

title: Pregnancy the first time and every time
answer: Yes. A girl can get pregnant the very first time she has sex, and every time she has sex without protection. Using a condom or another contraceptive method lowers the risk. A health worker can help you choose.
source: REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018; WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022

title: What is contraception and what methods exist
answer: Contraception helps you prevent pregnancy and decide if and when to have children. Methods include condoms, pills, implants, injections, IUDs and emergency pills. Condoms are the only method that also protects against STIs, including HIV. A health worker can help you choose the method that fits your life.
source: WHO Adolescent Contraception 2017; WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022

title: Are contraceptives safe for young people
answer: Yes. Young people can safely use any contraceptive method, and age alone is not a medical reason to refuse a method. Contraceptives are not only for married people. A health worker can explain what to expect, including common side effects.
source: WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022; WHO Adolescent Contraception 2017; REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018

title: Male condoms
answer: Condoms are worn on the penis and block sperm and infections. They are the only method that protects against both pregnancy and STIs, including HIV. Used correctly every time, about 2 in 100 women get pregnant in a year; as commonly used, about 13 in 100. Use a new condom each time and talk about it with your partner before sex. Using two condoms at once does not protect more and can make them break.
source: WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022; REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018

title: Birth control pills
answer: The combined pill is taken every day at the same time. As commonly used, about 7 in 100 women get pregnant in a year, and fewer than 1 in 100 if no pills are missed. Bleeding changes are common at first and not harmful. Pills do not protect against STIs. If you miss a pill, take it as soon as you remember and ask a health worker what else to do. Pills do not make you infertile; fertility returns when you stop.
source: WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022; REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018

title: Implant
answer: The implant is a small rod, about the size of a matchstick, placed under the skin of the upper arm by a trained provider. It protects against pregnancy for 3 to 5 years, depending on the type, and is one of the most effective methods. It can be removed at any time and fertility returns right away. Bleeding changes are common and not harmful. It does not protect against STIs.

title: Contraceptive injection
answer: The injection is given every 3 months (every 2 months for NET-EN). As commonly used, about 4 in 100 women get pregnant in a year. Bleeding changes are common and not harmful, and no one else can tell you are using it. It can take about 4 months longer to become pregnant after stopping. It does not protect against STIs.
source: WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022; WHO Adolescent Contraception 2017
reviewer_note: WHO notes DMPA is category 2 for under 18s (benefits generally outweigh risks).

title: IUD (coil)
answer: The copper IUD is a small device placed in the womb by a trained provider. It protects against pregnancy for up to 12 years and can be removed at any time. Periods may become heavier with more cramps in the first 3 to 6 months. It does not protect against STIs. IUDs can come out more often in women who have never given birth, so check with a health worker.

title: Emergency contraceptive pills
answer: Emergency pills can help prevent pregnancy after sex without protection, a broken condom or forced sex. Take them as soon as possible, ideally within 3 days. They can still help up to 5 days after. They do not end an existing pregnancy and do not protect against STIs. They are safe to use, even more than once, but a regular method works better. A copper IUD can also be used for emergency contraception. If your period is more than 7 days late afterwards, take a pregnancy test.
source: WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022; Rwanda HIV Guidelines 2022

title: Contraception myths
answer: Contraceptives are not only for married people. Pills do not make you infertile. Washing the vagina with Coca-Cola or Sprite after sex does not prevent pregnancy. Using two condoms does not protect more. The days between periods are not always safe, especially when periods are irregular.

title: Withdrawal and counting days
answer: Withdrawal (pulling out) is one of the least effective methods: about 20 in 100 women get pregnant in a year as commonly used. Counting days is also unreliable, especially when periods are irregular, as they often are in teenagers. A condom or another method protects better.
source: WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022; REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018

title: Permission and privacy for contraception
answer: WHO recommends that young people can get contraceptive information and services without needing a parent or guardian to approve, and with privacy and respect. Rwanda's CSE book states that adolescents have a right to information and services. Ask your health center about its rules and how it keeps your information private.
source: WHO Adolescent Contraception 2017; WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022; REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018
reviewer_note: Please confirm current Rwandan rules for minors accessing contraception.

title: Signs of pregnancy
answer: A missed period is a common first sign of pregnancy. Some people also feel sick, have tender breasts or feel very tired. A late period can have other causes, such as stress, so only a pregnancy test can tell you for sure.
reviewer_note: Signs other than missed period are general knowledge, not from the uploaded documents.

title: How to know if you are pregnant
answer: A pregnancy test can tell you. You can get one at a health center. If you took emergency pills and your period is more than 7 days late, take a pregnancy test. If it is positive, go to a health center for antenatal care as early as possible.

title: When can a girl get pregnant
answer: A girl can get pregnant any time she has sex without protection, even the first time. The most fertile time is around the middle of the cycle, but periods in teenagers can be very irregular, so no day is reliably safe. A condom or another method gives better protection.

title: Risks of teenage pregnancy
answer: Pregnancy at a young age brings higher health risks for the girl and the baby, and can affect her education and future work. Going for antenatal care early, eating well and having skilled care at birth reduce the risks. Contraception and staying in school help prevent early pregnancy.
source: WHO Adolescent Contraception 2017; WHO Adolescent SRHR 2018
reviewer_note: Second sentence (antenatal care advice) is general practice. Please confirm.

title: What to do if you are pregnant
answer: Go to a health center as early as you can for antenatal care. You will be offered tests, including HIV and syphilis, which protect you and your baby. Try to talk to an adult you trust. You have a right to respectful care without being judged.
source: Rwanda HIV Guidelines 2022; WHO Adolescent SRHR 2018

title: Worried about pregnancy after sex without protection
answer: Pregnancy is possible after sex without protection. Emergency contraceptive pills can lower the risk if taken as soon as possible, ideally within 3 days and up to 5 days. Go to a health center or pharmacy soon. If your period is more than 7 days late afterwards, take a pregnancy test.

title: What are STIs
answer: STIs are infections that pass from person to person through sexual contact. Anyone who has had sex can get one. Many STIs have no symptoms, especially in girls, so a person can have one without knowing. Testing and treatment protect you and your partner.

title: Signs of an STI
answer: Possible signs are a change in discharge, a new bad smell, itching, burning when passing urine, or sores. But many STIs show no signs at all. If you have had sex without a condom or you notice any of these, please get tested at a health center.
source: UNICEF/IMC Growing Healthy booklet 2015; REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018
reviewer_note: Burning with urine and sores are general knowledge; please confirm list.

title: Can STIs be cured
answer: Many STIs can be treated and cured with the right medicine, and early treatment prevents damage to your body. Some, such as HIV and herpes, cannot be cured but can be managed. Go to a health center for testing and treatment.
source: REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018; Rwanda HIV Guidelines 2022

title: Getting tested and treated for an STI
answer: You can get tested and treated at a health center. Treatment is usually very effective. Health workers should treat you with respect and keep your information private. Do not use herbs or ointments on your private parts.
source: REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018; WHO Adolescent Contraception 2017; UNICEF/IMC Growing Healthy booklet 2015
reviewer_note: Please confirm rules on parental permission for under-age clients.

title: Condoms and STI protection
answer: Condoms reduce the risk of many STIs when used correctly every time you have sex. They protect best against STIs spread by discharge, such as HIV, gonorrhea and chlamydia, and also help against herpes and HPV. Other methods such as pills, implants, injections and emergency pills do not protect against STIs.

title: Can you get an STI from toilets or swimming
answer: STIs are mainly spread through sexual contact with an infected person. You cannot get an STI from toilet seats, swimming pools, sharing food, hugging or other normal contact.
source: REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018; Rwanda HIV Guidelines 2022
reviewer_note: CSE says STIs occur through sexual contact; some infections can also pass by blood or from mother to baby. Wording says mainly. Please confirm.

title: HPV vaccine
answer: The HPV vaccine protects against the virus that can cause cervical cancer. Ask your school nurse or health center about the vaccine and who can get it.
reviewer_note: Please add Rwanda's national HPV vaccine schedule.

title: What is HIV and AIDS
answer: HIV is a virus that weakens the body's defense against disease. AIDS is the late stage of untreated HIV infection. With treatment, people living with HIV can stay healthy and live long lives.
source: REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018; Rwanda HIV Guidelines 2022

title: How HIV is passed on and how it is not
answer: HIV passes through unprotected sex, contact with infected blood and from mother to baby. It is not passed by touching, hugging, sneezing, sharing food, cups or toilets, swimming pools, mosquito bites, or tears and sweat.

title: How to prevent HIV
answer: Use condoms correctly every time you have sex; they prevent 80 to 95 percent of HIV transmission that would otherwise occur. Get tested, get STIs treated, and ask a health worker about PrEP (daily pills before exposure) and PEP (pills after exposure). Never share needles or blades.
source: WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022; Rwanda HIV Guidelines 2022
reviewer_note: Needles/blades sentence is general knowledge.

title: HIV testing
answer: Testing is voluntary and private. In Rwanda, people aged 12 and above can agree to a test themselves, and for children aged 10 to 11 a parent or guardian agrees. A self-test kit is for people aged 16 and above and is sold at health facilities and pharmacies. A positive self-test must be confirmed by a health worker.

title: HIV window period
answer: After infection, it can take from 2 weeks up to 3 to 6 months for a test to show positive. This is the window period. If you had a recent risk and tested negative, test again later. A negative self-test does not rule out HIV after recent exposure.
source: REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018; Rwanda HIV Guidelines 2022

title: PrEP
answer: PrEP is a daily pill that HIV-negative people at higher risk can take to prevent HIV. It is voluntary. You must test negative first and be tested again every 3 months. It reaches full protection after 7 daily doses. You should still use condoms for other protection. Ask a health worker if PrEP is right for you.

title: PEP after possible exposure
answer: PEP is a 28-day course of HIV medicine that lowers the chance of infection after possible exposure, for example after rape or a condom failing with a partner living with HIV. Start it as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours. Go to a health facility right away.

title: Treatment and living with HIV
answer: Everyone with HIV can start treatment (ART) on the same day as diagnosis. Taking medicine every day brings the virus to undetectable levels. Undetectable means untransmittable (U=U): the virus cannot pass to a sexual partner. Treatment is not a cure, so continue it for life, with support from a health worker.

title: HIV and pregnancy
answer: Pregnant women are offered an HIV test at antenatal care. If a mother is living with HIV, treatment and follow-up for the mother and baby greatly lower the chance of passing HIV to the baby. Go to antenatal care early.
reviewer_note: Please confirm wording of PMTCT statement against national PMTCT chapter.

title: Contraception for people living with HIV or at risk
answer: All family planning methods are safe for people at high risk of HIV or living with HIV, except spermicides containing nonoxynol-9. Condoms are still important to prevent HIV and other STIs. A health worker can help you choose a method that works with your HIV medicine.
source: WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022; WHO Adolescent Contraception 2017

title: What is a healthy relationship
answer: In a healthy relationship both people feel safe, respected and equal. You can say no without fear, talk honestly and make your own choices. Love is not control, threats or violence. If you feel afraid or controlled, talk to someone you trust.
source: UNESCO ITGSE; REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018
reviewer_note: Please check wording against ITGSE learning objectives.

title: Pressure to have sex
answer: You have the right to decide about your own body, and nobody should pressure you into sex. It is okay to say no or to wait. You can say, "I am not ready," or "If you respect me, you will wait." Talk with a trusted adult or a health worker if the pressure continues.
source: WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022; UNESCO ITGSE

title: Am I ready for sex
answer: Only you can decide, and there is no rush. Think about whether you feel ready, safe and free from pressure, and whether you can protect yourself with condoms or another method. Waiting is a valid choice. You can talk to a nurse or an adult you trust.
source: UNESCO ITGSE; REB/UNFPA CSE Reference Book 2018

title: Talking to a partner about condoms
answer: Talk about condoms before sex, when you are calm. You can say, "I want us both to be safe." Talking before sex makes it more likely that a condom will be used. If your partner refuses, you can say no to sex. A health worker can help you practise what to say.

title: Who can I talk to about these questions
answer: It is okay to want to know more and to ask for help. You can talk to a trusted teacher, friend, family member or a nurse at a health center. Health workers should not judge you and should keep your information private.
source: UNICEF/IMC Growing Healthy booklet 2015; WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022

title: Gender, equality and decisions
answer: Girls and women have the right to make their own decisions about sex and contraception, and boys and men share responsibility for the results of their actions. Respect and equality make relationships safer and healthier.

title: What is consent
answer: Consent means that a person freely says yes to sex and can change their mind at any time. Sex needs agreement from both people each time. Silence, fear or being drunk or drugged is not consent. Anyone can say no.

title: Sex with a person under 18
answer: In Rwanda, sex with a person under 18 is rape (statutory rape) even if the young person says yes. This protects children. If an adult is pursuing you or a friend, tell a trusted adult or call the child helpline on 116.
reviewer_note: Please confirm with legal advisor the current Rwandan law on age of consent.

title: Bad touch and what to do
answer: No one has the right to touch you in a way that feels wrong, scary or secret. It is never your fault. Say no if you can, get away to a safe place and tell an adult you trust. You can call 116 (child helpline, free) for help.

title: What to do after rape or sexual assault
answer: It was not your fault. Go as soon as you can to a health facility or an Isange One Stop Centre (call 3029). Care is free. If you go within 72 hours you can be given medicine to lower the chance of HIV (PEP) and emergency pills to prevent pregnancy. You can also be tested and get support. You can call 3512 for help. You do not have to report to the police to get health care.
reviewer_note: RBC page states services are free in district hospitals. Please confirm 'free' at Isange centres and 'no police report needed'.

title: Sexual harassment
answer: Touching someone's body or making sexual comments without permission is sexual harassment. It is not okay, whoever does it. You can tell a trusted adult, a teacher or the police on 3512.

title: Marriage does not mean consent to sex
answer: Agreeing to marry does not mean agreeing to sex. Everyone has the right to say yes or no each time. Forced sex inside marriage is still violence.
reviewer_note: Please confirm legal wording.

title: Privacy and confidentiality
answer: Health workers should respect your privacy. Young people have a right to private, respectful care. This tool does not ask your name and does not save your questions.
source: WHO Adolescent SRHR 2018; WHO/JHU Family Planning Handbook 2022
reviewer_note: Confirm that the platform design actually stores no questions before launch.

title: Where to get help and services
answer: You can go to your nearest health center or health post, or ask a community health worker. You can also call 114 (RBC free health line). For abuse, call 3512 (gender-based violence), 116 (child abuse) or 3029 (Isange One Stop Centre). For an emergency, call 112.
source: RBC website; Rwanda National Police; RIB
reviewer_note: Numbers checked on RBC and RIB websites in Oct 2026. Please verify before launch.

title: Enthusiastic consent: a clear yes
answer: Enthusiastic consent means both people clearly and happily want to do something together. It sounds like 'yes, I want to' and looks like someone who is relaxed, involved and comfortable. A quiet 'maybe', a shrug, a forced smile or a 'yes' given only to stop someone asking is not enthusiastic consent. If you are not sure the other person really wants it, stop and ask. Real consent is free, clear and willing, and it should feel good for both of you, not like a deal or a test.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Consent is ongoing, every time
answer: Consent is not a one-time permission. It must be given every time and for every new step, from start to finish. Agreeing to something last week, or even five minutes ago, does not mean agreeing now. People can feel differently on different days, and that is normal. Checking in during intimacy with simple questions like 'is this okay?' or 'do you want to continue?' shows respect. If the answer is unclear or the person goes quiet, stop. Respecting this keeps both people safe and trusted.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Withdrawing consent and stopping midway
answer: Anyone can change their mind at any moment, even in the middle of kissing, touching or sex. Saying 'stop', 'wait' or 'I don't want to anymore', or pulling away, means the other person must stop right away. It does not matter how far things have gone, whether clothes are off, or whether the person agreed earlier. Continuing after someone says stop is sexual assault. If someone ignored a stop, you can get help from the GBV line 3512, Isange on 3029, or a trusted adult.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Silence or not resisting is not consent
answer: Consent is an active, clear yes. Silence, not moving, not fighting back, or not saying no are NOT consent. Many people freeze or go quiet when they are scared or confused. Others stay silent because they fear the person or feel they have no choice. If someone is not clearly and freely saying yes, the right thing is to stop. Nobody should assume. If someone was touched or had sex while silent or frozen, it was not their fault, and help is available on 3512 or 116.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Consent when drunk or high
answer: A person who is very drunk or high on drugs cannot give real consent. Alcohol and drugs affect thinking, memory and the ability to decide or say no. Having sex with someone in that state is sexual assault, even if they seemed to agree or were flirting earlier. Being drunk never makes it the victim's fault, and it is never an excuse for the person who did it. If someone is too drunk, the respectful thing is to help them get home safely. Help after assault: 3029, 3512 or 112.

title: Consent when asleep or unconscious
answer: A person who is asleep, passed out, unconscious or half-awake cannot give consent. They cannot say yes or no, so any sexual touching or sex with them is sexual assault or rape. This is true even if the two people are dating, married or have had sex before. Waiting until someone wakes up and asking clearly is the only respectful choice. If this has happened to someone, it is not their fault, and they can get help from Isange on 3029 or the GBV line 3512.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Pressure, threats and coercion
answer: Consent must be given freely. A 'yes' that comes from threats, fear, force, blackmail or constant pressure is not real consent. This is called coercion. Examples: 'I will hurt you', 'I will tell everyone your secret', 'I will fail you', or nagging until the person gives up. Coercing someone into sex is a form of sexual violence. If anyone is being pressured or threatened, they deserve help: talk to a trusted adult, call 3512 (GBV line), 116 (child helpline) or 3029 (Isange).

title: Consent in a dating relationship
answer: Being someone's boyfriend or girlfriend does not mean you must have sex or do anything sexual. Each person in a relationship still has the right to say yes or no each time. A partner who truly cares will respect your choices and will not pressure, punish or leave you for saying no. Forced sex inside a relationship is still sexual violence. Healthy couples talk openly about what they are and are not ready for. If a partner forces or threatens, call 3512 or talk to a trusted adult.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Gifts or money do not buy consent
answer: Receiving gifts, money, phone credit, food, a drink, a lift or school fees never means a person owes anyone sex or touching. Consent cannot be bought or traded as repayment. Someone who gives gifts and then demands sex is using pressure, and this can be exploitation. A person can always say no and keep their dignity. If an adult is offering things in exchange for sex, it is wise to tell a trusted adult or call 116 or 3512 for advice.

title: Saying yes before does not mean yes now
answer: Having had sex or kissed someone before does not give them permission for the future. Every time is a new decision. A person may have agreed in the past but not want to today, and that must be respected. Former partners, ex-boyfriends or ex-girlfriends have no right to expect sex again. Saying 'but you did it before' is a form of pressure. Consent must be fresh, clear and freely given each time. If someone is being forced, help is available on 3512.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Yes to one thing is not yes to everything
answer: Agreeing to one activity does not mean agreeing to others. Saying yes to holding hands, kissing or touching does not mean saying yes to sex. Agreeing to sex with a condom does not mean agreeing to sex without one. Each new step needs its own clear yes. It is normal to enjoy one thing and not want the next. A respectful partner asks before moving further and accepts the answer. If someone pushes beyond what was agreed, that is not okay; support is available on 3512.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Removing a condom without agreement
answer: If two people agree to have sex with a condom, removing it or damaging it on purpose without the other person knowing or agreeing breaks consent. The person only agreed to protected sex. This puts them at risk of pregnancy, HIV and other infections, and it is a serious violation of trust and a form of sexual violence. Anyone this happens to can go to a health centre or Isange (3029) quickly, ideally within 72 hours, to get protection against HIV and pregnancy, and can call 3512 for support.

title: How to ask for consent
answer: Asking for consent is simple and respectful. Use clear words like 'Do you want to?', 'Is this okay?' or 'Do you want to stop?'. Ask before each new step, not just at the beginning. Listen to the answer and watch body language. If the answer is no, unsure, or the person seems uncomfortable, stop and accept it kindly. Asking does not ruin the mood; it shows care. Never ask again and again to wear someone down, because that becomes pressure.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: How to say no clearly
answer: You have the right to say no to any touching, kissing or sex, with anyone, at any time. You can say it simply: 'No', 'I don't want to', or 'Stop'. You do not have to explain or apologise. Use a firm voice, and move away if you can. If the person does not listen, leave, go to where other people are, and tell a trusted adult. Your no is enough. If you ever feel in danger, call 112, or 3512 for the GBV line.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Respecting a no and handling rejection
answer: When someone says no, the respectful response is to stop, accept it, and not take it as an insult. Do not argue, sulk, threaten, spread rumours or ask again and again. Feeling disappointed is normal, but the other person's body and choices belong to them. Handling rejection calmly shows maturity and makes you someone people can trust. Talking to a friend or doing something you enjoy can help with the feelings. Never punish someone for saying no.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Power differences and consent
answer: Consent is hard or impossible when one person has much more power, such as a teacher, boss, employer, landlord, older relative, leader or someone much older and richer. The less powerful person may say yes out of fear of losing marks, a job, money or a home. That is not free consent. People in authority must never ask for sex from those who depend on them. Such situations can be abuse or exploitation. Advice and help: 116 (children), 3512 (GBV line) or a trusted adult.

title: Body language and unclear signals
answer: Body language can show how someone feels. Pulling away, going stiff, turning the face, crying, pushing hands away, or being very quiet are signs to stop. Smiling or dressing nicely is not a sexual yes. Because signals can be confusing, the safest way is always to ask with words and wait for a clear yes. If you are unsure, stop. A real yes is clear in both words and body. Guessing is never good enough when it comes to someone's body.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Consent for photos and videos
answer: Taking or sharing pictures or videos of someone needs their permission, especially private or sexual ones. Agreeing to a photo does not mean agreeing to it being shared, posted or forwarded. Secretly filming someone while undressed, bathing or during sex is a serious violation. Images of anyone under 18 that are sexual are child sexual abuse material and must never be made or shared. If someone's private images are taken or shared, they can tell a trusted adult, keep evidence and call 116 or 3512.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Everyday consent: hugs and touching
answer: Consent is not only about sex. It also applies to everyday touch like hugs, holding hands, sitting on someone's lap, tickling or playful wrestling. Everyone, including children, can say 'no thank you' to touch they do not want. You can offer other ways to greet, like a wave or handshake. Asking 'can I hug you?' teaches respect. If someone keeps touching after being told no, that is not okay, and you can tell a trusted adult.

title: 'If you loved me' pressure
answer: Phrases like 'if you loved me you would', 'everyone is doing it', 'I'll leave you' or 'you are wasting my time' are emotional pressure. They try to make you feel guilty so you agree to sex. Love does not need to be proven with sex. A caring partner respects your decision and waits until you are truly ready, or accepts that you may never be. If someone keeps pressuring you, it is a warning sign. Talking to a trusted adult or calling 3512 can help.

title: Lying or tricking to get sex
answer: Consent must be based on honest information. Tricking someone into sex, for example by lying about using protection, pretending to be someone else, promising marriage or a job that is fake, or secretly drugging a drink, takes away the person's real choice. Deception and manipulation are not consent and can be forms of sexual violence or exploitation. If someone was tricked, it is not their fault. They can get support from a trusted adult, 3512 or Isange on 3029.

title: Peer pressure from friends to have sex
answer: Friends may tease, dare or say 'you are the only virgin left' to push someone into sex. Many young people say they are having sex when they are not. Deciding when to have sex is personal, and waiting is normal and healthy. A real friend respects your choice. You can say 'I'll decide for myself', change the subject, or spend time with friends who support you. Being pushed by a group into sex is pressure, not consent.

title: Freezing during an unwanted experience
answer: When people are very scared, their body can freeze. They may be unable to move, speak or shout. This is an automatic survival reaction, not a choice, and it does not mean they agreed. Many survivors blame themselves for not fighting back, but freezing is common and normal. Anyone who froze during unwanted touching or sex is not to blame. Talking to a counsellor can help with these feelings; Isange (3029) and the GBV line 3512 offer support.

title: Myth: 'no' secretly means 'yes'
answer: Some people believe that when a girl says no she really means yes, or that she is playing hard to get. This is a harmful myth. No means no. Not now means no. Maybe means not yet. Treating a no as a yes leads to sexual violence. If someone wants to say yes, they can say it clearly. Respecting a no, every time, protects people. Young people of any gender deserve to have their words believed.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Visiting someone's room is not consent
answer: Going to someone's house or room, staying late, accepting a drink, kissing or sleeping over does not mean agreeing to sex. Consent is only given with a clear yes for that act. A person can visit, chat or watch a film and still say no to anything sexual. If you plan to visit someone, it helps to tell a friend where you are and keep your phone charged. Anyone forced after a visit is not to blame; help is on 3512 or 3029.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Consent in sexting and online chats
answer: Consent matters online too. Sending sexual messages, photos or videos to someone who did not ask for them is harassment. Asking again and again for nudes is pressure. Even if someone agrees to sexy chat, they can stop at any time. For anyone under 18, sexual images are illegal to make or share and can cause lasting harm. You can block, refuse and report. If an adult sends sexual messages to a young person, tell a trusted adult or call 116.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What is body autonomy
answer: Body autonomy means your body belongs to you. You have the right to decide who touches you, how, and when, and to make choices about your own body and health. It also means respecting that other people's bodies belong to them. Body autonomy applies to children, teenagers and adults, girls and boys, and people with disabilities. No one, not a partner, relative or leader, has the right to use your body without your permission. If that right is violated, you can tell a trusted adult or call 116.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What are personal boundaries
answer: Personal boundaries are the limits you set about what you are comfortable with. They show others how you want to be treated: how close they stand, how they touch you, what they say to you, and what you share. Boundaries are different for everyone and can change over time. Healthy boundaries protect your safety and feelings and help relationships stay respectful. People who care about you will respect your boundaries, even if they do not fully understand them.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Types of boundaries
answer: There are different kinds of boundaries. Physical boundaries are about your body and personal space, like who can hug or touch you. Emotional boundaries protect your feelings, such as not being insulted or blamed. Sexual boundaries are about what sexual activity, if any, you agree to. Digital boundaries cover your phone, passwords, photos and online messages. Time and material boundaries are about your time, money and belongings. You can have clear limits in all of these areas.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: How to set a boundary
answer: To set a boundary, first know what makes you uncomfortable. Then say it clearly and calmly: 'Please don't touch me like that', 'I don't share my password', or 'I don't want to talk about that'. You do not need a long explanation. Repeat it if needed. If the person ignores you, move away and get support from a trusted adult. Setting boundaries can feel hard at first, but it gets easier with practice and it is a sign of self-respect.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: When someone keeps crossing your boundaries
answer: If someone keeps ignoring your limits after you have clearly said no, that is a serious warning sign. It shows they do not respect you. You can repeat your boundary firmly, spend less time alone with them, and stay near other people. Tell a trusted adult such as a parent, teacher or counsellor. If the person touches you sexually, threatens or harms you, it is abuse and you can call 116 (child helpline), 3512 (GBV line) or 112 in an emergency.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Children saying no to hugs from relatives
answer: Children often feel they must hug or kiss relatives or visitors to be polite. But children have the right to say no to touch they do not want, even from family. They can greet in other respectful ways, like a handshake, a wave or a kind word. Parents can support this by not forcing affection. Teaching children that their 'no' matters helps protect them from abuse, because they learn their body belongs to them. Any adult who gets angry about this is a reason to tell another trusted adult.

title: Using correct names for private parts
answer: Teaching children the correct names for their body parts, including private parts like penis, vulva and breasts, helps keep them safe. Children who know the right words can explain clearly if something wrong happens, and adults will understand them. It also shows that these body parts are normal, not shameful. Private parts are the parts covered by underwear. Children should know that no one should touch or look at them there, except to keep them clean or healthy, with a parent or carer present.

title: Teaching a younger child good touch and bad touch
answer: Older siblings and carers can teach young children simply. Good touch feels safe and kind, like a hug they want or a high five. Bad touch hurts, scares them, or touches their private parts. Confusing touch makes them feel uncomfortable or comes with 'keep it secret'. Teach them three steps: say 'No!', get away, and tell a trusted adult. Remind them it is never their fault and that they will not be in trouble for telling. The child helpline is 116.

title: Safe secrets and unsafe secrets
answer: A safe secret, or surprise, is something fun that will be shared soon, like a birthday gift. An unsafe secret is one that makes you feel scared, worried or uncomfortable, or that someone tells you never to share, especially about touching, photos or gifts. Abusers often say 'this is our secret'. Children and teens should know: you never have to keep an unsafe secret. Telling a trusted adult is the right thing, even if you promised. You can also call 116.

title: The underwear rule
answer: The underwear rule is an easy way to teach children: the parts of the body covered by underwear are private. No one should touch them, look at them, or ask the child to touch theirs. The only exceptions are a parent or carer helping with washing, or a health worker checking for health reasons with a parent present and with an explanation. If anyone breaks this rule, the child should say no, get away and tell a trusted adult or call 116.

title: Body privacy during medical exams
answer: Sometimes a health worker needs to examine private parts for a health reason. A good health worker will explain what they are doing and why, ask for your permission, and allow a parent, carer or another staff member to be present. You can ask questions, ask for a female or male provider if possible, and say if something hurts or feels wrong. An exam should never be secret or involve sexual comments. If something felt wrong, tell a trusted adult or call 116 or 3512.

title: Choosing a trusted adult
answer: A trusted adult is a grown-up who listens, believes you, keeps you safe and helps you get help. It might be a parent, grandparent, aunt, older sibling, teacher, school counsellor, nurse, religious leader or neighbour. Think of at least two or three people, in case one is not available or does not help. If the first adult does not believe you, keep telling until someone does. You can also call 116, the child helpline, to talk to someone.

title: It is okay to say no to an adult
answer: Children are taught to obey adults, and that is usually good. But no adult has the right to touch a child in a sexual way, ask them to keep unsafe secrets, show them sexual pictures or hurt them. In those cases, it is right to say no, get away and tell someone, even if the adult is a relative, teacher or leader. Saying no to protect yourself is not disrespect. Children can call 116 for help.

title: Respecting other people's bodies
answer: Just as your body belongs to you, other people's bodies belong to them. Grabbing, touching bottoms or breasts, lifting skirts, pulling down trousers, or touching someone in a sexual way without permission is never a joke. It is harassment or assault. Respect means asking first, keeping your hands to yourself, and stopping when someone says no or looks uncomfortable. Boys and girls both deserve this respect. Speaking up when friends do it helps make school and the community safer.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Boundaries in friendships
answer: Friends need boundaries too. A good friend respects when you say you do not want to share something, lend money, skip class, drink, or be touched in a certain way. It is okay to tell a friend 'I'm not comfortable with that' or 'please don't share my secrets'. A friend who mocks, threatens or keeps pushing after you say no is not respecting you. Healthy friendships feel safe, equal and kind. A teacher or counsellor can help if a friendship feels harmful.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Partner checking your phone and passwords
answer: You have a right to privacy, even in a relationship. A partner demanding your passwords, reading your messages, checking your call history, or telling you who you can chat with is crossing a digital boundary. It can be a sign of control, not love. Trust in a healthy relationship is built by honesty and respect, not by spying. You can say 'my phone is private'. If a partner threatens or punishes you for this, it is a warning sign; call 3512 for advice.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Respecting elders while protecting your body
answer: In Rwandan culture, young people are taught to respect elders, and that is a good value. But respect never means letting someone touch you sexually, hurt you or force you into something. Protecting your body is not disrespect. You can be polite and still say no, move away and tell another trusted adult. Good elders want children to be safe. If an older person abuses that respect, help is available from 116, 3512 or a school or community focal person.

title: Privacy when bathing and changing
answer: As children grow, they have a right to privacy when bathing, changing clothes and using the toilet. Others, including older relatives, should not watch, take photos, or come in without reason. Young children may need help washing, but that help should be about care, not watching or touching for other reasons. If someone keeps spying, filming, or insisting on being present when it is not needed, it is a warning sign and should be told to a trusted adult or reported to 116.

title: What is sexual abuse
answer: Sexual abuse is any sexual act or contact that a person does not agree to, cannot agree to, or is forced, tricked or pressured into. It includes unwanted touching, rape, forcing someone to touch another person, showing sexual images, sexual comments or messages, and taking sexual photos. Any sexual activity with a child is abuse. Abuse can be done by strangers, but most often by someone the person knows. It is never the victim's fault. Help: 116, 3512 or Isange on 3029.

title: What is child sexual abuse
answer: Child sexual abuse is when an adult, or an older or more powerful young person, involves a child (anyone under 18) in sexual activity. A child cannot consent to sex, so it is always abuse, even if the child seemed to agree or did not resist. It includes touching, rape, showing sexual images, making sexual photos or videos, and sexual talk. It is a serious crime in Rwanda. The child is never to blame. Report it to 116, 3512, Isange (3029) or police on 112.

title: Sexual abuse without touching
answer: Sexual abuse does not always involve touching. Non-contact abuse includes showing a child pornography or sexual pictures, exposing private parts to them, watching them undress or bathe for sexual reasons, making them watch sexual acts, sending sexual messages, or asking them to pose or undress for photos or videos. These acts harm children and are serious. If a child experiences this, they should tell a trusted adult. It can be reported to 116 or 3512.

title: Signs a child may be being abused
answer: Children who are being abused may not say it in words. Possible signs include sudden fear of a certain person or place, nightmares, bed-wetting, pain or bleeding in private parts, sexual knowledge too advanced for their age, new gifts or money from someone, withdrawal, sadness, anger, dropping marks or running away. These signs can have other causes, but they deserve gentle attention. Stay calm, listen and get help from 116, 3512 or Isange (3029).

title: Why children often do not tell about abuse
answer: Many abused children stay silent. They may be threatened, told it is a secret, or afraid no one will believe them. They may feel ashamed, think it is their fault, love the abuser, or fear breaking up the family or losing school fees or food. Young children may not have words for what happened. This is why adults should ask gently, listen, and believe children. Silence does not mean nothing happened. Help is available on 116 and 3512.

title: Abusers are often people the child knows
answer: Most sexual abuse is done by someone the child or young person knows and trusts, not a stranger. It may be a relative, family friend, neighbour, teacher, older student, employer, boyfriend or someone in the community. These people can use trust, gifts, power or secrecy. This is why safety rules apply to everyone, not just strangers. A child does not have to keep quiet because they know or love the person. Report concerns to 116 or 3512.

title: Abuse by a family member
answer: Sexual abuse can happen inside families, by a parent, step-parent, uncle, cousin, sibling or grandparent. It is just as serious as abuse by a stranger and is a crime. The family member is responsible, not the child. Families sometimes pressure victims to stay quiet to protect the family name, but the child's safety comes first. Another trusted adult, the child helpline 116, the GBV line 3512 or Isange (3029) can help keep the child safe.

title: What is incest
answer: Incest is sexual activity between close family members, such as a parent and child, siblings, or a grandparent and grandchild. When it involves a child, it is sexual abuse. Incest is harmful and is against the law in Rwanda. It often involves secrecy, threats and fear because the abuser lives close. The child or young person is never to blame. Anyone who knows about incest can seek help from 116, 3512, Isange (3029) or the police on 112.

title: Sexual abuse by teachers
answer: Teachers have a duty to protect students. Any sexual touching, sexual messages, requests for sex, or relationships between a teacher and a student are abuse of power and are not allowed. This includes asking a student to stay alone after class for sexual reasons or offering marks, money or favours. Students are never to blame. It can be reported to the head teacher, a school focal person, parents, 116, 3512 or RIB. A student can bring a friend when reporting.

title: Sexual abuse by neighbours
answer: Neighbours are often trusted and children may visit their homes, run errands or watch TV there. Sadly, some neighbours abuse this trust by touching children, offering sweets or money for secrets, or calling them inside alone. Children should know to stay in open places, go in pairs, and tell parents where they are going. If a neighbour behaves in a sexual or secretive way with a child, it should be reported to a parent, local leader, 116 or 3512.

title: Abuse of house helps by employers
answer: Young domestic workers, often called house helps, can be at risk of sexual abuse by employers or people in the house, because they live away from family and depend on the job. No job gives anyone the right to touch, rape or threaten a worker, or to withhold pay for sex. Domestic workers have rights. If a house help is being abused, they can contact 3512, Isange (3029), 116 if under 18, or the police on 112.

title: Abuse by religious leaders, coaches or mentors
answer: People in positions of trust, such as religious leaders, choir masters, sports coaches, youth leaders or mentors, can also abuse. They may use spiritual authority, selection for teams, trips or special attention to gain access. No leader is allowed to touch young people sexually or ask for secret meetings. Abuse is still abuse even if the person is respected in the community. Concerns can be reported to parents, another leader, 116, 3512 or RIB.

title: Boys can be sexually abused
answer: Boys and young men can be sexually abused, by men or by women. It is just as serious as abuse of girls. Boys often stay silent because of shame, fear of being laughed at, or myths that 'boys can't be victims' or 'he should be happy'. These ideas are false and harmful. Being abused does not change a boy's manhood or sexuality. Boys deserve to be believed and helped. They can call 116, 3512 or go to Isange (3029).

title: Women can also commit sexual abuse
answer: Most reported abusers are men, but women and girls can also sexually abuse children or young people. For example, an older woman may pressure a teenage boy into sex, or a female carer may touch a child sexually. This is still abuse and is never something a young person should feel lucky about. Victims of female abusers deserve the same belief and support. Report concerns to 116, 3512 or Isange (3029).

title: Sexual abuse between children
answer: Sometimes an older or stronger child forces, tricks or pressures a younger child into sexual acts. Curious play between children of similar age is different from this. Warning signs of harmful behaviour include a big age or size difference, force, threats, secrecy or acts copying adult sex. The child who was harmed needs protection and support, and the child who caused harm also needs help from adults. Parents, teachers or 116 can guide what to do.

title: Emotional effects of sexual abuse
answer: Sexual abuse can affect feelings for a long time. Survivors may feel fear, shame, guilt, anger, sadness, numbness or confusion. They may have nightmares, trouble sleeping or concentrating, avoid certain places, or lose trust in people. Some feel nothing at first. All these reactions are normal responses to something harmful. They are not a sign of weakness. Counselling and support really help. Isange One Stop Centres (3029) offer psychosocial support, and 3512 or 116 can link survivors to help.

title: Healing after abuse is possible
answer: Many survivors of sexual abuse go on to live happy, healthy lives. Healing takes time and looks different for each person. It helps to talk to someone safe, get counselling, keep up routines, rest, and spend time with supportive people. Some days will be harder than others, and that is normal. What happened does not define a person's worth or future. Isange One Stop Centres (3029), health centres and counsellors offer support, and 116 or 3512 can guide you.

title: When an abuser threatens or demands secrecy
answer: Abusers often use threats to keep victims quiet: 'No one will believe you', 'I'll hurt your family', 'You'll be expelled', or 'It's your fault'. These threats are tricks to keep control. Telling a trusted adult or helpline is still the safest choice, because they can help protect the victim and family. Children and young people will not be punished for telling. Call 116, 3512, Isange (3029) or 112 if there is immediate danger.

title: Body reactions do not mean consent
answer: Sometimes during unwanted touching, the body reacts physically on its own. This is a normal automatic reaction and does not mean the person wanted it or agreed. Abusers sometimes use this to make victims feel guilty or confused. Consent is about choice, not about how the body responds. A survivor whose body reacted is still a survivor and is not to blame. Talking to a counsellor can help; contact Isange (3029), 3512 or 116.

title: What is rape
answer: Rape is when someone forces or tricks another person into sexual intercourse, or any sexual penetration, without their consent. It includes using force, threats, drugs, alcohol, or taking advantage of someone who is asleep, very drunk, or too young to consent. Rape can happen to girls, boys, women and men, and by strangers, partners or family members. It is a serious crime in Rwanda. It is never the victim's fault. Help: Isange 3029, GBV line 3512, or 112.

title: What sexual assault includes
answer: Sexual assault is a broad term for any sexual contact or act without consent. It includes rape, but also unwanted touching or grabbing of private parts, breasts or bottom, forced kissing, forcing someone to touch another person sexually, and attempted rape. Even if there was no intercourse, it is still serious and harmful. Survivors deserve support. They can go to Isange One Stop Centre (3029), call 3512 or 116, or 112 in an emergency.

title: What is grooming
answer: Grooming is when someone builds trust and an emotional connection with a child or young person, and sometimes their family, so they can later abuse or exploit them. A groomer may give gifts, attention, compliments, money or special favours, then slowly introduce secrecy, sexual talk or touching. It can happen in person or online and can take weeks or months. Grooming is a form of abuse. If something feels wrong, tell a trusted adult or call 116.

title: Warning signs of grooming
answer: Signs that someone may be grooming a young person include: giving special gifts, money or phone credit; wanting time alone with them; asking them to keep secrets; telling them they are 'mature' or 'special'; talking about sex or bodies; testing boundaries with small touches; and trying to separate them from parents or friends. Any one sign may be innocent, but several together are a red flag. A young person noticing this can tell a trusted adult or call 116.

title: Online grooming
answer: Online grooming happens on social media, games and chat apps. An adult may pretend to be a teenager, give lots of compliments, ask personal questions, move the chat to a private app, ask for photos, send sexual content or ask to meet. They often say 'don't tell your parents'. Young people can protect themselves by not sharing personal details or photos, keeping accounts private, and blocking and reporting. Tell a trusted adult or call 116 about suspicious contacts.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Grooming with gifts, phones and money
answer: Some people use gifts like phones, airtime, clothes, money, school materials or treats to make a young person feel special or in debt. Later they may ask for secrecy, time alone, photos or sex, and say 'you owe me'. Gifts with hidden conditions are a warning sign. A young person never owes anyone their body. It is wise to tell a parent or trusted adult about gifts from older people, and call 116 or 3512 if it feels wrong.

title: Grooming the family
answer: Groomers often also win the trust of parents and family. They may help with money or school fees, offer lifts, babysit, or become a 'family friend' so they can spend time alone with a child without suspicion. Families then may not believe the child if something happens. Parents can protect children by noticing adults who seek a lot of alone time with one child and by listening carefully. Concerns can be shared with 116 or 3512.

title: What to do if you notice grooming
answer: If you notice an adult behaving in a grooming way toward a child or friend, such as secret gifts, private messages or trying to be alone with them, take it seriously. Do not confront the adult yourself if it could be unsafe. Gently talk to the young person, and tell a trusted adult such as a parent, teacher or school focal person. You can also call 116 (child helpline) or 3512 for advice. Speaking up early can prevent abuse.

title: An adult asking to meet alone in secret
answer: If an adult asks a young person to meet alone, especially in secret, at night, in a hotel, house or car, or tells them not to tell their parents, this is a serious warning sign. Safe adults do not ask children to keep meetings secret. The safest response is to say no, not go, and tell a trusted adult. If it is a teacher or employer, a parent or focal person can help. You can also call 116 or 3512.

title: Sugar daddies and sugar mummies
answer: A 'sugar daddy' or 'sugar mummy' is an older, richer person who gives money, gifts or help to a young person in exchange for a sexual relationship. It may seem attractive, but it is risky. The older person has more power, so the young person may not be able to say no, ask for condoms, or leave. It raises risks of HIV, pregnancy, violence and exploitation. If the young person is under 18, it is a crime. Advice: 3512 or 116.

title: Warning signs with a much older partner
answer: When one partner is much older, the relationship can become unequal. Warning signs include the older partner asking for secrecy, giving lots of money or gifts, controlling who you see, pressuring for sex, refusing condoms, or meeting only in hidden places. Older partners may know more and have more power. If the younger person is under 18, any sexual relationship with an adult is a crime. Talking to a trusted adult or calling 116 or 3512 can help.

title: Strangers online who want to meet
answer: People met online may not be who they say. A stranger who quickly wants to meet in person, asks to keep it secret, offers money or a job, or wants you to come alone, is a red flag. Many abusers and traffickers use this. Never meet an online contact alone or without telling a trusted adult. If a meeting happens, it should be in a busy public place with an adult aware. Report suspicious contacts to 116 or the police.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What is sexual exploitation
answer: Sexual exploitation is when someone takes advantage of another person's need, poverty, age or trust to get sex or sexual images, often in exchange for money, food, grades, a job, a place to stay or protection. The person exploited may seem to agree, but they are not truly free to say no. It is abuse of power. Exploiting a child is a serious crime. Help is available from 116, 3512 or Isange (3029).

title: Sex for grades
answer: When a teacher or lecturer asks for sex, touching or sexual photos in exchange for good marks, passing an exam or avoiding punishment, this is sexual exploitation and abuse of power. It is never the student's fault and the student does not have to agree. Students can keep messages as evidence, avoid being alone with the teacher, bring a friend, and report to the head teacher, a school focal person, parents, 116, 3512 or RIB.

title: Risks of sex for money or gifts
answer: Having sex in exchange for money, gifts, food, rent or transport, sometimes called transactional sex, puts young people at risk. It is often hard to insist on condoms or say no, which increases the chance of HIV, other infections and pregnancy. It can lead to violence, exploitation and feeling trapped. If someone is under 18, any adult involved is committing a crime. Young people in need can seek support from 3512, 116 or a social worker.

title: Sex for jobs
answer: Some employers, managers or recruiters ask for sex in exchange for a job, a promotion or keeping a job. This is sexual exploitation and harassment. A person seeking work should never have to give sex to get it. Warning signs include interviews in hotels or at night, private messages, and promises that sound too good. Keep evidence, bring someone with you to interviews, and report it to 3512, RIB or the police. Under 18s can call 116.

title: Sex in exchange for school fees
answer: Some young people are offered help with school fees, uniforms or materials in exchange for sex. This is sexual exploitation, and if the young person is under 18 it is a crime. Education is a right and should not cost anyone their body. There may be other options, like asking the school, local leaders, social workers or support programmes for help with fees. A young person facing this pressure can talk to a trusted adult or call 116 or 3512.

title: Sex in exchange for rides or transport
answer: Some drivers, moto riders or others may offer free rides and later expect sex, or ask for sex instead of the fare. No one owes sex for transport. This is exploitation, and if the young person is under 18 it is a crime. To stay safer, carry fare when possible, use known transport, tell someone where you are going, and avoid accepting free rides with conditions. Unsafe experiences can be reported to 112, 3512 or 116.

title: Commercial sexual exploitation of children
answer: Commercial sexual exploitation of children means using a child (under 18) for sex or sexual images in exchange for money, goods or anything of value, for the child or for someone else. This includes child prostitution, selling sexual images of children, and adults arranging sex with children. It is a serious crime and a form of child abuse. The child is a victim, never a criminal. Anyone who knows of this should call 116, 3512, RIB or police on 112.

title: Exploitation by officials or aid workers
answer: People who provide help, like officials, aid or NGO workers, security staff, community volunteers or food distributors, must never ask for sex in exchange for services, documents, food, money or protection. Help is free and is a right. Asking for sex in return is sexual exploitation and abuse and is not allowed. If this happens, it can be reported to the organisation's leaders, local authorities, RIB, 3512 or, for children, 116. Survivors will not lose the right to help.

title: Refusing an offer of money for sex
answer: If someone offers money, gifts or favours for sex, you can refuse clearly: 'No, I'm not interested.' You do not owe any explanation. Leave the situation, go where other people are, and avoid being alone with that person again. Return gifts if it feels safer. Tell a trusted adult, especially if the person is older, an employer or a teacher, or keeps insisting. Offers to someone under 18 should be reported to 116 or 3512.

title: What is gender-based violence
answer: Gender-based violence (GBV) is harm done to someone because of their gender, or because of unequal power between women and men. It includes physical, sexual, emotional and economic violence. It can happen at home, in relationships, at school, at work or online. Women and girls are affected most, but men and boys can also be victims. GBV is never acceptable and never the victim's fault. In Rwanda, help is available on 3512 (GBV line), 3029 (Isange), 116 and 112.

title: Main types of gender-based violence
answer: Gender-based violence has four main types. Physical violence: hitting, slapping, kicking, burning or using weapons. Sexual violence: rape, unwanted touching, forced sex, sexual harassment and exploitation. Emotional or psychological violence: insults, threats, humiliation, control and isolation. Economic violence: taking someone's money, stopping them from working or studying, or refusing basic needs. A person may experience more than one type. All are harmful. Help: 3512 or Isange (3029).

title: Physical violence
answer: Physical violence is using force to hurt someone. It includes hitting, slapping, pushing, kicking, choking, beating, burning, pulling hair or using objects or weapons. It can happen between partners, in families, or from others. Physical violence can cause injuries, long-term health problems and fear. It is never a way to show love or discipline a partner. If someone is in danger, call 112. For support, call 3512 or go to Isange One Stop Centre (3029).

title: Sexual violence as a type of GBV
answer: Sexual violence is any sexual act, attempt, comment or advance forced on someone without their consent, by anyone, in any setting, including at home or in marriage. It includes rape, unwanted touching, sexual harassment, forced marriage, sexual exploitation, trafficking for sex, and sharing sexual images without consent. It affects physical and mental health. It is never the survivor's fault. Isange One Stop Centres (3029) provide care, and early help within 72 hours is important.

title: Emotional and psychological violence
answer: Emotional or psychological violence hurts a person's mind and feelings. It includes insults, name-calling, shouting, humiliating someone in public, threats, blaming, constant criticism, jealousy, controlling where someone goes, cutting them off from friends and family, and threatening to harm themselves or others. It leaves no marks but can cause deep sadness, fear and low self-esteem. It is a real form of abuse. Support is available from 3512, Isange (3029) or a counsellor.

title: Economic violence
answer: Economic violence is controlling someone through money or resources. It includes taking a person's earnings, refusing money for food or health care, stopping someone from working or studying, selling their property without permission, denying inheritance, or making them ask for every coin. It keeps people dependent and makes it harder to leave abuse. Economic violence is a form of gender-based violence. Support and advice are available on 3512 or from local leaders and Isange (3029).

title: Men and boys as victims of GBV
answer: Men and boys can also experience gender-based violence, including sexual abuse, physical violence, emotional abuse and economic control by partners or others. Many do not report because of shame or the belief that men must be strong or that no one will believe them. These ideas stop men from getting help. Every survivor deserves respect and support, whatever their gender. Men and boys can call 3512, 116 (if under 18) or go to Isange (3029).

title: Why gender-based violence happens
answer: Gender-based violence happens mainly because of unequal power between men and women and harmful beliefs, such as men must control women, women must obey, or violence is a private family matter. Alcohol, poverty and stress can make it worse, but they are not excuses. The person who chooses violence is responsible, not the victim. GBV can be prevented through equality, respect, education and speaking out. Report violence to 3512 or 112.

title: Myth: beating shows love
answer: Some people believe that if a partner hits you, it shows they love you or care, or that a 'good' wife or girlfriend should accept beating. This is false. Love is shown through respect, kindness and safety, never through violence. Hitting a partner is abuse and is against the law. No one deserves to be beaten for any reason. If someone is being hurt, they can call 3512 (GBV line), go to Isange (3029), or call 112 in danger.

title: Is GBV against the law in Rwanda
answer: Yes. Rwanda has laws to prevent and punish gender-based violence, including rape, sexual abuse of children, harassment and domestic violence. Rwanda's constitution protects equality between women and men. Victims have the right to report, to be protected, and to receive care. Services like Isange One Stop Centres (3029), the GBV line 3512, the child helpline 116, RIB and the police (112) exist to support survivors and act on reports.

title: Health effects of gender-based violence
answer: Gender-based violence can harm health in many ways: injuries, chronic pain, unwanted pregnancy, HIV and other infections, problems during pregnancy, depression, anxiety, trouble sleeping, alcohol or drug use, and thoughts of self-harm. Children who experience or see violence may struggle at school and with feelings. Getting care early protects health. Isange One Stop Centres (3029) and health centres offer medical and psychosocial care, and 3512 can guide survivors.

title: Children who witness violence at home
answer: Children who see or hear violence between parents or carers are affected even if they are not hit. They may feel scared, anxious, sad or angry, have trouble sleeping or learning, or believe violence is normal. It is not their fault and they cannot fix it. Children can stay safe by going to a safe room or neighbour, and telling a trusted adult. The child helpline 116 and the GBV line 3512 can help families.

title: Physical and emotional abuse of children at home
answer: Child abuse at home is not only sexual. It also includes severe beating, burning, harsh punishment that injures, constant insults or threats, locking children up, and neglect, such as not giving food, care or schooling. These harm a child's body, feelings and development. Children have a right to be protected and treated with dignity. Discipline should teach, not hurt. Anyone worried about a child can call 116 (free child helpline) or 112 in danger.

title: How bystanders can safely help
answer: If you see someone being harassed, threatened or hurt, you can help without putting yourself in danger. You can: distract (ask the person the time or directions), get others involved, record the time and place, check on the person afterwards, or report it. Never fight an attacker yourself. In an emergency call 112. For GBV, call 3512. Small safe actions can stop violence and show survivors they are not alone.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Role of men and boys in ending GBV
answer: Men and boys play a big part in ending gender-based violence. They can treat girls and women as equals, respect consent, refuse to join jokes about rape or beating, speak up when friends are disrespectful, share housework, and support survivors. Being a strong man means being caring and fair, not controlling. Boys who learn respect grow into partners and fathers who protect families. Anyone who sees violence can report it to 3512.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What is intimate partner violence
answer: Intimate partner violence is abuse by a current or former husband, wife, boyfriend or girlfriend. It can be physical (hitting), sexual (forced sex), emotional (insults, threats, control) or economic (controlling money). It often gets worse over time. It can happen in young relationships too, not only in marriage. It is never the victim's fault and is not a private matter to hide. Support: 3512 (GBV line), Isange (3029), or 112 if in danger.

title: Warning signs of an abusive relationship
answer: Warning signs that a relationship may be abusive include: a partner who is very jealous, checks your phone, tells you who to see, insults or embarrasses you, threatens you, pressures you for sex, controls your money, blames you for their anger, or hurts you physically. You may feel scared, always 'walking on eggshells' or isolated. These are red flags. Talking to someone you trust or calling 3512 can help you think through what to do.

title: Jealousy is not love
answer: Some people think strong jealousy shows deep love. But extreme jealousy, like getting angry when you talk to friends, accusing you of cheating, following you, or demanding to know where you are all the time, is about control, not love. Over time it can lead to emotional and physical abuse. Healthy love includes trust and freedom. If a partner's jealousy makes someone afraid, it is a warning sign. Advice is available on 3512.

title: A partner who isolates you from others
answer: Isolation is when a partner tries to cut you off from family, friends, school, church or work. They may say your friends are bad, get angry when you go out, make you feel guilty for visiting family, or move you far away. This makes you depend only on them and makes abuse easier to hide. Staying connected to trusted people is important. If someone is being isolated or controlled, they can talk to a trusted person or call 3512.

title: Threats of self-harm used to control
answer: Some partners say 'I'll kill myself if you leave' or 'I'll hurt myself if you don't have sex with me'. This puts huge pressure on the other person and is a form of emotional control. You are not responsible for another person's choices, and you should not stay or agree to sex because of such threats. Take the threat seriously by telling a trusted adult or calling 112 if there is immediate danger. Support: 3512.

title: The cycle of violence
answer: Abuse in relationships often follows a cycle. Tension builds, then there is an outburst of violence. Next the abuser apologises, gives gifts, cries or promises to change, and things feel calm. Then tension builds again. This 'honeymoon' phase can make victims hope it will stop. But without real help, violence usually returns and often gets worse. Knowing the cycle can help someone see the pattern. Support: 3512 or Isange (3029).

title: Why people stay in abusive relationships
answer: People stay in abusive relationships for many reasons: fear of more violence, love and hope the partner will change, depending on them for money or a home, children, shame, family or community pressure, threats, or not knowing where to go. Leaving can be dangerous and hard. This is why we should never blame someone for staying. Instead, offer support and information. Help and safety planning are available on 3512 and at Isange (3029).

title: Helping a friend in an abusive relationship
answer: If a friend is in an abusive relationship, listen without judging, tell them it is not their fault, and let them know you care. Avoid ordering them to leave or insulting their partner, because this can push them away.
