Help them think about safety, offer to go with them to get help, and share numbers like 3512 (GBV line), 3029 (Isange) and 116 if under 18. Respect their choices, stay in touch, and call 112 if they are in immediate danger.

title: Dating violence among teenagers
answer: Violence can happen in teenage relationships too. It includes hitting, forcing sex or touching, threats, constant checking of phones, insults, spreading rumours, or sharing private photos. Young people may think this is normal or just jealousy, but it is abuse. Dating should feel safe, fun and respectful. Teens experiencing dating violence can talk to a parent, teacher, counsellor, or call 116 (under 18) or 3512.

title: Reproductive coercion
answer: Reproductive coercion is when a partner controls decisions about pregnancy. Examples include hiding or destroying contraception, refusing condoms, pressuring someone to get pregnant, or forcing someone to continue or end a pregnancy. It takes away a person's right to decide about their own body and future. It is a form of abuse. Health workers can offer private contraception options and support, and 3512 or Isange (3029) can help.

title: Leaving an abusive relationship safely
answer: Leaving an abusive partner can be the most dangerous time, so planning helps. A person can tell a trusted friend or relative, keep important documents, some money and a phone ready, know where to go (a relative's home or a safe place), and memorise helpline numbers. They can get support from 3512, Isange (3029) or the police. If in immediate danger, call 112. Leaving is a process, and support makes it safer.

title: Insults and humiliation in dating
answer: A partner who regularly calls you names, makes fun of your body, embarrasses you in front of others, says you are stupid or worthless, or posts mean things about you is being emotionally abusive. Over time this can make someone believe the insults and feel trapped. Healthy partners may disagree but still speak with respect. You deserve kindness. A trusted adult, counsellor, 116 (if under 18) or 3512 can help.

title: Can an abusive partner change
answer: Some people who are abusive can change, but only if they take full responsibility, stop blaming others, and get real help over a long time. Promises, tears and gifts after violence are not the same as change, and violence often returns. The victim cannot make the abuser change by being 'better'. Their safety comes first. Talking to a counsellor or calling 3512 can help someone decide what to do.

title: Is hitting just once still abuse
answer: Yes. Even one slap, push or hit is violence and is not acceptable. Many abusive relationships start with 'only once', followed by apologies. Often it happens again and gets worse. It is important to take the first incident seriously, talk to someone trusted, and think about safety. Violence is never caused by the victim's behaviour. Support and advice are available on 3512 (GBV line) and at Isange One Stop Centres (3029).

title: Tracking and online control by a partner
answer: Some partners use technology to control, for example tracking your location, installing spy apps, logging into your accounts, demanding constant photos of where you are, or threatening to post private messages. This is a form of abuse called digital or technology-facilitated abuse. You can change passwords, turn off location sharing, check app permissions and log out of other devices. A trusted adult or 3512 can help with safety.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What is child marriage
answer: Child marriage is any formal marriage or informal union where one or both people are under 18. It mostly affects girls. It often ends a girl's education, exposes her to early pregnancy and its dangers, and increases the risk of violence. Children cannot fully consent to marriage. In Rwanda, a child under 18 living as someone's wife is also a victim of a crime. Anyone worried about a child marriage can call 116, 3512 or local leaders.

title: Legal age for marriage in Rwanda
answer: In Rwanda, the law sets the minimum age for civil marriage at 21 years for both women and men. Only marriages registered by the civil authority are legally recognised. This protects young people so they can finish school and make choices freely. Living with someone as husband or wife does not make a person under 18 a legal spouse, and sex with a child under 18 is a crime. Questions can be asked to local authorities or 116.

title: Harms of child marriage
answer: Child marriage harms girls and boys. Girls often leave school, lose chances for work, and may become pregnant before their bodies are ready, which increases the risk of serious complications. Married children face more violence, isolation, depression and HIV risk, and have less power to make decisions. Their children may also face poorer health. Ending child marriage helps families and the whole country. Concerns can be reported to 116 or 3512.

title: What is forced marriage
answer: A forced marriage is when someone is made to marry without their full and free agreement, through pressure, threats, violence, or emotional blackmail from family or others. It can happen to children or adults, women or men. It is different from an arranged marriage where both people freely agree. Forced marriage is a violation of human rights. Anyone facing it can seek help from 3512, Isange (3029), 116 if under 18, local leaders or police on 112.

title: Getting help to stop a forced or child marriage
answer: If someone is being pressured to marry against their will or before 18, they can get help. They can talk to a trusted adult, teacher, school focal person, or local leader, call 116 (child helpline), 3512 (GBV line) or Isange (3029), or call 112 if in danger. It helps to act early, before the wedding. Friends who know about it can also report. Nobody has to accept a marriage they did not freely choose.

title: Girls under 18 living with a man as a wife
answer: Sometimes a girl under 18 goes to live with a man as his 'wife', with or without a ceremony. Even if she agreed or her family accepted, this is not a legal marriage, and sex with a child under 18 is a crime. She is a victim who needs protection, not blame. She has the right to return to school and get health care. Anyone aware of this can contact 116, 3512, Isange (3029) or local leaders.

title: Being pushed to marry the man who caused a pregnancy
answer: Some families push a pregnant girl to marry or move in with the man responsible, to 'protect the family name'. If she is under 18, this is child marriage and the man may have committed a crime. Even for adults, pregnancy is not a reason to be forced into marriage. A pregnant girl has the right to health care, support and to continue her education. She and her family can get advice from 116, 3512, Isange (3029) or local leaders.

title: Bride price does not mean ownership
answer: Bride price or dowry (inkwano) is a tradition of exchange between families. It does not mean a husband owns his wife, or that she must obey him in everything or accept violence or forced sex. Marriage is a partnership of equals, and both partners keep their rights and dignity. Using bride price to justify control or abuse is wrong. Anyone facing violence in marriage can call 3512 or go to Isange (3029).

title: Boys and forced marriage
answer: Forced and early marriage mostly affects girls, but boys can also be pushed to marry, for example after a pregnancy or by family arrangements. Boys forced to marry young may leave school, struggle with responsibilities, and lose their own choices. Every young person, girl or boy, has the right to decide freely if, when and whom to marry. Boys facing this can talk to a trusted adult or call 116 or 3512.

title: What is Isange One Stop Centre
answer: Isange One Stop Centres are places in Rwanda where survivors of gender-based violence and child abuse can get several services in one place: medical care, psychosocial support (counselling), legal advice and police/investigation services. This means survivors do not have to go from office to office telling their story many times. Isange centres are found in hospitals across the country. The toll-free number is 3029. Children, young people, women and men can all go there.

title: Calling Isange on 3029
answer: 3029 is the toll-free number for Isange One Stop Centres in Rwanda. Anyone can call to get advice after sexual or gender-based violence or child abuse, to find the nearest Isange centre, or to ask what to do next. You can call for yourself or for someone else. If a person is in immediate danger, calling 112 is fastest. For GBV support you can also call 3512, and children can call 116.

title: Do survivors pay at Isange
answer: Services at Isange One Stop Centres for survivors of gender-based violence and child abuse are free. This includes medical care, counselling, and help with reporting and legal steps. A survivor does not need money, health insurance, or a parent with them to be helped first. No one should stay away from Isange because they cannot pay. You can call 3029 to ask questions before going.

title: The 3512 GBV hotline
answer: 3512 is the toll-free gender-based violence hotline of the Rwanda National Police. Anyone can call it to report violence or abuse, including domestic violence, rape, child abuse, harassment or trafficking, or to ask for advice. You can call for yourself or to report something happening to someone else. In an emergency where someone is in danger right now, call 112.

title: The 116 child helpline
answer: 116 is Rwanda's free child helpline. Children and young people, or adults worried about a child, can call to report abuse, neglect, exploitation or child marriage, or to get advice and support. You do not need airtime to call. You can call if you are scared, if something happened to a friend or sibling, or if you just need to talk to someone about a worry. In immediate danger, call 112.

title: When to call 112
answer: 112 is Rwanda's emergency number for police and urgent help. Call it when someone is in immediate danger: being attacked, threatened with a weapon, locked in, seriously hurt, or when an attacker is still nearby. Say clearly where you are and what is happening. If it is not an emergency but you need advice or to report abuse, you can call 3512 (GBV), 116 (children) or 3029 (Isange).

title: What RIB does in abuse cases
answer: RIB, the Rwanda Investigation Bureau, is the government body that investigates crimes, including rape, child sexual abuse, gender-based violence, trafficking and cyber crimes. When a crime is reported, RIB investigators collect information and evidence and prepare the case for court. RIB has offices across the country and works with Isange One Stop Centres. A survivor or someone who knows about a crime can report to RIB, the police, 3512 or Isange (3029).

title: School focal persons and counsellors
answer: Many schools have a teacher or staff member who is a focal person for student welfare, guidance and counselling, or protection from abuse. Students can talk to them about harassment, abuse, pressure for sex, bullying or problems at home. They can listen, help keep the student safe, and connect them to services like Isange, 116 or the police. If the school focal person is part of the problem, a student can go to the head teacher, a parent or call 116.

title: Community helpers for child protection
answer: In the community, people who can help with abuse include local leaders at village and cell level, community health workers, social workers, child protection volunteers, and religious or youth leaders. They can listen, help a family find services, and connect a child or survivor to Isange (3029), the police or RIB. If a community helper does not act, you can still call 116 for children or 3512 for GBV directly.

title: Health centres can help after violence
answer: Any health centre or hospital can give first care after violence or sexual assault, such as treating injuries, protecting against HIV and pregnancy, and referring to Isange or counselling. If the nearest Isange One Stop Centre is far, going to the nearest health facility quickly is a good first step, especially within 72 hours after sexual violence. Health workers should treat survivors with respect and privacy.

title: Calling helplines without airtime
answer: The main help lines in Rwanda, 116 (child helpline), 3512 (GBV line), 3029 (Isange) and 112 (emergency), are toll-free, so you can call even without airtime. If you do not have a phone, you can borrow one from a trusted person, ask a teacher, local leader or health worker to call, or go directly to a police station, health centre or Isange. Help should never depend on having money.

title: What happens when you report abuse
answer: When abuse is reported, the person who reports is listened to, and the survivor's safety is checked first. They may be referred to Isange or a health facility for medical care and counselling. Police or RIB will take a statement and may investigate. For children, social workers or child protection staff help make sure the child is safe. Survivors can ask questions at every step and bring a trusted person. Reporting starts with 3512, 116, 3029 or 112.

title: What happens during a visit to Isange
answer: At Isange, staff welcome the survivor in a private space. A health worker checks for injuries and offers care, such as medicine to prevent HIV and pregnancy when needed, with the survivor's consent. A counsellor offers emotional support. Police or investigators can take a statement and collect evidence if the survivor wants to report. Legal advice is available. Children are helped together with a trusted adult or social worker. Everything is explained before it is done.

title: Reporting abuse by a family member
answer: Reporting a family member is very hard. People may fear breaking the family, losing support, or being blamed. But the child's or survivor's safety matters most, and staying silent usually lets abuse continue, sometimes to other children too. The abuser, not the person who reports, is responsible for any trouble. Services like 116, 3512 and Isange (3029) are used to these situations and can help plan for safety and support.

title: Reporting abuse for someone else
answer: Yes, you can report abuse even if it is happening to someone else, such as a friend, sibling, classmate or neighbour's child. You do not need proof; you only need a genuine worry. Share what you saw or heard. It is best to tell the person you are getting help, if it is safe. Call 116 for children, 3512 for GBV, 3029 for Isange, or 112 if someone is in immediate danger.

title: Is it too late to report old abuse
answer: It is never too late to tell someone and get support, even if the abuse happened months or years ago. Counselling can help with feelings at any time. Reporting to police or RIB is also possible for past abuse, although collecting physical evidence is easier soon after. Survivors can talk to Isange (3029), 3512 or 116 to learn about their options. Telling is a brave step whenever it happens.

title: Why getting help within 72 hours matters
answer: After sexual assault, getting to a health facility or Isange as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours (3 days), is very important. Medicine to prevent HIV (PEP) works best when started early and must begin within 72 hours. Emergency contraception to prevent pregnancy also works best soon after. Injuries can be treated and evidence collected. Even after 72 hours, survivors should still seek care and support. Call 3029 or 3512.

title: Keeping evidence after sexual assault
answer: If possible, before going for help after sexual assault, try not to wash, bathe, change clothes, or throw away anything worn. If clothes are changed, put them in a paper bag or cloth, not plastic. Keep messages, photos or call records. This can help investigators. But safety and health come first, and evidence is not required to get care. Go to Isange (3029), a health centre or the police as soon as possible.

title: Getting help even after washing
answer: Many survivors wash, change clothes or clean up after an assault. This is a very normal reaction, and it is not a mistake. They can still get medical care, protection against HIV and pregnancy, counselling, and they can still report. Investigators can use other information too. Please do not let washing stop anyone from seeking help. Go to Isange (3029), a health centre, or call 3512 as soon as possible.

title: Medical examination after sexual assault
answer: After sexual assault, a health worker may offer an examination to check for injuries, give treatment and, if the survivor agrees, collect evidence. The survivor should be told what will happen and can say yes or no to each part. They can ask for a trusted person to be with them, and children are examined with a parent, carer or social worker present. The exam is done privately and respectfully. Isange (3029) provides this care free.

title: Police or hospital first after assault
answer: After sexual assault, health comes first. The best place to go is an Isange One Stop Centre, because medical care, counselling and police are all in one place. If Isange is far, go to the nearest health facility first for urgent care, especially within 72 hours, and they can refer you. You can also call 3512 or 112, and police can help you get to care. There is no wrong door.

title: Reporting abuse or harassment at school
answer: Students who experience or see abuse or harassment at school can report it to a teacher they trust, the school focal person, the head teacher, or the school's guidance office. Bringing a friend or parent can help. If the person is a staff member or the school does not act, report to parents, the sector education office, 116, 3512 or RIB. Keep notes of dates and save any messages.

title: Fear of revenge after reporting
answer: Fear of revenge or threats is a common reason people do not report. When reporting, tell police, RIB or Isange about any threats, so they can consider safety measures. Staying with trusted people, avoiding being alone with the abuser, and keeping helpline numbers handy can help. Threatening a witness or survivor is itself wrong and should also be reported. If there is immediate danger, call 112.

title: Settling abuse privately with money
answer: Sometimes families agree to 'settle' rape or child abuse privately, with money, a cow, or a marriage, to avoid shame. This does not protect the survivor, and the abuser may harm others. Sexual abuse of a child and rape are serious crimes, not family disputes to be negotiated. Survivors deserve justice, care and support. Anyone aware of such a deal can call 116, 3512, RIB or Isange (3029).

title: Supporting a friend who was abused
answer: If a friend tells you they were abused, stay calm and listen. Say 'I believe you', 'It's not your fault' and 'Thank you for telling me'. Let them share at their own pace and do not push for details. Ask what they need, and help them reach a trusted adult or services like Isange (3029), 3512 or 116. If they are in danger or very hurt, call 112. Keep checking in, because support over time matters.

title: What not to say to a survivor
answer: Some words hurt survivors, even when meant well. Avoid asking 'why were you there?', 'what were you wearing?', 'why didn't you scream?' or 'are you sure?'. Do not tell them to forget it, keep quiet, or that they should have known better. Do not spread their story. Instead, say you believe them, that it is not their fault, and that help is available, such as 3512, 116 or Isange (3029).

title: Why believing survivors matters
answer: When survivors are believed, they are more likely to get care, report, and heal. When they are doubted or laughed at, they may stay silent and suffer alone, and the abuser may keep harming others. False reports are rare. You do not need to investigate; your role is to listen, believe and help them get support. Saying 'I believe you' can be one of the most powerful things you do. Help: 3512, 116, 3029.

title: Abuse is never the victim's fault
answer: Sexual abuse and violence are always the fault of the person who chose to do it, never the victim. It does not matter what the victim wore, where they were, whether they drank alcohol, knew the person, accepted gifts, flirted, or did not fight back. Many survivors feel guilt or shame, but the shame belongs to the abuser. Survivors deserve care and respect. Support is available from Isange (3029), 3512 and 116.

title: Should you keep a friend's abuse secret
answer: If a friend tells you about abuse and asks you to keep it secret, it can be hard to know what to do. Respect their trust, but if they are under 18, in danger, or the abuse is still happening, getting help from a trusted adult or 116 is the right thing, even if they are upset at first. Explain gently that you care and want them safe. Try to involve them in deciding who to tell.

title: Supporting a boy or man who was abused
answer: Male survivors often face extra shame and fear of being mocked. If a boy or man tells you he was abused, take it seriously. Do not joke, question his manhood, or say he should have fought back. Remind him that it is not his fault and that abuse does not change who he is or his sexuality. Encourage him to get support from Isange (3029), 3512 or 116, and offer to go with him.

title: Taking care of yourself while supporting someone
answer: Supporting a friend or family member through abuse can be emotionally heavy. You may feel angry, sad, scared or helpless. That is normal. You do not have to fix everything alone. Share the load by involving a trusted adult or professional, take breaks, sleep, and do things that calm you. You can talk to a counsellor too. Isange (3029), 116 and 3512 can advise supporters as well as survivors.

title: When a younger child tells you about abuse
answer: If a young child tells you someone touched them or hurt them, stay calm and listen. Use simple words: 'You did the right thing telling me', 'It is not your fault', 'I will help'. Do not ask many detailed questions or promise to keep it secret. Do not confront the abuser yourself. Tell a trusted adult right away, and call 116, 3512 or Isange (3029). If the child is in danger now, call 112.

title: What is victim blaming
answer: Victim blaming is when people suggest that a survivor caused the abuse, for example by saying 'she shouldn't have worn that', 'he should have been stronger' or 'why did she go there?'. This is unfair and harmful. It shifts responsibility away from the abuser, makes survivors feel ashamed, and stops others from reporting. We can challenge victim blaming by speaking up and putting responsibility where it belongs: on the person who did harm.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Stigma survivors face
answer: Survivors of sexual violence sometimes face gossip, rejection, being called 'spoiled', being blamed or teased at school, or pressure to keep quiet. This stigma adds pain and can stop people seeking help. Communities can reduce stigma by treating survivors with dignity, keeping their stories private, and stopping gossip. Survivors have the right to continue school, be treated equally and get support. Isange (3029), 3512 and 116 can help.

title: Myth: clothes cause rape
answer: Some people say short skirts, tight clothes or 'revealing' outfits cause rape. This is false. People of all ages are raped while wearing all kinds of clothes, including school uniforms and long dresses. Rape is caused by a person who chooses to ignore consent, not by clothing. Blaming clothes protects abusers and hurts survivors. Everyone has the right to dress as they choose and be safe. Help: 3512, 3029.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Myth: being out late invites rape
answer: Some people blame survivors for walking alone, being out at night, going to a party or visiting a friend. While staying safe is wise, being somewhere at a certain time never gives anyone permission to attack. Many assaults happen during the day and in homes, by people the survivor knows. The only cause of rape is the person who commits it. Survivors should get help without shame: call 3512 or go to Isange (3029).
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Myth: boys and men cannot be raped
answer: It is a myth that boys and men cannot be raped or sexually abused. Boys and men can be assaulted by men or women. Some people think a male body reaction means he wanted it, or that real men can always fight back. These beliefs are wrong and keep male survivors silent. Male survivors deserve to be believed and supported. They can get care at Isange (3029) and call 3512 or 116.

title: How to put on a male condom
answer: First check the expiry date and make sure the packet is not torn. Open it gently with your fingers, never with teeth, scissors or a blade. Put the condom on when the penis is hard and before it touches your partner's genitals. Check that the rim is on the outside so it rolls down easily. Pinch the tip to squeeze out air, then roll it all the way down to the base. If you start putting it on the wrong way, throw it away and use a new one.

title: How to take off a condom after sex
answer: Right after ejaculation, while the penis is still hard, hold the rim of the condom against the base of the penis and pull out slowly so no semen leaks. Move away from your partner's genitals before you slide the condom off. Be careful not to spill anything on your partner. If you want to have sex again, always use a brand new condom. Wash your hands after handling a used condom.

title: Where to throw away a used condom
answer: After taking a condom off, tie a knot at the open end so semen does not spill. Wrap it in paper or a small bag and put it in a rubbish bin or a pit latrine. Do not flush it in a flush toilet because it can block the pipes. Do not leave it on the ground, in the bush or where children could find and play with it. Wash your hands afterwards.

title: Checking a condom's expiry date
answer: Every condom packet has an expiry date, and sometimes a manufacturing date, printed on the wrapper or the box. Look for words like EXP or 'use by'. If the date has passed, the rubber may be weak and break more easily, so do not use it. When you get condoms from a shop, pharmacy or health center, check the date before you leave, and check it again before you use one.

title: Using an expired condom
answer: It is not a good idea to use an expired condom. Old rubber can become dry and weak, so it is more likely to tear and will not protect you well from pregnancy, HIV or other infections. If the only condom you have is expired, using it is still better than using nothing, but get new ones as soon as you can. Free condoms are available at health centers and youth corners.

title: How to store condoms
answer: Keep condoms in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight, heat and sharp objects. Heat and sun damage the rubber and make it weak. Do not keep them for long in a hot car, near a stove or in a tight back pocket. A small box or the side pocket of a bag works well. Before use, check that the packet still has air in it and is not torn or sticky.

title: Carrying condoms in a wallet or pocket
answer: It is fine to carry a condom in your wallet or pocket for a short time so you have it when you need it. But keeping it there for weeks is not good, because body heat, rubbing and bending can damage the packet and the condom inside. Replace a condom you have carried for a long time. A small case or a bag pocket is a better place to carry condoms.

title: Checking a condom packet before use
answer: Before opening, press the packet gently. You should feel a small cushion of air, which shows it is sealed. Do not use it if the packet is torn, flat, or has a hole. After opening, do not use the condom if it looks dry, cracked, sticky, discoloured, or the rubber breaks easily when you stretch it slightly. Throw it away and use a new one.

title: Condom put on inside out
answer: If you start putting a condom on the wrong way, it will not roll down. Do not just turn it over and use it, because the outside may now have pre-ejaculate (pre-cum) on it, which can contain sperm or germs. Throw that condom away and start again with a new one. To find the right side, the rolled rim should be on the outside, like a little hat.

title: Condom sizes
answer: Most male condoms are made to stretch and fit almost all penises well. Some brands also make larger or snugger sizes. A good fit means the condom rolls all the way down, stays on during sex and does not feel painfully tight. If standard condoms often feel too tight or keep slipping, you can try a different brand or size. A pharmacist or health worker can help you without judging.

title: Condom too tight or too loose
answer: A condom that is too tight may feel uncomfortable and can be more likely to tear. One that is too loose may slip off during sex. If either happens often, try another brand or size, make sure you roll it all the way to the base, and use enough water-based or silicone lubricant. Holding the rim when pulling out also stops slipping. If a condom slips or tears, think about emergency contraception.

title: Why you pinch the tip of a condom
answer: When you put on a condom, pinch the tip to squeeze out the air. This leaves a small empty space at the end to collect semen. If air stays trapped inside, the condom is more likely to burst during sex. Keep pinching the tip while you roll the condom down to the base of the penis.

title: When to put on a condom during sex
answer: Put the condom on as soon as the penis is hard and before it touches the vagina, anus or mouth of your partner. Pre-ejaculate (pre-cum) that comes out before ejaculation can carry sperm and infections like HIV. Putting the condom on only just before ejaculating is not safe. Keep it on from start to finish for every act of sex.

title: Losing an erection while wearing a condom
answer: Losing an erection sometimes is common, especially when you are nervous or new to condoms. If the penis goes soft, hold the rim of the condom and pull out so it does not slip off and spill. Take it off and use a new condom when you are hard again. Practising putting condoms on alone, and using lubricant, can help you feel more relaxed. If it happens very often, talk to a health worker.

title: What to do if a condom breaks
answer: Stay calm. Stop and pull out, and put on a new condom if you continue. To lower the chance of pregnancy, the girl can take emergency contraceptive pills as soon as possible, within 5 days, from a pharmacy or health center. Because of the risk of HIV and other infections, go to a health center as soon as you can, ideally within 72 hours, to ask about HIV prevention medicine and testing. You can call 114 for free advice.

title: Condom slipped off during sex
answer: If a condom slips off, stop and gently remove it. Semen may have entered the vagina or anus, so think of it like having sex without a condom. The girl can use emergency contraceptive pills as soon as possible, within 5 days. Visit a health center soon, ideally within 72 hours, to talk about HIV prevention medicine and STI testing. Next time, hold the rim when pulling out and check the condom fits well.

title: Getting a condom out of the vagina
answer: A condom cannot get lost inside the body, because the vagina ends at the cervix. Wash your hands, relax, squat or put one leg up, and gently reach in with your fingers to pull it out. Do not use sharp objects. If you cannot reach it, go to a health center where a nurse can remove it. Because semen may have leaked, think about emergency contraception and ask about HIV prevention.

title: Why condoms break and how to prevent it
answer: Condoms usually break because of how they are used. Common causes are expired or heat-damaged condoms, opening the packet with teeth, not leaving space at the tip, a dry vagina or anus, oil-based lubricants with latex, or using two condoms at once. To prevent breaks, check the date, store them well, pinch the tip, use water or silicone-based lubricant, and use one new condom each time.

title: Vaseline, oil or lotion with condoms
answer: Do not use oil-based products with latex condoms. Things like petroleum jelly (Vaseline), cooking oil, butter, body lotion, baby oil and some creams can weaken latex within a short time and make it break, even if you cannot see damage. Use water-based or silicone-based lubricant instead. If you need an oil-based product, choose a non-latex condom made of polyurethane or nitrile.

title: Using saliva as lubricant
answer: Saliva is not a good lubricant. It dries quickly, so the condom can rub and tear, and it may carry germs. Many condoms already have lubricant on them. If you need more, use a water-based or silicone-based lubricant from a pharmacy. Taking time for foreplay so the vagina becomes naturally wet also helps.

title: Lubricated and non-lubricated condoms
answer: Many male condoms come already lubricated, which makes them feel smoother and helps prevent tearing. Some are non-lubricated, which some people choose for oral sex. Both protect well when used correctly. If sex feels dry or rough with any condom, add a water-based or silicone-based lubricant. Never add oil-based products to latex condoms.

title: Wearing two condoms at once
answer: Wearing two male condoms at the same time does not give double protection. The two condoms rub against each other, which makes them more likely to tear or slip. One condom, used correctly every time, gives the best protection. For extra protection against pregnancy, combine one condom with another method like pills or an implant.

title: Using a male and female condom together
answer: Do not use a male condom and a female (internal) condom at the same time. They can rub against each other, causing one or both to tear, slip or be pushed out of place. Choose one type of condom and use it correctly. To add more pregnancy protection, use the condom with another method like the pill, an injection or an implant.

title: Reusing a condom
answer: A condom can only be used once. After sex, a used condom has semen on it and may be stretched or have tiny tears, so it will not protect you again. Never wash, turn over or reuse a condom, even with the same partner. Use a new condom for every act of sex. Condoms are free at health centers and youth corners, so you do not need to save them.

title: Allergy to latex condoms
answer: A few people are allergic to latex, the rubber in most condoms. Signs can include itching, redness, rash or swelling of the genitals after using a condom. Similar signs can also come from an infection, so see a nurse or health worker to find the cause. If it is a latex allergy, you can still use condoms made of polyurethane or nitrile, including the female condom.

title: Non-latex condom options
answer: Condoms that are not made of latex are made of materials like polyurethane or nitrile. They are good for people with a latex allergy and can be used with any type of lubricant, including oil-based ones. The female (internal) condom is usually made of nitrile. Non-latex condoms also protect against pregnancy, HIV and other STIs when used correctly. Ask at a pharmacy or health center if they are available.

title: Itching or burning after using a condom
answer: Itching or burning after sex with a condom can have different causes. It might be irritation from dryness or from a lubricant, a latex allergy, or an infection such as thrush or an STI. Do not try to guess. Visit a nurse or health worker at your nearest health center, who can check you and give the right treatment. Until then, avoid sex, wear clean cotton underwear and do not wash inside the vagina.

title: How effective male condoms are
answer: When male condoms are used correctly every time, about 2 out of 100 women become pregnant in a year. In real life, when people sometimes forget or make mistakes, about 13 out of 100 become pregnant. So condoms work very well, but only if you use one correctly from start to finish every time. They are also the only method that protects against pregnancy, HIV and other STIs together.

title: STIs that condoms protect against less well
answer: Condoms protect very well against infections spread through fluids, like HIV, gonorrhoea and chlamydia. They give less protection against infections spread by skin-to-skin contact, such as herpes, genital warts (HPV) and syphilis sores, if the sore or wart is in an area the condom does not cover. Condoms still lower the risk a lot. If you see sores or warts, avoid sex and visit a health center.

title: Where to get free condoms in Rwanda
answer: In Rwanda you can get free condoms at public health centers and health posts, and at youth corners or youth-friendly services. Some community health workers also give out condoms. You can buy condoms at pharmacies and many shops. You do not need to be married or to bring a parent. Call 114, the free RBC line, if you want to know the nearest place.

title: Feeling shy to get condoms
answer: Many people feel shy about getting condoms, but choosing to protect yourself is responsible and nothing to be ashamed of. Pharmacists and health workers give condoms every day and are there to help, not to judge. Youth corners are made for young people. You can go with a trusted friend, take them from a free condom box, or simply say 'condoms, please'.

title: Partner refuses to use a condom
answer: You have the right to decide about your body and to insist on protection. If your partner refuses a condom, you can say no to sex. A partner who pressures or forces you is not respecting you. If someone forces you to have sex, it is abuse; you can get help at Isange One Stop Centre (call 3029), the GBV line 3512, the child helpline 116, or 112 in an emergency.

title: Do condoms reduce sexual pleasure
answer: Some people say condoms feel a little different, but many couples enjoy sex with them. Condoms are thin and many are lubricated. Using extra water-based lubricant, finding a size and brand you like, and making putting it on part of foreplay can help. Knowing you are protected from pregnancy and infections can also help you relax and enjoy sex more.

title: Condoms for oral sex
answer: STIs like gonorrhoea, herpes and syphilis can pass during oral sex, and HIV can pass in rare cases. Using a condom on the penis during oral sex lowers this risk. Flavoured condoms are made for oral sex and can make it nicer. Do not use flavoured condoms for vaginal sex unless the packet says they are safe for it, because sugar in the flavour can cause irritation.

title: Condoms for anal sex
answer: Anal sex carries a higher risk of HIV and other STIs than vaginal sex, because the skin inside the anus is thin and can tear easily. Always use a condom with plenty of water-based or silicone-based lubricant, because the anus does not make its own wetness. Use a new condom every time. Pregnancy is unlikely from anal sex, but semen can leak near the vagina.

title: Are there tiny holes in condoms
answer: This is a myth. Good quality condoms are tested and have no holes that let HIV, other germs or sperm pass through. Laboratory tests show that latex blocks even very tiny germs. When condoms fail, it is usually because they break, slip or are not used every time. Use condoms correctly and consistently and they protect you very well.

title: Plastic bags instead of a condom
answer: Never use a plastic bag, cling film, a balloon or any homemade item instead of a condom. They do not fit, tear easily, slip off and can hurt the body. They do not protect against pregnancy, HIV or other infections. Real condoms are free at health centers and youth corners, and cheap at pharmacies. If you do not have a condom, it is safer to wait.

title: Practising how to use a condom
answer: Practising before you need a condom is a great idea. Boys can practise putting one on their own erect penis when alone. Anyone can practise on a banana or similar object, following the steps: check the date, open carefully, pinch the tip, roll down to the base. Practising helps you feel confident so you make fewer mistakes when it really matters.

title: Girls carrying condoms
answer: Yes, girls and young women can and should carry condoms if they think they might have sex. Protecting your own health is responsible, not shameful. Carrying condoms means you are not depending on your partner to remember. Female (internal) condoms are another option a girl can control herself. Anyone, girl or boy, can get condoms free at health centers and youth corners.

title: Myths that condoms harm health
answer: Condoms do not cause infertility, cancer, weakness or illness, and they do not get lost in the body or 'stay inside' a woman. They also do not contain HIV. Condoms are thin covers that stop sperm and germs, and they leave nothing behind in the body. Using them protects your future fertility by preventing infections that can cause infertility.

title: Condoms with spermicide
answer: Some condoms are coated with a spermicide called nonoxynol-9. They do not protect better against pregnancy than ordinary lubricated condoms, and the spermicide can irritate the vagina or anus. Frequent use of nonoxynol-9 may raise the risk of HIV infection. Ordinary condoms without spermicide are the better choice, especially for anal sex or for people at risk of HIV.

title: Using condoms when drinking alcohol
answer: Alcohol and drugs make it harder to think clearly. People who are drunk are more likely to forget condoms, use them wrongly, or have sex they did not plan or agree to. If you drink, carry condoms and decide before you go out. Remember that a person who is very drunk cannot give consent to sex. If something happened that you did not agree to, you can get help at Isange One Stop Centre (3029).

title: Are all condom brands safe
answer: Condoms from health centers, youth corners, pharmacies and shops that are sealed, in date and properly stored are tested for quality. Price does not decide safety: free condoms protect just as well as expensive ones. Avoid condoms that look old, damaged or have been kept in the sun, such as from hot roadside displays. Always check the packet and the expiry date.

title: What a female (internal) condom is
answer: A female condom, also called an internal condom, is a soft, thin pouch with a flexible ring at each end. It is put inside the vagina before sex and lines it, so sperm and germs cannot pass. It protects against pregnancy, HIV and other STIs. A woman can control it herself, and it does not need the man to have a full erection.

title: How to insert a female condom
answer: Check the expiry date and open the packet carefully. Find a comfortable position, like squatting or lifting one leg. Squeeze the inner ring at the closed end and push it into the vagina as far as it will go. Put a finger inside the condom and push the inner ring up. The outer ring stays outside, covering the opening. During sex, guide the penis into the condom.

title: How to remove a female condom
answer: After sex, and before standing up, hold the outer ring and twist it gently to close the condom and keep the semen inside. Then pull it out slowly. Wrap it in paper or a bag and put it in a bin or pit latrine, not a flush toilet. Use a new female condom every time you have sex.

title: Putting in a female condom before sex
answer: A female condom can be put in some hours before sex, up to about 8 hours before. This means you do not have to stop in the moment, and you can be ready and protected. Make sure it stays in place until sex is finished. Remove it after sex and use a new one the next time.

title: How effective female condoms are
answer: When the female condom is used correctly every time, about 5 out of 100 women get pregnant in a year. With typical use, when mistakes happen, about 21 out of 100 get pregnant. It works best when used every time, inserted properly, and the penis enters inside the condom. Using it with another method, like the pill, gives more pregnancy protection.

title: Female condoms and HIV/STI protection
answer: Yes. When used correctly every time, the female condom protects against HIV and other STIs, because it stops semen and body fluids passing between partners. It also covers part of the outer genitals. Like male condoms, it gives less protection against infections spread by skin contact outside the covered area. Use a new one every time.

title: Where to get female condoms in Rwanda
answer: Female condoms can be found at some health centers, youth corners and youth-friendly services, and in some pharmacies. They are less common than male condoms, so ask a nurse or pharmacist. If they do not have them, they can tell you where to find them. You can also call 114, the free RBC line, for information.

title: Female condom noise or discomfort
answer: Some people notice rustling sounds or feel the rings at first. Adding more lubricant, either inside the condom or on the penis, usually reduces noise and rubbing. Make sure the inner ring is pushed up high. With practice, most couples find it more comfortable. If you feel pain, stop and check the condom is in the right place, and talk to a health worker if pain continues.

title: Penis outside the female condom
answer: Sometimes the penis goes between the female condom and the vaginal wall, or the outer ring is pushed inside. If this happens, stop. Take the penis out, fix the condom, or replace it with a new one. Guide the penis into the condom with your hand. If semen went into the vagina outside the condom, think about emergency contraception and ask a health center about HIV prevention.

title: Reusing a female condom
answer: Female condoms are made to be used only once. Washing or reusing them is not recommended, because they may tear or carry germs and sperm. Use a new female condom each time you have sex, and throw the old one in a bin or pit latrine.

title: Female condoms and latex allergy
answer: Most female condoms are made of nitrile or polyurethane, not latex. This makes them a good choice if you or your partner are allergic to latex. They protect against pregnancy, HIV and other STIs. If you still get itching, swelling or rash, see a health worker to find the cause.

title: Lubricant with female condoms
answer: Female condoms usually come with lubricant already on them. Because they are made of nitrile or polyurethane, you can add any type of lubricant, including water-based, silicone-based or oil-based ones, without damaging them. Extra lubricant can make sex more comfortable and reduce noise. Do not use a male condom at the same time.

title: Female condom during your period
answer: Yes, you can use a female condom during your period. It still protects against pregnancy and STIs, including HIV. Pregnancy during a period is less likely but possible, and HIV and other infections can pass more easily when there is blood. Remove any tampon or menstrual cup before inserting the female condom.

title: Female condom feels hard to use at first
answer: Many people find the female condom a bit strange the first few times. It becomes easier with practice. You can practise putting it in alone before using it with a partner. Try different positions, use extra lubricant, and guide the penis in with your hand. A nurse at a health center or youth corner can show you how to use it.

title: How combined pills prevent pregnancy
answer: Combined pills contain two hormones, similar to the ones a woman's body makes. Taken every day, they mainly stop the ovaries from releasing an egg each month. They also make the mucus at the cervix thicker, so sperm cannot easily get through. If no egg is released, pregnancy cannot happen. They do not cause abortion.

title: Hormones in combined pills
answer: Combined pills contain two hormones: an estrogen and a progestin. These are man-made versions of hormones the body makes naturally. Today's pills have low amounts of hormones and are safe for most women and girls. This is different from progestin-only pills (mini-pills), which contain only a progestin and are often used by breastfeeding women.

title: When to start the combined pill
answer: You can start the combined pill any day of the month if it is reasonably sure you are not pregnant. If you start within 5 days after your period began, you are protected straight away. If you start at another time, use condoms or avoid sex for the first 7 days. A health worker will check you can use it safely and explain exactly how to begin.

title: How soon the pill starts working
answer: If you start combined pills within the first 5 days of your period, you are protected from pregnancy right away. If you start on any other day, it takes 7 days of taking pills every day to be protected, so use condoms or avoid sex during that time. Remember that pills never protect against HIV or other STIs.

title: Taking the pill at the same time every day
answer: Combined pills work best when you take one every day, at about the same time. This makes it a habit so you are less likely to forget. Being an hour or two late is usually not a problem for combined pills, but the more pills you miss, the higher the chance of pregnancy. Choose a time linked to something you do daily, like brushing your teeth.

title: 21-pill and 28-pill packs
answer: Combined pills come in different packs. In a 28-pill pack, the last pills are often a different colour and contain no hormones; they help you keep the daily habit, and you usually bleed during them. In a 21-pill pack, you take a short break with no pills before starting the next pack. Always follow your pack's leaflet and ask a provider if you are unsure.

title: Starting the next pill pack
answer: With a 28-pill pack, start the new pack the day after you finish the old one, with no break, even if you are still bleeding. With a 21-pill pack, take the break shown on the leaflet and start the new pack on time. Starting a new pack late is a common reason for pregnancy, so always have your next pack ready before the old one ends.

title: Forgot one combined pill
answer: If you forget one combined pill, take it as soon as you remember, then carry on with the rest of the pack as usual. Missing just one pill is usually not a big risk. Read the leaflet in your pack for exact advice, and if you are unsure, ask a pharmacist, nurse or call 114.

title: Missed several combined pills
answer: Missing several pills, or starting a pack late, raises the chance of pregnancy. Take a pill as soon as you remember and continue the pack, then use condoms or avoid sex for the next 7 days. Read your pack leaflet carefully. If you had unprotected sex recently, talk to a pharmacist or nurse quickly about emergency contraception. You can call 114 for free advice.

title: Vomiting or diarrhoea on the pill
answer: If you vomit soon after taking your pill, or have very bad diarrhoea, the pill may not be absorbed properly. This can be like missing a pill. Follow the advice in your pack leaflet, keep taking your pills, and use condoms until you are well and have taken pills normally for 7 days. If the sickness lasts more than a day or two, see a health worker.

title: Common side effects of combined pills
answer: Some people have side effects in the first few months, such as spotting between periods, nausea, headaches, sore breasts, slight weight change or mood changes. These are not harmful and often get better within about three months. Many people have no side effects at all. If side effects worry you or do not improve, talk to a health worker; another pill or method may suit you better.

title: Spotting between periods on the pill
answer: Light bleeding or spotting between periods is common in the first few months of taking the pill. It is not harmful and does not mean the pill is failing. Missing pills or taking them late can make it worse, so take one every day. If bleeding is heavy, lasts a long time, comes with pain, or starts after months of normal cycles, see a health worker.

title: Nausea from the pill
answer: Some people feel slightly sick in the first weeks of taking the pill. Taking it with food or at bedtime often helps. Nausea usually gets better after a few months. If you vomit soon after taking a pill, check your leaflet as it may count as a missed pill. If nausea continues or is strong, see a health worker; another pill type may suit you better.

title: Headaches on the pill
answer: Mild headaches can happen in the first months of taking the pill and often improve. Rest, water and ordinary pain relief from a pharmacy can help. But a new severe headache, a headache with blurred vision or flashing lights, or migraines that get worse are warning signs. Stop and see a health worker quickly, as the pill may not be safe for you.

title: Does the pill cause weight gain
answer: Research shows that most people do not gain much weight because of the combined pill. A few may notice small changes in weight or water, especially early on. Weight also changes naturally during the teenage years because of growth and diet. If you are worried about your weight, talk to a health worker, who can check if the pill or something else is the cause.

title: Pill, mood and skin
answer: Some people notice mood changes, like feeling low or irritable, when starting the pill, while others feel no change. The combined pill often improves acne for many people. If your mood becomes very low, you feel hopeless or think of harming yourself, talk to a health worker straight away; the pill can be changed. You can also get support by calling 114.

title: Who should not use combined pills
answer: Combined pills are safe for most young people, but not for everyone. They are usually not recommended for women with high blood pressure, migraine headaches with aura (flashing lights), a history of blood clots, stroke or heart disease, some liver diseases or breast cancer, smokers aged 35 and over, or women breastfeeding a baby under 6 months. A health worker will check before giving pills.

title: Warning signs on the combined pill
answer: Serious problems on the pill are rare, but know the danger signs: severe pain in the chest or belly, sudden shortness of breath, severe pain or swelling in one leg, a very bad headache, blurred vision or loss of sight, or weakness or numbness on one side of the body. If you have any of these, go to a health facility immediately or call 112.

title: How effective combined pills are
answer: When combined pills are taken every day without missing any, fewer than 1 in 100 women get pregnant in a year. In real life, when pills are sometimes missed or packs started late, about 7 in 100 women get pregnant in a year. The secret is to take one every day and start each new pack on time. Pills do not protect against HIV or other STIs.

title: Medicines that can make the pill less effective
answer: A few medicines can make combined and progestin-only pills work less well. These include some medicines for epilepsy (fits) and some for TB, such as rifampicin. Most everyday medicines do not interfere. Whenever a health worker or pharmacist gives you any medicine, tell them you use the pill, so they can advise if you need condoms or another method.

title: Antibiotics and the pill
answer: Most common antibiotics, like those used for chest or urine infections, do not make the pill less effective. The main exception is rifampicin and rifabutin, used for TB and some other infections. If you have vomiting or bad diarrhoea while sick, that can affect the pill. Always tell the health worker you use the pill when you get any medicine.

title: HIV medicines and the pill
answer: Women and girls living with HIV can use contraceptive pills. Some HIV medicines may affect how well hormonal methods work, while many do not. Tell your HIV clinic nurse or doctor that you want contraception, so they can check your medicines and help you choose the best method. Keep using condoms too, to protect your partner and yourself from other infections.

title: TB medicines and contraceptive pills
answer: Rifampicin and rifabutin, medicines used to treat TB, can make contraceptive pills much less effective. If you are on TB treatment and want to prevent pregnancy, talk to your health worker. They may advise condoms plus another method, such as an injection or an IUD, during treatment. Do not stop your TB medicines.

title: The pill and STI protection
answer: No. Combined and progestin-only pills only protect against pregnancy. They give no protection against HIV, chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis or other STIs. If there is any chance of infection, also use a condom every time you have sex. Using the pill together with condoms is called dual protection.

title: Fertility after stopping the pill
answer: The pill does not cause infertility. When you stop taking it, your ability to get pregnant comes back quickly, often within a month or so. Some people's periods take a few months to become regular again. This means if you stop the pill and do not want a baby, you need to start another method straight away.

title: Do you need breaks from the pill
answer: No. You do not need to take a 'rest' from the pill to let your body recover. It is safe to use for many years without breaks. Stopping and restarting actually increases the chance of unplanned pregnancy. If you want to stop for any reason, talk to a health worker about another method first.

title: Skipping the hormone-free week
answer: Some people use combined pills continuously, skipping the hormone-free pills or break, so that they bleed less often. WHO says this is safe for most users. Spotting between periods is common when doing this. Do it only after talking with a health worker, who can explain how with your type of pill.

title: The pill and cancer
answer: Using combined pills actually lowers the risk of cancer of the womb lining and of the ovaries, and this protection lasts for years after stopping. Studies on breast cancer and cervical cancer show small or unclear changes in risk while using pills. Overall, the pill is safe for most young people. Ask your health worker if you have worries or a family history of cancer.

title: Myth that pills build up in the body
answer: Pills do not collect in the stomach, womb or anywhere else in the body. Each pill dissolves and the hormones are used up and removed by the body every day. That is why you must take one every day. Pills also do not cause babies to be born with problems later or block the womb.

title: Sharing pills with a friend or sister
answer: It is not a good idea to take someone else's pills. Pills are not safe for every person, and a health worker should check your health first. You may also get the wrong type or not enough to take every day, which means you are not protected. Visit a health center, youth corner or pharmacy to get your own pills and proper advice.

title: Taking the pill only on days you have sex
answer: Regular contraceptive pills do not work if you only take them on the day you have sex. They must be taken every day, whether you have sex or not, to stop an egg being released. If you have sex only now and then, condoms may suit you better. After unprotected sex, emergency contraceptive pills are a different product made for that situation.

title: Getting pregnant while on the pill
answer: If you get pregnant while taking the pill, it will not harm the baby or cause birth defects. It also does not cause a miscarriage. If you think you might be pregnant, for example your period does not come and you missed pills, take a pregnancy test at a health center or pharmacy. If you are pregnant, stop the pill and see a health worker.

title: Where to get contraceptive pills in Rwanda
answer: In Rwanda you can get combined and progestin-only pills at public health centers and health posts, youth corners, and pharmacies. In many areas, community health workers can also give pills to continue a method. A health worker will ask some questions and may check your blood pressure. Call 114, the free RBC line, to find services near you.

title: The pill and alcohol
answer: Alcohol does not stop the pill from working. But drinking a lot can make you forget to take your pill, and if you vomit soon after taking it, it may not be absorbed, which is like missing a pill. Drinking also makes it more likely you will forget condoms. Keep your pill routine and check the leaflet if you vomit.

title: Tips to remember your pill
answer: Link your pill to something you do every day, like brushing your teeth or eating breakfast. Set a daily alarm on your phone. Keep the pack where you will see it. Check the day written on the pack to see if you took today's pill. Get your next pack before the old one ends. If you often forget, ask a health worker about a method you do not need to take daily.

title: No bleeding during the pill-free days
answer: Sometimes you may have no bleeding, or very little, during the hormone-free days. This is common and not harmful. If you took all your pills correctly, pregnancy is very unlikely. If you missed pills, had vomiting, or have no bleeding two months in a row, take a pregnancy test at a pharmacy or health center to be sure. Keep starting new packs on time.

title: Switching pill brands
answer: You can change from one combined pill brand to another, for example if you have side effects or your usual brand is not available. Usually you can start the new pack straight after finishing the old one without losing protection, but follow the advice of a health worker or pharmacist. Do not leave a gap between packs.

title: Smoking and the pill
answer: Smoking while using combined pills raises the risk of blood clots, heart attack and stroke, especially for women aged 35 and older. Young women who smoke can usually use combined pills, but stopping smoking is best for your health. Tell your health worker if you smoke; they may suggest a progestin-only pill or another method.

title: Combined pill while breastfeeding
answer: Combined pills are usually not recommended for women who are breastfeeding a baby less than 6 months old, because estrogen may reduce milk. Breastfeeding mothers can use progestin-only pills, condoms, LAM or other methods instead. After 6 months, combined pills can usually be used. A health worker can help a new mother choose.

title: Herbal remedies and the pill
answer: Some herbal products, like St John's wort, can make contraceptive pills less effective. Many traditional or herbal remedies have not been tested, so their effect is unknown. If you use any herbal or traditional medicine, tell the health worker or pharmacist so they can advise you. Using condoms as well gives extra protection.

title: Pill and breast tenderness or size
answer: Some people notice sore or slightly fuller breasts in the first months of taking the pill. This is usually mild and gets better with time. Wearing a supportive bra can help. The pill does not permanently change breast size. If you find a lump, have pain that does not go away, or notice discharge from the nipple, see a health worker.

title: Is there a pill for boys
answer: No. At present there is no contraceptive pill for males, and boys must never take a girl's contraceptive pills; they will not prevent pregnancy. Methods boys and men can use are condoms and withdrawal, and adult men can choose vasectomy. Boys can also support their partner's choice of method and share responsibility for protection.

title: The pill can make periods lighter and less painful
answer: Many people find that combined pills make their monthly bleeding lighter, more regular and less painful. They may also reduce some symptoms before periods. This is one of the benefits of the pill. Bleeding during the hormone-free days is usually shorter and lighter than a normal period. If you have very painful periods, talk to a health worker about your options.

title: Using the pill when not having sex
answer: Some girls and women use combined pills for reasons other than preventing pregnancy, such as painful or heavy periods or acne. Using the pill does not mean you are having sex. A health worker should check if the pill is safe for you and if it is the best treatment for your problem. Never take pills without advice.

title: Is bleeding on the pill a real period
answer: The bleeding you have during the hormone-free days of the pill is called a withdrawal bleed. It happens because the hormones stop for a few days, not because an egg was released. It is often lighter and shorter than a natural period. It is not needed for health, so it is fine if it is very light.

title: Periods after stopping the pill
answer: After stopping the pill, your natural periods usually come back within one to three months. At first they may be irregular, or similar to how they were before you started. If you have no period for three months after stopping, take a pregnancy test and see a health worker. Remember you can get pregnant as soon as you stop.

title: Check-up before starting pills
answer: Before giving you pills, a health worker will ask about your health, such as headaches, smoking, breastfeeding and medicines, and will usually measure your blood pressure. You do not need a pelvic exam, blood test or pregnancy test in most cases. These simple checks help make sure the pill is safe for you.

title: What progestin-only pills are
answer: Progestin-only pills, sometimes called mini-pills, contain only one hormone, a progestin, and no estrogen. They work mainly by thickening the mucus at the cervix so sperm cannot pass, and in some users by stopping eggs being released. They are taken every day with no break. They are often chosen by breastfeeding women and people who cannot use estrogen.

title: Difference between combined and progestin-only pills
answer: Combined pills contain two hormones, estrogen and progestin; progestin-only pills contain only progestin. Progestin-only pills are taken every day with no break, and timing is stricter. They are suitable for breastfeeding women and for some people who cannot use estrogen. Combined pills often make bleeding more regular, while progestin-only pills more often cause irregular bleeding.

title: Who can use progestin-only pills
answer: Almost all women and girls can use progestin-only pills, including those who are breastfeeding, those who smoke, those with high blood pressure that is controlled, and those who cannot take estrogen. A health worker will ask a few questions to check they are right for you, for example about current breast cancer or certain liver diseases.

title: Taking progestin-only pills on time
answer: Progestin-only pills must be taken at the same time every day, with no breaks between packs. For women who are not breastfeeding, taking a pill more than 3 hours late can reduce protection. Set a daily alarm and keep the pack where you see it. Breastfeeding women have a little more protection, but should still be on time.

title: Late or missed progestin-only pill
answer: If you are more than 3 hours late or miss a progestin-only pill, take one as soon as you remember and keep taking them at the usual time. Use condoms or avoid sex for the next 2 days. If you had sex in the last few days, ask a pharmacist or nurse about emergency contraception. Your pack leaflet also explains what to do.

title: Bleeding changes on progestin-only pills
answer: Changes in bleeding are common with progestin-only pills. You may have irregular bleeding, spotting, more frequent bleeding, or sometimes no bleeding at all. These are not harmful. Breastfeeding women often have no periods. If bleeding is very heavy or long, or you think you might be pregnant, see a health worker.

title: How effective progestin-only pills are
answer: For women who are not breastfeeding, progestin-only pills work about as well as combined pills: with typical use, about 7 in 100 women get pregnant in a year, and fewer than 1 in 100 with perfect use. For breastfeeding women they are even more effective. Taking every pill on time is the key.

title: Progestin-only pills while breastfeeding
answer: Progestin-only pills are a good choice for breastfeeding mothers. They do not reduce milk and do not harm the baby. A breastfeeding mother can start them at any time after birth. When breastfeeding stops or reduces, she can continue them or switch to another method; protection is strongest while breastfeeding.

title: Starting the progestin-only pill
answer: You can start progestin-only pills on any day if it is reasonably sure you are not pregnant. If you start within 5 days after your period begins, you are protected at once. At other times, use condoms or avoid sex for the first 2 days. Breastfeeding mothers will get specific advice from their health worker on when to start.

title: Side effects of progestin-only pills
answer: Besides bleeding changes, some people on progestin-only pills have headaches, dizziness, mood changes, sore breasts or stomach pain. These are usually mild and not harmful. Severe stomach pain could be a sign of a pregnancy outside the womb, which is rare but serious; go to a health facility straight away if that happens.

title: How long after sex EC pills work
answer: Emergency contraceptive pills can be taken up to 5 days (120 hours) after unprotected sex. The sooner you take them, the better they work, so do not wait until the next morning if you can get them today. Even on day 4 or 5 they can still help. A copper IUD can also be fitted within 5 days.

title: How EC pills work
answer: Emergency contraceptive pills work mainly by stopping or delaying the release of an egg from the ovary. If no egg is released while sperm are still alive in the body, fertilisation cannot happen. They do not work after an egg has been fertilised and they do not end a pregnancy that has already started.

title: EC is not abortion
answer: Emergency contraceptive pills are not abortion pills. They prevent pregnancy from starting, mainly by delaying the release of an egg. If a pregnancy has already begun, they do not end it and do not harm it. Using EC is a safe and responsible way to prevent an unplanned pregnancy after unprotected sex.

title: Taking EC when already pregnant
answer: If you are already pregnant, emergency contraceptive pills will not work, but they will not harm the pregnancy or the baby either. So if you took EC and later find out you were pregnant, there is no need to worry about damage from the pills. If your period is late, take a pregnancy test and talk to a health worker about your options and care.

title: Using EC more than once
answer: Yes, you can use emergency contraceptive pills more than once, and every time you need them. Using EC again is safe and does not cause infertility, cancer or other long-term harm. But if you often need EC, a regular method like pills, an injection, an implant or an IUD will protect you better. A health worker can help you choose.

title: Why EC is not for regular use
answer: Emergency contraception is safe, but it is meant as a backup, not an everyday method. It is less effective than regular methods like pills, injections, implants or IUDs, and using it often can make your bleeding irregular. If you have sex regularly, ask a health worker about a method that protects you all the time. Condoms also protect against STIs.

title: How effective EC pills are
answer: Emergency contraceptive pills greatly reduce the chance of pregnancy but do not remove it. For example, if 100 women had unprotected sex once in the middle of their cycle, about 8 might become pregnant without EC, but only about 1 or 2 with EC pills. They work best when taken as soon as possible. The copper IUD is even more effective as EC.

title: Side effects of EC pills
answer: Some people have mild side effects after taking emergency pills, such as nausea, stomach pain, tiredness, headache, sore breasts, dizziness or some spotting. These usually go away within a day or two. Your next period may come a little early or late. If you have severe stomach pain, go to a health facility quickly.

title: Vomiting after taking EC
answer: If you vomit within about 2 hours of taking an emergency contraceptive pill, it may not have been absorbed. Contact a pharmacist or health worker quickly; they may advise you to take it again. If vomiting continues, a copper IUD can be another option. Do not guess or take extra pills on your own.

title: Where to get EC in Rwanda
answer: In Rwanda, emergency contraceptive pills are available at health centers, youth corners and many pharmacies. Go as soon as possible after unprotected sex. A health center can also tell you about the copper IUD as emergency contraception. If you were forced to have sex, Isange One Stop Centre (3029) gives EC and other care for free. You can call 114 for advice.

title: Period after taking EC
answer: After emergency pills, your next period may come on time, a few days early or a few days late. It may also be a bit lighter or heavier than usual. This is normal. If your period is more than a week late, take a pregnancy test at a pharmacy or health center.

title: Spotting or bleeding after EC
answer: Some people have light spotting or bleeding a few days after taking emergency pills. This is a common side effect and is not harmful, but it is not your period and does not prove the pill worked. Wait for your normal period. If it is more than a week late, take a pregnancy test. If bleeding is heavy or painful, see a health worker.

title: Copper IUD as emergency contraception
answer: A copper IUD put into the womb within 5 days after unprotected sex is the most effective emergency contraception, preventing more than 99 out of 100 possible pregnancies. A trained provider at a health facility puts it in. It works even for people for whom pills may work less well. After that, it can stay in as a long-term method.

title: Most effective type of EC
answer: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception. Among pills, those containing ulipristal acetate are somewhat more effective than levonorgestrel pills, especially later in the 5-day window. All types work best when used as early as possible. Use whichever you can get quickly; any EC is better than none.

title: Types of EC pills
answer: There are three kinds of emergency contraceptive pills: progestin-only pills containing levonorgestrel (the most common), pills containing ulipristal acetate, and some ordinary combined pills used in a special way under a provider's guidance. Each has its own instructions. A pharmacist or health worker will give you the right one and explain how to take it.

title: EC after sexual assault
answer: If someone forced you to have sex, it is not your fault. Go to Isange One Stop Centre or the nearest health facility as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours. They can give emergency contraception, medicine to prevent HIV, care for injuries and support, free of charge. Call Isange on 3029, the GBV line 3512, the child helpline 116, or 112 in an emergency.

title: Boys getting EC for a partner
answer: A boy or man can go to a pharmacy or health center to get emergency contraceptive pills for his partner. This is a caring and responsible thing to do. It is still the girl's choice whether to take them, and she should take them as soon as possible. Both partners can also ask about condoms, HIV prevention and a regular method.

title: Body weight and EC
answer: Emergency contraceptive pills may work somewhat less well in women with a higher body weight, but they still help and should not be refused. If you are worried, ask a health worker; the copper IUD works equally well whatever your weight. Taking EC as soon as possible is important for everyone.

title: EC does not protect against STIs or HIV
answer: Emergency contraception only lowers the chance of pregnancy. It does not protect against HIV or other STIs. If you had sex without a condom, visit a health center soon, ideally within 72 hours, to ask about medicine to prevent HIV (PEP) and STI testing. Using condoms every time protects against both pregnancy and infections.

title: EC and future fertility
answer: Emergency contraceptive pills do not cause infertility, even if used many times. They do not stay in the body and do not damage the womb or ovaries. Your fertility returns straight away, which means you can get pregnant if you have unprotected sex again after taking them.

title: Is EC safe for teenagers
answer: Yes. Emergency contraceptive pills are safe for girls and young women of any age who have started having sex, including those who have just started their periods. There are no medical conditions that make EC pills unsafe for adolescents. You can get them at pharmacies, health centers and youth corners.

title: EC after missed regular pills
answer: If you missed several combined pills, or were late with a progestin-only pill, and had unprotected sex, emergency contraception may be needed. Talk to a pharmacist or health worker quickly, as it depends on how many pills you missed and when. Keep taking your regular pills, and use condoms until you are protected again.

title: Starting regular contraception after EC
answer: After using EC, you can start a regular method soon. After levonorgestrel or combined EC pills, you can usually start pills, injections or an implant right away. After ulipristal EC pills, wait 5 days before starting a hormonal method. Use condoms in the meantime. A health worker will explain what to do and may suggest a pregnancy test later.

title: Taking EC before sex
answer: Emergency contraceptive pills are meant to be taken after unprotected sex, not before. Taking them before sex does not give reliable protection for sex in the coming days. If you know you will have sex, use a condom or a regular method. Keep EC only as a backup for accidents.

title: Sex again after taking EC
answer: Emergency pills only protect against sex that happened before you took them. They do not protect you during the rest of the month. If you have sex again after taking EC, use a condom or start a regular method. Because EC can delay ovulation, you might release an egg later than usual and get pregnant.

title: EC while breastfeeding
answer: Breastfeeding mothers can use emergency contraception. Levonorgestrel emergency pills are safe while breastfeeding. With ulipristal pills, a provider may advise pausing breastfeeding for a short time. The copper IUD is also an option. Ask a pharmacist or health worker which is best for you and your baby.

title: Keeping EC at home in advance
answer: Some people choose to get emergency contraceptive pills before they need them and keep them at home. This is safe and means you can take them quickly if a condom breaks or you have unprotected sex, which makes them work better. Check the expiry date and store them in a cool, dry place. Ask a pharmacist or health worker.

title: When you need EC
answer: You may need emergency contraception after sex with no method, when a condom broke, slipped or leaked, after missing several pills, being late for an injection, if withdrawal failed, if you were forced to have sex, or if you made a mistake with any method. If you are not sure, ask a pharmacist or health worker quickly, or call 114.

title: How to know EC worked
