answer: The only sure sign that emergency contraception worked is getting your next period. Spotting soon after taking EC does not prove it worked. If your period is more than 7 days late, or is very light and unusual, take a pregnancy test at a pharmacy or health center. If you are worried, talk to a nurse or call 114.

title: Medicines that affect EC
answer: Some medicines, such as certain medicines for epilepsy, TB (rifampicin) and some HIV medicines, can make emergency pills work less well. If you take any regular medicine, tell the pharmacist or health worker when you ask for EC. They may suggest a different approach or the copper IUD, which is not affected by medicines.

title: EC near ovulation
answer: Emergency pills work by delaying the release of an egg. If the egg has already been released, the pills may not work as well. This is why taking them as soon as possible matters. Around the middle of the cycle, the copper IUD is the most reliable choice because it works even after ovulation. A health worker can advise you.

title: Ordinary pills as EC
answer: Some ordinary combined pills can be used as emergency contraception in a special way, but the right number depends on the brand, and they cause more nausea than dedicated EC pills. Do not try this on your own. Ask a pharmacist or health worker; dedicated emergency pills or a copper IUD are better choices if available.

title: Keeping a copper IUD after using it as EC
answer: If you get a copper IUD as emergency contraception, you can keep it as your regular method. It protects against pregnancy for many years and can be removed by a provider whenever you want. If you prefer another method, the IUD can be taken out at a later visit after the provider confirms you are not pregnant.

title: Unprotected sex more than 5 days ago
answer: Emergency contraception is not recommended more than 5 days after sex. If it has been longer, take a pregnancy test about 3 weeks after the sex, or when your period is late, at a pharmacy or health center. Talk to a health worker about your situation and start a regular method. You can call 114 for confidential advice.

title: EC and alcohol
answer: Drinking alcohol does not stop emergency contraceptive pills from working. But if you vomit within about 2 hours of taking EC, the pill may not be absorbed, so contact a pharmacist or health worker. Alcohol can also lead to unplanned sex without condoms, so plan protection before you drink.

title: What spermicides are
answer: Spermicides are products put deep into the vagina before sex to kill or stop sperm. They come as foam, gel, cream, tablets or film, and the most common one contains nonoxynol-9. Used alone, they are one of the least effective methods. They do not protect against HIV or other STIs.

title: How to use spermicide
answer: Spermicide must be put deep in the vagina, close to the cervix, shortly before sex. Some types work immediately and others need a few minutes to melt, so follow the package instructions on timing. Use more spermicide before each act of sex. Do not wash inside the vagina for several hours after sex.

title: How effective spermicide is
answer: Spermicide used alone is one of the least effective methods. With typical use, about 21 out of 100 women get pregnant in a year, and about 16 out of 100 even with correct use every time. It works better combined with a diaphragm, but other methods like condoms, pills, injections, implants or IUDs protect much better.

title: Spermicide and HIV risk
answer: Spermicides do not protect against HIV or other STIs. Frequent use of nonoxynol-9 can irritate the vagina or anus and cause small sores, which may actually raise the risk of getting HIV. For this reason, spermicides are not recommended for people at higher risk of HIV, and should never be used for anal sex. Condoms are the safer choice.

title: Spermicide irritation
answer: Some people get itching, burning or irritation in the vagina or on the penis from spermicide, especially when it is used often. If this happens, stop using it and choose another method. Because similar signs can come from an infection, see a nurse or health worker at your nearest health center if the irritation does not go away.

title: What a diaphragm is
answer: A diaphragm is a soft, shallow cup made of latex or silicone. It is put into the vagina before sex to cover the cervix, so sperm cannot enter the womb. It is used together with spermicide. Some diaphragms come in sizes and need fitting by a provider; one type fits most women. It can be washed and reused.

title: How to use a diaphragm
answer: Put spermicide in the diaphragm cup and around the rim. Squeeze it and push it into the vagina so it covers the cervix. It can be put in some hours before sex. Leave it in for at least 6 hours after the last sex, but not more than about 24 hours in total. Then remove it, wash it with mild soap and water, dry it and store it.

title: How effective a diaphragm is
answer: When a diaphragm with spermicide is used, about 17 out of 100 women get pregnant in a year with typical use, and about 16 out of 100 with correct use every time. It is less effective than pills, injections, implants or IUDs. Using it every time, with spermicide, and leaving it in long enough after sex helps it work best.

title: Diaphragm and STI protection
answer: A diaphragm does not protect against HIV or most other STIs. It only covers the cervix, so fluids still touch the vagina. If there is any risk of infection, also use condoms. Do not use a male or female condom made of latex with oil-based products if the diaphragm is latex.

title: What a cervical cap is
answer: A cervical cap is a small, soft cup, smaller than a diaphragm, that fits tightly over the cervix. It is used with spermicide and inserted before sex. It needs fitting by a trained provider. It is less effective than most other methods, especially for women who have given birth, and does not protect against HIV or STIs.

title: Getting a diaphragm or cervical cap in Rwanda
answer: Diaphragms and cervical caps are not commonly available in Rwanda. If you are interested, ask a nurse at a health center or youth corner, or a pharmacist, whether they can get one. They can also help you compare it with methods that are easier to find, such as condoms, pills, injections, implants and IUDs. You can call 114 for information.

title: How effective withdrawal is
answer: With withdrawal, the man pulls his penis out of the vagina before ejaculating. With typical use about 20 out of 100 women get pregnant in a year, and about 4 out of 100 when it is done correctly every time. It is one of the less effective methods. It costs nothing and is better than no method, but condoms or other methods protect much better.

title: Why withdrawal often fails
answer: Withdrawal fails because it needs perfect timing and self-control at the most exciting moment. Many men cannot always feel when they are about to ejaculate, or pull out too late. Semen near the vulva can also enter the vagina. Young or less experienced men may find it especially hard. Using condoms or another method is safer.

title: Who withdrawal may not suit
answer: Withdrawal may not suit men who ejaculate quickly or cannot tell when they are about to ejaculate, young men who are new to sex, or couples where pregnancy would be a serious problem. It also does not suit anyone at risk of HIV or STIs. In these cases, condoms or a more effective method are a better choice.

title: Making withdrawal safer with another method
answer: If you use withdrawal, adding another method makes pregnancy much less likely. Using a condom gives protection against both pregnancy and STIs. You could also combine it with pills, an injection or an implant. Keep emergency contraception in mind if he does not pull out in time.

title: Washing or peeing after sex myth
answer: Peeing, washing the vagina, jumping, or pushing after sex does not prevent pregnancy. Sperm swim into the womb very quickly, within minutes, and urine comes out of a different opening. Washing inside the vagina can also cause infections. If you had unprotected sex, emergency contraception within 5 days is the right step.

title: What fertility awareness methods are
answer: Fertility awareness methods help a woman know which days of her cycle she could get pregnant. On those fertile days, the couple avoids sex or uses condoms. Examples are the Standard Days Method with CycleBeads, the calendar method, the TwoDay Method using vaginal secretions, and the body temperature method. They need regular cycles or careful daily attention, and partner cooperation.

title: Standard Days Method
answer: The Standard Days Method is for women whose cycles are usually between 26 and 32 days long. Day 1 is the first day of the period. Days 8 to 19 are considered fertile, so on those days you avoid sex or use condoms. CycleBeads or a calendar help you keep count. If your cycles are often shorter or longer, this method will not work well.

title: Using CycleBeads
answer: CycleBeads are a string of coloured beads used with the Standard Days Method. Each bead is one day of your cycle. On the first day of your period, move the ring to the red bead, then move it one bead every day. White beads show fertile days, when you avoid sex or use condoms. Brown beads show days when pregnancy is unlikely. A health worker can explain them.

title: Calendar (rhythm) method
answer: The calendar or rhythm method uses a record of the length of your past cycles, usually at least 6, to estimate your fertile days. On those days you avoid sex or use condoms. It needs careful records and works poorly if your cycles change. Many young people have irregular cycles, so this method can be risky. A health worker can teach the calculation.

title: TwoDay Method
answer: The TwoDay Method uses vaginal secretions (discharge) to tell fertile days. Every afternoon or evening, check for any secretions. Ask yourself: did I notice secretions today? Did I notice them yesterday? If the answer to either is yes, today may be fertile, so avoid sex or use a condom. If both are no, pregnancy is unlikely today.

title: Body temperature method
answer: After an egg is released, body temperature at rest rises slightly and stays higher until the next period. In the basal body temperature method, you take your temperature every morning before getting up and record it. You avoid sex or use condoms from the start of the period until the temperature has been higher for 3 days in a row. It needs a thermometer and careful daily records.

title: Irregular periods and fertility awareness
answer: Fertility awareness methods based on counting days, like the Standard Days Method and calendar method, do not work well if your cycles are irregular, for example shorter than 26 or longer than 32 days. Irregular cycles are common in teenagers and after birth. Methods based on daily signs need training. Most people with irregular cycles are better protected by condoms or another method.

title: What HIV does to the immune system
answer: Your immune system is your body's defence team against germs. HIV is a virus that attacks this defence team, especially special white blood cells called CD4 cells. It gets inside them, makes copies of itself and slowly destroys them. Over time, without treatment, the body loses so many CD4 cells that it struggles to fight even simple infections. The good news is that HIV treatment stops the virus from multiplying, so the immune system can stay strong and recover.

title: What CD4 cells are
answer: CD4 cells are a type of white blood cell that act like leaders of your immune system. They help the body recognise and fight germs. HIV targets these cells and destroys them. A CD4 count is a blood test that shows how many of these cells you have, which tells health workers how strong your immune system is. When a person takes HIV treatment well, the CD4 count usually goes up again. Your nurse or health worker can explain your own results.

title: How long it takes HIV to become AIDS
answer: Without treatment, HIV usually damages the immune system slowly, often over many years, before it reaches the most serious stage called AIDS. The time is different for each person. Some people get sick sooner than others. With HIV treatment taken every day, most people never develop AIDS and can live long, healthy lives. That is why testing early and starting treatment quickly is so important. If you are worried, talk to a nurse at your nearest health center.

title: The stages of HIV infection
answer: HIV has three main stages if it is not treated. First is acute infection, in the first weeks, when the virus multiplies fast and some people feel like they have flu. Second is the chronic or silent stage, which can last years; the person may feel fine, but the virus keeps damaging the immune system. Third is AIDS, when the immune system is badly damaged and serious illnesses appear. Treatment can stop HIV from moving through these stages.

title: Acute HIV infection in the first weeks
answer: Acute HIV infection is the first few weeks after the virus enters the body. During this time HIV multiplies very fast, so the amount of virus in the blood is high and it is easier to pass to others. Some people get flu-like signs such as fever, sore throat, rash, tiredness or swollen glands, usually for a short time. Many people feel nothing at all. If you had a recent risk, see a health worker for testing and advice.

title: Why symptoms cannot tell you if you have HIV
answer: You cannot know if you have HIV by checking how you feel. Early signs like fever, rash or sore throat are the same as many common illnesses such as flu or malaria, and many people with HIV have no signs at all for years. Feeling healthy does not mean you are HIV negative, and feeling sick does not mean you are positive. The only way to know is to take an HIV test at a health center or youth corner.

title: You cannot tell someone's HIV status by looking
answer: There is no way to know if someone has HIV by looking at them. A person can look strong, healthy and beautiful and still have HIV. Many people living with HIV take treatment and look and feel well. Thin or sick-looking people may have other illnesses. Judging people by their appearance can give you a false feeling of safety. The only way to know anyone's status, including your own, is an HIV test.

title: Signs of advanced HIV
answer: When HIV is not treated for a long time, the immune system becomes weak. Then a person may have signs such as losing a lot of weight, long-lasting fever, night sweats, diarrhoea that does not stop, a cough for weeks, or repeated infections. These signs can also come from other illnesses like TB, so they do not prove HIV. Anyone with these signs should go to a health center soon to be checked and tested.

title: What opportunistic infections are
answer: Opportunistic infections are illnesses that take the 'opportunity' to attack when the immune system is weak. A healthy immune system can usually control them, but untreated HIV can let them cause serious disease. Examples include TB, some types of pneumonia, fungal infections in the mouth, and some brain infections. Taking HIV treatment every day keeps the immune system strong and greatly lowers the chance of these illnesses. Health workers can also give medicines to prevent some of them.

title: Which body fluids can carry HIV
answer: HIV is found in enough amount to infect someone only in certain body fluids: blood, semen (cum), pre-cum, vaginal fluids, rectal (anal) fluids and breast milk. HIV is passed when one of these fluids from a person with HIV gets into another person's body, for example through sex without a condom, sharing needles, or from mother to baby. These fluids need to reach the bloodstream or a mucous membrane, like the inside of the vagina, anus, penis tip or mouth.

title: Body fluids that do not pass HIV
answer: Saliva (spit), tears, sweat, urine (pee) and faeces (poo) do not pass HIV, unless they have visible blood in them. These fluids do not carry enough virus to infect anyone. So you cannot get HIV from someone's sweat during sports, from their tears, from being spat on, or from sharing a toilet. HIV is passed only through blood, semen, pre-cum, vaginal fluids, anal fluids and breast milk.

title: Can HIV survive outside the body
answer: HIV is a weak virus outside the human body. It cannot live long in air, water or on surfaces, and it cannot multiply outside a person. That is why you cannot get HIV from door handles, clothes, bed sheets, toilet seats or water. The real risk comes from fresh blood or body fluids getting directly into your body, like through shared needles. If you have to clean up blood, use gloves or a plastic bag on your hands.

title: Why the body cannot clear HIV by itself
answer: Many germs like flu are cleared by the immune system after some days. HIV is different. It hides inside immune cells and puts its own genetic material into them, so the body cannot fully remove it. This is why HIV stays for life. Treatment cannot remove it either, but it keeps the virus asleep and very low so the person stays healthy. This is also why HIV must be prevented and why treatment must be taken every day.

title: Can young people get HIV
answer: Yes. HIV can affect anyone of any age, including teenagers and young adults. Young people can get HIV through sex without a condom, sharing needles or sharp tools, or they may have been born with it. Being young does not protect you. The good news is that you can protect yourself by delaying sex, using condoms correctly every time, knowing your status, and asking about PrEP if you are at high risk. Youth corners at health centers can help.

title: Why girls and young women face higher HIV risk
answer: In many places, including Rwanda, girls and young women get HIV more often than boys their age. Reasons include the body, since the lining of a young vagina can tear more easily, relationships with older men who are more likely to have HIV, being pressured or forced into sex, and difficulty asking for condoms. Knowing this is not about blame. You have the right to say no, to insist on condoms, and to get testing and PrEP at a health center.

title: HIV risk from vaginal sex
answer: Vaginal sex without a condom is one of the most common ways HIV is passed, both from man to woman and from woman to man. The virus in semen, pre-cum or vaginal fluids can enter through the thin lining of the vagina or the penis. Risk is higher if there are sores, other STIs, bleeding, or if the partner with HIV is not on treatment. Using a condom correctly every time greatly lowers the risk.

title: HIV risk from anal sex
answer: Anal sex without a condom carries the highest risk of passing HIV during sex. The lining of the anus is thin and can tear easily, letting the virus get into the blood. The receptive partner, the one being penetrated, has the highest risk, but the other partner can also get HIV. This is true for any couple, whether man and woman or two men. Using a condom with plenty of water-based lubricant every time lowers the risk.

title: HIV risk from oral sex
answer: The risk of getting HIV from oral sex (mouth on penis, vagina or anus) is very low, much lower than vaginal or anal sex, but it is not zero. The risk goes up if there are cuts, sores or bleeding gums in the mouth, sores on the genitals, or if semen goes into the mouth. Oral sex can also pass other STIs. Using a condom or a barrier for oral sex lowers the risk.

title: Can HIV pass from having sex only once
answer: Yes, it is possible to get HIV from having sex only once without a condom, although it does not happen every time. Each time you have unprotected sex with someone who has HIV and is not on effective treatment, there is a chance the virus passes. You cannot know ahead which time it will happen. If you had sex without a condom in the last 72 hours, go to a health center quickly and ask about PEP.

title: HIV and sex during menstruation
answer: Having sex without a condom during a period can increase the risk of passing HIV, because menstrual blood can carry the virus if the woman has HIV, and the cervix may be more open. If a woman does not have HIV, sex during her period does not protect her either. Using a condom every time is the best way to protect both partners at any time of the month.

title: Can a woman pass HIV to a man
answer: Yes. A woman living with HIV who is not on effective treatment can pass HIV to a man during sex without a condom. The virus in vaginal fluids or menstrual blood can enter through the tip of the penis, the foreskin, or small cuts or sores. Some boys wrongly believe only men pass HIV. Condoms protect both partners, and a partner on treatment with an undetectable viral load does not pass HIV through sex.

title: HIV risk in sex between women
answer: The risk of HIV passing between two women during sex is very low, but it is possible if blood, such as menstrual blood or blood from cuts, or vaginal fluids pass between partners, or if sex toys are shared without cleaning or a new condom. Women who have sex with women can also have male partners or other risks. Using barriers, not sharing toys, and regular testing help keep you healthy.

title: HIV risk in sex between men
answer: Men who have sex with men can get HIV mainly through anal sex without a condom, which carries a high risk. Oral sex has a much lower risk. Using condoms with water-based lubricant every time, testing regularly, and asking about PrEP can greatly reduce the risk. Health services should treat everyone with respect and confidentiality. You can talk to a nurse at a health center or call 114 for advice without being judged.

title: Does the withdrawal method protect against HIV
answer: No. Pulling out before ejaculating (withdrawal) does not protect against HIV. Pre-cum, the fluid that comes out before ejaculation, can contain HIV, and vaginal or anal fluids can also pass the virus to the man. Withdrawal also often fails as a way to prevent pregnancy. To protect against HIV, use a condom from start to finish every time you have sex.

title: HIV through blood transfusion
answer: In Rwanda, donated blood is tested for HIV and other infections before it is given to patients, so the risk of getting HIV from a blood transfusion in a health facility is extremely low. Donating blood is also safe because a new, sterile needle is used for every donor. If you are worried about a transfusion, you can ask the health worker about it. Never accept blood or injections outside proper health facilities.

title: Sharing needles and syringes
answer: Sharing needles or syringes is a very high-risk way to get HIV, because tiny amounts of blood stay inside and go directly into the next person's blood. This includes needles for drugs, steroids, vitamins or any injection. Always use a new, sterile needle for every injection, and only get injections from trained health workers. If you use drugs, you can get confidential help and advice at a health center.

title: Tattoos, piercings and traditional cutting
answer: Getting a tattoo, ear or body piercing, or traditional cuts (scarification) can pass HIV and hepatitis if the needles, blades or ink are not new or properly sterilised, because they touch blood. To be safe, make sure a new needle or blade is used for you and that tools are sterilised. Never share tools with friends. If you are not sure about the safety of a place, it is better not to do it.

title: Can a baby get HIV through breastfeeding
answer: HIV can pass to a baby through breast milk if the mother has HIV and her virus is not controlled. When a mother living with HIV takes her treatment every day and her viral load stays very low, the risk becomes very small, and breastfeeding is usually recommended because it protects babies from other illnesses. Mothers living with HIV should follow advice from their health worker about feeding and baby testing.

title: Kissing and HIV
answer: You cannot get HIV from kissing, including deep or French kissing. Saliva does not carry enough virus to infect anyone. The only very rare exception would be if both people had open, bleeding sores or gums and a lot of blood was exchanged, which is extremely unlikely. So kissing a partner, family member or friend who has HIV is safe.

title: Mosquitoes do not spread HIV
answer: Mosquitoes and other insects cannot spread HIV. When a mosquito bites, it does not inject blood from the last person it bit. HIV also cannot live or multiply inside insects. That is why people in the same area get malaria from mosquitoes but not HIV. Still, protect yourself from mosquitoes with a bed net to avoid malaria.

title: Sharing cups, plates and food
answer: You cannot get HIV from sharing cups, plates, spoons, food or drinks with someone who has HIV. HIV does not pass through saliva or food. You can eat together, drink from the same cup and cook for each other safely. Treating people living with HIV differently at meals is discrimination and can hurt them. Washing dishes normally is enough.

title: Toilets and HIV
answer: You cannot get HIV from using a toilet, latrine or bathroom after someone with HIV. HIV does not survive on toilet seats and is not passed through urine or faeces. Washing hands after using the toilet is good for preventing other germs like diarrhoea, but there is no HIV risk from toilets.

title: Hugging, touching and shaking hands
answer: HIV is not passed by hugging, touching, holding hands, shaking hands, sleeping in the same room, or sitting next to someone. HIV is not spread through the air, coughing or sneezing either. You can be close friends, play and live with a person who has HIV without any risk. Your friendship and kindness can mean a lot to them.

title: Swimming and HIV
answer: You cannot get HIV from swimming in a pool, lake or river with someone who has HIV, or from sharing bath water. HIV cannot survive in water, and water greatly dilutes any body fluids. People living with HIV can swim and enjoy water activities like everyone else. Just follow normal safety rules about swimming.

title: Witchcraft does not cause HIV
answer: HIV is not caused by witchcraft, curses, poisoning or bad spirits. It is a virus that is passed only through certain body fluids, mainly through unprotected sex, sharing needles, and from mother to baby. Believing in witchcraft can make people avoid testing and treatment, which is dangerous. If you are worried about HIV, get tested at a health center, where treatment is available.

title: Living with and caring for someone with HIV
answer: It is safe to live in the same house, share a bed, use the same bathroom, wash clothes and cook for someone with HIV. Daily life together does not pass HIV. If you care for someone who is bleeding or has wounds, cover any cuts on your own hands and use gloves or a plastic bag when touching blood, then wash your hands. This is good practice for any wound, not just HIV.

title: Sharing a toothbrush
answer: Sharing a toothbrush is not a recognised way of getting HIV, and the risk is extremely low. However, toothbrushes can carry tiny amounts of blood from bleeding gums, which can pass other infections like hepatitis B. For good hygiene, everyone should have their own toothbrush and not share it.

title: Bites and scratches
answer: Getting HIV from a human bite is extremely rare. It could only happen if the biter had blood in their mouth and the bite broke the skin deeply. Scratches do not pass HIV. If you are bitten and the skin is broken, wash the wound well with soap and water and see a health worker, who can check for other infections and give advice. Animal bites do not pass HIV.

title: Blood contact during sports and fights
answer: The risk of HIV from blood contact during sports or a fight is extremely low. HIV can only pass if fresh blood from a person with HIV gets directly into an open wound or into your eyes or mouth. If there is bleeding, stop playing, cover the wound, clean blood with gloves or a barrier, and wash with soap and water. If you are worried about a big blood exposure, talk to a health worker.

title: How well condoms protect against HIV
answer: When used correctly every time, from start to finish, male and female condoms are very effective at preventing HIV and many other STIs, and they also prevent pregnancy. Most failures happen because condoms are not used every time, are put on late, are torn by nails or teeth, or are used with oil-based lubricants. Check the expiry date, open the packet carefully, and use a new condom for each act of sex. Free condoms are available at many health centers.

title: Male circumcision and HIV
answer: Voluntary medical male circumcision, done by a trained health worker, lowers a man's chance of getting HIV from vaginal sex with a woman by about half or more. But it does not give full protection, and it does not protect his partner. Circumcised men still need to use condoms and test for HIV. In Rwanda, safe circumcision is offered at health facilities. Traditional or unsafe circumcision with shared tools can spread infections.

title: How other STIs increase HIV risk
answer: Having another sexually transmitted infection, like syphilis, herpes, gonorrhoea or chlamydia, makes it easier to get HIV or pass it on. Sores and swelling in the genitals make an easy entry point for the virus. Many STIs have no symptoms, so regular check-ups are important. If you notice sores, unusual discharge, pain or itching, go to a health center for testing and treatment, and ask for an HIV test at the same time.

title: Alcohol and drugs raise HIV risk
answer: Alcohol and drugs do not give you HIV directly, but they make it harder to think clearly and make safe choices. People who are drunk or high are more likely to have sex without a condom, have sex they did not plan, or be taken advantage of. Sharing needles for drugs is also very risky. If you choose to drink, stay with trusted friends and always carry condoms. A health worker can help if alcohol or drugs are a problem.

title: Having many sexual partners and HIV risk
answer: Having more than one sexual partner, especially at the same time, increases the chance of HIV, because each partner may have other partners too, creating a network where HIV can spread quickly. You often cannot know your partners' status. Fewer partners, using condoms every time, testing together, and PrEP if you are at high risk all lower your risk. This is about staying safe, not about judging anyone.

title: Relationships with older partners and HIV
answer: Older partners have had more years and often more partners, so they are more likely to have HIV. When there is a big age or money gap, it can also be harder for a young person to refuse sex or insist on a condom. Gifts or money in exchange for sex can make you feel you owe something. You always have the right to say no. Talk to a trusted adult or health worker, or call 116 if you need help.

title: Being pricked by a used needle
answer: If you are pricked by a used needle or sharp object, do not panic. Let the wound bleed a little, wash it well with soap and running water, and do not squeeze hard or suck it. Go to a health center as soon as possible, ideally within a few hours and no later than 72 hours, so a health worker can check if you need PEP and other protection, like hepatitis B vaccination. The risk from a needle found outdoors is usually very low.

title: Safety of injections and care at health facilities
answer: In health facilities, health workers should use a new, sterile needle and syringe for every injection and clean or sterilised tools for procedures. The risk of getting HIV from proper medical care is extremely low. You have the right to ask if a needle is new. Avoid getting injections, drips or procedures from untrained people or in places where tools may be reused.

title: Washing or peeing after sex does not prevent HIV
answer: Washing your genitals, peeing, douching or using water, soap, salt or other products after sex does not prevent HIV or pregnancy. The virus can enter the body very quickly during sex. Washing inside the vagina can even irritate it and raise infection risk. If you had sex without a condom, go to a health center within 72 hours to ask about PEP and emergency contraception.

title: Touching and fingering without intercourse
answer: Touching, rubbing or fingering a partner's genitals without penetration by the penis carries little to no risk of HIV, as long as there are no cuts on the hands and no blood or semen gets inside the body. These activities can still pass some other STIs. Wash your hands, keep nails short, and remember that you have the right to decide what you are comfortable with.

title: Delaying sex to avoid HIV
answer: Not having sex (abstinence) or waiting until you are older and ready is the surest way to avoid getting HIV through sex. Waiting gives you time to learn about your body, build healthy relationships and make informed choices. It is your right to decide when you are ready, and no one should pressure you. If you do decide to have sex later, use condoms and get tested together with your partner.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Is being faithful enough to prevent HIV
answer: Being faithful to one partner lowers HIV risk only if both of you tested negative and both of you stay faithful. If one partner had earlier partners and has not tested, or has sex with others, the risk remains. You cannot be sure of another person's choices. The safest plan is to test together, keep testing, and use condoms until you both know your status.

title: Where to get an HIV test in Rwanda
answer: In Rwanda you can get an HIV test at public health centers, hospitals and many health posts, including youth corners that are friendly to young people. Some places also offer self-test kits. A nurse or counsellor will explain the test and keep your result private. You can ask a community health worker where the nearest testing place is, or call the free line 114 for information.

title: Is HIV testing free in Rwanda
answer: HIV testing is offered free of charge at public health facilities in Rwanda. You do not need to pay to know your status. If anyone asks you for money for an HIV test at a public facility, you can ask the health center management or call 114 for information. Private clinics may have their own fees, so ask before testing there.

title: Testing for HIV without a parent
answer: According to the Rwanda HIV Guidelines 2022, young people aged 12 and older can agree to an HIV test by themselves, without needing permission from a parent or guardian. A counsellor will talk with you first to make sure you understand the test and are ready. Your result is confidential. You may still choose to bring a trusted adult for support if you want.

title: Age for using an HIV self-test
answer: According to the Rwanda HIV Guidelines 2022, HIV self-testing is for people aged 16 and older. If you are younger than 16, you can still get tested by a health worker at a health center or youth corner, where you will also get counselling and support. Anyone using a self-test should confirm a reactive result at a health facility.

title: What an HIV self-test is
answer: An HIV self-test lets you test yourself privately, using a kit with either a mouth swab (oral fluid) or a finger-prick blood drop. You do the test yourself and read the result in a short time, following the instructions. It is a screening test: a reactive result must be confirmed at a health facility, and a non-reactive result may need repeating if you had a recent risk. It is for people 16 and older in Rwanda.

title: How to get an HIV self-test kit in Rwanda
answer: If you are 16 or older, you can ask for an HIV self-test kit at a health facility, and some places such as youth-friendly services may also offer them. Availability can differ from place to place. To find out where kits are available near you, ask a nurse at your health center or a community health worker, or call the free line 114.

title: How to use an oral HIV self-test
answer: Read the instructions carefully before starting. Do not eat, drink or brush your teeth just before the test if the instructions say so. Gently swab along your upper and lower gums with the pad, place it in the tube of liquid, and wait the exact time shown in the instructions before reading. Reading too early or too late can give a wrong result. If anything is unclear, ask a health worker or call 114 for help.

title: What a reactive self-test result means
answer: A reactive result on an HIV self-test means you might have HIV, but it is not a final diagnosis. You must go to a health facility for further testing to confirm the result. Try to go soon, and consider bringing someone you trust. If the result is confirmed, you can start free treatment right away and live a long, healthy life. You can call 114 for support and information.

title: What a non-reactive self-test result means
answer: A non-reactive self-test result usually means HIV was not found. But if you had a possible exposure in the last few weeks or months, the test may not yet detect it, so you may need to test again later; a health worker can tell you when. If you are at ongoing risk, keep using condoms, test regularly, and ask about PrEP.

title: How a rapid HIV test is done
answer: A rapid HIV test at a health facility usually uses a small drop of blood from a finger prick. The health worker puts the blood on a test strip and you get the result in a short time, often during the same visit. Before and after the test, a counsellor talks with you, answers your questions, and explains what the result means. It is quick, safe and private.

title: How long HIV test results take
answer: With a rapid HIV test at a health facility, results are usually ready in a short time, often within the same visit, so you can wait and get them with your counsellor. If more tests are needed to confirm a result, it may take a little longer, and the health worker will explain when to come back. Self-tests also give results in a short time; follow the waiting time in the instructions.

title: Does an HIV test hurt
answer: An HIV test is quick and causes very little pain. A finger-prick test feels like a small, fast pinch that lasts a second. Oral self-tests use a soft swab on your gums and do not hurt at all. Feeling nervous is normal. The counsellor will explain each step and you can ask questions at any time.

title: Is my HIV test result confidential
answer: Yes. Your HIV test and result are confidential. Health workers must not tell your parents, teachers, partner, friends or anyone else without your permission, except other health workers caring for you. If you are worried about privacy, ask the counsellor how your information will be kept. You decide whom to tell and when.

title: Counselling before and after an HIV test
answer: When you test at a health facility, a trained counsellor talks with you before the test to explain it, answer questions and check that you agree. After the test, they explain your result and what to do next. If negative, they talk about staying negative. If positive, they help you get confirmatory testing, start treatment, and find support. Counselling is private and you can ask anything.

title: What a negative HIV test result means
answer: A negative HIV test result means no HIV was found in your test. If you had a possible exposure recently, the test may be too early to show it, so the health worker may ask you to test again later. A negative result is a chance to keep protecting yourself: use condoms, limit partners, test regularly, and ask about PrEP if you are at high risk.

title: What a positive HIV test result means
answer: A positive HIV result, after confirmation, means you have HIV. It does not mean you have AIDS or that you will die soon. Today, free treatment in Rwanda lets people with HIV live long, healthy lives, study, work, love and have children. You can start treatment right away. The counsellor will support you, and you are not alone. Take time to breathe and ask every question you have.

title: What an inconclusive HIV test result means
answer: An inconclusive or indeterminate result means the test could not clearly show whether you have HIV or not. This can happen if you were infected very recently or for other technical reasons. It does not mean you are positive. The health worker will ask you to test again after some time, following national guidelines. Keep protecting yourself and your partners until you get a clear result.

title: Why a confirmatory HIV test is needed
answer: No single test is perfect. In Rwanda, a reactive or positive first test is checked with further tests, following national guidelines, before someone is told they have HIV. This makes sure the result is correct. Health workers also retest people before they start treatment. Confirmatory testing protects you from a wrong diagnosis, so always go back if you are asked.

title: Can an HIV test be wrong
answer: HIV tests are very accurate, but rarely a result can be wrong. A negative result may miss a very recent infection because of the window period. A first positive result is always confirmed with more tests to avoid mistakes. That is why health workers follow a set testing process. If you doubt your result, talk to the health worker about retesting rather than ignoring it.

title: How often young people should test for HIV
answer: How often you should test depends on your situation. If you are sexually active, testing at least once a year is a good habit. Test more often if you have a new partner, more than one partner, an STI, a partner with HIV, or if you are on PrEP. Always test after any possible exposure. A health worker can help you decide what is right for you.

title: Couples HIV testing
answer: Couples HIV testing means you and your partner test together and receive your results together with a counsellor. It helps you both know your status, plan how to protect each other, and support each other whatever the results. It also builds trust. Each person still has the right to decide. Ask at your health center or youth corner about testing together.

title: When a partner refuses to test for HIV
answer: If your partner refuses to test, try to talk calmly about why it matters to both of you, and suggest testing together or offering a self-test kit if they are 16 or older. A counsellor can help you plan the conversation. You cannot force anyone, but you can protect yourself: use condoms every time, test regularly, and ask about PrEP. If you feel unsafe or pressured, call 3512 or 116.

title: When one partner has HIV and the other does not
answer: A couple where one partner has HIV and the other does not is called a discordant couple, and it is more common than people think. Such couples can stay together and have a healthy relationship. When the partner with HIV takes treatment and keeps an undetectable viral load, HIV is not passed through sex. The negative partner can also use PrEP and condoms, and test regularly. A counsellor can support you both.

title: A partner's result does not tell you your own
answer: Your partner's HIV result only shows their status, not yours. Even if you have had sex together, one person can have HIV while the other does not, and someone can be in the window period. The only way to know your own status is to take your own test. Testing together as a couple is a good way to both know.

title: Testing before starting a sexual relationship
answer: Testing for HIV before you start having sex with a new partner is a smart and caring choice. It helps you both make decisions about protection and shows respect for each other's health. Remember that a recent risk may not show on the test yet, so keep using condoms, and consider testing again later. You can test together at a health center or youth corner.

title: Does a normal blood test check for HIV
answer: No. A normal blood test for things like malaria, blood count or sugar does not automatically test for HIV. HIV testing is done only with your knowledge and agreement, and with counselling. If you want to know your HIV status, you need to ask specifically for an HIV test. Never assume you are negative because you had other blood tests.

title: Can someone test me for HIV without my consent
answer: HIV testing should be voluntary. Health workers should explain the test and get your agreement before testing you, and young people 12 and older in Rwanda can give their own consent. No one, including a partner, school or employer, should force you to test or test you secretly. If you feel your rights were not respected, you can talk to the health facility management or call 114.

title: Feeling scared to take an HIV test
answer: It is very normal to feel afraid of an HIV test. Many people worry about the result or what others will think. Remember that knowing your status is a way of caring for yourself. If the result is negative, you can stay protected. If it is positive, free treatment lets you stay healthy, and starting early is best. You can bring a trusted friend or adult, and counsellors are there to support you.

title: Where to go after a reactive self-test
answer: After a reactive self-test, go to a health center or hospital as soon as you can and tell the nurse you had a reactive self-test. They will do confirmatory tests and, if HIV is confirmed, help you start free treatment, often the same day. You do not need to bring the kit, but you may. If you feel overwhelmed, talk to someone you trust or call 114.

title: HIV services at youth corners
answer: Youth corners are friendly spaces at many health centers in Rwanda designed for young people. There you can get information about HIV, testing, condoms, counselling and referrals for PrEP, PEP or treatment, often from staff or peer educators trained to work with youth. Services are private and you will not be judged. Ask at your local health center if it has a youth corner.

title: How community health workers can help with HIV
answer: Community health workers in your village can give you information about HIV, tell you where to get tested, help link you to the health center, and support people on treatment to keep taking their medicine. They are trained to respect privacy. If you are not sure where to start, a community health worker is a good person to ask, and you can also call 114.

title: Should I test if I have never had sex
answer: Most young people who have never had sex and have not shared needles or had blood exposures are at very low risk. But some children are born with HIV and do not know it, especially if their mother had HIV or they lost parents to illness. If you have ever wondered, testing is the only way to know. It is free, private, and young people 12 and older can consent themselves.

title: How babies are tested for HIV
answer: Babies born to mothers with HIV need a special HIV test, because the normal rapid test can show the mother's antibodies in the baby's blood even if the baby does not have HIV. Health workers test the baby at set times, including after breastfeeding ends. Mothers should keep all appointments so the baby can be checked and treated early if needed.

title: Telling my parents I took an HIV test
answer: You do not have to tell your parents that you tested for HIV; it is your choice and your result is private. Still, many young people find it helpful to have support from a trusted adult, especially if the result is positive. If you want to tell them, a counsellor can help you plan what to say or even be with you when you talk. Choose someone you feel safe with.

title: HIV testing after sexual assault
answer: If you were raped or sexually assaulted, go as soon as possible to a health facility or the Isange One Stop Centre, or call 3029 for free. They will test you for HIV, give PEP within 72 hours, offer emergency contraception, check for STIs, and give counselling and legal support. A baseline test is followed by later tests. What happened is not your fault, and you deserve care.

title: Giving an HIV self-test kit to a partner
answer: If you are 16 or older and got a self-test kit, you can offer one to your partner, if they are also 16 or older, so they can test privately. This can help partners who are shy about going to a clinic. Never force or trick someone into testing; it must be their choice. If their result is reactive, they should go to a health facility to confirm.

title: Unapproved HIV tests and home myths
answer: There is no reliable way to test for HIV with urine, looking at your skin, home remedies or tests sold by unknown sellers or on social media. Only approved HIV tests, done at health facilities or approved self-test kits used correctly, can tell your status. Fake tests can give wrong results and false peace of mind. Get tested at a health center or youth corner.

title: Why health workers ask about partners after a positive test
answer: After a positive HIV test, a health worker may ask about your sexual partners and children so they can also be offered testing. This is called partner notification or index testing. It is voluntary and done with your consent. You can choose to tell partners yourself, go with them, or ask the health worker to contact them without naming you. Your safety comes first; tell the health worker if you fear violence.

title: What an HIV test cannot tell you
answer: A standard HIV test tells you whether you have HIV. It does not tell you when you got it, who gave it to you, how strong your immune system is, or whether you have AIDS. Other tests, such as viral load and CD4 count, help with that after a diagnosis. Try not to blame yourself or others based on a test; focus on getting care and support.

title: Who PrEP is for
answer: PrEP is medicine taken by HIV-negative people to prevent HIV. It is for people at higher risk, for example someone whose partner has HIV and is not virally suppressed, someone with several partners or who often has sex without condoms, someone who recently had an STI, or someone who sells sex or injects drugs. A health worker will talk with you to see if PrEP is right for you.

title: Can teenagers take PrEP
answer: Yes. WHO says PrEP is safe for adolescents who are at substantial risk of HIV, and it can be offered to young people who are HIV negative and need it. A health worker will check your situation and test you first. Adolescents may need extra support to take PrEP every day. Ask at a health center or youth corner if you think PrEP could help you.

title: Where to get PrEP in Rwanda
answer: PrEP is offered at health facilities in Rwanda that provide HIV services. Ask a nurse at your health center or youth corner. They will talk with you about your risk, test you for HIV, and check if PrEP is right for you. Not every site may offer it, so if your health center does not, they can refer you. You can also call 114 to ask where PrEP is available.

title: When PrEP starts to protect you
answer: PrEP does not protect you from the first pill. It needs to be taken every day for some days, often about seven days, before it reaches a protective level in the body. Until then, use condoms or avoid sex. Your health worker will tell you exactly when you are protected and how to use PrEP correctly.

title: Why PrEP must be taken every day
answer: Oral PrEP works best when you take it every day, around the same time. Taking it daily keeps enough medicine in your body to block HIV. When people skip pills often, PrEP may not protect them. Linking your pill to a daily habit, using a phone alarm, or keeping pills in a safe, private place can help. Talk to your provider if daily pills are hard for you.

title: Forgetting a PrEP pill
answer: If you forget a PrEP pill, do not panic. Missing a single pill now and then is unlikely to make PrEP fail, but missing many pills lowers protection. Do not take extra pills without advice. Talk to your health provider about what to do when you forget, and ways to remember. If you missed many pills and had sex without a condom, see a health worker quickly, as you may need PEP.

title: PrEP side effects
answer: Most people take PrEP without problems. Some feel mild side effects in the first weeks, such as nausea, stomach upset, headache or tiredness, which usually go away on their own. Rarely, PrEP can affect the kidneys or bones, so health workers may do check-ups. Do not stop PrEP on your own because of side effects; talk to your health provider, who can help.

title: Stopping PrEP
answer: You can stop PrEP if your situation changes, for example if you are no longer at risk. But do not stop suddenly on your own. Talk to your health provider first, because you may need to keep taking PrEP for some days after your last possible exposure to stay protected, and you should have an HIV test. You can restart PrEP later if your risk returns.

title: HIV testing while on PrEP
answer: You need an HIV test before starting PrEP, because PrEP is only for people who are HIV negative. While on PrEP, you will have regular HIV tests, often every few months, when you collect your refills. This makes sure you are still negative and that PrEP is the right medicine for you. Keep all your clinic appointments.

title: PrEP does not prevent pregnancy or other STIs
answer: PrEP only protects against HIV. It does not prevent pregnancy, and it does not protect against other STIs like syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia or herpes. To prevent pregnancy, you need a contraceptive method, and to prevent other STIs, use condoms. Condoms protect against HIV, STIs and pregnancy all at once.

title: Using PrEP and condoms together
answer: Using PrEP and condoms together gives you the strongest protection. PrEP protects against HIV, while condoms protect against HIV, other STIs and pregnancy. Condoms also add protection on days when you may have missed PrEP pills. You and your partner can choose what works best, and a health worker can help you plan.

title: Taking PrEP with contraception
answer: Yes, PrEP can be used together with contraceptive methods such as pills, injections, implants or IUDs. PrEP does not reduce how well contraception works, and contraception does not stop PrEP from protecting against HIV. Using both helps you prevent HIV and unplanned pregnancy. Tell your health worker about all medicines you use.

title: Difference between PrEP and PEP
answer: PrEP means 'before exposure': HIV-negative people at ongoing risk take it regularly to prevent HIV. PEP means 'after exposure': it is an emergency medicine started within 72 hours after a possible HIV exposure, such as a broken condom or rape, and taken for 28 days. If you often need PEP, ask a health worker about PrEP.

title: Stigma about taking PrEP
answer: Taking PrEP is a responsible choice to protect your health. It does not mean you have HIV or that you are a bad person. Some people may misunderstand PrEP because the pills look like HIV treatment. You decide whom to tell. If you face judgement, a counsellor or peer educator can support you. Your health is what matters.

title: PrEP when your partner has HIV
answer: If your partner has HIV, PrEP can help protect you, especially while your partner is starting treatment or if their viral load is not yet undetectable. When your partner takes treatment well and is undetectable, HIV is not passed through sex. Talk with a health worker together about the best plan, which may include PrEP, condoms, and regular testing.

title: Is PrEP free in Rwanda
answer: PrEP is provided free of charge at public health facilities in Rwanda that offer it to people who need it. You will not be asked to pay for the pills or HIV tests that come with PrEP at public facilities. Ask your health center or youth corner about PrEP, or call 114 for information.

title: Long-term safety of PrEP
answer: PrEP has been used by many people around the world and is considered safe for most people, including young people. Rarely, it can affect kidney function or bone density, which is why health workers may check your health while you use it. Any effects found are usually reversible after stopping. Attend your check-ups and report any concerns to your provider.

title: Other forms of PrEP besides pills
answer: Besides daily pills, WHO has recommended other forms of PrEP, such as a vaginal ring that releases medicine and a long-acting injection. These may not be available everywhere. Ask a health worker at your health center which PrEP options are available in your area and which one fits you best.

title: Telling a partner or family about PrEP
answer: Whether you tell anyone about PrEP is your choice. Telling a partner can help you plan protection together and avoid misunderstandings if they see your pills. Telling a trusted family member may give you support to take it daily. Explain that PrEP is a prevention medicine for HIV-negative people. A counsellor can help you plan the conversation.

title: How soon to start PEP
answer: PEP must be started as soon as possible after a possible HIV exposure, ideally within a few hours, and no later than 72 hours (3 days). The sooner you start, the better it works. Do not wait until morning or after the weekend if you can avoid it. Go to the nearest health center or hospital and explain what happened.

title: When it is too late for PEP
answer: PEP is not given after 72 hours, because it is not likely to work then. If more than 72 hours have passed, still go to a health center. A health worker can test you, check for other STIs, offer emergency contraception if it is still useful, and tell you when to test again for HIV. They can also talk with you about PrEP for the future.

title: How long PEP lasts
answer: PEP is taken every day for 28 days (four weeks). It is important to finish the whole course, even if you feel fine, so it can work. Take it at the same time each day. If you have side effects or problems, do not stop on your own; talk to your health worker. You will also have follow-up HIV tests after finishing.

title: Where to get PEP in Rwanda
answer: You can get PEP at health centers and hospitals in Rwanda. If it is night or a weekend, go to a hospital emergency service or the nearest facility that is open. After sexual assault, go to an Isange One Stop Centre or call 3029. Tell the staff you need PEP and what happened. You can also call 114 for information.

title: PEP after rape
answer: If you were raped, go as soon as possible to the nearest health facility or Isange One Stop Centre, or call 3029 (free). They can give PEP within 72 hours to prevent HIV, emergency contraception, treatment for STIs, counselling, and help with reporting if you choose. Try not to wash or change clothes if you want to keep evidence, but do not delay care. It was not your fault.

title: PEP after a condom breaks
answer: If a condom breaks or slips off during sex and you do not know your partner's HIV status, or they have HIV and are not virally suppressed, go to a health center as soon as possible, within 72 hours, and ask about PEP. Also ask about emergency contraception and STI testing. Next time, check the expiry date, use water-based lubricant, and put the condom on correctly.

title: PEP after a needle injury
answer: After a needle-stick or sharp injury with possible blood exposure, wash the area with soap and water and go quickly to a health facility. A health worker will assess the risk, test you, and decide if PEP is needed, starting it as soon as possible within 72 hours. They may also check your hepatitis B protection. Follow-up testing will be planned.

title: PEP side effects and finishing the course
answer: Some people taking PEP feel mild side effects like nausea, tiredness, headache or stomach upset, which usually improve after a few days. It is important to finish all 28 days. Do not stop on your own; if side effects are hard to manage, talk to your health worker, who can help. Go to a health facility quickly if you develop a rash, yellow eyes or feel very unwell.

title: HIV testing after finishing PEP
answer: When you start PEP, you are tested for HIV. After finishing PEP, you need follow-up HIV tests at times your health worker will tell you, to make sure you did not get HIV. Keep using condoms until your follow-up tests are done. If your risk continues, ask about PrEP.

title: Using PEP more than once
answer: PEP can be given again if you have another possible HIV exposure, and a health worker will not refuse you because you used it before. But PEP is an emergency medicine, not a regular prevention method. If you keep needing PEP, it means you are at ongoing risk, and PrEP together with condoms may protect you better. Talk to a health worker about your options without fear of being judged.

title: Getting PEP without a parent
answer: Young people in Rwanda aged 12 and older can consent to HIV testing on their own, and PEP is started after an HIV test, so a parent should not be a barrier to getting urgent care. Go straight to a health facility within 72 hours and explain what happened. Health workers will keep your information private. If you can, bring a trusted adult for support, but do not delay.

title: Care after rape besides PEP
answer: After rape, PEP is only one part of care. At a health facility or Isange One Stop Centre (call 3029), you can also get emergency contraception to prevent pregnancy, tests and treatment for other STIs, care for injuries, counselling, and help with police and legal support if you choose. Follow-up visits are important. You deserve care and support, and what happened was not your fault.

title: Is PEP free in Rwanda
answer: PEP is provided free of charge at public health facilities in Rwanda, and care for survivors of sexual violence at Isange One Stop Centres is also free. Do not let worry about money stop you from going quickly. If you are asked to pay at a public facility, you can call 114 for information.

title: Does PEP always work
answer: PEP greatly lowers the chance of getting HIV when it is started early and taken every day for all 28 days, but it is not 100 percent effective. It works best when started within hours, not days. That is why follow-up HIV tests are needed after finishing. Keep using condoms during and after PEP until your follow-up tests are done.

title: PEP for children after sexual abuse
answer: Children who have been sexually abused can and should get PEP if it is within 72 hours, along with other care. Take the child to the nearest health facility or Isange One Stop Centre as soon as possible, or call 3029 or the child helpline 116. Health workers know how to care for children gently. The child needs comfort, safety and to hear that it is not their fault.

title: Helping a friend get PEP
answer: PEP must be prescribed by a health worker after an HIV test, so your friend needs to go to a health facility in person. You cannot collect PEP for them. You can help by encouraging them to go quickly, within 72 hours, and offering to go with them. Never share your own medicines. If your friend was assaulted, they can call 3029 for Isange.

title: What ART is
answer: ART stands for antiretroviral therapy. It is the medicine people living with HIV take every day to control the virus. ART stops HIV from making copies of itself, which lets the immune system recover and protects the person from getting sick. It does not cure HIV, but when taken well it allows people to live long, healthy lives and stops HIV from passing to sexual partners.

title: Starting ART on the day of diagnosis
answer: In Rwanda, everyone diagnosed with HIV is offered treatment, no matter their CD4 count, and many people can start ART on the same day or within a few days of diagnosis, once they are ready. Starting early protects your immune system and your partners. The health worker will counsel you and check for illnesses like TB first. If you need time, talk openly about it.

title: Why ART is for life
answer: ART controls HIV but does not remove it from the body. The virus hides in some cells, and if you stop treatment it comes back and starts damaging the immune system again. That is why ART is taken every day for life. Many people find it becomes a normal daily habit, like brushing teeth. Your health worker will support you along the way.

title: Why taking ART every day matters
answer: Taking ART every day, as your health worker advised, is called adherence. It keeps enough medicine in your blood to stop HIV from multiplying. When doses are often missed, the virus can grow again and may become resistant, meaning the medicine stops working. Good adherence keeps you healthy, makes your viral load undetectable, and protects your partners.

title: Tips to remember your ART
answer: Simple tricks can help you take ART every day: take it at the same time each day, link it to a daily habit like a meal or brushing teeth, set a phone alarm, use a pill box, and keep a small extra supply where you stay. Some young people ask a trusted friend or family member to remind them. Peer support groups also share helpful tips.

title: Missing a dose of ART
answer: If you miss a dose of ART, do not panic and do not stop your treatment. What to do depends on your medicine and how late you are, so talk to your health provider about the right plan and follow their advice. Never take extra pills without advice. If you miss doses often, tell your health worker honestly so they can help you find a solution.

title: Side effects of ART
answer: Most people take ART with few or no problems. Some have mild side effects at first, such as nausea, headache, tiredness, dizziness or strange dreams, which often improve within weeks. Do not stop your medicine because of side effects. Tell your health worker, who can help manage them or change the medicine if needed. Go to a health facility quickly if you have a serious rash, yellow eyes or feel very ill.

title: Stopping ART when you feel well
answer: Feeling well is a sign that ART is working, not that HIV is gone. If you stop your medicine, the virus will multiply again, your immune system will weaken, you can pass HIV to others, and the virus may become resistant. Never stop ART without talking to your health worker. If something makes it hard to continue, they can help.

title: HIV drug resistance
answer: Drug resistance happens when HIV changes so that a medicine no longer works against it. It usually develops when ART is taken irregularly or stopped and started. Resistant HIV is harder to treat and may need different medicines. You can prevent resistance by taking your ART every day as advised and going for your viral load tests.

title: What a viral load test is
answer: A viral load test measures how much HIV is in your blood. It shows whether your ART is working. The goal is a very low or undetectable viral load. In Rwanda, people on ART have viral load tests at regular times set by the guidelines. Your health worker will explain your results and what to do if the viral load is high.

title: Undetectable equals untransmittable
answer: When a person living with HIV takes ART every day and their viral load stays undetectable, they do not pass HIV to their sexual partners. This is called U=U: undetectable equals untransmittable. Their viral load must be confirmed by a test and they must keep taking treatment. U=U is about sexual transmission; it does not protect against other STIs or pregnancy.

title: How long it takes to become undetectable
answer: Most people who take ART every day reach an undetectable viral load within a few months, often by about six months. Your health worker will test your viral load to confirm. Until it is confirmed undetectable, use condoms to protect your partners. Taking every dose is the key to getting there and staying there.

title: What a high viral load result means
answer: A high viral load result while on ART means the virus is not fully controlled. The most common reason is missed doses, but other causes include vomiting, other medicines, or resistance. Your health worker will talk with you, offer adherence support, and repeat the test. If it stays high, they may change your medicine. Be honest about any problems so they can help.

title: Is HIV treatment free in Rwanda
answer: Yes. HIV treatment (ART), viral load tests and routine HIV care are provided free of charge at public health facilities in Rwanda. You do not need to pay for your ARVs. If you face any problem getting your medicine, talk to the health facility or call 114.

title: Collecting ART refills and changing clinic
answer: You collect your ART refills at the health facility where you are enrolled in care. If you move, go to university or change school, tell your health worker before you leave. They can transfer your care and records to a facility near your new home so your treatment continues without a gap. Do not wait until your pills run out.

title: Herbal medicine and ART
answer: Some herbal or traditional medicines can interfere with ART, making it work less well or causing side effects. Herbs cannot replace ART. Before taking any herbs, supplements or other medicines, tell your health worker. Never stop your ART to try herbal treatment.

title: Alcohol and drugs while on ART
answer: Alcohol and drugs can make you forget your ART doses, harm your liver, and lead to unsafe sex. Heavy drinking is especially harmful. If you drink, make sure you still take your medicine on time. If you find it hard to control alcohol or drug use, talk honestly with your health worker; they can help without judging you.

title: Taking ART at boarding school
answer: Many students living with HIV take ART at boarding school. Plan with your health worker and parent or guardian: you may get enough pills for the term, and some schools have a nurse or matron who can keep your medicine private and help you. You decide who knows. Set an alarm and keep pills in a safe place. Tell your health worker if you face problems.

title: Travelling with ART
answer: If you are travelling, take enough ART for the whole trip plus a few extra days, and keep it in your hand luggage, not in a bag that may be lost. Keep taking it at the same time each day. Tell your health worker before long trips so they can give you enough medicine or help you get refills where you are going.

title: Life expectancy with HIV on treatment
answer: Today, a young person who starts ART early and takes it every day can expect to live a long life, close to that of people without HIV. They can finish school, work, marry and have children. HIV is no longer a death sentence when treated. Taking your medicine, going for check-ups, and living healthily make the biggest difference.

title: Fewer clinic visits when stable on ART
answer: In Rwanda, people who are doing well on ART, with an undetectable viral load, may be offered easier care, such as fewer clinic visits, longer medicine refills, or group refills. This saves time and makes school or work easier. Your health worker will decide if you qualify. Keep your appointments and viral load tests so you can benefit.

title: Feeling tired of taking pills every day
answer: Many people living with HIV, especially young people, sometimes feel tired of taking pills every day. This is called pill fatigue, and it is normal. Talk about it with your health worker, counsellor or a peer support group. Remind yourself why your medicine matters: your health, your dreams and the people you love. Ask your health worker if simpler options are available.

title: Taking ART without others knowing
answer: If you are not ready to tell people about your HIV status, you can still take your medicine privately. You might take it at a time when you are alone, keep pills in a private container, and keep enough with you. Hiding medicine should never lead to missing doses. A counsellor can help you plan, and over time you may find someone you trust to support you.

title: Losing or running out of ART
answer: If you lose your ARVs or are about to run out, go to your health facility as soon as possible and explain. Do not wait until you have missed many doses. If you are away from home, go to the nearest public health facility that provides HIV care and tell them your situation. Keep a small extra supply and your clinic card to make this easier.

title: ART and meals
answer: Some HIV medicines can be taken with or without food, while others work better with food or may upset the stomach if taken without. Ask your health worker how to take your own medicine. Eating regular, balanced meals helps you feel well. If you do not have enough food, tell your health worker; they may connect you to support.

title: Taking ART when sick with another illness
answer: If you get sick with something else, like malaria, flu or diarrhoea, keep taking your ART unless a health worker tells you otherwise. Go to a health facility and tell them you are on ART, so they choose medicines that are safe to take together. If you vomit soon after taking your pills, ask your health worker what to do.

title: Missing an HIV clinic appointment
answer: If you miss an HIV clinic appointment, go back as soon as you can, even if it is late. Health workers will welcome you back and help you continue treatment. Do not be afraid of being scolded. It is better to return than to stay away. Call your facility or ask your community health worker if you need help getting there.

title: Feeling unwell soon after starting ART
answer: In the first weeks of ART, some people feel side effects, and a few may feel worse as the immune system wakes up and reacts to infections already in the body. This usually improves. Do not stop your medicine. Tell your health worker about any new symptoms. Go to a health facility right away if you have high fever, trouble breathing, serious rash or feel very ill.

title: Condoms when you are undetectable
answer: An undetectable viral load means you do not pass HIV through sex. But condoms are still useful because they protect against other STIs, such as syphilis or gonorrhoea, and prevent unplanned pregnancy. Also, if you miss doses, the viral load can rise again. Talk with your partner and health worker about what protection makes sense for you.

title: Never share your ART
answer: Never share your ARVs with anyone or take someone else's. Sharing means you will run short and miss doses, which can cause resistance. The other person may need a different medicine, a proper HIV test, or PEP, which a health worker must decide. If a friend needs HIV medicine, encourage them to go to a health facility.

title: Fasting and ART
answer: If you plan to fast for religious reasons, talk to your health worker before you start. Many people can adjust the time they take their ART so they keep taking it every day, for example before dawn or after sunset. Do not skip doses because of fasting. Religious leaders often agree that taking needed medicine is acceptable.

title: ART and teenage growth
answer: ART helps children and teenagers living with HIV grow and develop well. Untreated HIV can slow growth and delay puberty, but with good treatment most young people grow normally. Health workers check your weight and height at visits. If you are worried about your growth or body changes, talk to your health worker.

title: Why your ART may be changed
answer: Health workers sometimes change a person's ART. Reasons include side effects, a high viral load that does not come down, new and better medicines recommended in national guidelines, or changes such as growing older, pregnancy or other illnesses. A change is not a punishment. Ask your health worker why your medicine changed and how to take the new one.

title: Phases of the menstrual cycle
answer: The menstrual cycle has a few stages that repeat. First is your period, when the lining of the womb comes out as blood. Next, the lining starts to grow thick again while an egg gets ready in an ovary. Around the middle of the cycle, the egg is released (ovulation). After that, the body waits to see if a pregnancy starts. If it does not, hormone levels drop and the next period begins. The whole cycle usually takes about three to five weeks.

title: Hormones that control the cycle
answer: Your cycle is controlled by chemical messengers called hormones. The brain sends signals to the ovaries. The ovaries then make two main hormones: oestrogen, which helps the womb lining grow and an egg to mature, and progesterone, which keeps the lining ready after ovulation. When no pregnancy happens, these hormones fall and your period starts. Changes in these hormones can also affect your mood, skin and energy at different times of the month.

title: Why the womb lining sheds each month
answer: Each month the inside lining of your womb (uterus) grows thick and soft with blood and tissue. This is the body getting ready in case a pregnancy starts, because a fertilised egg would need that lining to grow. When no pregnancy happens, the body does not need the lining, so hormone levels drop and the lining breaks down. It leaves the body through the vagina as your period. Then a new lining starts to grow again.

title: What ovulation is
answer: Ovulation is when one of your ovaries releases a mature egg. The egg travels down a tube towards the womb. This usually happens once in each cycle, often about two weeks before your next period starts, but the exact day differs between people and from month to month. The egg lives for about one day. Ovulation is a normal sign that your reproductive system is working, and it is the time when pregnancy is most possible if there is sex.

title: Body signs of ovulation
answer: Some girls notice signs around ovulation, but many notice nothing, and that is normal. Common signs include clear, wet, slippery discharge that stretches like raw egg white, a mild ache on one side of the lower belly, slightly tender breasts, or feeling more energetic. Your body temperature also rises a little after ovulation. These signs can help you understand your body, but they are not an exact way to know the day, especially when cycles are still irregular.

title: Fertile days in the cycle
answer: Your fertile days are the days in your cycle when pregnancy can happen if you have sex. Sperm can live inside the body for up to about five days, and the egg lives about one day, so the fertile time is roughly the five days before ovulation plus the day of ovulation. Because ovulation often moves from month to month, especially in young people, it is hard to know these days exactly. Counting days is not a safe way to avoid pregnancy for most young people; talk to a health worker about reliable methods.

title: One-sided pain in the middle of the cycle
answer: Some girls feel a dull ache or short sharp twinges on one side of the lower belly around the middle of their cycle. This is often linked to ovulation, when an ovary releases an egg. It usually lasts from a few minutes to a day or two and may switch sides from month to month. Rest and warmth can help. If the pain is very strong, lasts longer, or comes with fever, vomiting or fainting, go to a health center quickly.

title: What counts as day one of the cycle
answer: Day one of your cycle is the first day of real period bleeding, when you need a pad or other product. Light brown spotting before the flow starts usually does not count. Count every day from day one until the day before your next period begins; that number is your cycle length.
