Knowing day one helps you notice your own pattern and gives useful information if you ever need to see a health worker about your periods.

title: Why cycle length differs from girl to girl
answer: Every body is different, so cycles are different too. One girl may bleed every 24 days and her friend every 33 days, and both can be healthy. Age, genes, stress, weight, sleep and illness can all affect how long a cycle is. In the first years after periods begin, the body is still learning a rhythm, so differences are very common. What matters most is knowing what is normal for you and noticing big changes.

title: Why first periods may be light or brown
answer: Your very first periods are often light, short, or brown in colour rather than bright red. This is because your hormones are just starting to work together and the womb lining may be thin. Brown blood is simply older blood that took longer to leave the body. Over the next months your flow often becomes more regular. If you have questions or the bleeding is very heavy, you can talk to a nurse at a health center.

title: What period blood is made of
answer: Period blood is not only blood. It is a mix of blood, pieces of the womb lining, mucus from the cervix and normal vaginal fluid. That is why it can look thicker than blood from a cut and can have small soft lumps. It is not dirty or poisonous. It is a normal body fluid, just like sweat or saliva, and it leaves the body because the lining is not needed that month.

title: Dark brown or black period blood
answer: Period blood can be bright red, dark red, brown or almost black, and all of these can be normal. Dark blood is usually older blood that stayed in the womb or vagina a little longer before coming out, so it has changed colour. This is common at the start or the end of a period, or in the morning after lying down. See a health worker if dark bleeding comes with a bad smell, fever, belly pain or itching.

title: Blood clots during a period
answer: Small soft clots, like jelly pieces smaller than a coin, are common, especially on heavy days or after lying down for a long time. They form when blood collects before it comes out. Clots are a reason to see a health worker if they are often bigger than a large coin, if you soak a pad every hour, or if you feel weak, dizzy or very tired. A nurse at your health center can check you.

title: How much blood is lost in a period
answer: It can look like a lot, but most people lose only a few tablespoons of blood over the whole period. The blood spreads out on a pad, so it seems like more. Your body makes new blood all the time, so a normal period does not leave you empty. If you soak through a pad every one to two hours, bleed more than seven days, or feel weak and dizzy, see a health worker.

title: Pink or watery period blood
answer: Sometimes period blood looks pink or watery, often at the very start or end of a period or when the flow is light. This usually happens because the blood is mixed with normal vaginal fluid. It is usually nothing to worry about. If watery bleeding comes with a bad smell, itching, pain, fever, or happens often between periods, visit a nurse at your health center to be checked.

title: Does an egg come out with period blood
answer: The egg released at ovulation is tiny, smaller than a grain of sand, so you cannot see it. If it is not fertilised, it breaks down within about a day and is absorbed or leaves the body without being noticed. The lumps you may see in period blood are clots or pieces of womb lining, not eggs. So there is no egg to look for in your pad.

title: How many eggs a girl is born with
answer: A baby girl is born with all the eggs she will ever have, about one to two million, stored in her ovaries. Many naturally disappear over time, so by puberty there are a few hundred thousand left. Usually only one egg is released each cycle. Having periods does not make you run out of eggs quickly, and your supply lasts until menopause, many years later.

title: Do friends' periods sync
answer: Many girls believe that friends or sisters who live together start bleeding at the same time. Studies have not shown that this really happens. Because cycles are different lengths, periods often overlap by chance and then drift apart again. So if your period starts on the same day as your roommate, it is most likely a coincidence. Either way, it is normal and nothing to worry about.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Do the ovaries take turns
answer: You have two ovaries, one on each side of the womb. It is often said that they take turns releasing an egg, but in reality it is quite random which ovary releases the egg in a given month. Sometimes the same side releases eggs several months in a row. If one ovary is removed or not working, the other one can still release eggs and periods can continue.

title: Where period blood comes out
answer: A girl has three openings between her legs. At the front is the urethra, where urine comes out. In the middle is the vagina, where period blood comes out. At the back is the anus, where stool comes out. Period blood flows from the womb through the cervix and out of the vagina. You cannot hold it in like urine, which is why you use a pad or other product.

title: Stretchy egg-white discharge mid-cycle
answer: Around the middle of your cycle, you may notice clear, wet, slippery discharge that stretches between your fingers, like raw egg white. This is cervical mucus, and it changes this way close to ovulation. It is normal and healthy. It usually has little or no smell and does not itch. After ovulation, it often becomes thicker and stickier or you may feel drier. Just wear clean cotton underwear and change it if it feels wet.

title: Discharge before the period starts
answer: In the days before your period, discharge is often thicker, white or creamy, and sometimes slightly sticky. This is caused by the hormone progesterone and is normal. Some girls also see a little brown discharge just before bleeding starts. If the discharge is lumpy and itchy, green or grey, smells bad, or comes with pain, see a nurse at your health center.

title: Brown discharge after the period ends
answer: It is common to see brown discharge for a day or two after your period seems finished. This is old blood leaving the womb slowly, and it turns brown because it has been in the body longer. A panty liner or a thin cloth can keep your underwear clean. See a health worker if the brown discharge goes on for many days, smells bad, itches, or comes with belly pain or fever.

title: Discharge that itches or smells bad
answer: Healthy discharge is clear or white with a mild smell. Some changes can mean an infection that needs treatment: discharge that is yellow, green or grey, thick and lumpy like porridge, foamy, or with a strong fishy or bad smell, or with itching, burning or pain. Infections are common and treatable, and they are not something to be ashamed of. Visit a nurse at your health center or youth corner, or call 114 for free advice. Do not wash inside your vagina to fix it.

title: Body temperature changes in the cycle
answer: After ovulation, the hormone progesterone makes your resting body temperature rise a little, by less than one degree. It stays slightly higher until your next period. Most people do not feel this change, and it can only be seen by measuring with a thermometer every morning before getting up. Feeling hot with sweating, shivering or headache is different and could be fever or malaria, so get tested at a health center.

title: Sore breasts before a period
answer: Many girls notice their breasts feel swollen, heavy or tender in the days before a period. This is caused by normal hormone changes and usually gets better once bleeding starts. Wearing a comfortable, supportive bra, using a warm or cool cloth, and cutting down on salty foods may help. If you find a lump that does not go away after your period, or the pain is in one spot and keeps getting worse, see a health worker.

title: Bloating before and during a period
answer: Feeling bloated, with a swollen or tight belly, is common just before and during a period. Hormones make the body hold on to more water and can slow digestion. It usually passes in a few days. Drinking plenty of water, eating less salty food, eating fruit and vegetables, and gentle walking can help. If your belly is very swollen and painful, or bloating lasts all month, see a health worker.

title: Pimples before a period
answer: Many young people get more pimples in the days before their period. Hormone changes make the skin produce more oil, which can block pores. Wash your face gently twice a day with clean water and mild soap, avoid squeezing pimples, and keep hands and phone screens clean. Drinking water and getting enough sleep also help. If pimples are very painful, leave scars or upset you a lot, a health worker can advise you.

title: Diarrhoea or constipation around periods
answer: Some girls get loose stools or need the toilet more often during their period. The same body chemicals that make the womb squeeze can also affect the gut. Others feel constipated before their period. Drink plenty of clean water, eat fruit, vegetables and beans, and move your body. If diarrhoea is severe, lasts more than two days, has blood, or you cannot keep fluids down, go to a health center.

title: Feeling tired during a period
answer: Feeling more tired than usual during your period is common. Hormone changes, cramps, poor sleep and losing some blood can all make you feel low in energy. Eat regular meals with iron-rich foods like beans, dark green leaves and small fish, drink water, rest when you can, and do gentle activity. If you feel extremely tired all the time, short of breath, or very pale, see a health worker, as this can be a sign of low blood (anaemia).

title: Headaches around a period
answer: Some girls get headaches just before or during their period because of falling hormone levels. Drinking enough water, eating regular meals, sleeping well, and resting in a quiet dark place can help. A pharmacist or health worker can tell you about safe pain relief. Go to a health center quickly if a headache is sudden and very severe, comes with fever, a stiff neck, confusion or weakness, or changes in your eyesight.

title: Food cravings before a period
answer: Feeling extra hungry or craving sweet or salty foods before your period is very common and is linked to hormone changes. It is okay to eat a little of what you want. Try to choose filling foods like sweet potatoes, beans, bananas, groundnuts and fruit, and eat regular meals so you do not get too hungry. Drinking water helps too. The cravings usually go away once your period starts or ends.

title: Sleep problems around a period
answer: Hormone changes, cramps, and worry about leaks can make it hard to sleep before or during your period. A regular bedtime, less tea or coffee in the evening, a warm cloth on your belly, and a night pad or extra protection can help you relax. Some girls feel more sleepy instead, which is also normal. If poor sleep lasts many weeks or you feel very sad, talk to a health worker.

title: What PMS is
answer: PMS stands for premenstrual syndrome. It is a group of body and mood changes that some people get in the one or two weeks before their period. Signs can include bloating, sore breasts, tiredness, headaches, cravings, pimples, and feeling sad, worried or easily annoyed. These changes are linked to hormones and usually stop a few days after bleeding begins. PMS is common and real, and you are not imagining it.

title: Mood swings and crying before a period
answer: Feeling happy one moment and sad or tearful the next is common in the days before a period. Hormone changes affect the brain chemicals that control mood. It does not mean something is wrong with you. Getting enough sleep, moving your body, eating regularly and talking with someone you trust can help. Knowing when your period is coming can also help you understand these feelings. If sadness is very strong or lasts beyond your period, talk to a health worker or call 114.

title: Feeling angry or irritable before a period
answer: Some girls feel short-tempered, impatient or easily annoyed before their period. This is a common part of PMS and is linked to hormone changes. You are still in charge of how you act, and these tips can help: take a short walk, breathe slowly, get enough sleep, and step away before an argument grows. It can help to explain to people close to you how you feel. If anger feels out of control, talk to a health worker or counsellor.

title: Very low mood before periods (PMDD)
answer: For a small number of people, mood changes before a period are so strong that they make school, home or friendships very hard, with deep sadness, hopelessness, anxiety or anger that lifts once the period starts. This can be a condition sometimes called PMDD, and it can be treated. Please talk to a health worker at your health center or youth corner. If you ever have thoughts of hurting yourself, tell a trusted adult now, call 114, or go to the nearest health facility.

title: Ways to cope with PMS
answer: Simple habits can make PMS easier. Mark your cycle on a calendar so you know when it is coming. Eat regular meals with fruit, vegetables and beans, and cut down on very salty or sugary foods. Drink water, sleep well, and move your body each day, even with a walk. Talk to friends or family about how you feel. If PMS still disrupts your life, a health worker can discuss other options with you.

title: Does the period come on the same date every month
answer: Your period does not usually come on the same calendar date each month. It follows your cycle length, not the calendar. For example, if your cycle is 28 days and your period started on 3 March, the next one may start around 31 March. Many cycles also change by a few days from month to month, which is normal. Marking each start day helps you learn your own pattern.

title: Why the period comes earlier each calendar month
answer: If your cycle is shorter than the number of days in a month, your period will start a little earlier in the month each time. For example, with a 28-day cycle, a period that started on 10 June may start around 8 July and then about 5 August. This is normal and does not mean your periods are coming too often. It is simply how cycle days fit into calendar months.

title: Choosing a period product
answer: There is no single best period product. Disposable pads are easy to use and to find in shops. Reusable cloth pads cost less over time if you have water and a sunny place to dry them. Menstrual cups last for years but need clean water and practice. Tampons are less common in Rwanda. Period underwear is another option. Think about cost, water, privacy, comfort and what you feel happy with. You can try different options over time.

title: How to put on a disposable pad
answer: Wash your hands first. Take the pad out of its wrapper and peel off the paper strip on the back. Press the sticky side onto the middle of your underwear, with the longer or wider end towards the back. If it has wings, fold them around the sides of your underwear and press them underneath. Pull up your underwear so the pad sits close to your body. Wash your hands again afterwards.

title: How often to change a pad
answer: Change your disposable pad every four to six hours, or sooner if it feels full, wet or uncomfortable. On heavy days you may need to change more often, and on light days less often, but try not to keep the same pad on all day. Changing regularly helps prevent leaks, smell, rashes and infections. At night you can wear one pad, ideally a longer night pad, and change it when you wake up.

title: Day pads, night pads and absorbency
answer: Pads come in different sizes and thicknesses. Thin or regular pads suit light or normal days. Super or maxi pads hold more blood for heavy days. Night pads are longer and wider at the back to stop leaks while you lie down. The drops or pictures on the packet show how much a pad can hold. Many girls use a mix: a larger pad on heavy days and at night, and a thinner one on light days.

title: Pads with wings or without
answer: Wings are the flaps on the sides of some pads. You fold them under your underwear so the pad stays in place and blood is less likely to leak at the sides. Pads with wings are helpful when you are walking, playing sport or sleeping. Pads without wings can be fine on light days or with tight underwear. Both work the same way, so choose what feels comfortable and fits your budget.

title: Panty liners for daily use
answer: Panty liners are very thin pads. They are useful for very light bleeding, spotting at the start or end of a period, or as backup with a cup. They are not needed every day for normal discharge, which is healthy. Wearing liners all the time can trap moisture and cause irritation. If you use one, change it several times a day. Clean cotton underwear changed daily is usually enough for normal discharge.

title: Pad rash and chafing
answer: A pad can rub your inner thighs or skin and cause a red, sore rash, especially when it is hot, damp, or you walk a lot. To help: change pads often, keep the area clean and dry, wear soft cotton underwear that fits well, and choose unscented pads. Washing with clean water and patting dry helps. A little plain petroleum jelly on the outer skin of the thighs can reduce rubbing. If the rash has blisters, pus or does not heal, see a nurse.

title: Making a cloth pad at home
answer: You can make a simple reusable pad from clean, soft cotton cloth, like an old cotton shirt or towel. Cut several layers into a long rectangle, fold or stitch them together so they are thick enough to absorb, and make sure the outside is smooth. Avoid nylon or rough fabric. Wash the cloth well and dry it in the sun before first use. You can attach it with a safety pin or wear close-fitting underwear to hold it in place.

title: How to wash reusable cloth pads
answer: Soak or rinse a used cloth pad in cold water first, because hot water can set the stain. Then wash it well with soap and clean water, rubbing until the water runs clear. Rinse to remove all soap. Dry it completely, ideally in direct sunlight, which helps kill germs. If you can, iron it once dry. Wash your hands before and after. Never use a pad that is still damp, as it can cause infections.

title: Drying reusable pads in the sun
answer: Sunlight and air are the best way to dry cloth pads because they help kill germs and stop bad smells. Many girls feel shy and hide wet pads under the bed or under other clothes, but cloths that stay damp can cause infections. If you want privacy, hang the pad in the sun with a light cloth over it, or dry it in a sunny spot inside. Make sure it is completely dry before you use it.

title: Storing clean reusable pads
answer: Once your cloth pads are clean and completely dry, fold them and keep them in a clean, dry bag, box or cloth pouch. Store them away from dust, damp places, insects and dirty clothes. A small clean bag also makes it easy to carry a spare to school. Keep used pads separate in a plastic or waterproof bag until you can wash them. Check stored pads before use; wash again if they smell or look dirty.

title: When to replace reusable pads
answer: Good reusable pads can last many months, often around a year or more, depending on how often you use and wash them. Replace a pad when the cloth becomes thin, torn, hard, or no longer absorbs well, or if it keeps a bad smell even after careful washing and sun drying. Having several pads lets each one rest and dry fully, which makes them last longer.

title: Reusable versus disposable pads
answer: Disposable pads are used once and thrown away. They are easy to use, good when you are away from water, but they cost money every month and create waste. Reusable pads cost more at first but can last a long time, saving money and making less rubbish. They need water, soap, a private place to wash, and sun to dry. Both are safe when used properly. Some girls use reusables at home and disposables at school.

title: What a menstrual cup is
answer: A menstrual cup is a small, soft, bell-shaped cup, usually made of medical-grade silicone. You fold it and put it inside your vagina, where it opens and collects period blood instead of soaking it up. You empty it, rinse it and put it back. One cup can last several years if you look after it, which can save money. It takes some practice to learn, and you need clean water and soap to use it safely.

title: How to insert a menstrual cup
answer: Wash your hands well. Fold the clean cup, for example into a C shape, so it is narrow. Relax and sit, squat or stand with one leg up. Gently push the folded cup into your vagina, aiming towards your lower back, not straight up. Let it open; you can turn it slightly or run a finger around it to check it has opened. It should sit lower than a tampon and you should not feel it. Practise at home first.

title: How to remove a menstrual cup
answer: Wash your hands. Sit or squat and relax your muscles. Gently pull the stem until you can reach the base of the cup. Pinch the base to break the seal, because pulling only the stem can hurt. Keep it upright as you slide it out slowly, then empty the blood into the toilet or latrine. Rinse it with clean water and reinsert, or wash and store it. If you cannot remove it after trying calmly, a nurse can help.

title: Cleaning and boiling a menstrual cup
answer: During your period, empty the cup, rinse it with clean water and, if possible, wash it with mild unscented soap before putting it back. At the end of each period, boil it in a pot of water for several minutes, then let it dry and store it in a breathable cloth bag, not a closed plastic box. Use clean water; if your water is not safe, use boiled water to rinse. Do not use strong chemicals or perfumed soap.

title: Menstrual cup leaking
answer: A cup may leak if it has not fully opened, sits too high or at the wrong angle, is too full, or is the wrong size. Try emptying it more often on heavy days, checking it has popped open by running a finger around it, and placing it a little lower, aiming towards your back. Wearing a liner while you learn can help. Most people get better with practice over a few periods.

title: Can a cup or tampon get lost inside
answer: No, a cup or tampon cannot get lost inside your body. The top of the vagina is closed by the cervix, which only has a tiny opening, so nothing can go up into your belly. Sometimes it moves higher and is harder to reach. Relax, squat, and gently bear down as if passing stool, and it will usually move lower. If you still cannot reach it, see a nurse; this is common and they can help.

title: Can young girls use a menstrual cup
answer: Yes, girls who have started their periods can use a menstrual cup, and many brands make smaller sizes. It may take more practice at first, and that is okay. Some girls prefer to wait until they feel more comfortable with their bodies. Being relaxed helps, as does practising at home. You can choose to use one or not; pads are just as good. Ask a nurse or trusted adult if you have questions.

title: Choosing a menstrual cup size
answer: Most cup brands make a smaller size and a larger size. The smaller size is usually recommended for young people, those who have not given birth, and those with a lighter flow. A softer, smaller cup can also be easier to fold and insert. The packet or leaflet will explain the brand's sizes. If the cup is uncomfortable or leaks often, a different size or brand may suit you better.

title: What a tampon is
answer: A tampon is a small tube of soft absorbent material, usually cotton, with a string at one end. You put it inside your vagina, where it soaks up blood before it leaves the body. The string stays outside so you can pull it out. Tampons come in different sizes for light or heavy flow. They are less common and harder to find in Rwanda than pads, and they must be changed regularly.

title: How to insert a tampon
answer: Wash your hands. Choose the lowest absorbency that suits your flow. Unwrap the tampon and get into a relaxed position, like squatting or one foot on the toilet. With an applicator, hold it at the grip, gently push the tip into your vagina aiming towards your lower back, push the inner tube to release the tampon, then pull out the applicator. Without an applicator, push it in with a clean finger. The string should hang outside. If it hurts, it may not be far enough in.

title: How often to change a tampon
answer: Change a tampon every four to eight hours, and never leave one in for more than eight hours. Use the lowest absorbency that works for your flow, and do not use a tampon when you are not bleeding. Leaving a tampon in too long increases the risk of a rare but serious illness called toxic shock syndrome. If you sleep more than eight hours, a pad at night is a safer choice.

title: Toxic shock syndrome warning signs
answer: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a rare but serious illness linked mostly to leaving tampons, and sometimes cups, in too long. Warning signs include sudden high fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, a rash that looks like sunburn, dizziness or fainting, muscle aches and confusion. If you have these signs while using a tampon or cup, remove it and go to a health facility immediately or call 912 for an ambulance. Tell the health worker you were using a tampon or cup.

title: Peeing with a tampon or cup inside
answer: Yes, you can pee with a tampon or menstrual cup in. Urine comes out of a different, smaller opening (the urethra) in front of the vagina, so it does not pass through the tampon or cup. You can hold a tampon string to one side if you want to keep it dry. You can also pass stool normally, though some people check their cup has not moved afterwards.

title: Do tampons or cups affect virginity
answer: Using a tampon or menstrual cup does not take away your virginity. Virginity is about whether a person has had sex, not about a product used for periods. The hymen is a thin, stretchy piece of tissue at the vaginal opening that is different in every girl. It can stretch with many activities, like sport, and it cannot prove whether someone has had sex. You can choose any product you feel comfortable with.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Period underwear
answer: Period underwear looks like normal underwear but has special absorbent layers in the crotch that soak up blood and keep you feeling dry. Some can be worn alone on light days, while others are used as backup with a pad or cup. They can be washed and reused many times. They cost more at first and can be hard to find, and you need enough pairs and time to wash and dry them between uses.

title: Washing period underwear
answer: After wearing period underwear, rinse it in cold water until the water runs mostly clear. Then wash it with mild soap by hand or in a gentle wash, without bleach or fabric softener, which can damage the absorbent layer. Hang it to dry fully in the sun or open air; do not wear it damp. Follow any instructions on the label. With good care, a pair can last for a long time.

title: What to use when you have no pad right now
answer: If your period starts and you have no pad, do not panic. For now you can fold clean toilet paper or tissue thickly into your underwear, or use a clean, soft cotton cloth or handkerchief. Change it often. Ask a friend, teacher, school matron, nurse or older woman you trust; many will gladly help. Tie a sweater around your waist if you are worried about a stain. Then get a proper pad or cloth as soon as you can.

title: Unsafe materials to use as pads
answer: Some things girls use when they have no pads can harm the body. Do not use dirty rags, mattress foam, paper like newspaper, plastic, leaves, soil, ash, or cloth that is still damp. These can scratch the skin, cause rashes and infections, or not absorb blood well. If you use cloth, it must be clean cotton, washed with soap and fully dried in the sun. If you cannot get safe materials, ask a health worker or teacher for help.

title: Using toilet paper as a pad
answer: Toilet paper can be used for a short time in an emergency, folded thickly in your underwear. It is not a good choice for a whole period, because it breaks apart, does not hold much blood, and can leave small pieces on your skin. Change it often and wipe away any bits. As soon as you can, switch to a pad or clean cotton cloth. Do not put toilet paper inside the vagina.

title: Using cotton wool as a pad
answer: Cotton wool is soft and absorbs well, but loose cotton wool can stick to your skin and pubic hair and leave fibres behind. If you use it, wrap it inside a piece of clean cotton cloth or gauze so it holds together, and change it often. Never put loose cotton wool inside your vagina. It can be a short-term option, but pads or clean cloth pads are better for regular use.

title: Using a baby diaper as a pad
answer: A clean, unused baby diaper (nappy) can work as an emergency pad, especially at night on heavy days, because it is made to absorb a lot. It may feel bulky and can be warm. Change it every few hours just as you would a pad, and dispose of it the same way. It should not replace pads all the time if they are available, but it is safe for short use.

title: Putting pads into a pit latrine
answer: Many girls drop used disposable pads into pit latrines. This fills the pit faster, can block the latrine, and plastic in pads does not break down. Where possible, wrap the used pad in paper or its wrapper and put it in a covered bin, then empty the bin into a rubbish pit or as your community or school advises. If your school has a special bin or incinerator for pads, use it. Ask your school matron what to do.

title: Flushing pads in a flush toilet
answer: Do not flush pads, tampons, panty liners or their wrappers down a flush toilet, even if the toilet seems strong. They swell with water and can block pipes and drains, causing overflow. Wrap the used product in its wrapper or toilet paper and put it in the bin. If a bathroom has no bin, wrap it and carry it in a small bag until you find one. Menstrual cup blood can be emptied into the toilet.

title: Burning used pads
answer: In some homes and schools, used pads are burned. Burning in a proper incinerator is a safe way to destroy them. Burning pads in an open fire can produce smoke from the plastic that is bad to breathe, so stand away from the smoke and do it in an open area, away from homes and children. Never burn pads in a cooking fire. Bury or put them in a covered rubbish pit if burning is not possible.

title: Reusing a disposable pad
answer: Disposable pads are made to be used only once. Washing and reusing them is not safe because they do not get clean inside, they break apart, and they can grow germs that cause infections. If money is tight, reusable cloth pads or a menstrual cup are safer ways to save. You can also ask a teacher, school matron or health worker if they know of support for pads in your area.

title: Scented pads and allergies
answer: Some pads have perfume or other added chemicals. They can irritate the sensitive skin around the vulva and cause itching, burning or a rash. You do not need a scented pad to stay fresh; changing pads often and washing with water is enough. If a pad brand makes you itchy, try an unscented brand or cloth pads. If itching continues after changing products, or you have unusual discharge, see a nurse.

title: Wearing two pads at once
answer: Some girls wear two pads at once on heavy days to avoid leaks. It is okay for a short time, but it can feel bulky and rub, and it may not stop leaks better than one larger night pad that fits well. Placing one pad a little further back is useful when lying down. If you regularly need two pads or soak through one in an hour or two, your bleeding may be heavy, so see a health worker.

title: Washing during a period with little water
answer: Even with little water you can stay clean. Use a small basin or jerrycan cup: wash your hands, then pour clean water over your vulva from front to back, using a clean cloth if you like. Wash outer skin and between the folds, then pat dry with a clean cloth. Once or twice a day is enough. Save some water for washing hands after changing your pad. Clean, dry underwear also helps you feel fresh.

title: Should you wash inside the vagina
answer: No, you do not need to wash inside your vagina, even during your period. The vagina cleans itself with natural discharge and has healthy bacteria that protect it. Washing or squirting water, soap, herbs or other products inside (douching) can upset this balance and cause infections. Only wash the outside area, the vulva, with clean water. If you notice a bad smell or itching, see a nurse instead of washing inside.

title: Which soap to use on private parts
answer: Clean water is enough to wash your vulva, even during your period. If you want to use soap, choose a mild, unscented soap on the outside skin only and rinse well. Strong, perfumed or antiseptic soaps, vaginal washes and sprays can dry and irritate the skin and upset the natural balance, leading to itching or infection. Never put soap inside the vagina.

title: Washing hands when changing products
answer: Wash your hands with soap and water before and after you change a pad, cloth, tampon or cup. Washing before stops germs from your hands reaching your private parts, and washing after removes blood from your hands. This is especially important before inserting a cup or tampon. If there is no water at school, carry a small bottle of water and soap, or hand sanitiser, and wash properly when you can.

title: Can bathing make bleeding heavier
answer: Bathing or showering, with warm or cold water, does not make your period heavier or stop it. Washing is healthy and helps you feel fresh. Sometimes blood seems to flow while you bathe because warm water relaxes your body and gravity helps it come out, but the total amount does not change. Keep bathing as usual during your period; a warm bath can even ease cramps.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Washing hair during a period
answer: It is safe to wash your hair during your period. Some people believe that washing hair while menstruating causes illness, headaches or heavier bleeding, but this is not true. Washing your hair and body keeps you clean and helps you feel good. Dry your hair if the weather is cold so you stay comfortable. You can follow your normal routine.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Shaving or trimming pubic hair during a period
answer: Pubic hair is normal and you do not need to remove it, during your period or at any time. It does not make periods dirty. If you choose to trim or shave, you can do it during your period, but use your own clean razor or scissors, never share, and be gentle because skin can be more sensitive. Trimming with scissors is less likely to cause cuts and ingrown hairs than shaving.

title: How often to change underwear during a period
answer: Change into clean underwear at least once a day during your period, and change it sooner if blood leaks onto it or it feels damp. Cotton underwear is best because it lets air through and is easy to wash. Wash used underwear in cold water first to remove blood, then with soap. Dry it in the sun. Having a spare pair in your bag is helpful in case of leaks.

title: Strong fishy smell after a period
answer: A mild smell is normal, but a strong fishy smell that stays after your period has ended, often with thin grey or white discharge, can be a sign of a common imbalance of vaginal bacteria. It is not caused by being dirty, and it can be treated. Do not wash inside or use perfume to cover it, as this can make it worse. See a nurse at your health center or youth corner for a check.

title: Itching during a period
answer: Itching during your period is often caused by a damp pad, perfumed products, rough cloth, or heat and sweat. Change pads often, use unscented products, wear cotton underwear, and keep the area clean and dry. If the itching is strong, lasts after your period, or comes with thick white or coloured discharge, sores, or a bad smell, it may be an infection, so see a nurse at your health center.

title: Stopping leaks at night
answer: To avoid night leaks, change to a fresh pad just before bed and use a longer night pad or a thicker cloth pad. Place the pad a little further back, since blood flows backwards when you lie down. Close-fitting underwear or shorts keep it in place. Sleeping on your side with knees bent can help. Putting an old towel or cloth under you protects your bedding. If you leak every night despite this, talk to a health worker about heavy bleeding.

title: Getting blood stains out of clothes
answer: Act quickly if you can. Rinse the stain from the back of the cloth with cold water; never use hot water first, because heat sets the stain. Rub in soap and scrub gently, then rinse. For old stains, soak the cloth in cold water with soap or a little salt for some time, then wash again. Dry it in the sun, which can also help lighten stains. Blood stains are normal; everyone who menstruates deals with them.

title: A stain on your uniform at school
answer: A period stain can happen to anyone, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. If it happens at school, tie a sweater or jacket around your waist and go to the toilet. Ask a friend you trust, a female teacher or the school matron or nurse for a pad and help. You can rinse the stain with cold water. If you need to, ask to go home to change. Most people understand more than you think.

title: Carrying a period kit
answer: A small period kit in your school bag helps you feel ready. It can include: two or three pads or clean cloth pads, a spare pair of underwear, a small plastic or waterproof bag for used products, some tissue, and a small piece of soap or sanitiser. A sweater can cover stains. Put everything in a small pouch so it stays clean and private. Refill it after each period.

title: Can people tell I am on my period
answer: Most of the time, nobody can tell that you are on your period. Pads are not visible under clothes, and a well-cleaned body does not smell. Many girls feel worried that everyone knows, but other people are usually busy with their own thoughts. Changing your pad regularly, washing daily and wearing comfortable clothes help you feel confident. Your period is private, and you only share it if you want to.

title: Hot water bottle for cramps
answer: Warmth on your lower belly or lower back can relax the muscles of the womb and ease period cramps. You can use a hot water bottle, a plastic bottle filled with warm (not boiling) water and wrapped in cloth, or a warm towel. Always keep a cloth between the heat and your skin to avoid burns, and do not sleep with something very hot against you. A warm bath or shower can help too.

title: Exercise and stretching for cramps
answer: Gentle movement can reduce period cramps for many girls. Walking, light jogging, dancing or stretching increases blood flow and helps the body release natural chemicals that reduce pain. Try lying on your back with your knees pulled to your chest, kneeling and stretching your arms forward on the floor, or slowly rocking your hips. Breathe slowly and deeply. Stop if anything makes the pain much worse.

title: Foods and drinks that help period pain
answer: Some foods and drinks may help you feel better during your period. Warm drinks like ginger tea or warm water can be soothing. Drinking plenty of water helps with bloating. Eating fruit, vegetables, beans, whole grains, groundnuts and small fish gives your body energy and iron. Cutting down on very salty foods, sugary drinks, and lots of coffee may reduce bloating and discomfort. Eat regular meals so you do not feel weak.

title: Pain medicine for period cramps
answer: Common pain medicines sold in pharmacies, such as ibuprofen or paracetamol, can ease period cramps for many people. Ask a pharmacist or health worker which one is right for you and how much to take for your age and weight, and always follow the instructions on the packet. Some work best taken when pain first starts, with food. Do not take medicines prescribed for someone else. If pain medicine does not help, see a health worker.

title: Massage for period cramps
answer: Gently rubbing your lower belly or lower back can help relax tight muscles and ease cramps. Use your fingertips or the palm of your hand and make slow circles below your belly button, or ask someone you trust to rub your lower back. A little plain oil or lotion can make it more comfortable. Combine it with warmth and rest. Stop if pressing makes the pain sharper.

title: Herbal and traditional remedies for cramps
answer: Many families have traditional remedies for period pain. Simple things like warm ginger or lemon tea are generally safe. Be careful with unknown herbal mixtures, roots, or medicines from traditional healers, because the strength and safety are not known and some can harm your liver, kidneys or womb. Never put herbs inside your vagina. If you want to try a remedy, ask a health worker first, especially if your pain is severe.

title: Lower back pain during periods
answer: Many girls feel aching in the lower back during their period. The same muscle squeezing that causes cramps in the womb can spread pain to the back. Warmth on your lower back, gentle stretching, a back rub, rest, and pain relief from a pharmacy can help. If the back pain is severe, on one side, or comes with fever, pain when peeing, or vomiting, see a health worker because it may be something else.

title: Leg pain during periods
answer: Some girls feel aching or heaviness in their thighs or legs during their period. This happens because cramping pain from the womb can spread along nerves into the legs. Warmth, gentle stretching, walking, raising your legs while resting, and pain relief from a pharmacy can help. See a health worker if one leg is swollen, red, hot or very painful, or if the pain is severe and does not go away after your period.

title: Nausea and vomiting with period pain
answer: Some girls feel sick to their stomach or vomit when period cramps are strong. The body chemicals that cause cramps can also affect the stomach. Rest, sip water or warm ginger tea, eat small light meals, and use warmth on your belly. If you vomit many times, cannot keep fluids down, feel very weak, or have severe pain or fever, go to a health center right away.

title: Fainting or dizziness during a period
answer: Feeling light-headed during your period can happen from strong pain, not eating, not drinking enough, or standing for a long time. Sit or lie down with your legs up, drink water, and eat something. If you actually faint, feel dizzy often, are very pale, or your bleeding is heavy, go to a health center; this can be a sign of low blood. If someone faints and does not wake quickly, call 912 or 112.

title: Signs period pain needs a health worker
answer: Mild to moderate cramps are common, but some pain needs a health check. See a health worker if your pain stops you from going to school or doing daily activities, does not improve with rest, warmth or pharmacy pain relief, keeps getting worse over months, or comes with very heavy bleeding. Go to a health facility right away if pain is sudden and severe, or comes with fever, fainting or vomiting. You do not have to just put up with it.

title: Period pain that started years after the first period
answer: Cramps often start in the first few years of having periods. If your periods were mostly painless and then became painful years later, or the pain is much worse than before, it is a good idea to see a health worker. Sometimes this is linked to a condition in the womb or pelvis, such as endometriosis or infection, that can be checked and treated. A nurse at your health center can advise you and refer you if needed.

title: Does period pain get better with age
answer: For many people, period pain becomes milder as they get older, often by their twenties. Some notice less pain after giving birth, but that is not true for everyone and is not a reason to have a baby. You do not need to wait to feel better: warmth, movement, rest and pharmacy pain relief help now, and a health worker can discuss other options if pain is strong.

title: Fever with period pain
answer: Periods do not normally cause a fever. If you have a fever with belly or pelvic pain, it may be a sign of infection, malaria, or another illness that needs attention. Go to a health center soon, especially if you also have unusual or bad-smelling discharge, pain during sex, vomiting, or feel very weak. If you use a tampon or cup and get a sudden high fever with a rash, remove it and go to a health facility immediately.

title: Pain when peeing during a period
answer: Burning or pain when you pee, needing to pee very often, or cloudy or smelly urine can be signs of a urine infection. These can happen at any time, including during your period. Drinking plenty of water and changing pads often help, but an infection needs a check and treatment. Visit a health center. Go urgently if you have fever, back pain on one side, or vomiting.

title: What counts as a heavy period
answer: Your period may be heavy if you need to change a pad every one to two hours for several hours in a row, need to use two pads at once, bleed through at night often, pass clots bigger than a large coin, or bleed for more than seven days. Heavy periods can make you tired, weak or short of breath. If this sounds like you, see a health worker. If you soak a pad every hour and feel dizzy or faint, go to a health facility now.

title: Causes of heavy periods
answer: In the first years after periods start, heavy bleeding is often due to hormones that are not yet balanced, because ovulation does not happen every month. Other possible causes include bleeding disorders, thyroid problems, some contraceptive methods, growths in the womb such as fibroids or polyps, and infections. Only a health worker can find the cause. If your periods are heavy, visit your health center so you can be checked and helped.

title: Period lasting longer than seven days
answer: Most periods last between two and seven days. If your bleeding goes on for more than seven days, especially more than once, see a health worker. It can happen when hormones are not yet balanced, especially in the first years, but it can also cause low blood (anaemia) or be a sign of another problem. If you bleed heavily for a long time and feel weak, dizzy or short of breath, go to a health facility quickly.

title: Two periods in one month
answer: It is possible to have two periods in one calendar month and still be healthy. If your cycle is short, for example 21 to 24 days, one period may come at the start of the month and another at the end. In the first years, cycles also vary. But if bleeding comes every two weeks or less, happens often, or is heavy, see a health worker to check what is happening.

title: Very light periods
answer: Some people have light periods that need only a few pads, and this can be normal, especially in the first years or if light periods are usual for you. Periods can also become lighter because of stress, weight loss, intense exercise, illness or some contraceptive methods. If your period suddenly becomes much lighter than usual and stays that way, or you also have other changes, a health worker can check you. Pregnancy should also be considered if you have had sex.

title: A missed period when not pregnant
answer: Missing one period can happen for reasons other than pregnancy. Common causes include stress, exams, illness, travel, big changes in weight, not eating enough, very intense exercise, and, in the first years, hormones that are still settling. Some contraceptive methods can also stop periods. If you have had sex, a pregnancy test is the only way to rule out pregnancy. If you miss more than one period or are worried, see a health worker.

title: No period for three months or more
answer: If you used to have periods and they have stopped for three months or more, see a health worker. Possible causes include pregnancy, big weight loss or very low body weight, too much exercise, long-term stress, illness, hormone conditions such as PCOS or thyroid problems, and some contraceptive methods. The health worker may ask questions, check you and do simple tests. Getting checked early helps protect your health.

title: Period a few days late
answer: A period that is a few days late is very common and usually nothing to worry about. Cycle length can change a little each month, especially with stress, illness, travel or changes in sleep or eating. In the first years after periods begin, being late is even more common. If you have had sex, a pregnancy test can give you an answer. If you are late often or by a week or more, talk to a health worker.

title: Period coming early
answer: Your period may come a few days earlier than expected because of stress, illness, changes in weight, travel, intense exercise, or hormones that are still settling in the first years. Some contraceptive methods can also change bleeding. One early period is usually nothing to worry about. If your periods often come less than three weeks apart, or bleeding is very heavy, see a health worker.

title: Spotting between periods
answer: Spotting means light bleeding or brown marks between periods, needing only a liner or none. It can happen in the first years of periods, around ovulation, with some contraceptive methods, or from stress. But it can also be a sign of infection or another problem, especially if it happens often, after sex, or with pain, bad-smelling discharge or fever. If spotting keeps happening, see a health worker at your health center.

title: Light bleeding around ovulation
answer: A few people notice a small amount of pink or brown spotting around the middle of their cycle, at about the time of ovulation. It is caused by a short dip in hormones and usually lasts a day or two. It is generally harmless. If the bleeding is heavier, lasts longer, comes with pain or bad-smelling discharge, or happens after sex, see a health worker to be checked.

title: Spotting a few days before the period
answer: Many people see light brown or pink spotting a day or two before their period properly starts. This is often the first sign that the womb lining is beginning to shed and is usually normal. It often leads into the full flow. You can use a liner or a thin pad. If spotting before your period lasts many days, is getting longer each month, or comes with pain, see a health worker.

title: Period stops then starts again
answer: Sometimes a period seems to stop for a day and then starts again. This is quite common, especially in the first years. Flow can slow and then pick up as the lining sheds, and lying down or being very active can change how blood flows out. It is usually still the same period. If bleeding restarts many days later, is very heavy, or this keeps happening, see a health worker.

title: Being underweight and periods
answer: Your body needs enough energy from food to have regular periods. If you lose a lot of weight, are very thin, do not eat enough, or skip meals often, your periods may become irregular or stop. This is the body protecting itself. Eating regular, balanced meals usually helps periods return. If you are trying to lose weight, feel afraid of eating, or your periods have stopped, please talk to a health worker.

title: Weight gain and periods
answer: Gaining a lot of weight can change hormone levels and sometimes make periods irregular, less frequent or heavier. Some conditions, like PCOS, can cause both weight gain and irregular periods. Eating balanced meals and being active are good for your whole body, including your cycle. If your periods have become irregular and you have gained weight, see a health worker for advice and a check, rather than trying extreme diets.

title: Illness like malaria and periods
answer: Being sick, for example with malaria, a bad flu, typhoid or another illness with fever, can put stress on your body and delay or change your next period. Some medicines can also affect bleeding. Usually the cycle goes back to normal after you recover. Focus on getting treatment and resting. If your periods do not return to normal within a couple of months after you are well, see a health worker.

title: Too much exercise and missing periods
answer: Regular exercise is good for you and can ease cramps. But very intense training, such as long-distance running or many hours of sport every day, especially without eating enough, can make periods irregular or stop. This can also weaken bones over time. If you are an athlete and your periods have become irregular or stopped, eat enough to match your training and see a health worker.

title: Travel and changes in routine affecting periods
answer: Big changes in routine, like travelling, moving to boarding school, changing sleep times, or starting a new job, can affect the hormones that control your cycle. Your period may come earlier or later than usual, or be different for a month or two. This is common and usually settles once your body adjusts. Pack extra pads when travelling, just in case.

title: Alcohol, smoking and periods
answer: Drinking alcohol and smoking are harmful for young bodies, and they can also affect periods. They can make cramps, PMS, mood changes and irregular cycles worse, and alcohol can make you dehydrated and more tired during your period. The best choice for your health is to avoid them. If you find it hard to stop drinking or smoking, a health worker or youth corner can support you without judging.

title: Anaemia from heavy periods
answer: Anaemia means your blood has too few red blood cells or too little iron to carry oxygen well. Heavy or long periods are a common cause in girls and young women. Signs include feeling very tired or weak, pale skin, inner eyelids or nails, dizziness, headaches, fast heartbeat and shortness of breath. A simple blood test at a health center can check for it. If you have these signs, see a health worker; they can treat it and look at the cause.

title: Iron-rich foods in Rwanda
answer: Your body uses iron to make blood, and you lose some iron each period. Good local sources include beans, peas and lentils, dark green leaves like isombe (cassava leaves) and dodo (amaranth), small fish like sambaza, eggs, meat, and liver. Groundnuts and sorghum also help. Try to include some of these foods in your meals every day, especially during and after your period.

title: Helping your body absorb iron
answer: Your body takes in iron from beans and green leaves better when you eat them with foods rich in vitamin C, like oranges, passion fruit, tomatoes, guava, mango or pineapple. Drinking tea or coffee with meals can reduce how much iron you absorb, so have them between meals instead. Do not take iron tablets unless a health worker advises it, as too much iron can be harmful.

title: Drinking enough water during a period
answer: Drinking enough clean water during your period helps with bloating, headaches, tiredness and constipation. Some girls drink less so they do not have to visit the toilet at school, but this can make you feel worse. Carry a bottle of clean water, and include fruits and soups. Your urine should be pale yellow; dark urine means you need to drink more.

title: What endometriosis is
answer: Endometriosis is a long-term condition where tissue similar to the womb lining grows outside the womb, for example on the ovaries or in the pelvis. This tissue can cause pain, especially around periods. It can start in teenage years, but it often takes time to be recognised. It is not caused by anything you did, and it is not an infection. It can be managed, so if you have strong period pain, talk to a health worker.

title: Signs that may point to endometriosis
answer: Possible signs include period pain that is very strong and stops daily activities, pain that does not improve with pharmacy pain relief, pain in the pelvis at other times of the month, pain when passing stool or urine during periods, heavy periods, and feeling very tired. These signs can have other causes too, and only a health professional can tell. If you have them, see a health worker and describe your pain clearly; you deserve to be taken seriously.

title: What PCOS is
answer: PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome) is a common hormone condition where the ovaries do not release eggs regularly and the body may make more of the hormones usually found in higher amounts in males. It can affect periods, skin, hair and weight. The word cyst can sound scary, but these are small fluid sacs, not cancer. PCOS can be managed with healthy habits and treatment from a health professional.

title: Signs that may point to PCOS
answer: Possible signs of PCOS include periods that are very irregular, far apart (more than about 35 days), or missing for months; extra hair on the face, chest or belly; strong acne; thinning hair on the head; dark velvety skin patches on the neck or armpits; and weight gain. In the first years after periods begin, irregular cycles are common, so these signs can be hard to judge. If you notice several of them, see a health worker.

title: What fibroids are
answer: Fibroids are growths made of muscle in or on the wall of the womb. They are not cancer. They are common in adult women, especially from their thirties onward, and are rare in teenagers. Many cause no problems, but some can cause heavy or long periods, pain, a swollen belly or needing to pee often. If your mother or another woman has fibroids, a health professional can explain the treatment options for her.

title: Ovarian cysts
answer: An ovarian cyst is a small sac filled with fluid on an ovary. Many cysts form naturally during the cycle and go away on their own without causing problems. Some can cause pain on one side of the lower belly, bloating or changes in periods. Go to a health facility immediately if you have sudden, severe pain on one side, especially with vomiting, fever, or fainting, because a cyst can sometimes twist or burst.

title: Thyroid problems and periods
answer: The thyroid is a small gland in your neck that makes hormones controlling energy and growth. If it makes too much or too little hormone, periods can become irregular, very light, heavy or stop. Other signs may include big changes in weight, feeling very tired or restless, feeling too hot or too cold, or a swelling in the neck. A health worker can check this with simple tests and refer you if needed.

title: Bleeding easily and heavy periods
answer: Some people have a condition where their blood does not clot as well as it should. Signs include very heavy periods from the very first period, frequent or long nosebleeds, bleeding gums, bruising easily, or bleeding a long time after a small cut or tooth removal. These conditions often run in families. If this sounds like you, see a health worker; tests can find out what is going on and treatment can help.

title: Will irregular periods affect having children later
answer: Irregular periods are very common in the first few years and usually do not affect being able to have children later. When they continue into adulthood, they can sometimes be linked to conditions that affect ovulation, such as PCOS, and many of these can be treated. If you are worried, the best step is to see a health worker, who can check your health now. Worrying alone will not help, but getting information will.

title: Is it possible to stop or delay a period
answer: There is no safe home trick to stop or delay a period. Some hormonal family planning methods can change bleeding or make periods lighter, but they should only be used after talking with a health worker, who can explain options and side effects. Never take tablets from friends or unknown sellers to stop a period. If your period worries you before a big event, a health worker can give advice.

title: Does the HPV vaccine affect periods
answer: The HPV vaccine protects against the virus that causes most cervical cancer. Large studies around the world have shown that it does not harm periods or fertility and does not make girls unable to have children. Some girls may notice changes in their period around the time of vaccination, but these are usually due to normal cycle changes in the teenage years. If you have concerns, ask a health worker.

title: Is having periods a sign of good health
answer: Regular periods are one sign that your body is growing and your hormones are working. Health workers sometimes call the cycle a vital sign because changes can tell them something about your health, such as stress, low weight, anaemia or a hormone problem. Noticing your pattern helps you spot changes early. Having irregular periods at times does not mean you are sick, but long changes are worth checking.

title: Can period products cause infertility
answer: No. Pads, cloth pads, tampons, menstrual cups and period underwear do not cause infertility or damage your womb when used and cleaned properly. They only collect blood. What matters is hygiene: change products regularly, keep reusable ones clean and dry, and follow time limits for tampons and cups. If you notice pain, itching, or a bad smell, see a nurse, but using these products will not stop you having children.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What happens at a health center visit for period problems
answer: When you visit a health center about your period, a nurse or doctor will ask questions: when your periods started, how often they come, how long they last, how heavy they are, and about pain. Writing down your period dates first helps. They may check your weight and blood pressure, and sometimes do a blood or urine test. An internal exam is not always needed, and they should explain and ask your permission before any exam.

title: Feeling shy to talk to a male health worker about periods
answer: It is normal to feel shy, but male and female health workers are trained to talk about periods and the body, and they see these questions every day. Your period is a normal health topic, not something shameful. You can ask to bring a friend or relative with you, or ask if a female health worker is available. Being honest about your symptoms helps them help you.

title: Getting period help at a youth corner
answer: Many health centers in Rwanda have youth corners or youth-friendly services where young people can ask questions privately and without judgment. You can go there to talk about period pain, irregular or heavy periods, discharge, or how to manage your period. Staff and peer educators can give information and refer you to a nurse if needed. Ask at your nearest health center whether they have a youth corner.

title: Calling 114 about period worries
answer: You can call 114, the free Rwanda Biomedical Centre health line, to ask questions about your period, such as pain, heavy bleeding, missed periods or discharge. It is free, and you do not have to give your name if you do not want to. They can give you information and tell you where to get care. In an emergency, like fainting or very heavy bleeding, call 912 or 112, or go straight to a health facility.

title: Talking to your parent about periods
answer: Talking to your mother or another parent about periods can feel awkward, but most parents want to help. Choose a calm, private moment, for example while walking or cooking together. You can start simply: I want to ask you something about periods, or My period started and I need pads. If talking is hard, you could write a note. If a parent is not available, an aunt, older sister, teacher or nurse can help.

title: Talking to a father or guardian about periods
answer: If you live with your father, a grandfather or another guardian, you can still ask for help with periods. Many fathers and guardians want to support their daughters but may not know what to say. Be simple and clear: I have my period and I need pads, or I need money for period supplies. You can also ask a trusted woman, such as an aunt, neighbour, teacher or community health worker, to help or to talk with your guardian.

title: Telling a teacher or school matron about your period
answer: Teachers, the school matron, school nurse or the person responsible for girls' health at school are there to help. You can quietly tell a female teacher or matron that you have your period and need a pad, need to use the washroom, or are in pain and need to rest. You do not have to explain in front of the class. Many schools keep spare pads or have a girls' room for this reason.

title: Feeling embarrassed to buy pads at a shop
answer: Buying pads is as normal as buying soap or toothpaste, and shopkeepers sell them every day. Many people, including adults, have felt shy at first. You can bring a friend, write it on a shopping list, buy them with other items, or ask a trusted family member to buy them for you. Remember: about half of all people menstruate at some time in their lives, so there is nothing to be ashamed of.

title: Keeping your period private at home
answer: Wanting privacy during your period is normal. Keep pads or cloth pads in a small bag or box that belongs to you. Wrap used disposable pads well before putting them in a bin. Dry cloth pads in the sun with a light cloth over them if you prefer. You can ask your family for a private time or place to wash. Your period is not shameful, but you can decide who knows about it.

title: Periods and girls with disabilities
answer: Girls with disabilities have periods just like other girls and have the same right to information, products, privacy and dignity. Some may need extra support, such as pads that are easier to put on, a seat or rail in the toilet, picture guides, or a trusted helper. Carers should explain each step, respect privacy and ask the girl what she prefers. A health worker can help find solutions that suit her needs.

title: Menstrual cup discoloration and smell
answer: Over time, a menstrual cup may become a bit stained or yellowed. This is normal and does not make it unsafe if you clean it properly. Rinsing it in cold water first, washing with mild soap and boiling it between periods helps. If your cup smells bad even after cleaning, boil it again and dry it in the open air. Replace the cup if it becomes sticky, cracked, torn, or the smell will not go.

title: Menstrual Hygiene Day
answer: Menstrual Hygiene Day is marked around the world on 28 May each year. The date was chosen because many periods last about five days and many cycles are about 28 days. The day raises awareness that periods are normal, breaks silence and shame, and calls for girls and women everywhere to have products, water, toilets, information and dignity. Schools and communities in Rwanda often hold activities on this day.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Is period blood dirty
answer: Period blood is not dirty, impure or dangerous. It is made of blood and womb lining and is as clean as blood from any other part of the body. It may smell when it meets air and bacteria outside the body, which is why we change pads and wash. A girl on her period is not unclean, and she can touch people, objects and food normally. Periods are a healthy part of life.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Swimming during a period
answer: Yes, you can swim during your period. Water pressure slows the flow while you are in the water, and swimming is healthy exercise that can even ease cramps. A pad will soak up water and will not work in the water, so many people use a tampon or menstrual cup for swimming. If you do not use these, you might choose to skip swimming on heavy days, and that is okay too. Swimming does not spread infections or harm the water.

title: Playing football and sports during a period
answer: You can play football, netball, volleyball, run and do any sport during your period. Exercise is safe and can reduce cramps and improve your mood. Wear a well-fitted pad with wings, a cup, or a tampon, close-fitting underwear or shorts under your sports clothes, and change your product before playing. Drink water. If you feel very tired, dizzy or have strong pain on a particular day, it is fine to rest.

title: Does exercise make bleeding heavier
answer: Exercise does not make your period heavier overall or cause you to lose more blood. Sometimes blood flows out a little faster while you move because your muscles push it out, which may make it feel heavier for a while, but the total amount stays the same. Changing your product before exercise and wearing comfortable, close-fitting clothes helps. If your bleeding is very heavy in general, see a health worker.

title: PE class during a period
answer: You can join physical education (PE) lessons during your period. It is healthy and may help with cramps. Change your pad before class and wear shorts or tights under your sports clothes if you are worried about leaks. If you have strong pain, dizziness or very heavy bleeding that day, you can quietly tell your teacher and ask to rest. You do not have to explain details in front of others.

title: Traditional dance during a period
answer: Dancing, including traditional Rwandan dance, is safe during your period. Movement can help relieve cramps and lift your mood. Use a product that you trust for active movement, such as a pad with wings, a cup or a tampon, and wear shorts or tights under your costume. Change before you perform. If cramps are strong or you feel dizzy, rest; otherwise there is no reason to stop dancing.

title: Farm work and carrying loads during a period
answer: You can do normal work like farming, fetching water or carrying things during your period. It will not harm your womb or make you bleed more overall. Wear a secure pad or cloth, change it regularly, drink water and take breaks. If you have strong cramps, heavy bleeding, or feel dizzy, it is fine to rest or ask someone to share the work. Talk to a health worker if pain stops you working every month.

title: Practical period planning on exam day
answer: If your period may come during exams, prepare: pack spare pads, underwear, a small bag for used products and water. Change your pad just before the exam starts, and use a bigger pad for long papers. Wear dark clothes if you feel more comfortable. If you need to use the toilet during the exam, ask the invigilator quietly. Eat breakfast and, if cramps are common for you, ask a health worker beforehand about safe pain relief.

title: Concentrating in class during a period
answer: Cramps, tiredness and worry about leaks can make it hard to focus. Changing your pad at break times, eating breakfast, drinking water and using warmth or pain relief before school can help. Sitting comfortably and taking deep breaths eases cramps. Knowing you have spare supplies reduces worry. If you often cannot concentrate because of period pain or heavy bleeding, tell a teacher or school nurse and see a health worker.

title: Managing periods at boarding school
answer: At boarding school, plan ahead: bring enough pads or cloth pads for the term, plus spare underwear and a bag for used products. Keep a small calendar of your dates. Learn where the bins, washing area and matron's room are. Many schools have a matron or nurse who can help with pads, pain or stains. Friends can support each other too. If you run out of supplies, tell the matron quickly rather than using unsafe materials.

title: Washing and drying pads at boarding school
answer: In boarding school, washing cloth pads can feel hard because of little privacy and water. Wash them in a basin with soap and cold water in the washing area, and dry them in a sunny place; a light cloth or peg bag over them gives privacy. Do not hide damp pads in your box or under the mattress. Ask the matron where girls can dry them. Some girls use disposables at school and reusables at home.

title: Missing school because of periods
answer: Some girls miss school during their period because of pain, no pads, fear of leaks, or no water or private toilet at school. Missing days can hurt your learning, and you deserve support. Plan supplies, use comfort measures for pain, and speak to a teacher, matron or school health worker. If pain or bleeding keeps you home every month, see a health worker. If you have no products, ask your school or health center about support.

title: Getting your first period at school
answer: If your first period starts at school, stay calm; this happens to many girls. Go to the toilet and use toilet paper or a clean cloth for now. Then quietly tell a female teacher, the matron, school nurse or a trusted friend, who can give you a pad and help you. If your clothes are stained, tie a sweater around your waist. When you get home, tell a parent or trusted adult so they can help you get supplies.

title: School toilets with no water
answer: If your school toilets have no water, carry a small bottle of water, a piece of soap or sanitiser, and some tissue in your period kit. Use them to wash your hands and clean up when you change. Wrap used pads and put them in a bin or carry them in a bag. You can ask your school club, teachers or parents' committee to help improve water and bins for girls; that is a fair request.

title: Being teased at school about periods
answer: Being teased about your period can hurt, but you have done nothing wrong. Periods are normal and healthy. You can calmly say it is a normal body thing, walk away, or stay with friends who support you. Tell a teacher, matron or school counsellor if teasing continues; schools should stop bullying. Remember, those who tease often do not understand periods. You deserve respect.

title: How pregnancy happens step by step
answer: Pregnancy starts when a sperm from a male joins an egg from a female. During vaginal sex, sperm come out of the penis into the vagina. They swim through the cervix and womb into the fallopian tubes. If an egg has been released that month, one sperm can join it. This is called fertilisation. The joined cell moves to the womb and attaches to its lining. When it attaches and keeps growing, a pregnancy has begun.

title: What sperm is
answer: Sperm are tiny cells made in the testicles of a boy or man after puberty starts. They are so small you cannot see them without a microscope. Each sperm has a head, which carries half of the information needed to make a baby, and a tail that helps it swim. Sperm leave the body in a whitish fluid called semen when a male ejaculates. One drop of semen can contain very many sperm.

title: What an egg (ovum) is
answer: An egg, also called an ovum, is a tiny cell stored in the ovaries of a girl or woman. Girls are born with all their eggs already inside. After puberty, usually one egg becomes mature and is released each cycle. The egg carries half of the information needed to make a baby. It is very small, about the size of a dot. If it does not meet a sperm, it breaks down and leaves the body.

title: What fertilisation means
answer: Fertilisation is the moment when one sperm enters an egg and they join together. The sperm and egg each carry half of the information needed to make a person, so together they make one new cell. This cell starts dividing into more cells as it travels to the womb. Fertilisation alone does not mean pregnancy has fully started; the growing cells must also attach to the lining of the womb.

title: Where in the body fertilisation happens
answer: Fertilisation usually happens in one of the fallopian tubes. These are two thin tubes that connect the ovaries to the womb. After an egg is released from an ovary, it moves into a tube. If sperm are there, one may join with the egg. The fertilised egg then moves slowly down the tube into the womb over several days, where it can attach and grow.

title: What implantation is
answer: Implantation is when the fertilised egg, now a small ball of cells, attaches itself to the lining of the womb. This usually happens about 6 to 10 days after fertilisation. Once it attaches, the body starts making the pregnancy hormone that pregnancy tests detect. Some people notice light spotting around this time, but many notice nothing at all. Not every fertilised egg implants.

title: How long sperm can live inside the body
answer: Sperm can stay alive inside a woman's body for up to about 5 days. This is why sex a few days before ovulation can still lead to pregnancy: sperm can wait in the tubes until an egg is released. Outside the body, on skin or in the air, sperm dry out and die quickly. Because sperm live for days inside, it is hard to know exactly which sex led to a pregnancy.

title: How long an egg lives after ovulation
answer: After an egg is released from the ovary, it can only be fertilised for a short time, about 12 to 24 hours. If no sperm reaches it in that time, the egg breaks down and the body later sheds the womb lining as a period. Because sperm can live for several days, though, sex in the days before ovulation can still cause pregnancy.

title: When a boy becomes able to cause pregnancy
answer: A boy can make a girl pregnant once his body starts making sperm during puberty. This often begins somewhere between about 11 and 15 years old, but it differs for each boy. A sign is having wet dreams or ejaculating, but sperm may be present even before he notices this. So a young boy who has started puberty can cause a pregnancy, even the first time he has sex.

title: When ovulation happens in the cycle
answer: Ovulation usually happens about 14 days before the next period starts, not 14 days after the last one. In a 28-day cycle, that is around day 14, counting from the first day of bleeding. But cycles differ from person to person and month to month, especially in teenagers. Stress, illness and travel can move ovulation earlier or later, so you cannot know the exact day for sure.

title: Chance of pregnancy from one act of unprotected sex
answer: Pregnancy can happen after having unprotected vaginal sex just once. The chance depends on where you are in your cycle: it is highest in the few days before and on the day of ovulation, and lower at other times. But because young people's cycles are hard to predict, any single time carries a real chance. If it happened, emergency contraception or a pregnancy test at the right time can help; a health worker can advise you.

title: Pregnancy from sex with a virgin boy
answer: Yes, a girl can get pregnant from sex with a boy who has never had sex before. If he has started puberty, his semen and pre-cum can contain sperm from the very first time. Being a virgin does not make a boy's sperm weaker or harmless. The same is true for the girl: a first time can lead to pregnancy for either partner.

title: Ovulation when periods are irregular
answer: If your periods are irregular, ovulation can happen at different times each month, and you cannot predict it by counting days. This is common in the first few years after periods start. It means you could get pregnant on days you think are safe. You might also ovulate before a period you were not expecting. If you are having sex, talk to a health worker about reliable contraception.

title: Myth of completely safe days
