answer: There is no day in the cycle that is completely safe from pregnancy for everyone. Pregnancy is less likely on some days, but because ovulation can come early or late and sperm can live up to 5 days, sex on a day you thought was safe can still lead to pregnancy. This is especially true for teenagers, whose cycles are often irregular. Reliable contraception is much safer than counting days.

title: Only one sperm is needed
answer: Only one sperm is needed to fertilise an egg. Millions of sperm are released in each ejaculation, but most never reach the egg. Once one sperm enters the egg, the egg changes so that other sperm cannot get in. This is why even a small amount of semen near or in the vagina can lead to pregnancy.

title: How twins happen
answer: Twins can happen in two ways. Identical twins form when one fertilised egg splits into two, so the babies share the same genes. Non-identical twins form when two eggs are released at the same time and each is fertilised by a different sperm. Twins can run in some families, especially non-identical twins. A health worker can see twins on an ultrasound during pregnancy.

title: What decides if the baby is a boy or girl
answer: A baby's sex is decided at fertilisation by the sperm. Every egg carries an X chromosome. A sperm carries either an X or a Y. If an X sperm joins the egg, the baby will usually be a girl. If a Y sperm joins, the baby will usually be a boy. The woman's body does not decide this, so a woman should never be blamed for having girls or boys.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Pregnancy before the first period
answer: Yes, it is possible. A girl releases her first egg about two weeks before her first period. If she has vaginal sex, or sperm gets into the vagina, around that time, she could get pregnant even though she has never bled. Because you cannot know when your first egg will come, not having had a period yet does not protect you.

title: Pregnancy without orgasm
answer: Yes, a girl can get pregnant even if she does not have an orgasm or does not enjoy sex. Pregnancy depends on sperm reaching an egg, not on how the girl feels. A girl's pleasure or climax has nothing to do with whether she conceives. If sex happened without protection, the chance of pregnancy is there whether or not she enjoyed it.

title: How soon after sex pregnancy can begin
answer: Pregnancy does not start at the exact moment of sex. Sperm may reach the egg within minutes or hours, but if there is no egg yet, sperm can wait up to about 5 days. After fertilisation, it takes about 6 to 10 more days for the fertilised egg to attach to the womb. So pregnancy can begin from a few days up to about two weeks after sex.

title: How long sperm take to reach the egg
answer: After ejaculation in the vagina, some sperm can reach the fallopian tubes within minutes to an hour. Others swim more slowly or wait in the cervix and tubes for a few days. Getting up, washing or peeing after sex does not stop sperm that are already on their way. This is why emergency contraception, if used, should be taken as soon as possible.

title: Pregnancy from sex during your period
answer: Pregnancy from sex during a period is less likely, but it is possible. Sperm can live up to about 5 days inside the body. If your period is short or your cycle is short or irregular, you could ovulate soon after your period ends, and sperm from sex during your period could still be alive. So sex during a period is not a reliable way to avoid pregnancy.

title: Pregnancy from sex right after your period
answer: Yes, you can get pregnant from sex right after your period ends. Some people, especially those with short or irregular cycles, ovulate only a few days after bleeding stops. Sperm can live up to about 5 days and wait for the egg. So the days just after a period are not safe days. If you had unprotected sex, see a health worker if you are worried.

title: Pregnancy from sex just before your period
answer: Pregnancy from sex in the few days just before a period is less likely, because ovulation has usually already happened. But it is not impossible. Many young people cannot know exactly when their next period will come, and ovulation can happen later than expected. What you think is the week before your period might actually be your fertile time. So these days are not guaranteed safe.

title: Pregnancy from sex standing up
answer: Yes, you can get pregnant from sex standing up. The position does not matter. Sperm swim actively and do not depend on gravity, so they can reach the womb in any position. Standing, sitting, lying down or any other position all carry the same chance of pregnancy if there is unprotected vaginal sex.

title: Sperm in a swimming pool or bath water
answer: You cannot get pregnant from sperm in a swimming pool, lake or shared bath water. Sperm die quickly in water, especially water with chlorine, soap or heat, and they become very spread out. For pregnancy to happen, sperm must be put directly into or right at the vagina. Being in the same water as a boy, or after him, will not make you pregnant.

title: Having sex in water
answer: Yes, you can get pregnant from having sex in water, such as a lake, pool or bath. When the penis is in the vagina, sperm go straight into the body, just as they would on land. Water does not wash sperm away or kill them before they enter. Sex in water also carries the same risk of STIs.

title: Pregnancy when the hymen is not broken
answer: Yes, a girl can get pregnant even if her hymen seems not broken or she did not bleed. The hymen is a thin, stretchy tissue with an opening, and it is different in every girl. Sperm can pass through that opening. Bleeding or not bleeding during sex says nothing about whether pregnancy can happen, or about whether a girl has had sex before.

title: Pregnancy without penetration
answer: Pregnancy without the penis entering the vagina is unlikely but possible. If a boy ejaculates, or pre-cum leaks, on or very near the opening of the vagina, sperm can swim inside. Rubbing genitals together without clothes carries this small risk. If clothes are on and no semen touches the vulva, pregnancy cannot happen. If you are worried, a health worker can help you.

title: Pre-cum and pregnancy
answer: Pre-cum is a small amount of clear fluid that comes out of the penis when a boy is aroused, before he ejaculates. It can sometimes carry sperm. So pregnancy is possible even if the boy pulls out before he finishes or never ejaculates. The risk is smaller than with full ejaculation, but it is real. Condoms used from the start protect against this.

title: Sperm on clothes or bedsheets
answer: You cannot get pregnant from sperm on clothes, bedsheets, chairs or towels that later touch you. Sperm die quickly once semen dries or is exposed to air, and they cannot swim through fabric. For pregnancy, fresh semen needs to get into or right at the vagina. Sitting on a sheet or wearing clothes with old semen on them will not cause pregnancy.

title: Sperm on fingers touching the vagina
answer: Pregnancy from fingers is very unlikely. It could only happen if fresh, wet semen were on the fingers and was pushed right into the vagina immediately. Once semen has dried or been wiped off, the sperm are no longer able to cause pregnancy. If there was no semen on the fingers, there is no chance at all. A health worker can answer worries in private.

title: Kissing and pregnancy
answer: No, kissing cannot make you pregnant. This includes kissing on the lips, deep kissing with tongues, or kissing other parts of the body. Pregnancy only happens when sperm reach the vagina. Saliva does not contain sperm. You can enjoy kissing without any worry about pregnancy, though it is always your choice whether to kiss someone.

title: Oral sex and pregnancy
answer: You cannot get pregnant from oral sex, which means using the mouth on a partner's genitals. The mouth and stomach are not connected to the womb. Pregnancy only happens if sperm get into or right at the vagina. But oral sex can pass some sexually transmitted infections, so it is not free of all risks. Condoms or barriers can reduce that risk.

title: Swallowing sperm
answer: Swallowing semen cannot make you pregnant. Anything you swallow goes into your stomach, where it is digested like food. The digestive system is completely separate from the womb, so sperm in the mouth or stomach can never reach an egg. Semen can carry some infections, though, so oral sex is not completely risk free.

title: Anal sex and pregnancy
answer: Pregnancy cannot happen directly from anal sex, because the anus is not connected to the womb. However, semen can sometimes leak from the anus towards the vagina, which carries a small chance of pregnancy. Anal sex also has a higher risk of passing HIV and other STIs, so using a condom with lubricant is important for protection.

title: Pregnancy while breastfeeding
answer: Yes, you can get pregnant while breastfeeding. Breastfeeding only gives good protection if all three are true: the baby is less than 6 months old, the baby gets only breast milk day and night, and your period has not come back. If any of these changes, pregnancy is possible. A health worker can help you choose a family planning method that is safe while breastfeeding.

title: Pregnancy before periods return after giving birth
answer: Yes. After giving birth, you can release an egg before your first period comes back. This means you can become pregnant again without ever seeing a period. Ovulation can return within weeks if you are not fully breastfeeding. Getting pregnant very soon after a birth is hard on the body, so talk to a health worker about family planning before you start having sex again.

title: How soon pregnancy can happen after a miscarriage or abortion
answer: Fertility can return very quickly after a miscarriage or an abortion. You may release an egg as soon as about two weeks later, even before your next period. This means you can become pregnant again soon if you have unprotected sex. Health workers usually advise waiting at least 6 months before trying for another pregnancy, and can help you choose contraception right away.

title: Toilet seats and pregnancy
answer: You cannot get pregnant from a toilet seat, even if a boy or man used it before you. Sperm cannot survive long outside the body, and they cannot jump or travel from a seat into the vagina. Pregnancy only happens when sperm get directly into or right at the vagina, usually during sex.

title: Masturbating alone cannot cause pregnancy
answer: Touching your own body for pleasure, called masturbation, cannot make you pregnant. Pregnancy needs sperm from a male to reach an egg. If a girl touches herself alone, there is no sperm involved, so pregnancy is impossible. Masturbation is a private choice; it does not harm your body or your future ability to have children.

title: Hugging or sleeping in the same bed
answer: Hugging, cuddling, holding hands or sleeping next to a boy in the same bed cannot make you pregnant as long as there is no sexual contact where semen reaches the vagina. Pregnancy does not pass through the air, skin or clothes. If you are worried about something that happened, you can talk privately with a health worker or call 114.

title: Semen on the thighs or outside the vulva
answer: If a boy ejaculates on your thighs, belly or the outer part of the vulva, pregnancy is unlikely but possible if fresh semen gets to the opening of the vagina. Sperm can swim in wet semen. The further away from the vagina, the lower the risk; semen on the belly or legs that is wiped off is very low risk. If you are worried, speak with a health worker soon.

title: Dried semen and pregnancy
answer: Dried semen cannot cause pregnancy. Once semen dries on skin, clothes or sheets, the sperm in it die and cannot swim. Even if dried semen gets wet again, the sperm do not come back to life. Only fresh, wet semen that gets into or right at the vagina can lead to pregnancy.

title: Sharing towels and pregnancy
answer: You cannot get pregnant from using a towel that a boy or man used before. Any semen on a towel spreads out, dries and the sperm die quickly. They cannot travel into the vagina from a towel. For good hygiene, it is still better to use your own towel, because sharing towels can pass some skin infections.

title: Wet dreams and pregnancy
answer: A wet dream is when a boy ejaculates while sleeping. It is a normal part of puberty. A boy's wet dream cannot make anyone pregnant unless his fresh semen gets into or right at a girl's vagina, which does not happen when he is simply asleep in his own bed. A wet dream does mean his body is making sperm and could cause pregnancy during sex.

title: Sex through underwear or clothes
answer: If both of you have clothes or underwear on, and the penis does not touch the vulva directly, pregnancy is extremely unlikely. Sperm cannot swim through fabric. A small risk exists only if clothes are moved aside or fresh semen soaks through and touches the vaginal opening. Dry rubbing with clothes still on does not normally lead to pregnancy.

title: Quick or short sex and pregnancy
answer: Even very quick sex can lead to pregnancy. How long sex lasts does not matter; what matters is whether sperm get into the vagina. Pre-cum can contain sperm even in the first seconds, and a boy can ejaculate very quickly. So sex that lasted only a minute, or stopped early, can still cause pregnancy.

title: Girl on top position myth
answer: Some people believe a girl cannot get pregnant if she is on top during sex, because sperm will flow out. This is not true. Sperm swim strongly and quickly towards the womb, whatever the position. No sex position prevents pregnancy. Only correct use of contraception reduces the chance of pregnancy.

title: Jumping or moving after sex myth
answer: Jumping up and down, dancing, squatting or shaking after sex does not stop pregnancy. Sperm move quickly into the cervix and womb, where movement cannot push them out. Any semen that leaks out of the vagina afterwards does not mean all the sperm left. If you had unprotected sex, the chance of pregnancy is the same whatever you do with your body afterwards.

title: Drinks after sex do not prevent pregnancy
answer: Drinking soda, salt water, lemon juice, strong tea or any other drink after sex does not prevent pregnancy. What you drink goes to your stomach, not your womb, so it cannot reach sperm or an egg. Some mixtures can make you sick. If you had unprotected sex and want to prevent pregnancy, emergency contraception from a health center or pharmacy works best when taken soon.

title: Hot bath after sex myth
answer: Taking a hot bath, sitting in hot water or using steam after sex does not prevent pregnancy. Sperm that have entered the cervix and womb are inside your body, where outside heat cannot reach them. Very hot water can also burn your skin. A hot bath is not a form of contraception.

title: Myth: too young or too small to get pregnant
answer: A girl's height, weight or age does not stop pregnancy. Once a girl has started releasing eggs, which can be even before her first period, she can get pregnant, even if she looks small or young. Pregnancy in a young body has higher health risks. If a young girl is having sex, especially with an adult, she should get help from a trusted adult or call 116.

title: Holding breath or sneezing myth
answer: Holding your breath, coughing or sneezing during or after sex does not prevent pregnancy. These actions do not affect sperm inside the vagina or womb. There is no breathing trick or body trick that stops pregnancy. Only contraception, used correctly, lowers the chance of pregnancy.

title: Herbs or traditional medicine to prevent pregnancy
answer: There is no proof that herbs, roots or traditional mixtures prevent pregnancy. Some can make you very sick or harm your liver or kidneys. Relying on them can lead to an unplanned pregnancy. Safe and effective contraception and emergency contraception are available at health centers. A nurse or community health worker can explain your choices privately.

title: Myth: having sex often prevents pregnancy
answer: Having sex often does not make a girl unable to get pregnant. Some believe the body gets used to sperm or that frequent sex weakens sperm. This is false. Every time unprotected vaginal sex happens, there is a chance of pregnancy, especially around ovulation. Having sex more often actually increases the total chance of pregnancy over time.

title: Time of day myth
answer: The time of day you have sex does not change the chance of pregnancy. Morning, afternoon or night are the same. What matters is where you are in your cycle and whether sperm reach the vagina. Sperm can live up to about 5 days inside the body, so the hour of sex makes no real difference.

title: Circumcised boy myth
answer: Circumcision does not affect a boy's ability to cause pregnancy. A circumcised boy makes sperm in exactly the same way as an uncircumcised boy. Male circumcision lowers some risk of getting HIV for men, but it does not prevent pregnancy and does not replace condoms.

title: Body size myth: thin or big girls
answer: A girl's body size does not protect her from pregnancy. Thin girls and big girls can both get pregnant if they are releasing eggs. Very low or very high body weight can sometimes make periods irregular, but irregular periods do not mean you cannot conceive. You may still ovulate without knowing when.

title: Exercise or sport after sex myth
answer: Running, playing football or doing exercise after sex does not prevent pregnancy. Sperm that have entered the cervix and womb are protected inside your body, and movement cannot shake them out. Exercise is healthy, but it is not a form of contraception.

title: Can a boy get pregnant
answer: No. A boy's body does not have a womb or ovaries, so a boy cannot get pregnant. Pregnancy needs an egg and a womb where a baby can grow. Boys produce sperm, which can cause a pregnancy in a girl or woman. So boys share responsibility for preventing unplanned pregnancy.

title: Painkillers or antibiotics after sex myth
answer: Painkillers, antibiotics, malaria medicine or other ordinary medicines do not prevent pregnancy. Taking them after sex will not stop sperm or an egg. Taking medicines you do not need can be harmful. If you had unprotected sex, the right option is emergency contraception from a health center or pharmacy, taken as soon as possible.

title: Pregnancy if the man is much older
answer: An older man can still make a girl pregnant. Men keep making sperm for most of their lives, even into old age. So a man's age does not protect against pregnancy. If you are under 18 and an adult man is having sex with you, this is against the law in Rwanda and is not your fault. You can get help at Isange One Stop Centre (3029), or call 116 or 3512.

title: Getting pregnant while already pregnant
answer: Once a pregnancy has started, the body normally stops releasing eggs, so getting pregnant again during a pregnancy is extremely rare. If you are pregnant, you do not need to worry about a second pregnancy. However, sex during pregnancy can still pass STIs and HIV, so condoms are still important.

title: Objects or sex toys with semen on them
answer: If fresh, wet semen is on a sex toy, finger or object and it is put into the vagina right away, there is a small chance of pregnancy. Once semen dries or is washed off, there is no risk. Sharing sex toys can also pass STIs, so wash them or cover them with a new condom for each person.

title: Can you feel the moment you get pregnant
answer: No, you cannot feel the moment of fertilisation or implantation. Some people say they just knew, but there is no reliable feeling. Early signs like a missed period, nausea or sore breasts usually appear a week or more later, and they can also have other causes. The only way to know is a pregnancy test at the right time.

title: No pregnancy without sperm contact
answer: If no sperm or semen touched your vagina or vulva, you cannot be pregnant. Pregnancy is not caused by thoughts, dreams, being alone with a boy, looking at sexual images or touching yourself. Feeling worried can sometimes cause symptoms like a late period or stomach upset, but these do not mean pregnancy. If worry is hard to manage, you can call 114.

title: Touching a boy's penis with your hand
answer: Touching a boy's penis with your hand cannot make you pregnant, even if he ejaculates on your hand. Pregnancy can only happen if fresh semen then gets into or right at your vagina. Wiping or washing your hands afterwards removes any risk. A hand job alone, with no semen near the vagina, carries no chance of pregnancy.

title: Sweat or saliva cannot cause pregnancy
answer: Sweat, saliva, tears and urine do not contain sperm, so they cannot cause pregnancy. Only semen and pre-cum from a male can carry sperm. Being sweaty together, sharing a cup or licking skin cannot make anyone pregnant.

title: Pregnancy when periods have stopped for a while
answer: If your periods have stopped for a few months, for example because of stress, weight loss, illness or heavy sport, you may still release an egg at any time. Often an egg is released before the period returns, so you can get pregnant without warning. Missing periods is not a safe sign that you cannot conceive. A health worker can check why your periods stopped.

title: Charms or rituals do not prevent pregnancy
answer: Charms, strings tied around the waist, rituals or special words cannot prevent pregnancy. Pregnancy is a physical process: sperm meet an egg. Only medical contraception, used correctly, reduces the chance. Your beliefs are your own, but for protection against pregnancy, talk to a health worker about methods that are proven to work.

title: Alcohol before sex does not prevent pregnancy
answer: Drinking alcohol, by the girl or the boy, does not prevent pregnancy. Alcohol does not kill sperm or stop eggs. In fact, alcohol makes it more likely that people forget or misuse condoms and make choices they regret. Remember that a person who is very drunk cannot give consent.

title: Stress does not stop pregnancy after sex
answer: Feeling worried, scared or not relaxed during sex does not stop you from getting pregnant. Stress can sometimes delay ovulation or a period, but you cannot count on it to prevent pregnancy. Many girls have become pregnant during stressful times. Only contraception reliably lowers the chance.

title: Being sick does not prevent pregnancy
answer: Having a cold, malaria or another illness does not stop you from getting pregnant if you have unprotected sex. Illness can sometimes make periods late or irregular, but ovulation may still happen. Some medicines you take when sick, like certain TB or HIV medicines, can affect hormonal contraception, so tell your health worker if you use family planning.

title: Semen leaking out after sex
answer: It is normal for some semen to leak out of the vagina after sex. This does not mean all the sperm left your body. Many sperm have already swum into the cervix and womb within minutes. So semen coming out afterwards does not lower the chance of pregnancy much.

title: Getting pregnant while having an STI
answer: Yes, you can get pregnant while you have a sexually transmitted infection. Having an STI does not protect against pregnancy. Some untreated STIs can be passed to the baby or cause problems in pregnancy, and over time can damage the tubes. If you have signs of an STI or had unprotected sex, get tested and treated at a health center.

title: Sex between two girls and pregnancy
answer: Two girls cannot make each other pregnant, because pregnancy needs sperm, which only males produce. Sexual touching between two girls carries no chance of pregnancy. It can still pass some infections, so the same advice about hygiene and STI care applies. If you have questions about your feelings or body, you can talk confidentially with a health worker.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Myth: pregnancy only happens if you want a baby
answer: Pregnancy does not depend on love, wanting a baby or the girl's intentions. Some people think a girl only conceives if she really wants to or is in love. This is not true. The body responds to sperm and eggs, not feelings. Any unprotected vaginal sex can lead to pregnancy, whether it was planned, wanted or not.

title: When to take a pregnancy test after sex
answer: A urine pregnancy test works best from the first day your period is late, or about 3 weeks after the sex you are worried about. Testing earlier may give a negative result even if you are pregnant, because the pregnancy hormone is still too low. If your test is negative but your period still does not come, test again a week later or visit a health center.

title: How to use and read a urine pregnancy test
answer: Read the instructions on the test first. Usually you collect some urine in a clean cup, or hold the tip in your urine stream, then wait the time shown, often a few minutes. One line (the control line) means negative. Two lines, even if the second is light, usually mean positive. If no control line appears, the test did not work; use a new one. A health worker can do the test with you.

title: Where to get a pregnancy test in Rwanda
answer: In Rwanda you can get a pregnancy test at a health center, and many health posts and youth corners can also help. Pharmacies sell urine pregnancy tests. A community health worker can tell you where to go near you. At a health center, a nurse can test you, explain the result and talk with you about next steps. You can also call 114 for free information.

title: Late period but negative pregnancy test
answer: A late period with a negative test can happen for several reasons. You may have tested too early, or used a lot of water before testing. Stress, illness, weight change, travel or some contraceptives can also delay periods, and teenage cycles are often irregular. Test again in about a week using morning urine. If your period has not come or you are worried, see a health worker.

title: Faint line on a pregnancy test
answer: A faint second line that appears within the time written in the instructions usually means the test is positive. It is often faint when the pregnancy is very early and the hormone level is still low. A line that only appears long after the reading time may not count. To be sure, test again in a few days with morning urine, or visit a health center to confirm.

title: Blood pregnancy test
answer: A blood pregnancy test measures the pregnancy hormone in your blood. It can find a pregnancy a little earlier than a urine test and can show how much hormone there is. It is done at a health facility by a health worker. Most of the time a urine test is enough, but a health worker may use a blood test if results are unclear or there are concerns about the pregnancy.

title: Options for an unplanned pregnancy
answer: If you are pregnant and did not plan it, you have choices, and you deserve support to make them. Options include continuing the pregnancy and raising the child, with help from family or others, or continuing the pregnancy and arranging adoption or care by relatives. In Rwanda the law allows ending a pregnancy only in certain cases decided with a doctor. A health worker can explain all options confidentially, without judging you.

title: What the law in Rwanda says about abortion
answer: In Rwanda, the law allows abortion only in certain situations, and it must be decided with and done by a doctor at a health facility. Ending a pregnancy outside these rules is illegal and often unsafe. If you are pregnant and worried, talk to a health worker at a health center as early as possible. They can explain your legal options in private and help you get safe care.

title: Dangers of unsafe abortion
answer: An unsafe abortion is one done by someone without training, in an unclean place, or by drinking or inserting harmful things. It can cause very heavy bleeding, severe infection, damage to the womb, being unable to have children later, and even death. Please do not try to end a pregnancy yourself or with an untrained person. Go to a health center, where a health worker can help you safely and confidentially.

title: Post-abortion care is your right
answer: If you have bleeding, pain, fever or bad-smelling discharge after a miscarriage or after something was done to end a pregnancy, go to a health facility immediately or call 912. This is called post-abortion care, and every woman and girl has the right to receive it, without being judged. Health workers are there to save your life and health. Waiting can be very dangerous.

title: Pregnancy after rape or abuse by an adult
answer: If you became pregnant after rape, or you are under 18 and an adult man made you pregnant, it is not your fault, and what happened is a crime in Rwanda. You deserve care and protection. Go to Isange One Stop Centre (3029) or a health facility, where you can get medical care, counselling and help with legal options. You can also call 116 (child helpline) or 3512.

title: How to tell your parents you are pregnant
answer: Telling your parents can feel very scary, but most families want to help once the first shock passes. Choose a calm moment and, if it helps, bring a trusted adult such as an aunt, teacher or health worker. You can start simply: 'I have something important to tell you and I need your help.' Give them time to react. If you fear violence or being sent away, call 116 first.

title: Responsibility of the boy or man in a pregnancy
answer: A pregnancy is made by two people, so the boy or man shares responsibility. This means being honest, supporting the girl's health and decisions, going with her to the health center if she wants, and helping to care for the child if the pregnancy continues. Both parents are responsible for supporting their child. Running away or blaming her is not fair. Talk to a trusted adult or health worker for advice.

title: Staying in or returning to school when pregnant in Rwanda
answer: Being pregnant does not have to end your education. In Rwanda, pregnant girls and young mothers are encouraged to continue their studies and to return to school after giving birth. Talk to your head teacher, school counsellor or a trusted teacher about your situation. Family members can help with childcare. If you are told to leave school, ask for help from local leaders or call 116.

title: Where pregnant teenagers can get support in Rwanda
answer: You do not have to face pregnancy alone. A health center can start antenatal care and offer counselling. Community health workers can visit you and link you to services. Youth corners offer friendly advice. Your sector social affairs office and local leaders may help with family problems. For emotional support call 114; if you are in danger at home call 116, 3512 or Isange One Stop Centre (3029).

title: Signs of a miscarriage
answer: A miscarriage is the loss of a pregnancy before the baby can survive, usually in the first months. Signs can include bleeding from the vagina, which may be light or heavy, cramping or pain in the lower belly or back, and passing clots or tissue. Some early pregnancy symptoms may suddenly stop. If you are pregnant and have bleeding or pain, go to a health facility. If bleeding is heavy or you feel faint, call 912.

title: Miscarriage is not your fault
answer: Most miscarriages happen because the pregnancy was not developing normally from the start, and nothing could have prevented them. They are not caused by normal work, exercise, sex, stress, or a small fall. It is normal to feel sad, angry, guilty or relieved afterwards. Your feelings are valid. Talk to someone you trust, or call 114. A health check after a miscarriage is also important.

title: Warning signs of ectopic pregnancy
answer: An ectopic pregnancy grows outside the womb, usually in a tube. It cannot continue and can be life-threatening. Warning signs, often in the first weeks, include strong pain on one side of the lower belly, bleeding or spotting, pain at the tip of the shoulder, dizziness or fainting. If you might be pregnant and have these signs, go to a health facility now or call 912 or 112.

title: Bleeding in early pregnancy
answer: Some light spotting can happen early in pregnancy, for example around the time the pregnancy attaches to the womb. But bleeding in pregnancy can also be a sign of a miscarriage or an ectopic pregnancy. So any bleeding while pregnant should be checked at a health center. Go immediately, or call 912, if bleeding is heavy, or comes with strong pain, fever or fainting.

title: Healthy timing and spacing of pregnancies
answer: For the health of mother and baby, it is best to wait until at least age 18 before a first pregnancy, when the body is more ready. After a birth, waiting at least 2 years before trying to get pregnant again is healthier. After a miscarriage or abortion, waiting at least 6 months is advised. A health worker can help you plan and choose contraception until you are ready.

title: What antenatal care is
answer: Antenatal care (ANC) is the regular health check-ups you get from a nurse, midwife or doctor while you are pregnant. At these visits the health worker checks your health and the baby's growth, offers tests, gives vaccines and supplements, and answers your questions. ANC also helps you plan where and how you will give birth. In Rwanda you can get antenatal care at your nearest health center. It is for every pregnant person, whatever your age or situation.

title: Why antenatal care matters
answer: Antenatal care helps you and your baby stay healthy. Health workers can find problems early, like high blood pressure, anaemia, infections or a baby that is not growing well, and treat them before they become dangerous. You get vaccines, supplements and advice on food, rest and danger signs. Mothers who attend antenatal care regularly are more likely to have a safe birth and a healthy baby. Even if you feel fine, the check-ups are still important.

title: When to start antenatal care
answer: Start antenatal care as early as possible, ideally in the first 12 weeks (first three months) of pregnancy. Go as soon as you think you are pregnant or have a positive test. Starting early lets the health worker confirm how far along you are, check your health, offer important tests and give supplements that help the baby's early development. If you are already further along, it is never too late. Go to your nearest health center now.

title: How many antenatal care contacts are recommended
answer: WHO recommends at least eight antenatal care contacts during pregnancy. The first should be in the first 12 weeks, then around 20 and 26 weeks, then more often near the end of pregnancy, at about 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks. Your health center may use its own schedule, so ask them when to come back. If you have a health problem, you may need extra visits. Write down each appointment date so you do not miss it.

title: What happens at the first antenatal visit
answer: At your first antenatal visit, the health worker will ask about your health, your last period and any past pregnancies. They will check your weight, height and blood pressure and may examine your belly. You will be offered blood and urine tests, including tests for HIV, syphilis and anaemia. You may get a tetanus vaccine and iron and folic acid. They will estimate your due date and explain danger signs. It is a good time to ask any question.

title: What happens at later antenatal visits
answer: At later antenatal visits, the health worker checks your blood pressure and weight, measures your belly to see if the baby is growing well, and listens to the baby's heartbeat. Near the end of pregnancy they check the baby's position. They may repeat some tests, continue your supplements and ask how you feel. They also help you make a birth plan and remind you of danger signs. Tell them about any pain, bleeding or worries.

title: Blood tests during antenatal care
answer: During antenatal care you will be offered blood tests that protect you and your baby. These usually check your blood level for anaemia, your blood group, and infections like HIV, syphilis and sometimes hepatitis B. Some infections can pass to the baby, but if they are found early, treatment can protect the baby. The tests are confidential, and the health worker should explain each one and the results to you. You can ask questions before agreeing.

title: Urine test in pregnancy
answer: At antenatal visits you may be asked for a small urine sample. Health workers use it to look for protein, which can be a sign of a serious blood pressure problem called pre-eclampsia, and for sugar or signs of a urine infection. Urine infections in pregnancy can be harmless to treat but risky if ignored. Giving a sample is simple and painless. If you have pain or burning when you pass urine, tell the nurse.

title: Blood pressure checks in pregnancy
answer: Your blood pressure is checked at every antenatal visit because high blood pressure in pregnancy can be dangerous for you and your baby. It often has no signs at first, so the check is the only way to catch it early. The test is quick: a cuff is put on your arm and squeezes for a moment. If your blood pressure is high, the health worker will explain what to do and may ask you to come back more often.

title: Preparing for an antenatal visit
answer: Before an antenatal visit, gather your antenatal booklet, your mutuelle card and any vaccination card you have. Write down questions or worries so you do not forget them, such as pains, discharge, sleep or food. Eat something before you go, as you may wait for a while, and bring water. You can bring your partner or a trusted person. Be honest with the health worker about your health, medicines and feelings; it helps them care for you.

title: Ultrasound scan in pregnancy
answer: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves to show a picture of the baby on a screen. It is safe and does not hurt. WHO recommends one scan before 24 weeks of pregnancy. It helps check how far along you are, the baby's growth, the placenta and whether there is more than one baby. Not every health center has a scanner, so you may be referred to a hospital. Ask your health worker when and where you can have it.

title: Tetanus vaccine in pregnancy
answer: Tetanus is a serious infection that can kill newborn babies, often through an unclean umbilical cord or an unsafe birth. A tetanus vaccine given during pregnancy protects both you and your baby. It is safe in pregnancy. How many injections you need depends on how many you have had before, so bring any vaccination card you have. Your health worker at antenatal care will tell you when to get each dose.

title: Iron and folic acid supplements in pregnancy
answer: Pregnant women are usually given iron and folic acid tablets at antenatal care. Iron helps prevent anaemia (weak blood), which can make you tired and make birth riskier. Folic acid helps the baby's brain and spine develop well. Take them exactly as your health worker explains and do not share them. They can sometimes cause stomach upset or dark stools; if this bothers you, tell the nurse rather than stopping on your own.

title: Anaemia in pregnancy
answer: Anaemia means your blood does not have enough healthy red cells to carry oxygen. It is common in pregnancy. Signs can include feeling very tired, weak, dizzy, short of breath, or having pale eyelids, palms or lips. Anaemia can make bleeding at birth more dangerous and affect the baby's growth. Health workers test for it at antenatal care. Eating iron-rich foods, taking supplements as advised and preventing malaria all help. If you notice these signs, see a health worker.

title: Sleeping under a mosquito net in pregnancy
answer: Malaria is more dangerous during pregnancy, so the best daily protection is to sleep under an insecticide-treated mosquito net every night, all year. Tuck the net in well and repair any holes. Also keep the area around your home free of standing water and close doors and windows in the evening. In Rwanda, pregnant women can often receive a treated net through antenatal care, so ask at your health center if you do not have one.

title: Why malaria is dangerous in pregnancy
answer: Malaria can be more severe during pregnancy. It can cause serious anaemia in the mother, and can lead to miscarriage, early birth, a small baby or stillbirth. Signs include fever, chills, headache and body pain. If you are pregnant and have a fever, go to the health center the same day to be tested; do not wait or treat yourself at home. Malaria in pregnancy needs medicine chosen by a health worker that is safe for the baby.

title: Deworming during pregnancy
answer: Intestinal worms can take nutrients from your body and add to anaemia. In places where worms are common, health workers may give a deworming medicine to pregnant women after the first three months of pregnancy, when it is considered safe. Do not take deworming medicine on your own in early pregnancy; ask at antenatal care. You can also prevent worms by washing hands with soap, wearing shoes, drinking safe water and washing fruit and vegetables.

title: Partner attending antenatal care
answer: Your partner is welcome and encouraged to come with you to antenatal care, especially the first visit. In Rwanda, couples are encouraged to attend together. The partner can be tested for HIV and other infections, learn about danger signs, help plan for the birth and better support you. If your partner cannot or will not come, you can still get full care on your own. Your care does not depend on bringing anyone.

title: Health insurance for pregnancy care
answer: In Rwanda, community-based health insurance (mutuelle de santé) helps cover care at public health centers and hospitals, including antenatal care, giving birth and postnatal care. Make sure your mutuelle is paid and up to date before your due date, and carry your card. If you are unsure whether you are covered or cannot afford it, talk to your community health worker, the health center or local leaders, or call 114 for information.

title: Going to antenatal care alone as a young person
answer: Yes, you can go to antenatal care even if you are young and even if you go alone. Health workers are there to care for you and your baby, not to judge you. You have a right to respectful, private care. Bringing a trusted adult, friend or partner can help you feel supported, but it is not required to be seen. If you feel unsure, a community health worker or a youth corner can help you get started.

title: Missing an antenatal appointment
answer: If you missed an antenatal appointment, do not worry or feel ashamed, just go back to the health center as soon as you can. Health workers would rather see you late than not at all. Tell them which visit you missed so they can catch up on tests or vaccines. If you have danger signs like bleeding, severe headache or fever, go immediately, without waiting for your next appointment.

title: Keeping your antenatal care booklet
answer: At antenatal care you usually receive a card or booklet where health workers write your test results, vaccines, blood pressure, the baby's growth and your due date. Keep it safe and dry, and bring it to every visit and when you go to give birth. It helps any health worker understand your pregnancy quickly, especially in an emergency. If you lose it, tell the health center so they can help replace the information.

title: Community health workers and pregnancy
answer: Community health workers (CHWs) in your village can support you during pregnancy. They can encourage you to start antenatal care early, remind you of appointments, teach you about danger signs, help you plan for birth and visit you and your baby after birth. They can also help you get to the health center in an emergency. If you do not know your CHW, ask a neighbour, your local leader or the health center.

title: Fear of being judged at antenatal care
answer: Many young people worry that nurses will judge or scold them for being pregnant. You have the right to respectful, confidential care, whatever your age or situation. Most health workers want to help you have a healthy pregnancy. Going to care is a brave and responsible choice for your baby. If you are treated badly, you can ask to see another health worker or the person in charge, or call 114. Please do not let fear keep you away.

title: Weight gain in pregnancy
answer: Gaining weight during pregnancy is normal and healthy. It comes from the growing baby, placenta, extra blood, fluid and some stored fat for breastfeeding. Most weight is gained in the second half of pregnancy. How much is right depends on your weight before pregnancy, so the health worker weighs you at each visit. Gaining too little or too much can both be a concern. Do not try to diet or lose weight while pregnant; ask your health worker for advice.

title: Taking medicines while pregnant
answer: Some medicines can harm a baby, especially in the first months of pregnancy. Before taking any medicine, including painkillers, pharmacy medicines or ones left over at home, ask a health worker or pharmacist and tell them you are pregnant. Do not stop medicine for a long-term illness without advice either, as that can also be risky. When you are sick, the best place to get safe treatment is the health center.

title: Traditional herbs during pregnancy
answer: Some people use traditional herbs or remedies during pregnancy, for example to make labour faster. Many herbs have not been tested for safety, and some can harm the baby, cause strong contractions or bleeding. It is safest not to take herbal mixtures while pregnant or in labour unless a health worker says it is safe. If family members pressure you, you can explain that the nurse asked you to check first.

title: Healthy eating in pregnancy
answer: A healthy pregnancy diet includes a variety of foods every day: staples like sweet potatoes, cassava, maize or rice; beans, peas, groundnuts, eggs, fish or meat for protein; dark green vegetables like dodo (amaranth) and cassava leaves; fruits; and milk if you can. Eat an extra small meal or snack each day. Use iodised salt, limit sugary drinks and very salty food, and drink clean water. Good food helps your baby grow and keeps you strong.

title: The eating for two myth
answer: You do not need to eat twice as much when pregnant. Your body needs only a little more food, roughly one extra small meal or healthy snack a day, especially in the second half of pregnancy. What matters more is eating a variety of nutritious foods. Eating far too much can lead to unhealthy weight gain, while eating too little can harm the baby's growth. Listen to your hunger and ask your health worker if you are unsure.

title: Iron-rich foods in pregnancy
answer: Iron helps your body make blood for you and your baby. Good sources of iron include beans, peas, lentils, dark green leafy vegetables like amaranth (dodo) and cassava leaves, eggs, liver, meat, fish and small dried fish (indagara). Eating fruits with vitamin C, like oranges, passion fruit or tomatoes, at the same meal helps your body absorb iron. Tea or coffee with meals can reduce iron absorption, so have them between meals instead.

title: Food safety in pregnancy
answer: During pregnancy your body is more sensitive to some food infections, which can harm the baby. Wash hands before cooking and eating, wash fruit and vegetables with clean water, cook meat, fish and eggs well until no pink or runny parts remain, and drink boiled or pasteurised milk. Avoid food left uncovered for a long time and drink safe water. These simple steps help prevent food poisoning and infections.

title: Food taboos in pregnancy
answer: In some families, pregnant women are told not to eat certain foods, like eggs, meat or some fruits, because of beliefs that they harm the baby or make birth difficult. Most of these beliefs are not true, and avoiding healthy foods can leave you and your baby without important nutrients. Eggs, meat, fish, milk and fruits are good in pregnancy if prepared safely. If you are unsure about a food, ask your health worker.

title: Food cravings in pregnancy
answer: Many pregnant women suddenly want certain foods, or dislike foods they used to enjoy. This is common and is linked to body changes in pregnancy. It is usually fine to enjoy foods you crave in reasonable amounts, as long as your overall diet stays varied and healthy. Try not to fill up on sugary drinks, sweets or very salty snacks. If you crave things that are not food, like soil or chalk, tell a health worker.

title: Eating soil or clay in pregnancy
answer: Some pregnant women feel a strong urge to eat soil, clay, chalk or other non-food things. This is called pica and may be linked to low iron (anaemia). Eating soil or clay can expose you to worms, germs and harmful substances, and can stop your body from absorbing nutrients. Try to avoid it and tell your health worker about the urge. They can check your blood and give advice or treatment.

title: Drinking enough water in pregnancy
answer: Your body needs more fluids in pregnancy for the extra blood and the fluid around the baby. Drink clean, safe water often through the day, more when it is hot or after activity. Boil or treat water if you are not sure it is safe. Enough fluids can help with constipation and tiredness. Your urine should be pale; dark urine can mean you need more water. Limit sugary sodas.

title: Tea and coffee in pregnancy
answer: Tea, coffee and some sodas and energy drinks contain caffeine. Large amounts of caffeine in pregnancy may affect the baby's growth, so it is wise to keep them to a small amount each day and avoid energy drinks. Drinking tea with meals can also reduce how much iron you absorb, so have it between meals. Water, milk and fresh fruit juice are good choices. Ask your health worker if you drink a lot of coffee or tea.

title: Eating well on a small budget in pregnancy
answer: You can eat well in pregnancy without expensive food. Beans, peas, groundnuts and small dried fish are cheap sources of protein and iron. Dark green leaves like amaranth and pumpkin or cassava leaves are nutritious and can be grown at home. Eggs, seasonal fruits, sweet potatoes and sorghum porridge are also good. If your family is struggling to get enough food, tell your community health worker or health center, as support programs may exist.

title: Iodised salt in pregnancy
answer: Iodine is important for the baby's brain development. A lack of iodine in pregnancy can harm the baby's growth and learning. The easiest way to get enough iodine is to use iodised salt in your cooking instead of non-iodised salt. You only need normal amounts; do not add a lot of extra salt. Store salt in a covered container away from heat and sunlight so it keeps its iodine.

title: Vegetarian diet in pregnancy
answer: If you do not eat meat or fish, you can still have a healthy pregnancy. Eat plenty of beans, peas, lentils, soybeans, groundnuts and other nuts for protein and iron. If you eat eggs and milk, they are excellent. Add dark green vegetables and fruits rich in vitamin C to help absorb iron. Take your iron and folic acid supplements as advised. Tell your health worker about your diet so they can check you have enough nutrients.

title: Milk and calcium in pregnancy
answer: Calcium helps build your baby's bones and teeth and helps protect you, including against some blood pressure problems. Good sources include milk, yoghurt (ikivuguto), small fish eaten with their bones like indagara, dark green leafy vegetables and beans. Drink milk that is boiled or pasteurised. If you cannot get milk, eat the other calcium foods. Your health worker may also advise a calcium supplement.

title: Exercise during pregnancy
answer: Being active during a healthy pregnancy is good for you. Gentle activity like walking, light housework, stretching or dancing can help with back pain, sleep, mood and constipation, and prepares your body for birth. Aim to be active a little most days. Avoid activities where you could fall or be hit in the belly, and stop and rest if you feel pain, dizziness, bleeding or are very short of breath. Ask your health worker what is safe for you.

title: Heavy work and carrying loads in pregnancy
answer: Many pregnant women in Rwanda farm, fetch water and carry loads. Light work is usually fine, but very heavy lifting, carrying heavy loads for a long time and work that makes you exhausted can strain your back and may be risky, especially later in pregnancy. Bend your knees when lifting, carry smaller amounts, take breaks and ask family to share heavy tasks. Stop and seek care if you get belly pain or bleeding.

title: Rest and sleep in pregnancy
answer: Your body works hard to grow a baby, so you need more rest than usual. Try to sleep enough at night and rest during the day if you can, even for a short time with your feet up. Feeling tired is common, especially in the first and last months. Ask family or friends to help with chores. If you feel extremely tired, weak or breathless all the time, tell a health worker, as it can be a sign of anaemia.

title: Sleeping position in late pregnancy
answer: In the last months of pregnancy, it is safest to sleep on your side, either left or right, rather than flat on your back. Lying on your back for a long time can press on large blood vessels and reduce blood flow to you and the baby. A pillow or folded cloth between your knees or behind your back can make side sleeping more comfortable. If you wake up on your back, just turn onto your side.

title: Taking care of yourself at school while pregnant
answer: If you are attending school while pregnant, small steps can help you stay well. Carry water and a healthy snack, eat regular meals, and use the toilet when you need to. Take short breaks to stand or stretch if you sit for long. Avoid heavy sports or lifting. Plan your antenatal visits and tell a trusted teacher or school nurse so they can support you. Know the danger signs and go to the health center if any appear.

title: Working while pregnant
answer: Most women can keep working during a healthy pregnancy. Take regular breaks, drink water, eat snacks and avoid standing or sitting for very long periods. Avoid heavy lifting, very long hours and contact with harmful chemicals, pesticides or smoke. If your work is very physical or makes you feel unwell, talk to your employer about lighter tasks. Ask your health worker if your type of work is safe for you and your baby.

title: Travelling during pregnancy
answer: Travel is usually fine during a healthy pregnancy. On long bus or car trips, stop or stand up to walk often, drink water and wear your seatbelt with the lap part below your belly. Carry your antenatal booklet. In the last weeks before your due date, avoid long trips far from the health facility where you plan to give birth. If you have had bleeding or other problems, ask your health worker before travelling.

title: Riding a motorbike taxi or bicycle in pregnancy
answer: Motorbike taxis and bicycles carry a risk of falling, and a fall or bump on rough roads could hurt you and the baby. If you must use a moto, wear a helmet, sit properly, ask the driver to go slowly and avoid very bumpy roads. As your belly grows and your balance changes, it is safer to walk short distances or use a car or bus. In labour or an emergency, call 912 for an ambulance if possible.

title: Personal hygiene in pregnancy
answer: Keeping clean helps prevent infections during pregnancy. Bathe daily with clean water and mild soap, and wash your genital area from front to back with plain water; do not wash inside the vagina or use strong soaps, sprays or herbs there. Wear clean, loose cotton underwear and change it daily. Wash your hands with soap after using the toilet and before eating or cooking. Tell a health worker about itching, smelly discharge or sores.

title: Danger signs in pregnancy
answer: Some signs mean you or your baby may be in danger and you need care right away. Go to a health facility now, or call 912 for an ambulance or 112, if you have: bleeding from the vagina, a severe headache or blurred vision, fits, high fever, severe belly pain, fast or difficult breathing, swelling of the face and hands, fluid leaking from the vagina, or the baby moving less or not at all. Do not wait to see if it gets better.

title: Is sex safe during pregnancy
answer: For most women with a healthy pregnancy, sex is safe throughout pregnancy. The baby is protected by the fluid around it, the strong muscles of the womb and a plug of mucus in the cervix, so sex cannot hurt the baby. As your belly grows, some positions may be more comfortable than others. You never have to have sex if you do not want to. Ask your health worker if your pregnancy has any problems.

title: When to avoid sex during pregnancy
answer: Your health worker may advise you not to have sex if you have bleeding from the vagina, your waters have broken or are leaking, you have been told the placenta is low, you have signs of early labour, or you have had problems like early births before. Also stop and seek care if sex causes pain or bleeding. If you or your partner may have a sexually transmitted infection, get tested and treated first.

title: Condoms during pregnancy
answer: You cannot get pregnant again while you are already pregnant, but condoms are still important. Sexually transmitted infections, including HIV, can harm you and your baby, and new infections during pregnancy can pass to the baby. If you are not sure of your partner's status, or either of you has other partners, use a condom every time. You and your partner can both get tested at antenatal care.

title: Changes in sexual desire during pregnancy
answer: It is normal for your interest in sex to change during pregnancy. Some women want sex less, especially with nausea or tiredness in the early months or discomfort near the end. Others want it more, often in the middle months. Your partner's feelings may change too. Talk openly and kindly with each other. Closeness can also mean cuddling, massage or simply spending time together. All these feelings are normal.

title: Partner pressuring you for sex in pregnancy
answer: Being pregnant does not mean you must have sex whenever your partner wants. You always have the right to say no, at any time, including in marriage or a relationship. If your partner forces, threatens or hurts you, that is violence and it is not your fault. You can get help from the health center, Isange One Stop Centre (3029), the GBV line 3512, or 112 in an emergency. Your safety and your baby's safety matter.

title: Nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy
answer: Feeling sick or vomiting, often called morning sickness, is very common in the first three months and can happen at any time of day. It usually improves after about 12 to 16 weeks. Eating small amounts often, starting the day with something dry like bread, avoiding strong smells and greasy food, and sipping water between meals can help. Ginger may also help some women. Rest when you can. Ask a health worker before taking any medicine.

title: Severe vomiting in pregnancy
answer: Some vomiting is normal in early pregnancy, but go to a health facility quickly if you cannot keep any food or drink down for a day, you pass very little or dark urine, you feel very weak or dizzy, you are losing weight, or you vomit blood. Severe vomiting can cause dehydration and needs treatment from a health worker. It is not your fault and it can be treated.

title: Heartburn in pregnancy
answer: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest or throat, common in pregnancy because hormones relax the stomach valve and the growing baby presses on the stomach. Eating smaller meals more often, avoiding spicy, fatty or fried foods, not lying down right after eating, and raising your head with an extra pillow at night can help. If it is severe or does not improve, see a health worker before taking any medicine.

title: Constipation in pregnancy
answer: Constipation, meaning hard or infrequent stools, is common in pregnancy because hormones slow the gut, and iron tablets can add to it. Drink plenty of clean water, eat high-fibre foods like beans, vegetables, fruits such as papaya and whole grains, and stay active by walking. Go to the toilet when you feel the urge. If it lasts or is very painful, or you see blood, talk to a health worker rather than buying laxatives.

title: Back pain in pregnancy
answer: Back pain is common, especially later in pregnancy, as your belly grows and hormones loosen your joints. It can help to stand and sit up straight, bend your knees when lifting, avoid heavy loads, wear flat shoes, sleep on your side with a pillow between your knees, and do gentle stretching or walking. A warm cloth or massage may ease it. If back pain comes in waves, is severe, or comes with bleeding or fever, go to a health facility.

title: Swollen feet in pregnancy
answer: Mild swelling of the feet and ankles is common in later pregnancy, especially at the end of the day or in hot weather. Resting with your feet raised, avoiding standing for long periods, lying on your side, walking gently and wearing comfortable shoes can help. However, swelling that comes on suddenly, or swelling of the face and hands, especially with headache or blurred vision, can be a danger sign. Go to a health facility immediately if this happens.

title: Tiredness in pregnancy
answer: Feeling very tired is common in pregnancy, especially in the first three months and the last weeks. Your body is working hard to grow the baby. Rest when you can, sleep enough, eat regular healthy meals, drink water and take your iron and folic acid as advised. Gentle activity can also boost energy. If you are exhausted all the time, breathless or pale, tell a health worker, as you may need a check for anaemia.

title: Passing urine often in pregnancy
answer: Needing to urinate more often is normal in early pregnancy because of hormones and more blood flow, and again in late pregnancy when the baby presses on your bladder. Do not drink less water to avoid it; instead, go to the toilet whenever you need. Leaning forward when you urinate can help empty your bladder. If it burns, hurts, smells bad or you see blood, see a health worker, as it could be an infection.

title: Baby moving less
answer: Most women start feeling the baby move between about 16 and 24 weeks. After that, you should feel your baby move every day. Each baby has its own pattern. If you notice your baby is moving less than usual, has changed its pattern, or has stopped moving, do not wait until the next day or your next appointment. Lie on your side and pay attention; if movements are still reduced, go to a health facility immediately to have the baby checked.

title: Feeling dizzy in pregnancy
answer: Feeling a little dizzy or light-headed can happen in pregnancy, especially when standing up quickly, being in a hot place, or going long without food. Get up slowly, eat small meals regularly, drink water and sit or lie on your side if you feel faint. Dizziness can also be linked to anaemia. If you faint, or dizziness comes with bleeding, belly pain, severe headache or blurred vision, go to a health facility immediately.

title: Breast changes in pregnancy
answer: During pregnancy your breasts prepare to make milk. They may feel tender, sore, heavy or bigger, the nipples and the dark area around them may get darker, and veins may show more. Later, a little yellowish fluid called colostrum may leak. These changes are normal. A comfortable, supportive bra or cloth can help. Tell a health worker if you notice a hard lump, redness, or pain with fever.

title: Vaginal discharge in pregnancy
answer: It is normal to have more vaginal discharge during pregnancy. Healthy discharge is thin, clear or white and has little smell. Wear clean cotton underwear and avoid washing inside the vagina. See a health worker if the discharge is yellow, green or grey, smells bad, is thick like curds, or comes with itching, burning or pain, as it may be an infection. A sudden gush or steady leak of watery fluid needs care immediately.

title: Signs that labour has started
answer: Signs that labour may be starting include: contractions (tightening of the belly with pain) that come regularly and get stronger, longer and closer together; a sticky pinkish or bloody mucus from the vagina, called a show; your waters breaking, which can be a gush or a trickle of fluid; and lower back pain that comes and goes. When contractions are regular, or your waters break, go to the health facility. If you see heavy bleeding or green or brown fluid, go immediately.

title: Mild headaches in pregnancy
answer: Mild headaches are common in early pregnancy, often linked to hormones, tiredness, hunger, not drinking enough or stress. Rest in a quiet place, drink water, eat regularly and try to relax. Ask a health worker before taking any painkiller. A headache that is severe, does not go away, or comes with blurred vision, swelling of the face or hands, or upper belly pain, especially after 20 weeks, is a danger sign; go to a health facility immediately.

title: Mild breathlessness in pregnancy
answer: Feeling a bit short of breath is common in pregnancy, especially later, because the growing baby pushes up under your lungs and your body needs more oxygen. Slow down, rest, sit up straight and take breaks when climbing hills or stairs. Sleeping propped up may help. Feeling very breathless can also be due to anaemia. If you suddenly struggle to breathe, have chest pain, or your lips look blue, go to a health facility immediately.

title: Trouble sleeping in pregnancy
answer: Many pregnant women find it hard to sleep, especially later on, because of a big belly, needing to urinate, heartburn, leg cramps, the baby moving, or worries. Try lying on your side with a pillow between your knees, eating dinner earlier, keeping a regular bedtime and resting during the day. Gentle activity in the day may help. Do not take sleeping medicines without a health worker's advice. If worries keep you awake, talk to someone you trust.

title: Mood swings in pregnancy
answer: During pregnancy, changing hormones, tiredness and worries about the future can make your moods change quickly. You may feel happy one moment and teary or irritable the next. This is common. Rest, eat well, stay active, and talk about your feelings with someone you trust. Sharing worries with your health worker also helps. If sadness or worry lasts for weeks or stops you from coping, ask for help.

title: Depression and anxiety during pregnancy
answer: Some women feel very sad, hopeless, worried or anxious for weeks during pregnancy. This is more than normal mood swings and can be depression or anxiety, which are common and treatable. It is not a weakness. If you lose interest in things, cannot sleep or eat, feel worthless or cannot cope, talk to a health worker at antenatal care or call 114. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, get help right away by calling 112 or going to the nearest health facility.

title: Why give birth at a health facility
answer: Giving birth at a health facility with a skilled birth attendant, such as a midwife, nurse or doctor, is the safest choice. Problems like heavy bleeding, a long or blocked labour, high blood pressure or a baby who cannot breathe can happen suddenly, even in healthy pregnancies. At a facility, health workers can act quickly, give treatment and refer you if needed. In Rwanda, mutuelle de santé helps cover birth at public facilities. Plan early how you will get there.

title: Practice contractions in pregnancy
answer: In the second half of pregnancy, you may feel your belly tighten and become hard for a short time, then relax. These are often practice contractions (Braxton Hicks). They are usually irregular, not very painful, and ease when you change position, rest or drink water. Real labour contractions get stronger, longer and closer together. If tightenings become regular or painful, especially before 37 weeks, or come with bleeding or fluid, go to the health facility.

title: Postnatal care and danger signs after birth
answer: After birth, you and your baby need check-ups. WHO recommends at least four postnatal checks: in the first 24 hours, around day 3, between days 7 and 14, and at six weeks. Go to a health facility now, or call 912, if you have heavy bleeding (soaking a pad in less than an hour), fever, smelly discharge, severe headache or blurred vision, fits, difficulty breathing, severe belly pain, or a painful swollen leg. Community health workers can also visit you at home.

title: Pain when urinating in pregnancy
answer: Burning or pain when you pass urine, needing to go urgently, cloudy or smelly urine, or blood in urine can be signs of a urine infection. These infections are more common in pregnancy and, if untreated, can spread to the kidneys and lead to early labour. Do not ignore them. Go to your health center to be checked and treated with medicine that is safe in pregnancy. Drink plenty of water.

title: Exclusive breastfeeding for six months
answer: WHO recommends giving your baby only breast milk for the first six months: no water, other milk, porridge, juice or food. Breast milk has everything your baby needs, including water, even in hot weather, and protects against diarrhoea and infections. Start breastfeeding within the first hour after birth and feed whenever the baby wants, day and night. After six months, add other healthy foods and keep breastfeeding up to two years or beyond. Medicines prescribed by a health worker are allowed.

title: Danger signs in a newborn
answer: Take your baby to a health facility immediately if the baby: is not feeding well or stops breastfeeding; has fits; breathes fast or with difficulty, or the chest pulls in; feels hot (fever) or too cold; moves only when touched or not at all; has yellow skin in the first day or yellow palms and soles; or has redness, pus or a bad smell around the cord. Newborns can get very sick quickly, so do not wait. Call 912 for an ambulance if needed.

title: Age puberty starts in girls
answer: Most girls start puberty somewhere between about 8 and 13 years old. The first sign is usually small breast buds, then hair under the arms and around the genitals, a growth spurt and later the first period. Every girl has her own timing, so starting earlier or later than your friends is usually normal. If you have questions about your own timing, a nurse at your health center can check and reassure you.

title: Age puberty starts in boys
answer: Most boys start puberty somewhere between about 9 and 14 years old, often a little later than girls. The first sign is usually the testicles and scrotum getting bigger. After that come pubic hair, a bigger penis, a growth spurt, a deeper voice and later facial hair. Every boy has his own timing. If you are unsure about yours, a nurse at the health center can check you privately.

title: Puberty starting very early
answer: If a girl shows breast growth or pubic hair before about age 8, or a boy shows genital growth, pubic hair or a deep voice before about age 9, this is called early puberty. Sometimes it is just the child's natural timing, but sometimes there is a medical cause that can be treated. Please take the child to a health center so a nurse or doctor can check. It is not the child's fault.

title: Puberty starting late
answer: Some young people start puberty later than others, and this is often normal, especially if parents were also late. But if a girl has no breast development by about 13, or a boy has no growth of the testicles by about 14, it is a good idea to see a health worker. They can check your growth and health and explain what is happening. Late puberty can often be helped.

title: Why friends develop at different times
answer: Friends of the same age can look very different during puberty. Your timing depends mostly on your genes, which come from your family, and also on things like food and general health. One friend may look grown up at 12 while another starts at 14. Both are normal. Your body is not in a race. It will develop at the pace that is right for you.

title: How long puberty lasts
answer: Puberty usually lasts several years, often about 4 to 5 years, but it can be shorter or longer. Changes come little by little, not all at once. For many girls it is mostly finished by around 15 to 17, and for many boys by around 16 to 18, though some boys keep growing and getting more facial hair into their early twenties.

title: What causes puberty to start
answer: Puberty starts when a part of your brain sends chemical messages, called hormones, to your body. In girls these messages tell the ovaries to make more estrogen. In boys they tell the testicles to make more testosterone. These hormones cause the changes you notice, like body hair, growth, breasts or a deeper voice. Nothing you do or eat switches it on. It happens naturally when your body is ready.

title: What hormones are
answer: Hormones are natural chemical messengers made in your body. They travel in your blood and tell different parts of your body what to do. During puberty, estrogen (mainly in girls) and testosterone (mainly in boys) increase. Both girls and boys have some of each. These hormones cause body changes and can also affect your feelings, energy and skin. Changing hormone levels are a normal part of growing up.

title: First sign of puberty in girls
answer: For most girls the first sign of puberty is breast budding: a small, firm bump under one or both nipples, which can feel a bit sore. Soon after, hair may start to grow around the genitals and under the arms. A growth spurt follows, and the first period usually comes about two years after breasts start growing. Some girls notice pubic hair first, which is also normal.

title: First sign of puberty in boys
answer: For most boys the first sign of puberty is that the testicles get bigger and the skin of the scrotum becomes thinner, a bit darker and hangs lower. Many boys do not notice this at first. Next, pubic hair starts to grow and the penis gets longer and wider. The growth spurt, voice change and facial hair usually come later.

title: Food and puberty timing
answer: Good food helps your body grow and develop well. Young people who do not get enough food over a long time may start puberty later and grow less. Children who carry a lot of extra body weight may start a little earlier. There is no special food that makes puberty come faster or slower. Eating a mix of beans, vegetables, fruit, grains, and milk, eggs, fish or meat when you can supports healthy growth.

title: Growing pains in the legs
answer: Many children and young teens get aching legs, often in the thighs, calves or behind the knees, especially in the evening or at night. These are often called growing pains. They usually come and go and leave no damage. Gentle stretching, rest and rubbing the legs can help. See a health worker if the pain is in a joint, is very strong, happens in only one leg, or comes with swelling, redness, fever or limping.

title: Growth spurt in girls
answer: Girls usually have their fastest growth in height early in puberty, often around ages 10 to 14, soon after breasts start growing. During this time you may grow several centimetres a year. Your hips also widen and body shape changes. After the first period, growth slows down, and most girls reach close to their adult height a couple of years after that.

title: Growth spurt in boys
answer: Boys usually have their growth spurt a bit later than girls, often around ages 12 to 16. During the spurt a boy can grow quickly in height, then his shoulders get broader and muscles get stronger. That is why girls are often taller than boys for a while at the start of secondary school. Most boys catch up and keep growing for longer.

title: When you stop growing taller
answer: Most girls reach close to their adult height around 15 or 16, a couple of years after their first period. Most boys keep growing until around 17 or 18, and some grow a little more after that. Your final height depends mostly on your family's genes, and also on good food, sleep and health during childhood and puberty.

title: Ways to increase height
answer: Your adult height is mostly decided by your genes. No pill, herb, special drink or stretching exercise has been shown to make you much taller, and some products sold for height can be harmful. What helps you reach your natural height is eating enough healthy food, sleeping well, being active and avoiding smoking and alcohol. If you are worried about your growth, a health worker can measure and check you.

title: Being short for your age
answer: Being shorter than friends is very common during puberty, especially if you start later. Many late starters catch up and keep growing after others have stopped. Height also runs in families. Being short does not make you less healthy or less valuable. If you are much shorter than others your age, or seem to have stopped growing, a health worker can check your growth and nutrition.

title: Being very tall for your age
answer: Some young people grow tall early and stand above everyone else. This is usually normal and often runs in families. Girls in particular may be taller than boys for a while because they start their growth spurt earlier. Being tall is nothing to be ashamed of. Stand up straight and be proud. If growth seems extremely fast or unusual, a health worker can check.

title: Clumsiness during a growth spurt
answer: During a growth spurt your hands, feet, arms and legs can grow before the rest of your body catches up. Your brain needs some time to get used to your new size, so you may feel clumsy, bump into things or drop things more. This is normal and gets better with time. Sport and regular activity can help your balance and coordination.

title: Feeling very hungry in puberty
answer: Your body uses a lot of energy to grow during puberty, so feeling hungry more often is normal. Try to fill up on healthy foods like beans, sweet potatoes, cassava, maize, fruit, vegetables, groundnuts, eggs and milk when you can. Eat regular meals and healthy snacks instead of lots of sweets, sugary drinks or fried snacks. If you are hungry because there is not enough food at home, tell a trusted adult or community health worker.

title: Healthy eating during puberty
answer: Your body needs good food to grow during puberty. Try to eat a mix every day: grains or starchy foods for energy, beans, peas, groundnuts, eggs, fish, milk or meat for building the body, and fruit and green vegetables for vitamins. Foods with iron, like beans and dark green leaves, are important, especially for girls. Drink clean water, and limit sugary drinks and very salty or fried snacks.

title: Sleep and tiredness in teenagers
answer: During puberty many young people feel tired and find it hard to wake up. Your body is growing, and your sleep pattern naturally shifts later. Teens need about 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night. Try to go to bed at a regular time and put phones away before sleep. If you feel very tired all the time even with enough sleep, see a health worker to check for problems like low iron.

title: Sport and exercise during puberty
