answer: Being active is great for your body and mind during puberty. Sport, dancing, walking, football or games help build strong bones and muscles, improve sleep and mood, and reduce stress. Aim for about an hour of activity most days. Girls and boys can both play sport during puberty, including during periods. Drink water, warm up and rest if something hurts.

title: How breasts develop
answer: Breasts develop slowly over several years, often from around age 8 to 13 until the late teens. First a small bud forms under the nipple. Then the breast and the darker area around the nipple, called the areola, get bigger. Breasts keep changing shape and size for a few years. Every girl's breasts grow at their own speed, and the final size and shape are different for everyone.

title: Sore or tender breast buds
answer: When breasts start to grow, it is common for them to feel sore, tender or itchy, and the bud under the nipple can hurt when touched or bumped. This is caused by normal growth and usually settles over time. Wearing a soft, comfortable top or bra and protecting your chest during sport can help. If there is redness, heat, pus or fever, see a health worker.

title: Lump under the nipple in a young girl
answer: A small, firm, coin-sized lump just under the nipple in a girl starting puberty is usually a breast bud, the first stage of breast growth. It can be on one side first and be tender. This is normal and not cancer. The other side often follows within months. If a lump is somewhere else in the breast, grows quickly, is red and hot, or you are worried, see a health worker.

title: Uneven breasts
answer: It is very common for one breast to grow faster or end up a little bigger than the other. Many adult women have breasts of slightly different sizes. While you are growing, the difference may be bigger, and it often becomes smaller over time. This is normal and healthy. A soft or padded bra can help if it bothers you. See a health worker if one breast suddenly changes shape or has a lump.

title: Large breasts and back pain
answer: Some girls develop large breasts, sometimes early. This is normal, but it can bring unwanted attention or cause back, neck or shoulder aches. A well-fitting, supportive bra with wide straps can help a lot, as can good posture and exercises that strengthen your back. Nobody has the right to touch or comment on your body. If the pain is strong, see a health worker for advice.

title: Flattening or binding breasts
answer: Some girls or families try to stop breasts growing by pressing, binding tightly, or using hot objects on the chest. This does not stop development and can cause pain, burns, infections, lumps and damage to the breast. It is harmful and should not be done. If someone is doing this to you, or you feel unsafe about your developing body, talk to a trusted adult, a nurse, or call 116 for free.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: When to start wearing a bra
answer: There is no fixed age to start wearing a bra. Some girls like one when their breasts start to grow, for comfort or privacy, and others wait. A bra is not needed for health, but it can make sport and walking more comfortable. Choose one that fits well: it should not dig in, leave marks or let the breasts spill out. A soft cotton crop top is a good first choice.

title: Hair around the nipples
answer: It is normal for a few dark hairs to grow around the nipples in both girls and boys. They often appear during puberty because of hormone changes. They are harmless. You can leave them, or carefully trim them with small clean scissors. Pulling them out can cause ingrown hairs or infection. If you also notice a lot of new hair on your face, chest or belly as a girl, see a health worker.

title: Inverted or flat nipples
answer: Some people have nipples that point inward or are flat instead of sticking out. If you have had them like this since your breasts started growing, it is usually a normal variation and many women with such nipples can still breastfeed. A nipple that was normal and suddenly turns inward, or has discharge, a lump or skin changes, should be checked by a health worker.

title: Fluid coming from the nipple
answer: Sometimes squeezing the nipple can bring out a little clear or milky fluid, especially when breasts are developing. This can happen in girls and boys and is often harmless. Try not to keep squeezing, as that can make it continue. See a health worker if fluid comes out on its own, is bloody, comes from one side only, or if you have a lump, pain or could be pregnant.

title: Breast lump in a teenage girl
answer: Breasts can feel lumpy during puberty because they are made of glands and tissue that are still growing. Most lumps in teenage girls are harmless, and breast cancer is very rare at this age. Still, if you find a new lump that does not go away after your next period, grows, is hard, or comes with skin or nipple changes, see a health worker so they can examine it.

title: Getting to know your breasts
answer: It is good to know how your breasts normally look and feel. This is called breast awareness. Now and then, look in a mirror and gently feel your breasts and armpits with flat fingers. Breasts can feel different at different times of your monthly cycle. If you notice a new lump, skin dimpling, nipple changes or discharge, see a health worker. Most changes are harmless, but it is good to check.

title: Breast growth in boys
answer: Many boys get a little breast swelling during puberty, on one or both sides. It is caused by normal hormone changes and is common. It can feel tender. In most boys it goes away on its own within months to about two years. It does not mean you are turning into a girl. If it is very large, keeps growing, or you are worried, see a health worker.

title: Painful lump under a boy's nipple
answer: A tender, firm lump under one or both nipples is common in boys during puberty. It is usually normal breast tissue growing because of hormones and is not cancer. It often gets softer and disappears with time. Avoid squeezing or pressing it. See a health worker if the lump is hard, not under the nipple, growing fast, very painful, or has fluid or blood coming out.

title: Do breasts keep growing after puberty
answer: Breasts usually finish most of their growth by the late teens, but they can keep changing a little after that. Breast size can change with weight gain or loss, during your monthly cycle, during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and with age. So it is normal if your breasts look a little different from year to year. Sudden changes in one breast only should be checked by a health worker.

title: When a boy's voice changes
answer: A boy's voice usually starts to get deeper sometime between about 12 and 15, but it can be earlier or later. This happens because testosterone makes the voice box and vocal cords grow longer and thicker. The change can take months to finish. Every boy's timing is different, so if your voice has not changed yet while your friends' have, give it time.

title: Voice cracking
answer: While your voice box is growing, your voice may suddenly jump from low to high or squeak, especially when you are excited or speaking loudly. This is called voice cracking and it is completely normal. Your brain and vocal cords are getting used to the new size. It usually settles within a few months as your new, deeper voice becomes steady. Try not to worry if people laugh; it happens to most boys.

title: Do girls' voices change
answer: Yes, girls' voices also change during puberty, but much less than boys'. A girl's voice box grows a little, so her voice may become slightly lower and fuller. Most people do not notice a big difference. Girls do not usually get the sudden cracking that many boys have. Every voice is different, and a deeper or higher voice in a girl is normal.

title: Adam's apple
answer: The Adam's apple is the bump at the front of the neck. It is the voice box, also called the larynx. During puberty, the voice box grows bigger, especially in boys, so the bump often becomes easier to see. Girls have one too, but it is usually smaller. Its size varies from person to person and does not show how manly someone is.

title: Pubic hair growth
answer: Pubic hair is the hair that grows around the genitals in both girls and boys during puberty. It starts as a few soft, straight hairs and slowly becomes thicker, darker and curlier, spreading over the area. This hair is normal and helps protect the skin from rubbing. The amount, colour and texture are different for everyone.

title: Armpit hair
answer: Hair under the arms usually starts to grow a little after pubic hair, in both girls and boys. It is a normal part of puberty. Armpit hair can hold sweat, so washing your armpits every day with soap and water helps control smell. Whether you keep it or remove it is your personal choice; it is not needed for health either way.

title: When a boy's beard starts
answer: Facial hair in boys usually comes after pubic and armpit hair. It often starts as soft hair on the upper lip, then on the chin and sides of the face. For many boys this starts around 14 to 17, and a full beard may not grow until the late teens or twenties. Some men never grow much facial hair, and that is normal too.

title: No beard yet
answer: Not having a beard or moustache yet is very common, even in the late teens. Facial hair depends on your genes and family, and some men only grow a little hair all their life. It does not mean you are less of a man or that your body is not working. There is no safe cream or medicine that makes a beard grow. Give your body time.

title: Does shaving make hair grow thicker
answer: No. Shaving does not make hair grow back thicker, darker or faster. When hair is cut at the skin it has a blunt tip, so the new stubble can feel rougher and look darker for a while, but the hair itself has not changed. Hair naturally gets thicker during puberty because of hormones, which is why people sometimes blame shaving.

title: How to shave your face safely
answer: Use your own clean razor and never share it. Wash your face with warm water first to soften the hair, then use soap or shaving foam. Shave gently in the direction the hair grows, without pressing hard. Rinse the razor often. Afterwards rinse with cool water and pat dry. Replace blunt blades, since they cause cuts and bumps. Electric clippers can be gentler for curly hair.

title: Should I remove pubic hair
answer: You do not need to remove pubic hair. It is normal and helps protect the skin of the genitals from rubbing and dirt. Removing it is not cleaner or healthier. If you choose to remove or trim it, that is your choice, but shaving can cause cuts, itching, bumps and infections. Keeping the area clean with water and mild soap on the outside is what matters most.

title: Trimming pubic hair safely
answer: If you want to make pubic hair shorter, trimming with clean small scissors or clippers is gentler than shaving. Use your own tools and do not share them. If you shave, wet the skin, use soap, shave slowly in the direction the hair grows and use a new or clean razor. Never use sharp blades you cannot control, and stop if the skin is cut, sore or infected.

title: Razor bumps and ingrown hairs
answer: Razor bumps are small, itchy or sore spots that appear after shaving, often when curly hair grows back into the skin. To reduce them, shave less often, use a clean sharp razor, shave in the direction the hair grows, or trim instead of shaving close. Do not pick or dig out the hairs. See a health worker if bumps become very painful, swollen, filled with pus, or keep coming back.

title: Sharing razors and blades
answer: Do not share razors, blades or clippers with anyone, even family or friends. Shaving can cause tiny cuts, and a shared blade can carry blood from one person to another, which can spread infections such as HIV or hepatitis B and C. Use your own razor, keep it clean and dry, and throw away old blades safely. The same applies to tools used for cutting or piercing the skin.

title: Hair on a girl's upper lip or face
answer: Many girls have some fine or darker hair on the upper lip, chin or cheeks. This is common and often runs in families. You can leave it, or trim, pluck or gently remove it if it bothers you. If a girl suddenly grows a lot of thick, dark hair on the face, chest or belly, especially with very irregular periods or bad acne, she should see a health worker to check her hormones.

title: Lots of body hair in girls
answer: Girls naturally grow hair on the legs, arms and around the genitals, and the amount varies a lot between families. This is usually normal. But if a girl grows a lot of thick, dark hair in places like the chest, back, belly or face, together with irregular periods, acne or rapid weight gain, it can be a sign of a hormone imbalance that can be treated. See a health worker to get checked.

title: Removing leg and arm hair
answer: Hair on your legs and arms is normal, and removing it is a personal choice, not a health need. If you want to remove it, you can shave with your own clean razor and soap, or trim it. Shave gently in the direction the hair grows to avoid cuts and bumps. Do not use harsh chemicals, fire, or sharp blades not made for shaving. Moisturise dry skin afterwards.

title: Hair removal creams and waxing
answer: Hair removal creams and waxing can work, but they can also burn, sting or irritate the skin. If you try a cream, test a small patch first, follow the instructions exactly, and never use it on the genitals, face or broken skin unless the product says it is safe there. Hot wax can burn, so ask an experienced adult to help. Stop if your skin turns red, painful or blistered.

title: Chest hair in boys
answer: Chest hair in boys usually comes late in puberty, often in the late teens or twenties, and sometimes later. Some men get a lot, some only a little, and some none at all. This depends mostly on your genes. Having or not having chest hair does not show how healthy or manly you are. There is no need to remove it unless you want to.

title: Plucking hairs with tweezers
answer: Plucking a few hairs with clean tweezers, like stray eyebrow hairs, is usually fine. Pull in the direction the hair grows and clean the area afterwards. Plucking can hurt and may cause redness, ingrown hairs or small infections, especially in areas with curly hair like the pubic area or armpits. Do not pluck hairs growing from moles, and do not share tweezers.

title: Oily hair and scalp
answer: During puberty the glands in your scalp make more oil, so your hair may look greasy faster or you may get dandruff. Washing your hair regularly with a mild shampoo or soap and rinsing well helps. Avoid putting heavy oils near your forehead, as they can cause pimples. If your scalp is very itchy, flaky, red or has sores, see a health worker.

title: Why acne happens in puberty
answer: Acne, or pimples, is very common during puberty. Hormones make the skin produce more oil. The oil, plus dead skin cells, can block tiny holes in the skin called pores. Germs that live on the skin can then cause red, swollen spots, blackheads or whiteheads. Acne often appears on the face, chest and back. It is not caused by being dirty and usually improves with age.

title: Caring for skin with acne
answer: Wash your face gently twice a day with mild soap and clean water, and after sweating. Do not scrub hard, as this irritates the skin. Avoid heavy oils, petroleum jelly or thick creams on the face, and keep hair oils off your forehead. Keep hands and phones away from your face. Be patient; changes take weeks. A health worker or pharmacist can suggest suitable treatments if acne bothers you.

title: Squeezing pimples
answer: It is best not to squeeze, pop or pick pimples. Squeezing can push germs deeper into the skin, making spots bigger and more painful, and can leave dark marks or scars. Let pimples heal on their own and wash your face gently. If a spot is very large, painful and deep, or keeps coming back in the same place, a health worker can help.

title: Acne myths
answer: Many beliefs about acne are not true. Acne is not caused by being dirty, by masturbation, by having or not having sex, or by thinking about sex. It is not contagious, so you cannot catch it from someone. Sun does not cure it. Acne is mainly caused by hormones and oil in puberty, and it often runs in families. Some people notice certain foods make it worse, but food is not the main cause.

title: Severe or painful acne
answer: If your acne is very painful, has deep lumps or cysts, leaves scars or dark marks, spreads widely, or makes you feel very sad or ashamed, it is worth getting help. Go to your health center. A health worker can examine your skin and, if needed, recommend treatment or refer you to a skin specialist. Do not use strong products or medicines from friends or the market without advice.

title: Pimples on the back and chest
answer: Acne can also appear on the back, chest and shoulders because these areas have many oil glands. Shower or wash after sport or sweating, wear clean, loose cotton clothes, and change sweaty shirts quickly. Use a mild soap and do not scrub hard. Avoid tight straps that rub. If spots are painful or leave scars, see a health worker for advice.

title: Oily skin
answer: Oily or shiny skin is common in puberty because hormones make oil glands more active. Wash your face gently with mild soap and water twice a day and after sport. Pat dry with a clean towel. Avoid putting thick oils or petroleum jelly on your face. Do not wash too often or scrub hard, because that can irritate the skin and make it produce even more oil.

title: Dark marks after pimples
answer: After a pimple heals, it can leave a dark spot, especially on darker skin. These marks usually fade slowly over months. You can help by not picking or squeezing pimples, washing gently, and protecting your face from strong sun with a hat. Avoid bleaching creams, as they can harm your skin. If marks or scars bother you a lot, a health worker can give advice.

title: Why stretch marks appear
answer: Stretch marks are lines on the skin that appear when the body grows quickly, as it often does in puberty. They are common on the hips, thighs, buttocks, breasts, back and arms, in both girls and boys. They may first look pink, purple or dark, and later fade. Stretch marks are harmless and very common. They do not mean you are unhealthy.

title: Can stretch marks go away
answer: Stretch marks usually fade over time, becoming lighter and less noticeable, but they often do not disappear completely. Creams and oils sold to remove them have little proven effect, though moisturising can keep skin soft. Most people have some stretch marks, and they are nothing to be ashamed of. If the marks are very wide, many, and appear with other changes, a health worker can check.

title: Darker skin on armpits, inner thighs or genitals
answer: It is normal for the skin of the genitals, nipples, armpits and inner thighs to get a bit darker during puberty because of hormones. This is not dirt and cannot be scrubbed away; scrubbing hard can damage the skin. If you notice thick, velvety dark skin on the back of the neck or in skin folds, see a health worker, as this can sometimes be linked to weight or blood sugar.

title: Itchy rash in the groin or between the thighs
answer: Warm, sweaty, rubbing skin between the thighs or in the groin can cause chafing or a fungal rash, which may be red, itchy and spread at the edges. Wash and dry the area well, wear clean loose cotton underwear and change out of sweaty clothes. Do not share towels. If the rash does not improve, spreads, has sores, or affects the genitals themselves, see a health worker.

title: Sweating more in puberty
answer: During puberty your sweat glands become more active, especially in the armpits, groin, hands and feet. So you sweat more, especially when hot, active or nervous. Sweat itself is mostly water and salt and helps cool your body. Drink plenty of water, wear light cotton clothes and wash daily. Sweating more is a normal sign that your body is growing up.

title: Why body odour starts
answer: Body odour, or a strong smell, often starts in puberty. New sweat glands in the armpits and groin make a sweat that has no smell at first, but germs on the skin break it down and cause the smell. This is normal and happens to everyone. It does not mean you are dirty. Washing daily and wearing clean clothes keeps it under control.

title: How to control body odour
answer: Wash your whole body every day with soap and water, especially armpits, groin and feet, and dry well. Wear clean underwear and clothes each day, and wash clothes often, especially after sport. Cotton clothes let skin breathe. Deodorant or antiperspirant can help if you want. If a strong smell continues despite good washing, see a health worker.

title: Using deodorant
answer: Deodorant reduces smell, and antiperspirant reduces sweating. Both are generally safe for teenagers to use on clean, dry armpits. Do not put them on broken or freshly shaved skin, as they can sting. Never spray them near your face or breathe them in, and never use them on your genitals. If a product causes a rash, stop using it. You do not have to use one; daily washing works well.

title: Smelly feet
answer: Feet have many sweat glands, and in puberty they often sweat more. Shoes trap the sweat, so germs grow and cause a smell. Wash your feet every day with soap, dry well between the toes, wear clean dry socks and change them daily. Let shoes air out and dry, and swap pairs if you can. If skin between the toes is itchy, cracked or peeling, see a health worker.

title: Very heavy sweating
answer: Some people sweat a lot more than others, for example dripping hands or soaked armpits even when not hot or active. This can be embarrassing but is usually harmless. Wear light cotton clothes, carry a small towel and wash daily. If sweating is so heavy it disturbs your daily life, happens at night, or comes with weight loss, fever or a fast heartbeat, see a health worker.

title: How often to change underwear
answer: Change your underwear every day, and more often if it gets wet from sweat or sport. Wash underwear with soap and water, rinse it well and dry it fully, ideally in the sun, before wearing it again. Cotton underwear is best because it lets the skin breathe. Do not share underwear with others. Clean, dry underwear helps prevent smell, itching and infections.

title: Bad breath and teeth care
answer: Bad breath often comes from food and germs left in the mouth. Brush your teeth twice a day, especially before bed, with fluoride toothpaste, and brush your tongue too. Drink water, eat fewer sugary snacks and drinks, and avoid smoking. If you still have bad breath, bleeding gums or tooth pain, see a health worker or dentist, as you may need a check-up.

title: What the vulva is
answer: The vulva is the outside part of a girl's genitals, the part you can see between the legs. It includes the mons pubis (the soft area where pubic hair grows), the outer and inner lips (labia), the clitoris, the opening of the urethra where urine comes out, and the opening of the vagina. Many people call all of this the vagina, but the vagina is actually inside.

title: Inner and outer labia
answer: The labia are the lips of the vulva. The outer labia are the larger, padded folds on the outside, which grow pubic hair in puberty. The inner labia are thinner folds of skin inside them, without hair, that surround the openings of the vagina and urethra. They protect these openings. The inner labia often get bigger and darker during puberty.

title: Labia of different sizes
answer: Labia come in many shapes, sizes and colours. It is very common for the inner lips to be longer than the outer lips, to hang out, or for one side to be longer than the other. They may be pink, brown or dark, smooth or wrinkly. All of this is normal. See a health worker only if they cause pain, swelling, sores or itching.

title: Labia stretching practice
answer: In some communities girls are told to pull and stretch their inner labia. This practice is not needed for health, hygiene, childbirth or a good relationship. Every vulva is normal as it is. You have the right to decide about your own body, and no one should force or pressure you. If stretching has caused pain, sores, swelling or infection, stop and see a health worker.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What the vagina is
answer: The vagina is a stretchy, muscular tube inside a girl's body. It connects the vulva on the outside to the uterus (womb) inside. Menstrual blood flows out through it, and it is where a baby comes out during birth. It makes a little fluid, called discharge, which keeps it clean and healthy. The vagina is separate from the hole where urine comes out.

title: Is my vagina too small
answer: Many girls worry their vagina looks too small, especially when they cannot see it or when using a tampon seems hard. The vagina is very stretchy and grows during puberty. Its walls usually rest touching each other and expand when needed. Feeling tense or nervous can make muscles tight. If you have pain, cannot insert anything at all, or have no period by 15, see a health worker.

title: What the clitoris is
answer: The clitoris is a small, sensitive part of the vulva, found at the top where the inner lips meet, under a small hood of skin. Only a small part is visible; the rest is inside the body. It has many nerve endings and is linked to sexual feelings and pleasure. Its size and how much it shows differ from girl to girl, and all are normal.

title: Vulva shape and colour differences
answer: Every vulva looks different, just like faces. The size of the lips and clitoris, the colour of the skin, and the amount of pubic hair all vary. The skin can be darker than the rest of your body. Pictures in media often do not show this variety. If your vulva looks different from someone else's, that does not mean something is wrong. See a health worker only for pain, sores, lumps or itching.

title: What the uterus is
answer: The uterus, also called the womb, is a hollow, muscular organ inside a girl's lower belly, shaped a bit like an upside-down pear. Each month during the menstrual cycle, its lining thickens. If there is no pregnancy, the lining comes out as a period. If a pregnancy happens, a baby grows inside the uterus. It is very small before puberty and grows as the body matures.

title: What the ovaries are
answer: The ovaries are two small organs, about the size of a large grape or almond, on each side of the uterus. They hold a girl's eggs from birth. During puberty they start making the hormones estrogen and progesterone, and they begin releasing an egg about once a month. This is part of the menstrual cycle that leads to periods.

title: What the fallopian tubes are
answer: The fallopian tubes are two thin tubes that connect the ovaries to the uterus. When an ovary releases an egg, the egg travels through a tube towards the uterus. If sperm meets the egg in the tube, fertilisation can happen. Infections like some STIs can damage the tubes, which is one reason to protect your reproductive health.

title: What the cervix is
answer: The cervix is the narrow, lower part of the uterus that opens into the top of the vagina. It has a very small opening that lets menstrual blood out. During childbirth it opens wide so the baby can pass. Rwanda offers the HPV vaccine to girls, which helps protect against cervical cancer later in life. Ask at your school or health center about it.

title: Girls' three openings
answer: Girls have three openings between the legs. At the front is the urethra, a tiny hole where urine comes out. Behind it is the vaginal opening, where menstrual blood and discharge come out. At the back is the anus, where stool comes out. Urine does not come out of the vagina. Knowing this helps with hygiene, like wiping from front to back.

title: White discharge before the first period
answer: Many girls notice a white or clear, slightly sticky fluid in their underwear several months before their first period. This is normal vaginal discharge caused by rising hormones. It keeps the vagina clean and healthy. It may change a little in amount through the month. See a health worker if it smells bad, is green, grey or like cottage cheese, or comes with itching, pain or sores.

title: Normal smell of the vulva
answer: A healthy vulva and vagina have a mild, natural smell, which can change slightly during the month or after sport. This is normal and does not need perfume or special washes. Daily washing of the outside with water and mild soap is enough. A strong fishy or bad smell, especially with unusual discharge, itching or pain, can be a sign of infection, so see a health worker.

title: How girls should wash the vulva
answer: Wash the outside of the vulva once or twice a day with clean water, and mild unscented soap if you like, gently separating the lips. Do not put soap or water inside the vagina; it cleans itself. Rinse well and pat dry with a clean towel. Wear clean cotton underwear. Avoid perfumed products, strong soaps, sprays and herbs on the genitals.

title: Itching around the vulva
answer: Itching around the vulva can come from sweat, tight or synthetic underwear, perfumed soap, shaving, or an infection. Wear clean, loose cotton underwear, wash the outside with plain water, dry well and avoid scented products. Do not scratch. If itching lasts more than a few days, or comes with unusual discharge, sores, swelling or pain, see a health worker for a check.

title: Looking at your own genitals
answer: It is okay and healthy to look at your own genitals, for example with a small mirror in private. Knowing what your body normally looks like helps you understand it and notice changes, like sores or lumps, that need a check. It is your body, and being curious about it is normal. Make sure your hands and mirror are clean.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Hips widening and curves in girls
answer: During puberty, a girl's hips usually get wider and her body stores more fat on the hips, thighs, buttocks and breasts. This is caused by estrogen and prepares the body for adulthood. Gaining some weight and getting curves is normal and healthy, not a sign of being fat. Body shapes differ a lot, and every shape is normal.

title: How girls' reproductive organs work together
answer: A girl's reproductive system includes the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and vagina. After puberty starts, the ovaries release an egg about once a month. The egg moves through a fallopian tube to the uterus, whose lining has thickened. If the egg is not fertilised, the lining comes out through the cervix and vagina as a period. This cycle repeats about monthly.

title: Parts of the penis
answer: The penis has a shaft (the long part) and a head called the glans at the end, which is very sensitive. Inside runs the urethra, a tube that carries urine and, after puberty, semen out of the body, but never at the same time. In uncircumcised boys, the head is covered by a fold of skin called the foreskin. The penis has spongy tissue that fills with blood during an erection.

title: What the foreskin is
answer: The foreskin is the fold of skin that covers and protects the head of the penis in boys who are not circumcised. In young boys it is often tight and cannot be pulled back, which is normal. It usually loosens gradually during childhood and puberty. When a boy is circumcised, the foreskin is removed. Never force the foreskin back.

title: What the testicles do
answer: The testicles, also called testes or balls, are two oval organs inside the scrotum. From puberty they make sperm and the hormone testosterone. Testosterone causes many boy changes, like a deeper voice, more body hair and muscles. Sperm leave the body in semen during ejaculation. The testicles are sensitive, so protect them during sport.

title: Why the scrotum hangs and changes
answer: The scrotum is the bag of skin that holds the testicles. It hangs outside the body because sperm grow best a little cooler than body temperature. When it is cold, the scrotum tightens and pulls the testicles closer to the body; when warm, it relaxes and hangs lower. In puberty it gets bigger, darker and may grow hair. All of this is normal.

title: One testicle hangs lower
answer: It is very common and normal for one testicle to hang lower than the other, often the left one. This helps them not press against each other when you walk or sit. It is not a sign of a problem. However, if a testicle suddenly moves higher, becomes painful, swollen or hard, go to a health facility straight away.

title: Only one or no testicle in the scrotum
answer: Sometimes a testicle does not move down into the scrotum before birth, or moves back up. If you can feel only one testicle, or none, in your scrotum, it is important to see a health worker. It is often treatable, and it is better to check early because an undescended testicle can affect fertility later. It is nothing to be ashamed of.

title: When the penis grows in puberty
answer: The penis usually starts growing longer and then wider a little after the testicles begin to grow, often from around ages 11 to 15. It keeps growing gradually for several years, often until about 16 to 18. Every boy's timing is different. If you are early in puberty, your penis has likely not finished growing yet.

title: Curved penis
answer: It is common for an erect penis to curve a little to the left, right, up or down. This is usually normal and does not affect urinating or sex. See a health worker if the bend is strong, gets worse over time, is painful, or you feel a hard lump in the shaft. Masturbation does not cause a curve.

title: Penis and scrotum shrinking in the cold
answer: When you are cold, swimming, scared or stressed, the penis and scrotum often shrink and pull closer to the body. This is the body's normal way of protecting and keeping them warm. It is temporary, and they return to their usual size when you warm up or relax. It does not mean your penis is getting smaller permanently.

title: How boys should wash the penis
answer: Wash your penis and scrotum every day with clean water and mild soap. If you are not circumcised, gently pull the foreskin back as far as it goes easily, rinse the head with water, then pull the foreskin back over the head. Never force it. Rinse off all soap and dry well. Wash the skin between the scrotum and thighs too, and wear clean cotton underwear.

title: White stuff under the foreskin
answer: A white or cream-coloured, cheesy substance under the foreskin is called smegma. It is made of dead skin cells and natural oils and is normal. If it builds up it can smell and cause irritation, so wash under the foreskin gently every day with water. If there is redness, pain, swelling, a discharge from the urethra or a bad smell that continues, see a health worker.

title: Tight foreskin
answer: In many young boys the foreskin cannot be pulled back, and this is normal. It usually loosens with time, often by the teen years. Never force it, as this can cause tears and scarring. If your foreskin is still very tight in your teens, makes urine spray or balloon, causes pain during erections, or keeps getting infected, see a health worker. There are simple treatments.

title: Foreskin stuck behind the head of the penis
answer: If the foreskin has been pulled back and will not go back over the head of the penis, and the head is swelling or hurting, this is an emergency. The swelling can cut off blood flow. Go to a health facility now, or call 112 or 912 for help. Do not wait for it to get better by itself. To prevent it, always slide the foreskin back over the head after washing, urinating or sex.

title: Red, sore head of the penis
answer: Redness, soreness, itching or swelling of the head of the penis or under the foreskin can be caused by not washing well, strong soaps, or an infection. Wash gently with plain water every day, dry well and avoid perfumed products. If it does not get better in a few days, or there is pus, a bad smell, sores, pain when peeing or discharge, see a health worker. Do not use creams from friends.

title: Small bumps on the penis
answer: Many boys and men have tiny, painless, skin-coloured or white bumps in rows around the rim of the penis head, or small pale spots on the shaft or scrotum. These are often normal skin features and are not infections. Do not pick or try to remove them. But because some infections also cause bumps, if you are unsure, or bumps are new, painful, growing, or you have had sex, see a health worker.

title: Lumpy veins in the scrotum
answer: Some boys notice soft, lumpy veins above a testicle, often on the left, that feel like a bag of worms and are more visible when standing. These are swollen veins called a varicocele. They are common and often harmless. See a health worker if they ache, if that testicle seems smaller, or if you are worried. They can check and advise whether treatment is needed.

title: Tight underwear and the testicles
answer: The testicles work best when slightly cooler than the body. Very tight or hot underwear worn all the time may make them too warm and uncomfortable, and can cause sweating and rashes. Loose, clean cotton underwear is a good everyday choice. Supportive underwear is useful during sport. Underwear choice is not a cause of serious problems, so do not worry if you sometimes wear tight pants.

title: Urine and semen use the same tube
answer: In boys, both urine and semen leave the body through the same tube, the urethra, which runs through the penis. But they never come out at the same time. When the penis is erect, a small muscle closes the way from the bladder, so urine cannot mix with semen. That is why it is hard to pee with an erection. Waiting a few minutes helps.

title: How an erection happens
answer: An erection happens when the spongy tissue inside the penis fills with blood, making it bigger, harder and stand away from the body. It can be caused by sexual thoughts or touch, but also by nothing at all, such as during sleep or when nervous. There is no bone in the penis. After a while, or after ejaculation, blood flows back out and the penis becomes soft again.

title: Handling an erection in public
answer: Unexpected erections at school or in public are very common during puberty and usually go away within a few minutes. Most people do not notice. To feel more comfortable, you can sit down, hold a bag or book in front of you, untuck your shirt, or think about something else, like counting backwards. Wearing fitted underwear can help. It is not something to be ashamed of.

title: Erections before puberty
answer: Baby boys and young boys can have erections too. This is a normal body reflex, for example when the bladder is full, when touched during washing, or for no reason. It does not mean the child is thinking about sex. Parents do not need to worry or punish the child. Explain simply that the body does this sometimes and teach that private parts are private.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What semen is
answer: Semen is the whitish, sticky fluid that comes out of the penis when a male ejaculates. It contains millions of sperm from the testicles, mixed with fluid from glands such as the prostate, which helps the sperm move and stay alive. A boy can start producing semen during puberty. Semen can cause pregnancy and can carry infections like HIV.

title: How sperm travel out of the body
answer: Sperm are made in the testicles and stored in a coiled tube at the back of each testicle. When a male ejaculates, sperm move up through tubes called the vas deferens, mix with fluids from glands to form semen, and then leave through the urethra in the penis. The whole journey happens in seconds during ejaculation.

title: First ejaculation
answer: A boy's first ejaculation usually happens around ages 12 to 15, sometimes earlier or later. It may happen during sleep as a wet dream, during masturbation, or without a clear reason. The first semen may be clear or watery and small in amount. This is a normal sign that the body has started making sperm. It means a boy can now cause a pregnancy.

title: Can sperm run out
answer: No. From puberty, the testicles make new sperm every day, millions of them, for the rest of a man's life. Ejaculating often does not use up your supply or affect your ability to have children later. If a man ejaculates many times in a short time, there may be less semen for a while, but the body quickly makes more.

title: Is holding in semen harmful
answer: No. Not ejaculating does not harm your body. Sperm that are not released are simply broken down and absorbed by the body, and sometimes semen comes out naturally in a wet dream. You do not need sex or masturbation to stay healthy. Choosing not to have sex is safe and healthy. Anyone who says you need sex to avoid illness is wrong.

title: Never having a wet dream
answer: Not every boy has wet dreams. Some have many, some have only a few, and some never have them at all. All of these are normal and do not mean anything is wrong with your body or your fertility. Wet dreams may also happen less often if you ejaculate in other ways. If you have no other signs of puberty by around 14, see a health worker.

title: How often wet dreams happen
answer: How often wet dreams happen is different for everyone. Some boys have them several times a month, others only now and then, and they often become less frequent as boys get older or start ejaculating in other ways. There is no number that is too many or too few. Having many wet dreams does not cause weakness or illness.

title: Cleaning up after a wet dream
answer: If you wake up after a wet dream, simply wipe yourself with a cloth or tissue, wash your genitals with water, and change into clean underwear. Rinse the stained underwear or sheet with cold water and soap, then wash as usual. Semen washes out easily. Keeping a spare pair of underwear near your bed can help. There is nothing shameful about it.

title: Do girls have wet dreams
answer: Yes, girls can also have sexual dreams that cause excitement, wetness in the vagina, or even an orgasm while sleeping. This is normal and harmless, just like wet dreams in boys. Dreams about sex do not mean you have done something wrong or that you want to act on them. They are a normal part of growing up.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What male circumcision is
answer: Male circumcision is a small operation that removes the foreskin, the skin covering the head of the penis. It can be done for babies, boys or men. When done by a trained health worker in a health facility with clean tools, it is safe. After healing, the penis works normally for urinating, sex and having children.

title: Getting circumcised in Rwanda
answer: In Rwanda, voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) is offered at many public health facilities by trained health workers. To find out where and when it is available near you, ask at your health center, a youth corner or your community health worker, or call 114 for free. Before the operation you will get counselling and usually an offer of an HIV test.

title: Health benefits of male circumcision
answer: Besides lowering a man's risk of getting HIV from vaginal sex, medical circumcision makes it easier to keep the penis clean and lowers the risk of some other infections, such as some STIs and infections under the foreskin. It does not give full protection against HIV or other STIs, so condoms and testing are still needed. The choice to be circumcised should be voluntary.

title: What happens during medical circumcision
answer: Before medical circumcision, a health worker explains the procedure and checks your health. The penis is numbed with an injection, so you should feel little pain during the operation, which usually takes less than an hour. You go home the same day with a dressing and instructions. Some soreness is normal for a few days, and you will be asked to return for follow-up checks.

title: Caring for the wound after circumcision
answer: After circumcision, keep the dressing clean and dry and follow the health worker's instructions about when to remove it. Wear clean, loose-fitting underwear that supports the penis. Rest and avoid heavy work or sport for a few days. Wash your hands before touching the area. Go to all your follow-up visits. Healing usually takes about six weeks.

title: Waiting before sex after circumcision
answer: After medical circumcision, you should not have sex or masturbate for at least six weeks, until the wound has fully healed. Sex before healing can open the wound and greatly increase the risk of getting or passing on HIV and other infections. Even after healing, keep using condoms, because circumcision only gives partial protection.

title: Danger signs after circumcision
answer: Go back to the health facility immediately if, after circumcision, you have bleeding that soaks the dressing, pain that keeps getting worse, a lot of swelling, pus or a bad smell from the wound, fever, or difficulty passing urine. These can be signs of bleeding or infection that need quick treatment. If you cannot reach the clinic, call 112 or 912.

title: Risks of unsafe or traditional circumcision
answer: Circumcision done outside a health facility, by someone without training or with unclean or shared blades, can cause heavy bleeding, serious infection, injury to the penis, and can spread HIV and hepatitis through blood. It may not remove the foreskin properly. If you want to be circumcised, go to a health facility where trained workers use sterile tools.

title: Age and consent for circumcision
answer: Medical circumcision should be a choice made with full information, not something forced. Health workers will explain the benefits and risks and ask for your agreement. For young adolescents, a parent or guardian is usually involved in giving consent. Ask at your health center what is needed for your age. You can also ask questions and take time to decide.

title: Myths about circumcision
answer: Medical circumcision does not make the penis smaller, does not reduce fertility, and does not stop a man from enjoying sex. It does not make a man fully safe from HIV, so it is not a reason to stop using condoms. It also does not make someone more of a man. Ask a health worker if you hear other rumours.

title: Cutting of girls' genitals
answer: Cutting or removing parts of a girl's genitals, sometimes called female circumcision or female genital mutilation, has no health benefits. It causes pain, bleeding, infections, problems with urine, periods and childbirth, and emotional harm. It is a violation of girls' rights. It is not the same as male circumcision. If a girl is at risk, call 116 (child helpline) or 3512, or go to Isange One Stop Centre.

title: Masturbation myths about infertility and illness
answer: Masturbation does not cause infertility, impotence, madness, blindness, weakness, hair on the palms, acne or a small penis. It does not use up sperm or damage the vagina, uterus or ovaries. These are old myths. Masturbation is a private choice; some people do it and some do not. If you have pain or another worry, a health worker can help without judging.

title: How much masturbation is too much
answer: There is no normal number for how often someone masturbates. It becomes a problem only if it gets in the way of daily life, such as school, sleep, friendships or chores, if it causes soreness, or if you feel you cannot stop and it upsets you. If that happens, try staying busy with activities, and talk to a counsellor or health worker who will not judge you.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Do girls masturbate
answer: Yes, many girls and women masturbate, just as many boys do, and many others do not. Both are normal. It is a private way some people learn about their own body and feelings. It does not harm the vagina or future fertility. It is a personal choice, and nobody should make you feel ashamed whether you do or do not.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Keeping masturbation safe and clean
answer: If you masturbate, do it in private, with clean hands and clean, short nails. Do not put sharp, dirty, or breakable objects, or things that could get stuck, into your vagina or anus, and do not put anything into the urethra. Do not use harsh soaps, oils or chemicals on your genitals. If you have pain, bleeding, or something gets stuck, go to a health facility.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What a crush is
answer: A crush is a strong feeling of liking or being attracted to someone. You might think about them often, feel excited when you see them, or feel shy around them. Crushes are a normal part of growing up and can happen at any age. You can have a crush on a classmate, a neighbour or even a famous person. Having a crush does not mean you must act on it. It is simply a feeling, and it often passes with time.

title: Is it normal to have a crush
answer: Yes, having crushes is very normal, especially during puberty when your body and feelings are changing. Some people have many crushes, some have few or none, and all of these are okay. A crush shows that you are developing feelings of attraction, which is part of growing up. You do not need to feel ashamed or guilty about it. What matters is how you behave: respect yourself, respect the other person, and make choices that fit your values.

title: Having a crush on a teacher or older adult
answer: It is common to admire or have a crush on a teacher, coach or another older adult, often because they are kind, smart or confident. These feelings are normal, but a romantic relationship between a young person and a teacher or adult responsible for them is never okay. Adults have a duty to protect you and keep clear boundaries. Enjoy the feeling privately and let it fade. If an adult ever responds with romantic attention, tell a trusted adult or call 116.

title: Crush on someone who is already dating
answer: Liking someone who is already in a relationship can feel painful. Your feelings are real, but it is best to respect their relationship. Trying to break them up or compete can hurt everyone, including you. Give yourself some distance, spend time with friends and focus on things you enjoy. Over time the feeling usually becomes weaker. If they become single later, you can decide then. Someone worth dating will choose you freely, not because you pushed them.

title: How to know if someone likes you
answer: There is no sure sign, but some clues are: they try to spend time with you, talk or text often, remember small things you said, seem a little nervous or smile a lot around you, and show interest in your life. Still, people are different, and these signs can also just mean friendship. Try not to guess too much or rely on rumours. The only way to know for sure is through honest, respectful communication when you feel ready.

title: Someone is giving you mixed signals
answer: Mixed signals happen when someone seems interested one day and distant the next. This can be confusing and stressful. They might be unsure of their feelings, shy, busy, or not interested in a relationship. You cannot read their mind, so try not to spend too much energy guessing. If it matters to you, calmly ask them how they feel. If the answer stays unclear, it is okay to step back and protect your peace. You deserve clear and kind treatment.

title: Deciding whether to tell your crush how you feel
answer: Telling your crush how you feel is your choice. It can bring relief and clarity, but there is also a chance they do not feel the same. Before deciding, ask yourself: Am I ready to hear either answer? Could this affect our friendship? If you decide to tell them, choose a private, calm moment in a safe place and keep it simple, for example: I enjoy spending time with you and I like you. Respect whatever answer they give.

title: How to ask someone out
answer: Many young people first get to know each other through school, church, sports or group activities. If you want to ask someone out, suggest something simple, safe and public, like talking after class or joining friends for an activity. Be honest and polite: I would like to spend more time with you, would you like that? Accept the answer, yes or no, with respect. Make sure the plan fits your age, school rules and family values.

title: Being turned down by your crush
answer: Hearing no from someone you like can hurt. It is okay to feel sad, embarrassed or disappointed. Their answer is not a judgement of your value; people simply have different feelings and reasons. Respect their decision and do not keep pushing. Talk to a friend you trust, do things you enjoy and give yourself time. Being brave enough to ask shows courage, and the right person for you will want to be with you freely.

title: Saying no when someone asks you out
answer: You have the right to say no if you are not interested or not ready to date. Be clear, kind and honest: Thank you for asking, but I am not interested in dating you. You do not need to give a long explanation or make up excuses. Avoid laughing at them or telling others, because asking takes courage. If they keep pushing after your clear no, that is not okay; talk to a trusted adult or teacher.

title: Feeling shy around your crush
answer: Feeling shy, nervous or tongue-tied around someone you like is very common. Your heart may beat faster or you may forget what to say. To feel more relaxed, start with small, normal conversations, such as about school or a shared hobby. Spend time in groups so there is less pressure. Remind yourself that the other person may feel nervous too. Being yourself is more attractive than trying to act perfect.

title: When a crush takes over your thoughts
answer: When you like someone, it is normal to think about them a lot. But if it starts affecting your sleep, studies or friendships, it helps to take back some control. Keep busy with schoolwork, sports, music, church or youth groups. Limit how often you check their social media. Talk with friends about other topics. Write your feelings in a notebook. Strong feelings often calm down with time. If you feel very low, talk to a trusted adult.

title: Love versus infatuation
answer: Infatuation is a strong, exciting attraction that often comes quickly. It is based mostly on looks or an idea of the person, and it can fade fast. Love usually grows slowly. It means knowing the real person, including their faults, caring about their wellbeing, trusting each other and wanting good things for them even when it is not exciting. Infatuation is about how someone makes you feel; love is also about how you treat each other over time.

title: Can teenagers really be in love
answer: Yes, young people can feel deep and real feelings of love. These feelings are important and deserve to be taken seriously. At the same time, during your teenage years you are still learning who you are, what you value and what you want in the future. Many teenage relationships change or end as people grow, and that is normal. Enjoy healthy friendships and feelings, while keeping your education, values and goals as priorities.

title: Love at first sight
answer: Many people feel a strong attraction the first time they see someone. That instant spark is real, but it is usually attraction or infatuation rather than love. Love grows as you get to know a person: their character, how they treat others, and whether you share values. A first impression can be a good start, but take time to see if the person is kind, honest and respectful before giving your heart fully.

title: Body reactions when you are attracted to someone
answer: When you are attracted to someone, your body can react. Your heart may beat faster, your face may feel hot, your hands may sweat, and you may feel butterflies in your stomach. These reactions come from hormones and excitement and are completely normal. They do not mean you must do anything. You are always in control of how you act, and you can enjoy the feelings while making choices that fit your values.

title: What attraction is
answer: Attraction is feeling drawn to someone. It can be physical (liking how someone looks), emotional (feeling close and understood), or about their personality, like their humour or kindness. Attraction often becomes stronger during puberty because of hormones. It is natural and can be toward different people at different times. Feeling attracted to someone is not wrong, and it does not mean you have to start a relationship or do anything sexual.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What dating means
answer: Dating means two people spending time together to get to know each other because they like each other in a romantic way. For young people, dating can be as simple as talking, walking home together, or meeting with a group of friends. Dating does not mean having sex. Every family, religion and culture has its own views on dating, so it helps to understand your family's values and talk with them.

title: The right age to start dating
answer: There is no single right age that fits everyone. It depends on your maturity, your family's values, your religion and culture, and whether you feel ready. Many families prefer young people to wait until they are older. Ask yourself: Do I understand myself? Can I say no to things I don't want? Can I keep up with school? Talking with your parents or a trusted adult can help you decide.

title: Things to think about when dating young
answer: Dating at a young age can feel exciting, but it also brings challenges. Young couples may face pressure to have sex before they are ready, strong emotions that distract from school, and conflict with family rules. Relationships with much older partners carry extra risks. If you choose to date, keep it public and in groups, stay focused on school, stick to your values, and keep talking with a trusted adult.

title: Not interested in dating yet
answer: It is completely okay not to want a boyfriend or girlfriend yet. Everyone develops at their own pace. Many young people prefer to focus on school, friends, sports, faith or hobbies. Not dating does not mean something is wrong with you. You have the right to decide what you want and when you want it. When you feel ready in the future, you can make that choice for yourself.

title: How much to share with friends about your relationship
answer: You can choose how much of your relationship to share with friends. Sharing a little with trusted friends can bring support and advice. But sharing private details, especially about your partner's body, secrets or arguments, can break trust and hurt them. Agree together on what you are both comfortable sharing, online and offline. Gossip spreads fast. Respecting each other's privacy is part of a healthy relationship.

title: Staying safe on a first date
answer: For a first date, choose a public place where other people are around, during the day, such as a park, a café, a church event or a sports match. Tell a parent or trusted adult where you are going and when you will return. Have a way to get home on your own and keep your phone charged. Avoid alcohol. If anything feels uncomfortable, it is okay to leave. A good date should feel relaxed and respectful.

title: Getting to know someone in a group
answer: Spending time in groups is a great way for young people to get to know someone they like. Group activities, such as sports, youth clubs, choir, school events or studying together, take away pressure and help you see how the person behaves with others. Groups also make it easier to avoid situations where you might feel pressured. Many parents feel more comfortable with group outings too.

title: What to talk about on a date
answer: Good conversation is about being curious and listening. You can talk about school, favourite music or films, sports, hobbies, dreams for the future or funny experiences. Ask open questions, like what do you enjoy doing at weekends? Listen to the answers and share about yourself too. Do not push them to share very private things. A short silence is normal. Being yourself and being respectful matter more than having perfect words.

title: Difference between a friend and a boyfriend or girlfriend
answer: A friendship is based on caring, trust and enjoying time together. A romantic relationship includes those things plus romantic attraction and the wish to be close in a special way. Both should be respectful and equal. Sometimes it is hard to know which one you have, so honest talking helps. Many good romantic relationships start with a strong friendship.

title: Can boys and girls be just friends
answer: Yes, boys and girls can be close friends without any romance. These friendships help you learn respect, understand different points of view and build communication skills. Sometimes others may tease you or assume you are dating; you can simply explain that you are friends. If romantic feelings develop on either side, talk honestly. Friendships between boys and girls are healthy and valuable.

title: Falling for your best friend
answer: Developing romantic feelings for a best friend is common because you already trust and care about each other. Before sharing, think about how much the friendship means to you and whether you can handle either answer. If you decide to tell them, do it privately and gently, and let them know the friendship matters most. If they don't feel the same, give both of you some time; many friendships survive this.

title: You and a friend like the same person
answer: It can be hard when you and a friend like the same person. Talk honestly with your friend about it before anything happens. Remember that the person you both like will make their own choice, and it is not a competition. Ask yourselves whether a crush is worth damaging your friendship. Treat each other kindly whatever happens. Good friends find ways to stay respectful even when feelings are complicated.

title: Dating a friend's ex
answer: Dating a friend's ex can hurt your friendship, even if their relationship ended long ago. Before you act, think about how your friend might feel. If the friendship matters to you, talk with your friend openly and listen to their feelings. They don't own their ex, but honesty shows respect. Hiding it often causes bigger problems later. Decide with care, knowing that both friendships and relationships need trust.

title: Age gaps between young people who date
answer: Even a few years can make a big difference when you are young. For example, a 14-year-old and an 18-year-old are at very different stages: the older person may have more experience, freedom and power, which can lead to pressure. A sexual relationship between an adult and someone under 18 can also be against the law. It is safest to date people close to your own age. If an older person pressures you, talk to a trusted adult or call 116.

title: Can long-distance relationships work
answer: Long-distance relationships can work, but they need effort, trust and good communication. Being apart can bring loneliness, jealousy and misunderstandings. Couples who manage well usually agree on how and when to communicate, stay honest, and keep living full lives with friends and school. It is also okay to realise that the distance is too hard. What matters is that both of you feel respected and happy.

title: Dating a classmate
answer: Dating a classmate can be nice because you see each other often and share experiences. But it can also be hard: arguments or a breakup may make class uncomfortable, and others may gossip. If you choose to date a classmate, keep class time for learning, avoid public drama, and respect school rules. Agree that if things end, you will both stay respectful.

title: Tips for a healthy long-distance relationship
answer: If you are apart, a few habits help: agree on a communication routine that suits both of you without needing to talk all day; be honest about your feelings; trust each other instead of checking up constantly; share small moments through messages or calls; and plan to see each other when possible and allowed. Keep enjoying your own friends and studies. Talking every minute is not a sign of love; respect and trust are.

title: Relationships at boarding school
answer: At boarding school you spend most of your time with other students away from family, so feelings and relationships can grow quickly. Remember that your main goal is your education. Follow school rules, avoid going to hidden or isolated places alone with someone, and do not let anyone pressure you into sex. If you need advice, talk to a matron, patron, school counsellor, school nurse or a teacher you trust.

title: Balancing a relationship and school
answer: Your education opens doors for your future, so keep it a priority. Set clear times for study and stick to them. Tell your partner when you need to focus, and support each other's goals, for example by revising together. A caring partner will want you to succeed, not distract you. If a relationship keeps pulling you away from school and your marks keep dropping, it may be time to rethink it.

title: Partner does not support your goals
answer: A loving partner encourages your dreams. If your partner laughs at your goals, says school is a waste, pushes you to drop out, or gets angry when you succeed, that is a warning sign. You deserve someone who wants the best for you. Tell them how it makes you feel. If nothing changes, think about whether the relationship is good for you, and talk to a trusted adult.

title: How to be a good boyfriend or girlfriend
answer: Being a good partner means treating the other person with respect, kindness and honesty. Listen when they talk, keep your promises, and support their goals and friendships. Respect their boundaries, including when they say no. Talk through problems calmly instead of shouting or ignoring them. Apologise when you are wrong. Show care in small ways, like a kind message. A good partner helps the other person feel safe and valued.

title: Partner texts and calls all the time
answer: Talking often can feel nice at first, but if your partner calls or texts all day, demands instant replies, or gets angry when you are busy, it can become controlling. You have the right to time for school, family, friends and rest. Explain kindly that you care but need space at certain times. A healthy partner will understand. If they keep demanding or threatening, that is a warning sign; talk to a trusted adult.

title: Keeping your friends while dating
answer: When you start dating, it is easy to spend all your time with your partner, but your friends and family still matter. They support you, have fun with you and help you see things clearly. Make time for friends, keep your hobbies, and don't cancel plans every time your partner calls. A healthy relationship adds to your life; it does not replace everything else.

title: Handling your own jealous feelings
answer: Jealousy is a feeling of worry or fear that you might lose someone, or that someone else has what you want. Almost everyone feels jealous sometimes, and having the feeling is okay. What matters is what you do with it. Try to understand why you feel it, talk calmly with your partner or friend, and build your own confidence. Checking their phone, controlling them or accusing them only makes things worse.

title: Building trust in a relationship
answer: Trust grows slowly through actions over time. You build it by being honest, keeping promises, respecting privacy and treating your partner the same whether they are present or not. Talk openly about worries instead of hiding them. Trust also means giving your partner freedom to have friends and their own life. Without trust, a relationship becomes stressful and full of suspicion.

title: Rebuilding trust after a lie
answer: Broken trust can sometimes be rebuilt, but it takes time and effort from both people. The person who broke it needs to admit what happened honestly, apologise sincerely, and show change through consistent actions. The hurt person needs time and can set fair conditions. Rebuilding trust cannot be forced. If the same hurt keeps happening, it may be healthier to end the relationship.

title: When your partner lies to you
answer: Finding out your partner lied can hurt and leave you confused. Talk to them calmly about what you found and how it made you feel. Listen to their explanation, but notice whether the lie was a one-time mistake or part of a pattern. Frequent lies, especially about important things like other partners or where they go, damage the relationship. You deserve honesty. Talk with a trusted friend or adult if you feel unsure.

title: Good communication between partners
answer: Good communication means sharing your thoughts and feelings honestly and respectfully, and listening to your partner too. Use I statements, like I feel hurt when plans change without telling me, instead of blaming. Talk face to face about important things when possible, because messages are easily misunderstood. Choose a calm moment, listen without interrupting, and be open to compromise. Couples who communicate well solve problems before they grow big.

title: Is it normal for couples to argue
answer: Disagreements happen in every relationship and friendship because people have different opinions and needs, so arguing sometimes is normal. What matters is how you argue. Healthy disagreements stay respectful: no insults, threats, hitting or forcing. Both people get to speak and try to find a solution. If arguments happen all the time, make you afraid, or always end with one person getting their way, the relationship may be unhealthy.

title: Solving a disagreement fairly
answer: To solve a disagreement fairly, calm down first, then talk at a good time. Focus on the problem, not on attacking the person. Each person explains their view using I statements while the other listens. Look for a solution that works for both, or a fair compromise. Avoid bringing up old fights. If things get heated, take a break and come back later. Fair conflict leaves both people feeling respected.

title: How to apologise properly
answer: A good apology is sincere and specific. Say what you did, admit it was wrong, and recognise how it affected the other person: I'm sorry I shared your secret; I understand it hurt you. Avoid excuses or saying sorry, but. Then say how you will do better, and actually change. You cannot force forgiveness, so give the person time. Apologising is a sign of maturity and respect.

title: Forgiving someone who hurt you
answer: Forgiving means choosing to let go of anger about something that hurt you. It can bring peace and help repair relationships. Forgiving does not mean forgetting, pretending it didn't hurt, or accepting the same harm again. You can forgive someone and still decide to set limits or end the relationship. Take your time. Your safety and wellbeing always come first, especially if the hurt keeps happening.

title: The silent treatment
answer: The silent treatment means refusing to talk to someone to punish them or get your way. Taking a short break to calm down is healthy, but ignoring someone for days to make them feel guilty is hurtful and harms the relationship. If you need space, say so: I need some time to calm down, let's talk tomorrow. If your partner often uses silence to control you, talk about it or ask a trusted adult for advice.

title: Signs it may be time to end a relationship
answer: Some signs a relationship may be ending: you argue more and talk less, you no longer enjoy time together, one or both of you feel unhappy most of the time, trust is gone, or you want very different things. Relationships change and not all of them last, which is normal. Talk honestly with your partner about how you feel. Sometimes problems can be fixed; sometimes ending is the healthiest choice.

title: How to break up kindly
answer: If you decide to end a relationship, be honest and kind. Tell the person in person in a safe place, or by phone if meeting is not possible. Be clear: I've decided to end our relationship. Give a short, honest reason without insulting them. Expect sadness or anger and stay calm. Don't keep sending mixed signals afterwards. If you are worried about how they will react, tell a trusted adult and choose a public place.

title: Coping with a breakup
answer: Breakups can hurt a lot, even when you are young. Feeling sad, angry or lost is normal. Let yourself feel the pain. Talk to friends or family you trust, stay active, keep a routine for sleep and study, and do things you enjoy. Avoid constantly contacting your ex or checking their profiles. The pain usually becomes lighter with time. If sadness lasts a long time or you feel hopeless, talk to a counsellor, nurse or trusted adult, or call 116.

title: Staying friends with an ex
answer: Some people can stay friends after a breakup and some cannot, at least not right away. Friendship works best when both people have healed, respect each other's new lives, and are not secretly hoping to get back together. Give yourselves some time apart first. If staying friends keeps causing pain, jealousy or confusion, it is okay to keep your distance. Your peace matters.

title: Getting back together with an ex
answer: Getting back together can work if the reasons you broke up have truly been solved and both people want it. Ask yourself: Why did we end? Has anything really changed? Am I going back because I'm lonely, or because the relationship was healthy? If the breakup was about disrespect, control, cheating or violence, going back often brings the same problems. Take your time and talk with someone you trust.

title: What counts as cheating
answer: Cheating usually means breaking the promise of being faithful in a relationship, for example by secretly dating, kissing or having sex with someone else. Couples can have different ideas about what counts as cheating, such as flirty messages or secret chats, so it helps to talk about your expectations early. Cheating hurts trust deeply. Having sex with more than one person also increases the risk of HIV and other infections.

title: When you think your partner is cheating
answer: If you suspect your partner is cheating, try not to act on rumours alone or spy on their phone. Notice what is making you worried, then talk calmly and honestly with them about your feelings and listen to their answer. If trust is gone and you still feel unsure, think about whether the relationship gives you peace. If you have had sex, getting tested for HIV and STIs at a health center is a good idea.

title: Your partner cheated on you
answer: Learning that your partner cheated can be very painful. You may feel angry, sad or embarrassed; these feelings are normal, and it is not your fault. Take time before deciding what to do. Some couples try to rebuild trust; others decide to end the relationship. Both choices are valid. Talk to someone you trust. If you have had sex with this partner, visit a health center for HIV and STI testing.

title: What peer pressure is
answer: Peer pressure is when people your age influence you to do something, or not do something, to fit in. It can be direct, like being dared or teased, or quiet, like feeling you must copy others to be accepted. Peer pressure can be positive, like friends encouraging you to study, or negative, like pushing you to drink, skip school or start a relationship. Knowing your own values helps you decide for yourself.

title: Saying no to friends who pressure you
answer: Saying no is easier if you plan ahead. Be clear and confident: No thanks, I'm not into that. Repeat it if needed. You can give a reason or suggest something else to do. Stay close to friends who share your values. Leave the situation if the pressure continues. Real friends respect your choices. If people reject you for saying no, they may not be good friends for you.

title: Myth that everyone your age is having sex
answer: Friends may say everyone is having sex, but this is often not true. Many young people, especially younger teenagers, have not had sex, and some people exaggerate or lie to look experienced. Whether others are having sex or not, your choice should be based on your own readiness, values and safety. Waiting is normal, and many young people choose to wait.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Why some young people choose to wait for sex
answer: Many young people choose to delay sex. Reasons include not feeling ready, wanting to focus on school and goals, religious or family values, avoiding pregnancy, HIV and other infections, and wanting to wait for the right person or for marriage. Delaying sex is a healthy and respected choice. It does not mean you don't love your partner. You can show love in many other ways.

title: What abstinence means
answer: Abstinence means choosing not to have sex. Some people abstain until they are older, until marriage, or until they feel ready. When practised every time, abstinence prevents pregnancy and greatly lowers the risk of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. It is a personal choice anyone can make, including people who have had sex before. It works best when you are clear about your decision and have support from people who respect it.

title: Telling your partner you want to wait
answer: Be honest early and clearly: I care about you, but I've decided to wait before having sex. Choose a calm moment, not when you are already alone and things are getting physical. You don't have to justify your decision, but you can share your reasons if you want. A partner who respects you will accept it. If they pressure you or threaten to leave, that tells you something important about the relationship.

title: What sex is
answer: Sex, or sexual intercourse, usually means intimate sexual contact between two people, for example when a man's penis enters a woman's vagina. Sex can lead to pregnancy and can pass on HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. People may have sex to express love, for pleasure, or to have children. It should always be a free and informed choice between people who are old enough and ready.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Is sex the same as love
answer: Sex and love are different. Love is about caring, trust, respect and commitment, and it can exist without sex. Sex is a physical act that can happen with or without love. Having sex does not prove love and cannot make someone stay. You can show love by spending time together, listening, supporting each other's goals and being honest.

title: Deciding if you are ready to kiss
answer: Kissing is one way people show affection, and many young people wonder about it. It is okay to wait until you feel ready, and you never have to kiss anyone. Both people should want it; ask if you are not sure. Think about your values, your family's views and whether kissing might lead to pressure for more. Feeling nervous about a first kiss is normal, and it's fine if it feels awkward.

title: What virginity means
