answer: Virginity usually describes a person who has never had sexual intercourse. Different cultures and religions have different ideas about virginity and its importance. Being a virgin or not does not change your value as a person, and nobody has the right to check or judge it. It is completely okay to be a virgin at any age. Whether and when to have sex is a personal decision.

title: Myths about telling if someone is a virgin
answer: You cannot tell if someone is a virgin by looking at them, how they walk, or by checking their body. A common myth is that all girls bleed the first time they have sex or that the hymen proves virginity. In fact, many girls don't bleed, and the hymen can stretch through sport or everyday activity. Virginity tests are not accurate and violate a person's dignity.

title: Talking with parents about relationships
answer: Talking with your parents or guardians about relationships can feel awkward, but they can offer love, guidance and protection. Choose a calm time, like while cooking or walking together. Start small: Can I ask you something about relationships? You can use a TV show or school lesson to begin. Be honest and listen to their advice. If talking to a parent is too hard, another trusted adult like an aunt, uncle or teacher can help.

title: Parents who forbid dating
answer: Many parents forbid dating because they want to protect you, keep you focused on school, or follow family or religious values. It can feel unfair, but try to understand their reasons. Ask calmly why they feel that way and share your feelings. You may agree on rules, like meeting friends in groups. Hiding a relationship brings stress and makes it harder to get help if something goes wrong; honesty builds trust and often more freedom later.

title: When parents won't talk about sex
answer: Some parents avoid talking about sex because they feel shy, were never taught themselves, or worry that talking will encourage sex. If your parents won't talk, it is not your fault and your questions are still valid. You can get correct information from a trusted aunt or uncle, a teacher, a nurse at the health center, or by calling 114 for free. Avoid relying only on friends or the internet.

title: Religious values and dating
answer: Many religions have teachings about relationships, respect and sex. Some encourage young people to wait before dating, others allow friendships or courtship with guidance, and many teach that sex belongs in marriage. You can talk with your parents, a religious leader or youth group about what your faith teaches. Many young people of faith have caring, respectful relationships that follow their values. Choose what fits your beliefs and keeps you safe.

title: Accepting gifts from a partner
answer: Small gifts between partners, like a snack, a card or a book, can be a nice way to show care. Think more carefully about big or expensive gifts like phones or clothes. Ask yourself: Do I feel I owe something? Would I still feel free to say no or leave? A real gift never comes with conditions. If gifts make you feel pressured, it is okay to refuse them and talk honestly about it.

title: Sexting and sending nude photos
answer: Sexting means sending sexual messages, photos or videos by phone or online. Once you send something, you lose control of it: it can be saved, screenshotted, shared after a breakup or used to threaten you, causing shame and stress. For people under 18, making or sharing sexual images can be against the law, even of yourself. The safest choice is not to send them. If a photo has been shared, it is not your fault; tell a trusted adult or call 116.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Online friendships and fake profiles
answer: Online friendships can be fun, but you can't always know who someone really is. Some people use fake names, ages or photos. Warning signs include refusing video calls, stories that keep changing, or asking for money, photos or secrecy. Keep personal details like your address, school and routine private. Never send money or private photos. Tell a trusted adult about online friends, and block and report anyone who makes you uncomfortable.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What sexual orientation means
answer: Sexual orientation describes who a person is emotionally, romantically or sexually attracted to. Some people are attracted to people of a different sex, some to the same sex, some to more than one sex, and some feel little or no sexual attraction. Many young people feel unsure for a while, which is normal; you don't need a label. Having these feelings is not your fault. Everyone deserves respect, dignity and health care.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Is being gay a disease
answer: No. Health organisations, including the World Health Organization, do not consider homosexuality a disease or mental illness, so it does not need to be cured or treated. Trying to change someone's orientation can cause serious harm. It is also a myth that people become gay from friends, films or the internet. People of every orientation deserve respect, safety and good health care. If you are struggling, a nurse or counsellor can help confidentially.

title: What gender identity means
answer: Gender identity is a person's inner sense of being a boy or man, a girl or woman, or something else. For most people it matches the sex they were assigned at birth; for some it does not, and they may describe themselves as transgender. Sex refers to the body, while many gender roles are learned from society. Gender identity is different from sexual orientation. Everyone deserves respect and health care.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Being ready for marriage
answer: Being ready for marriage involves much more than love. It includes emotional maturity, good communication and problem-solving, financial stability, finishing education or training, shared values, and both people freely choosing each other. It also means being ready to plan a family together. Taking time to grow and reach your goals first often leads to stronger marriages. Marriage should never be forced or happen in childhood.

title: What youth-friendly health services are
answer: Youth-friendly health services are health services set up so young people feel welcome, safe and respected. Staff are trained to listen without judging, keep what you say private and explain things clearly. You can get information, counselling, condoms and other contraception, HIV and STI testing, pregnancy tests and support. Many health centres in Rwanda have a youth-friendly space. You do not need a special reason to visit. Asking about your body and health is normal and smart.

title: How youth-friendly staff should treat you
answer: At a youth-friendly service, staff should greet you kindly, listen to you, and talk with you in a private space. They should not shout, laugh at you, judge you or lecture you about your choices. They should explain things in words you understand, answer your questions honestly and keep your information private. You can refuse anything you do not want. If you are not treated well, you can ask for another provider or speak to the person in charge.

title: What a youth corner is
answer: A youth corner is a special space, often inside a health centre or youth centre, where young people can get SRH information and services in a relaxed and private setting. You may find trained staff or peer educators, leaflets, condoms and a place to ask questions. Some youth corners also offer counselling, HIV testing or a referral to the nurse. Ask at the reception of your health centre whether there is a youth corner and when it is open.

title: What happens at a youth centre
answer: Youth centres are community places where young people meet for sports, games, clubs, training and learning. Many also share SRH information through peer educators, talks and drama, and some have a youth corner offering counselling, condoms and HIV testing or referral. Going to a youth centre is a good way to learn, make friends and get support from people your age. Your sector or district office can tell you if there is a youth centre near you.

title: Finding a youth-friendly service near you
answer: To find a youth-friendly service near you, ask at your nearest health centre whether they have a youth corner or a nurse who works with young people. You can also ask your community health worker, a school nurse or teacher, a youth centre, or call 114 for free health information. If the nearest place has no special youth space, you can still get SRH services there, because health centres serve young people too.

title: Using an ordinary health centre as a young person
answer: Yes, you can use an ordinary public health centre even if it has no special youth space. Health centres serve everyone, including young people, and the nurses there can give SRH information, counselling, testing and many contraceptive methods. You do not need to be sick to go. Tell the person at reception you want to talk to a nurse about a health question. You have the right to be treated with respect, whatever your age.

title: Youth peer educators
answer: Peer educators are young people trained to share correct SRH information with others their age. You may meet them at schools, youth centres, youth corners or community events. They can answer simple questions, give leaflets or condoms in some places, and help you find a nurse or counsellor. Because they are close to your age, they can be easier to talk to. They are not health workers, so for tests, treatment or personal health problems they should refer you to a health facility.

title: Bringing a friend to a health visit
answer: You can bring a friend or a trusted person with you to the health centre for support. Many young people feel braver with someone they trust. When you talk to the nurse, you can choose whether your friend stays in the room or waits outside. The nurse may ask to speak to you alone for part of the visit, to make sure you can talk freely. Only bring someone you trust to keep your information private.

title: What to do if the clinic is closed
answer: If you arrive and the health centre or youth corner is closed, do not give up. Ask a guard or staff member when it opens, and go back then. You can also contact your community health worker, visit a health post or call 114 for free health advice. If it is an emergency, such as heavy bleeding, severe pain or someone who has fainted, call 912 for an ambulance or 112, or go straight to the nearest hospital.

title: Long waiting times at the clinic
answer: Health centres can be busy, so you may have to wait. It can help to go early in the day, bring something to read and ask at reception roughly how long it will take. If you need to be back at school or home, tell the staff. If you feel very unwell while waiting, such as bleeding a lot, fainting or having strong pain, tell a staff member straight away so they can see you sooner.

title: SRH services young people can get
answer: Young people can get many SRH services at health facilities. These include correct information and counselling, condoms and other contraception, emergency contraception, pregnancy tests, care during pregnancy, HIV testing and treatment, STI testing and treatment, care for period problems, and support after sexual violence. Some places also offer counselling for stress and relationships. If one place does not offer a service, the staff can refer you to one that does.

title: Health services for young people out of school
answer: If you are not in school, you have the same right to SRH information and services as students. You can go to a health centre, health post, youth centre or youth corner, or talk to your community health worker. Some youth centres and community groups run sessions for young people who work or stay at home. You can also call 114 for free health information. Being out of school should never stop you from getting care.

title: Health post versus health centre
answer: In Rwanda, a health post is a small facility close to the community that gives basic care, such as treatment of common illnesses and some family planning and testing services. A health centre is bigger, has more nurses and can offer more services, like a wider choice of contraception, HIV care, antenatal care and deliveries. If a health post cannot help you, they will send you to the health centre.

title: Services offered at a health centre
answer: A health centre is usually where you go first for most health needs. Nurses there can give consultations, family planning, HIV and STI testing and treatment, pregnancy tests, antenatal care, deliveries, vaccinations and counselling. Many have a laboratory for simple tests. If you need care they cannot give, such as a specialist or surgery, they will refer you to the district hospital. Bring your mutuelle card if you have one.

title: What a district hospital is for
answer: A district hospital gives more advanced care than a health centre. It has doctors, more equipment and can handle problems like difficult pregnancies and births, surgery, serious infections and emergencies. In most cases you go to the district hospital after being referred by a health centre, which helps your mutuelle cover the cost. In an emergency, go to the nearest hospital directly or call 912 for an ambulance.

title: Referrals and referral letters
answer: A referral is when a health worker sends you to another place for care they cannot give, for example from a health post to a health centre, or from a health centre to a district hospital. They usually give you a referral letter or note explaining your problem. Keep it safe and take it with you, along with your mutuelle card. Going through referral helps the next team understand your needs and usually helps your mutuelle cover the care.

title: Higher-level referral hospitals
answer: Above district hospitals, Rwanda has provincial and national referral hospitals with specialist doctors and equipment for complex problems. Most people only go there when a district hospital refers them. You do not need to go there for everyday SRH needs like contraception, testing or counselling, which your health centre can provide. If a doctor refers you to a referral hospital, ask them to explain why and what to bring.

title: Where to go first for a health problem
answer: For most SRH questions and health problems, start close to home. You can talk to your community health worker, or go to a health post or your health centre. They can help with most needs and will refer you to a hospital if needed. You can also call 114 for free advice about where to go. Only go straight to a hospital, or call 912, in an emergency.

title: When to go straight to a hospital
answer: Go straight to the nearest hospital, or call 912 for an ambulance or 112, if there are danger signs. These include very heavy bleeding, fainting, strong pain in the belly, high fever with weakness, trouble breathing, a serious injury, being attacked or raped, or bleeding or strong pain during pregnancy. Do not wait to see if it goes away. Ask someone to go with you if you can.

title: Emergency care without a parent present
answer: In an emergency, you should get care quickly even if your parents or guardian are not with you. Health workers will treat urgent problems first. If you are under 18, they may later try to contact your parent, guardian or another trusted adult, and they will ask you who that should be. If you are scared about your family's reaction, tell the health worker so they can support you.

title: Private clinics versus public facilities
answer: Public facilities, like health posts, health centres and district hospitals, are run by the government and many SRH services there are free or low cost, and mutuelle de sante is accepted. Private clinics can be faster or closer for some people, but they usually cost more and may not accept mutuelle. Both should give you respectful and private care. Before getting care at a private clinic, ask what it will cost.

title: Going to a health centre outside your area
answer: Some young people prefer a health centre further from home because they worry about meeting people they know. You can usually seek care at another public facility, but rules about mutuelle cover and referrals may be different there, so ask at reception first. Remember that health workers everywhere must keep your information private. In an emergency, always go to the nearest facility.

title: What a community health worker is
answer: A community health worker, often called an abajyanama b'ubuzima, is a person chosen by the community and trained to help with health in the village. They give health advice, treat some common illnesses in children, follow up pregnant women, share family planning information and help people get to the health centre when needed. They live near you, so they are easy to reach. They work closely with the health centre.

title: SRH help from a community health worker
answer: Your community health worker can give you correct information about SRH topics such as family planning, pregnancy, HIV and STIs, and tell you where to get services. Some can provide condoms and certain contraceptive methods. They can follow up pregnant girls and women and help you get to the health centre. If you have a question you feel shy to ask at the clinic, your community health worker can be a good first step.

title: Contraception from community health workers
answer: In Rwanda, some community health workers are trained to give certain family planning methods in the village, such as condoms and some pills or injections, and to explain how to use them. They will refer you to the health centre for other methods, like implants or the IUD, or if you have health questions they cannot answer. Ask your community health worker which methods they can give.

title: Privacy with a community health worker
answer: Community health workers are expected to keep what you tell them private, just like nurses. They should not share your questions or health information with your family or neighbours. If you are worried, you can ask them directly: will you keep this between us? If you still feel uncomfortable because they know your family, you can go to the health centre or call 114 instead.

title: Finding your community health worker
answer: Every village in Rwanda usually has community health workers. To find yours, ask your parents, a neighbour, your village leader or the staff at your health centre. They can tell you who the community health worker is and where they live. You can visit them or ask for their phone number so you can contact them when you need advice.

title: What community health workers cannot do
answer: Community health workers are helpful, but they are not nurses or doctors. They cannot do most laboratory tests, examine you fully, give many medicines or provide methods such as implants and IUDs. For STI symptoms, pregnancy problems, HIV care, injuries or anything serious, they will refer you to a health centre or hospital. If they tell you to go to the health centre, try to go soon.

title: SRH items you can get at a pharmacy
answer: At a pharmacy you can usually buy condoms, pregnancy tests, sanitary pads, some contraceptive pills and emergency contraception, and simple pain relief for period cramps. Pharmacists can also give advice and tell you when you need to see a nurse or doctor. Many other medicines, including antibiotics, need a prescription from a health worker. Remember that condoms and many SRH services are also free at public health facilities.

title: Questions to ask a pharmacist
answer: Pharmacists are trained health professionals, and you can ask them questions. Useful questions include: what is this medicine for, how and when should I take it, what side effects can happen, can I take it with my other medicines, what should I do if I miss a dose, and when should I see a nurse or doctor. You can ask to speak quietly at the side if you want privacy.

title: Why not to buy antibiotics without a prescription
answer: Antibiotics only work for certain infections, and the right one depends on the cause. If you buy antibiotics without seeing a health worker, you may take the wrong medicine, not take enough, or hide a problem that needs real treatment. This can make you sicker and helps germs become resistant, so antibiotics stop working for everyone. If you think you have an infection, including an STI, go to a health centre to be checked and treated properly.

title: Why not to take someone else's medicine
answer: Medicine given to a friend or family member was chosen for their body and their problem, not yours. Even if your symptoms look the same, the cause may be different. Taking someone else's medicine can be harmful, can cause bad reactions and can delay the right treatment. Do not share your own medicine either. Go to a health worker so you get checked and receive the medicine that is right for you.

title: Checking that a medicine is safe to use
answer: Before using any medicine or product, check that the package is sealed and not damaged, and look for the expiry date. Do not use anything that is past its expiry date, looks different from usual or has no clear label. Buy only from registered pharmacies or get it from a health facility. If you are unsure, ask the pharmacist or nurse to check it for you.

title: Pharmacy or health centre: which to choose
answer: A pharmacy is useful for quick things like condoms, pregnancy tests, pads or advice about a medicine you already have. Go to a health centre when you need to be examined, tested or treated, for example for possible STI symptoms, unusual bleeding, pain, HIV testing, starting most contraceptive methods or pregnancy care. Health centres are also where many SRH services are free. When in doubt, choose the health centre.

title: Medicines from the street or market
answer: Medicines sold in markets, on the street or by people walking around are not checked and can be fake, expired or the wrong medicine. They may not work, can make you sick and can delay real treatment. This includes pills sold to treat STIs, end a pregnancy or improve sex. Get medicines only from a registered pharmacy or a health facility, and see a health worker first.

title: Traditional or herbal remedies for SRH problems
answer: Some people use traditional or herbal remedies for problems like period pain, infections or wanting a baby. Many have not been tested for safety, and some can be harmful or delay treatment that works. If you have a health problem, see a health worker first. If you are using or thinking about a herbal remedy, tell the nurse or doctor, so they can advise you safely.

title: What happens at a first SRH visit
answer: At your first SRH visit, you usually register at reception, then wait to see a nurse. The nurse will ask why you came and some questions about your health, periods or relationships, so they can help you properly. They will explain your options and may offer tests, such as a pregnancy or HIV test, only with your agreement. An examination is done only if needed and only if you agree. You can ask questions at any time.

title: What to say to a nurse
answer: You do not need special words. You can start simply: I have a question about my body, or I want to talk about family planning, or I am worried I might have an infection. Say what you feel and how long it has been happening. If it is hard to say aloud, you can write it on paper and show the nurse. Nurses hear these questions every day and are there to help, not judge.

title: Feeling shy or ashamed to ask for help
answer: Feeling shy or ashamed about SRH questions is very common, and it is okay. Your body and your health are important, and asking questions is a sign that you care for yourself. Health workers hear the same questions every day and are trained not to judge. It can help to bring a trusted friend, write your question on paper, or start with a peer educator or community health worker. You deserve answers and care.

title: Preparing questions before a visit
answer: Preparing before a health visit helps you remember everything. Write down what you want to ask, what you are feeling and since when, the date of your last period if you are a girl, and any medicines you take. Keep the paper in your pocket and read from it if you feel nervous. During the visit, you can also write down what the nurse tells you so you do not forget.

title: When you do not understand the health worker
answer: If you do not understand what a nurse or doctor says, it is okay to say so. You can ask them to explain again more slowly, use simpler words, or speak in Kinyarwanda or another language you understand better. You can also ask them to write it down or draw it. A good way to check is to repeat back in your own words what you heard. You have the right to understand your own health care.

title: Asking for a female or male provider
answer: Many young people feel more comfortable talking to, or being examined by, a provider of the same sex. You can ask politely: is there a female nurse, or a male nurse, I could see? If one is available, the staff will usually try to arrange it. If not, you can ask for another person to be in the room, come back another day, or go to another facility. Your comfort matters.

title: Saying no to a test or treatment
answer: You have the right to agree or say no to any test, examination or treatment after it is explained to you. Health workers should tell you what it is for, how it is done and what could happen if you do not have it. You can ask for time to think or to talk with someone you trust. Saying no to one thing does not mean you lose the right to other care.

title: Why being honest with a health worker matters
answer: Health workers can only help you properly if they know what is really going on. Being honest about your symptoms, your periods, sex, medicines you have taken or anything that happened helps them choose the right tests and care. They are there to help, not to punish or report you for having sex. What you share should be kept private. If a question feels hard, you can say: this is difficult for me to talk about.

title: Questions to ask about medicine you are given
answer: When a health worker gives you medicine, it is good to ask: what is it for, how and when do I take it, for how many days, what should I avoid, what side effects can happen, and when should I come back. Ask what to do if you forget to take it. Finish the full course if told to, even if you feel better. If something worries you later, go back or call 114.

title: What to bring to the health centre
answer: When you go to a health centre, it helps to bring your mutuelle card if you have one, any referral letter, health booklet or old results, and any medicine you are taking. You may also want your list of questions, a pen and a little water or food if the wait is long. If you do not have a mutuelle card or documents with you, still go, especially if you need urgent care.

title: Why follow-up visits matter
answer: Sometimes a health worker asks you to come back on a certain date. Follow-up visits are used to check results, see if treatment worked, give the next dose of a method such as an injection, or check on a pregnancy. Missing them can mean a problem is not fully treated or your protection runs out. If you cannot make the date, go as soon as you can or tell the health centre.

title: Why health workers ask personal questions
answer: Nurses and doctors may ask personal questions, such as about your periods, sexual activity, partners or condom use. They are not being nosy or judging you. These answers help them understand your risks, choose the right tests and give you the right method or treatment. You can ask why they need to know. If a question makes you uncomfortable, you can say so, and they should explain.

title: When the health worker knows your family
answer: In small communities, the nurse may know your parents or neighbours. Health workers must still keep your information private, whoever they know. If you are worried, you can tell them: I am worried because you know my family, can I trust that this stays private? If you still feel uncomfortable, you can ask to see a different provider, call 114, or visit another facility.

title: Fear of being seen at the clinic
answer: Many young people worry that someone will see them at the health centre and guess why. Remember that people go to health centres for many reasons, like malaria, vaccines, check-ups or visiting someone. Nobody needs to know why you are there. You can go with a friend, go to a youth centre or youth corner, or visit another facility. Your health is more important than other people's opinions.

title: When a health worker is rude to you
answer: You deserve to be treated with respect at every health facility. If a health worker shouts at you, ignores you, insults you or makes fun of you, it is not your fault. Stay calm if you can, and say clearly what you need. You can ask to see another provider or speak to the person in charge of the facility. Please do not give up on your health; most health workers want to help.

title: Asking to see a different provider
answer: If you feel uncomfortable with a nurse or doctor, you can politely ask to see someone else. You do not need to give a long reason. You can say: I would feel more comfortable talking to another nurse, please. If no one else is available that day, you can come back another time or go to another health facility. You have the right to feel safe and respected.

title: Making a complaint at a health facility
answer: If you had a bad experience, you can speak to the person in charge, such as the head of the health centre or hospital manager. Explain calmly what happened, when, and who was involved, and say what you would like to change. You can bring a parent, teacher or trusted adult with you. Many facilities also have a suggestion box. Complaints help improve services for other young people too.

title: Being refused a service because of your age
answer: Young people have a right to SRH information and care. If you are told you are too young for a service, ask politely why, and which service you can get. Some services may have age rules, but you should still get information, counselling and referral. For example, in Rwanda young people aged 12 and above can consent to HIV testing themselves. If you feel unfairly refused, ask for another provider, the person in charge, or call 114.

title: Being asked for money or favours for care
answer: No health worker should ask you for a bribe, a gift, sex or any favour in exchange for care. That is wrong and against the rules. You should only pay official charges, and many SRH services at public facilities are free or low cost. If this happens, do not agree. Tell a trusted adult, the person in charge of the facility, or call 3512 if anything sexual was asked of you.

title: When a health worker behaves sexually toward you
answer: A health worker must never touch you in a sexual way, make sexual comments or ask you for a relationship. Any examination should be explained first and done only with your agreement. If a health worker behaves sexually toward you, it is not your fault. Leave if you feel unsafe, tell a trusted adult, and report it to the facility manager, the police on 3512, or 116 if you are a child.

title: When a health worker shares your information
answer: Health workers must keep your health information private. If you find out that a nurse, doctor or other staff member told people about your visit, test results or problem without your permission, that is wrong. You can talk to the person in charge of the facility, with a trusted adult if you like. It is not your fault, and you still have the right to go on getting care.

title: Being judged for being sexually active
answer: Some health workers may share personal opinions about young people having sex, but their job is to give you correct information and care, not to judge you. You have the right to services whether or not you are married or sexually active. If a provider lectures you, you can say: I came for help and information. If the judgement continues, ask for another provider or speak to the person in charge.

title: Will the nurse tell my parents
answer: In general, health workers keep what young people tell them private and do not call parents just because you asked about SRH or got a service. They may encourage you to talk with a parent or trusted adult, because family support can help. They might need to involve others if your life or safety is in danger, and they should explain this to you. You can ask the nurse at the start what stays private.

title: Who can see your medical records
answer: Your medical record or health booklet holds information about your visits, tests and treatment. It should only be seen by the health workers caring for you. Staff must not show it to other people without your permission, except in special situations allowed by the rules, such as some legal cases. If you carry a health booklet, keep it in a safe place, since others at home could read it.

title: When a health worker may need to share information
answer: Health workers keep most things private, but there are a few situations where they may need to involve others to protect you or someone else. For example, if you are being abused, if your life is in danger, or if you might seriously harm yourself. Even then, a good health worker will explain what they need to do, who they will tell and why, and will try to include you in the decision.

title: Talking to a school nurse or school health worker
answer: If your school has a nurse, health worker or school health club, they can be a helpful first person to talk to about periods, puberty, worries or symptoms. They should keep your questions private and treat you with respect. They can also refer you to the health centre. If something is very serious, such as abuse, they may need to involve others to protect you, and they should explain this to you.

title: Using mutuelle and keeping your visit private
answer: Using your family's mutuelle card helps pay for care, but some young people worry the family will find out about the visit. Health workers should still keep the reason for your visit private. Many SRH services at public facilities, such as condoms, family planning and HIV testing, are free or low cost. If privacy worries you, ask the nurse at the start how your visit will be recorded.

title: Will my partner be told my results
answer: Your test results are yours, and health workers should not tell your boyfriend, girlfriend, husband or wife without your agreement. For some infections, like HIV or other STIs, it is important that partners get tested and treated too. A counsellor can help you plan how to tell your partner, or offer ways to inform them safely. If you fear violence from your partner, tell the health worker.

title: Will my school find out about my clinic visit
answer: Health facilities do not usually contact schools about a student's visit, and your teachers do not have a right to your health information. If you need a note to explain why you missed class, you can ask the nurse for one that does not give private details. If you are in boarding school and need permission to go out, you can simply say you need to go to the health centre.

title: Going to a health centre without your parents
answer: Young people can go to a health centre on their own to get SRH information, counselling and many services. You do not need a parent to ask questions or learn about your body. For some services, the rules may depend on your age, and the nurse will explain this. Going with a parent or trusted adult can be helpful, but if you cannot, you can still go and ask for help.

title: HIV testing for children under 12
answer: For children under 12, a parent or guardian usually needs to give consent for an HIV test. If you are younger than 12 and worried about HIV, talk to a trusted adult, such as a parent, relative, teacher or community health worker, who can go with you to the health centre. You can also call 114 or 116 for advice. Health workers will support you kindly.

title: Getting SRH information without permission
answer: You do not need anyone's permission to get correct information about your body, puberty, relationships and sexual health. Learning about these things is part of your right to information and to health. You can ask a health worker, teacher, community health worker, peer educator or a trusted adult, read reliable materials, or call 114. Having information helps you make safe, healthy choices.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Not sure if you need a parent's consent
answer: Rules about age and consent can be different for different services, and they can change. If you are not sure whether you need a parent's permission, ask the nurse at the health centre or call 114 before you go. Even if a service needs consent, you can still get information, counselling and support. A health worker can also help you think about how to talk to a parent or another trusted adult.

title: Going with a trusted adult who is not your parent
answer: If you cannot talk to your parents, another trusted adult can support you at the health centre, such as an aunt, uncle, older sibling, teacher, godparent, mentor or community health worker. Choose someone who is kind, keeps things private and respects your choices. They can help you feel calm, ask questions with you and help you get there. You can still speak to the nurse alone if you wish.

title: What informed consent means
answer: Informed consent means you agree to a test or treatment after the health worker has clearly explained what it is, why it is needed, the benefits, the risks, other options and what happens if you say no. You should be free to ask questions and to decide without pressure. Consent can be withdrawn: you can change your mind at any time. Your agreement should be real, not forced.

title: How parents can support a child's access to services
answer: As a parent, you can help your child stay healthy by showing that health questions are normal. Tell them where the health centre and community health worker are, that health workers are there to help, and that they can come to you without being punished. Offer to go with them, but respect that they may want to talk to a nurse alone. A child who feels supported is more likely to seek care early.

title: What mutuelle de sante is
answer: Mutuelle de sante is Rwanda's community-based health insurance. Families pay a yearly contribution, and in return members pay only a small part of the cost when they get care at public health facilities. It helps people get health care without large costs. Most Rwandans are members. If you are not sure whether you are covered, ask your parents, your sector office or your health centre.

title: How mutuelle de sante works
answer: With mutuelle, your household pays a yearly contribution for each member. When you get care, you show your mutuelle card and pay a small share of the cost, often called the ticket moderateur, while mutuelle pays the rest. To get the most from it, start at your health centre and follow referrals to the hospital. Contribution amounts depend on rules set by the government, so ask your sector office for details.

title: Who is covered by family mutuelle
answer: Mutuelle is usually paid per household, and each household member who is paid for is covered. Children and young people are normally covered under their family's membership. If you are not sure whether your name is included, ask your parents or guardian, or check at your sector office or health centre. If you live away from your family, ask the sector office how you can be covered.

title: When your family has no mutuelle
answer: If your family does not have mutuelle this year, you can still go to a health facility. Many SRH services at public facilities, like condoms, family planning and HIV testing, are free or low cost. For other care you may need to pay the full price, so ask about costs first. Talk to your sector office or social affairs officer, who can explain options for families who struggle to pay. In an emergency, always seek care.

title: Are SRH services free at public facilities
answer: Many SRH services at public health facilities in Rwanda are free or low cost. For example, condoms, family planning counselling and methods, and HIV testing are usually offered free, and care after sexual violence is free. Some other care may have a small charge, which mutuelle can help with. Prices can change, so if you are worried about cost, ask at reception or call 114 before you go.

title: Asking about costs before care
answer: It is okay to ask how much something costs before you receive it. You can say: before we start, can you tell me if there is a charge? Ask whether mutuelle covers it, and if there are cheaper or free options. At private clinics and pharmacies, prices are often higher, so asking first helps you avoid surprises. Never let cost stop you from getting emergency care.

title: Lost or forgotten mutuelle card
answer: If you lost or forgot your mutuelle card, tell the staff at the health facility. They may be able to check your membership in their system. To replace a lost card, ask at your sector office or health centre what to do. If you need urgent care, do not delay because of a missing card; go to the facility and explain.

title: When money worries stop you seeking care
answer: Worry about money should not stop you from looking after your health. Many SRH services at public health facilities, such as condoms, family planning and HIV testing, are free or low cost. Talk to the nurse about your situation; they may suggest cheaper options. Your community health worker or sector social affairs officer may know about support. If something is serious or urgent, go first and sort out payment later.

title: What the 114 line is for
answer: 114 is a free health information line run by Rwanda Biomedical Centre (RBC). You can call it to ask health questions, including about HIV, STIs, contraception and other SRH topics, and to find out where to get services. It is a good number to call if you are unsure where to go or want advice before visiting a health centre. In an emergency, call 912 or 112.

title: What the 912 line is for
answer: 912 is the number to call for an ambulance in Rwanda. Use it for medical emergencies, such as very heavy bleeding, someone fainting or not waking, severe pain, trouble breathing, a serious injury, or a pregnant woman with danger signs. Stay calm, say where you are and what is happening, and follow their advice until help arrives.

title: What happens when you call a helpline
answer: When you call a helpline, a trained person will answer, listen and ask a few questions to understand what is happening and how they can help. They may give advice, tell you where to get services, or send help if you are in danger. You can take your time, cry or pause. Share what you feel comfortable sharing, but give your location if you need urgent help.

title: Calling a helpline for a friend
answer: Yes, you can call a helpline for a friend, a sibling or another child you are worried about. Explain what you know, where they are and whether they are in danger now. You do not need to have all the facts. It is good to tell your friend that you want to get them help, but if they are in danger, call even if they are unsure. Look after your own safety too.

title: Getting help when you have no phone
answer: If you do not have a phone, you can still get help. Ask a trusted adult, teacher, neighbour or friend to let you use theirs, or to call for you. You can also go in person to a health centre, community health worker, police station, your village or sector leaders, or an Isange One Stop Centre. In an emergency, ask anyone nearby to call 112 or 912.

title: Feeling nervous to call a helpline
answer: It is normal to feel nervous before calling a helpline. The people who answer are trained to listen kindly and they talk to many young people. You can start with something simple, like: I need some advice, or I am worried about something. You can write down what you want to say first, or ask a trusted friend to sit with you. Making the call is a brave step.

title: Judging if SRH information online is reliable
answer: To check if SRH information online is reliable, ask: who wrote it, and are they a health organisation such as the Ministry of Health, RBC, WHO or UNICEF? Is it recent? Does it use facts rather than fear or jokes? Is someone trying to sell you something? Does it agree with what health workers say? If you are not sure, do not act on it; ask a nurse or call 114.

title: Trusted sources of SRH information
answer: Trusted sources of SRH information include health workers at health centres, community health workers, school nurses and trained teachers, the 114 health line, and materials from the Rwanda Ministry of Health, RBC, WHO, UNICEF and UNFPA. Trained peer educators can also help. Friends, social media and songs may sometimes be right, but they often mix facts with myths, so check what you hear with a trusted source.

title: Checking a WhatsApp health message before sharing
answer: Many health messages forwarded on WhatsApp or social media are false, such as claims that a method causes infertility or that a herb cures HIV. Before you believe or share one, check who created it, whether it names a trusted source, and whether a health worker agrees. If you cannot check it, do not forward it. Sharing false health messages can scare people away from care that keeps them safe.

title: Influencers selling health products
answer: Some social media influencers and online sellers promote products like pills to enlarge body parts, creams to make the vagina tighter, teas to prevent pregnancy or medicines to cure STIs. These are often untested, useless or harmful, and they make money from your worries. Health claims that sound too good to be true usually are. Talk to a health worker before using any product for your body.

title: Pornography is not sex education
answer: Pornography is made to entertain and make money, not to teach. It often shows sex that is unrealistic, without condoms or consent, and bodies that do not look like most people's. Learning from it can create false ideas about what sex, bodies and relationships should be like, and can lead to pressure and unsafe choices. For correct information, use trusted sources like health workers, teachers and reliable materials.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Buying SRH medicines online or from social media sellers
answer: Medicines sold through social media, WhatsApp or unknown websites can be fake, expired, the wrong strength or dangerous. You cannot check where they came from, and some sellers take money and send nothing. This is especially risky for medicines claiming to cure STIs, prevent or end pregnancy, or boost sex. Get medicines only from a health facility or registered pharmacy, after talking to a health worker.

title: Asking a health worker to check something you read
answer: If you read or hear something about SRH that worries or confuses you, it is a good idea to ask a health worker about it. You can say: I read online that... is it true? Nurses, community health workers and the 114 line are used to these questions and will not laugh at you. Checking first can stop you from making a choice based on a myth.

title: Searching symptoms online cannot diagnose you
answer: Searching your symptoms online can give you ideas, but it cannot tell you what you really have. Many different problems have similar signs, and the internet often shows the worst possibilities, which can scare you, or tells you it is nothing when it needs care. Only a health worker who can talk with you, examine you if needed and do tests can find the cause. Use online information as a reason to get checked.

title: Health advice from friends
answer: Friends can be a great support, and it is good to talk with them. But friends may share things they heard that are not true, like myths about periods, condoms or contraception. Before you act on a friend's advice about your body or health, check it with a trusted source, like a health worker, a trained teacher or the 114 line. You can then share the correct facts with your friends too.

title: Keeping your privacy when searching SRH online
answer: If you share a phone or computer, others may see what you searched or read. To protect your privacy, you can use a private or incognito browser window, clear your search history, log out of accounts and avoid saving private photos or messages. Do not share personal details or photos with strangers online. Learning about your health is nothing to be ashamed of, but you have the right to privacy.

title: Scary stories online about contraception
answer: You may see scary stories online claiming that contraception causes infertility, cancer or birth defects. Most of these are myths or personal stories that are not the full picture. Modern contraceptive methods are well studied and safe for most young people, though some people get side effects. If a story worries you, do not stop or avoid a method on your own; talk with a health worker who can explain the facts.

title: Sharing your health problem in group chats
answer: It can feel helpful to ask friends in a group chat about a health problem, but messages and photos can be screenshotted and shared with many people. Never send photos of your private parts, even to ask for advice. For personal health questions, it is safer to talk to one trusted person, a health worker, or call 114. Protecting your privacy protects your dignity and safety.

title: Why health myths are harmful
answer: Health myths can cause real harm. They can stop people from using condoms or contraception, from getting tested, or from going to a health centre early. They can lead people to use dangerous remedies, and they can create stigma against people living with HIV or girls who have periods. Learning correct facts and gently correcting myths when you hear them helps protect you and your community.

title: Myth: asking about sex means you are having it
answer: Some people think that a young person who asks about sex, condoms or contraception must already be having sex or be badly behaved. This is a myth. Asking questions shows you are curious, responsible and want to make good decisions. Many young people ask to understand their bodies, to help a friend, or to be ready for the future. You deserve honest answers without being judged.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What comprehensive sexuality education is
answer: Comprehensive sexuality education, or CSE, is teaching that helps young people learn correct, age-appropriate information about their bodies, puberty, relationships, values, consent, gender, health and rights. It also builds skills like communicating, making decisions and saying no. Its goal is to help young people stay healthy, safe and respectful, and to make good choices at each stage of life.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What CSE covers in Rwandan schools
answer: In Rwanda, comprehensive sexuality education is part of the school curriculum and is taught through subjects such as biology and social studies, and through school clubs. Topics include body changes during puberty, menstruation, reproduction, relationships and values, gender equality, preventing pregnancy, HIV and other STIs, avoiding violence and abuse, and where to get help. Lessons are planned to match each age.

title: Does sexuality education encourage early sex
answer: No. Research reviewed by UNESCO shows that good sexuality education does not make young people start sex earlier or have more sex. Instead, it can help young people delay their first sex, have fewer partners and use condoms or contraception when they do have sex. Correct information and skills help young people make safer choices, while silence and myths leave them at more risk.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Why CSE is taught in schools
answer: Schools teach comprehensive sexuality education because young people need correct information before they face changes and choices. Many young people do not get this information at home, and myths from friends and the internet can be harmful. CSE helps reduce early pregnancy, HIV, STIs and violence, and supports respect between girls and boys. Schools can reach many young people with accurate, age-appropriate lessons.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Age-appropriate CSE at different ages
answer: Sexuality education starts early and grows with the child. Young children learn simple things, like names of body parts, families, friendship and that no one should touch them in a way that feels wrong. Older children learn about puberty and periods. Teenagers learn more about relationships, consent, pregnancy, HIV and STIs. Information is given in a way that suits each age, so children are not overwhelmed.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: How parents can work with schools on CSE
answer: Parents are a child's first teachers, and schools work best when families are involved. You can ask the school what topics are covered and see materials, attend parents' meetings, and talk at home about what your child learns. Your child can bring questions home, and you can add your family's values to the facts. Working together, parents and teachers give children a consistent, caring message.

title: CSE, culture, values and religion
answer: Comprehensive sexuality education respects culture and values. It teaches facts and also encourages respect, responsibility, kindness and healthy relationships, which are shared by most cultures and religions. It does not tell young people to have sex. Families and faith communities can add their own values, and many religious leaders support giving young people correct information to keep them safe.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: When a CSE lesson makes you uncomfortable
answer: It is normal to feel shy or uncomfortable in sexuality education lessons, especially at first. Many classmates feel the same. If a lesson brings up something painful, such as abuse or a hard experience, you can quietly tell the teacher, school counsellor or a trusted adult. You can also ask questions privately after class. Your feelings matter, and support is available.

title: Asking questions anonymously in class
answer: Many teachers use a question box, where students write questions on paper without their name and the teacher answers them for the whole class. This lets you ask about anything without feeling embarrassed. If your class does not have one, you can suggest it to your teacher, write a question privately, or ask after class. Every question is a good question.

title: CSE for students with disabilities
answer: Young people with disabilities have the same right to sexuality education as everyone else. They go through puberty, have feelings and relationships, and need to know how to stay safe and healthy. Lessons can be adapted, for example using sign language, braille, pictures, simple words or more time. If a student is missing out, parents and teachers can ask the school how to make lessons accessible.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: What is chlamydia
answer: Chlamydia is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in the world. It is caused by bacteria and passes from one person to another during sex. Many young people who have it feel completely fine, so they do not know they have it. The good news is that chlamydia can be cured with the right medicine from a health worker. If you think you may have been exposed, visit the nearest health center or youth corner for a test.

title: How chlamydia spreads
answer: Chlamydia spreads through vaginal, anal or oral sex without a condom with someone who has the infection. It can pass even if the penis does not fully enter or there is no ejaculation, because the bacteria live in body fluids and genital areas. A mother can also pass it to her baby during birth. You cannot get chlamydia from hugging, sharing plates, toilet seats or swimming. Using condoms every time you have sex greatly lowers the risk.

title: Chlamydia signs in girls and women
answer: Most girls and women with chlamydia have no signs at all. When signs do appear, they can include unusual vaginal discharge, a burning feeling when urinating, bleeding between periods or after sex, pain during sex, or pain in the lower belly. These signs can also be caused by other infections, so only a test at a health center can tell what is going on. If you notice any of them, please see a nurse soon.

title: Chlamydia signs in boys and men
answer: Many boys and men with chlamydia notice nothing. Some get a clear or cloudy discharge from the tip of the penis, burning or pain when urinating, itching inside the penis, or pain and swelling in one testicle. Infection in the anus or throat often has no signs. Other infections can cause the same problems, so the only way to know is a test at a health center. Testicle pain should always be checked quickly.

title: Chlamydia often has no symptoms
answer: Yes, chlamydia is often called a silent infection. Most women and many men who have it feel healthy and see nothing unusual. Even without symptoms, the infection can still be passed to partners and can slowly harm the body, especially a girl's womb and tubes. This is why testing matters if you have had sex without a condom or have a new partner, even when you feel fine. Ask for a test at a health center or youth corner.

title: Testing for chlamydia
answer: Testing for chlamydia is simple and usually does not hurt. Depending on what is available, a health worker may ask for a urine sample or take a swab from the vagina, cervix, penis, throat or anus. In some places, a health worker may decide on treatment based on your signs if lab tests are not available. Ask at your nearest health center or youth corner, or call 114 for free advice on where to go.

title: Is chlamydia curable
answer: Yes. Chlamydia can be cured with antibiotics given by a health worker. It is important to take all the medicine exactly as told, avoid sex until you and your partner have both finished treatment, and make sure your partner is treated too, or you can catch it again. Being cured once does not protect you in the future. Do not buy medicine on your own; get the right treatment at a health center.

title: Chlamydia complications
answer: If chlamydia is not treated, it can spread in a girl's body to the womb and fallopian tubes and cause pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). This can lead to long-lasting belly pain, difficulty getting pregnant, or a pregnancy growing outside the womb, which is dangerous. In boys it can cause painful swelling of the testicles. Untreated chlamydia also makes it easier to get HIV. Early testing and treatment prevent these problems.

title: Chlamydia in pregnancy and the baby
answer: A pregnant woman with chlamydia can pass it to her baby during birth. The baby may then get an eye infection or a lung infection (pneumonia). Chlamydia in pregnancy may also raise the risk of the baby being born early. The infection can be safely treated during pregnancy with medicine chosen by a health worker. If you are pregnant and worried about any STI, tell the nurse at your antenatal visit.

title: What is gonorrhoea
answer: Gonorrhoea (sometimes spelled gonorrhea) is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by bacteria. It can infect the penis, vagina, cervix, anus, throat and sometimes the eyes. Some people notice discharge or pain when urinating, but many, especially girls, have no signs. Gonorrhoea can be cured with the right medicine from a health worker, but it is becoming harder to treat because some bacteria resist medicines. Get tested at a health center if you are worried.

title: How gonorrhoea spreads
answer: Gonorrhoea passes during vaginal, anal or oral sex without a condom with a person who has the infection. It can spread even if there is no ejaculation. A mother can pass it to her baby during birth. It does not spread through hugging, sharing cups, handshakes or toilet seats. Using a condom correctly every time you have sex, and getting tested with your partner, lowers the risk a lot.

title: Gonorrhoea signs in boys and men
answer: Boys and men with gonorrhoea often notice signs a few days after sex. These can include a thick white, yellow or green discharge from the penis, burning or pain when urinating, and sometimes pain or swelling in a testicle. Some men have no signs at all. Other infections can look the same, so only a test at a health center can tell. Please go soon, and avoid sex until you are checked.

title: Gonorrhoea signs in girls and women
answer: Many girls and women with gonorrhoea have no signs, or the signs are mild and easy to confuse with other problems. Possible signs include more vaginal discharge than usual, burning when urinating, bleeding between periods or after sex, and pain in the lower belly. If it spreads to the womb and tubes, it can cause fever and strong belly pain. Only a test at a health center can tell what the cause is.

title: Testing for gonorrhoea
answer: A gonorrhoea test may use a urine sample or a swab from the place that could be infected, such as the cervix, penis, throat or anus. In some health facilities, the nurse may treat based on your signs if a lab test is not available. Tell the health worker honestly what kind of sex you had so they test the right places. Your information should be kept private. Ask at your nearest health center or youth corner.

title: Is gonorrhoea curable
answer: Yes, gonorrhoea can be cured with the right antibiotics from a health worker. But the bacteria are learning to resist many medicines, so it is very important to get treatment at a health facility rather than buying pills on your own. Take all the medicine as told, avoid sex until treatment is finished, and make sure your partner is treated too. If signs do not go away, go back to the health center.

title: Gonorrhoea complications
answer: Untreated gonorrhoea can cause serious problems. In girls and women, it can spread to the womb and tubes (PID), causing long-term pain, trouble getting pregnant, or a pregnancy outside the womb. In boys and men, it can cause painful swelling of the testicles and, rarely, affect fertility. Rarely, it spreads to the blood and joints. It also makes HIV easier to catch. Early testing and treatment prevent these problems.

title: Gonorrhoea in pregnancy and newborn eyes
answer: A pregnant woman with gonorrhoea can pass it to her baby during birth. The baby can get a serious eye infection that, without quick treatment, may damage the eyes and even cause blindness. Gonorrhoea in pregnancy may also lead to early birth. Gonorrhoea can be treated safely during pregnancy. If a newborn has swollen, red eyes with pus, take the baby to a health facility right away.

title: Gonorrhoea in the throat or anus
answer: Gonorrhoea can infect the throat after oral sex and the anus after anal sex. Infection in these places often causes no signs. Sometimes the throat is sore, or the anus has itching, discharge, pain or bleeding. Because these infections are easy to miss, tell the health worker about the kinds of sex you have had so they can test the right places. Using condoms for oral and anal sex lowers the risk.

title: What is syphilis
answer: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by bacteria. It develops in stages. It often starts with a painless sore, then may cause a rash, and then can hide in the body for years without signs. If it is never treated, it can later damage the brain, nerves, eyes and heart. Syphilis can be found with a simple blood test and cured with the right medicine from a health worker.

title: How syphilis spreads
answer: Syphilis spreads mainly through vaginal, anal or oral sex, when skin or mucous membranes touch a syphilis sore or rash. The sores can be hidden inside the vagina, anus or mouth, so a person may not know they have one. A pregnant woman can also pass syphilis to her baby. It does not spread through toilet seats, sharing clothes or eating together. Condoms lower the risk when they cover the sore area.

title: First stage of syphilis: painless sore
answer: The first sign of syphilis is often a single sore, called a chancre. It usually appears around 3 weeks after infection where the bacteria entered, such as the penis, vagina, anus or mouth. It is usually firm, round and painless, so many people do not notice it. The sore heals on its own in a few weeks, but the infection stays in the body. Any genital sore should be checked at a health center.

title: Second stage of syphilis: rash
answer: If syphilis is not treated, a second stage can start weeks after the sore. The most common sign is a rash that does not usually itch, often on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, but it can be anywhere. Some people also get fever, tiredness, swollen glands, sore throat, patchy hair loss or sores in the mouth. These signs go away by themselves, but the infection does not. Get tested at a health center.

title: Hidden and late stages of syphilis
answer: After the early signs fade, syphilis can stay hidden in the body for many years with no symptoms. This is called latent syphilis. In some people who are never treated, it later causes late (tertiary) syphilis, which can seriously damage the brain, nerves, eyes, heart, blood vessels and bones. This damage can be life-threatening. Testing and treatment at any stage stops the infection from going further, so getting checked is always worth it.

title: Testing for syphilis
answer: Syphilis is usually found with a blood test, often a quick finger-prick rapid test that gives results the same day. Some rapid tests check for HIV and syphilis together. A health worker may also look at any sores. Because some syphilis tests can stay positive even after past treatment, the health worker will explain what your result means. Ask for a syphilis test at your nearest health center or youth corner.

title: Is syphilis curable
answer: Yes, syphilis can be cured with antibiotics from a health worker, most often given as an injection. Early treatment is simple and stops the infection from causing more harm. Treatment cannot always undo damage that late syphilis has already done to organs, which is why early testing matters. Avoid sex until the health worker says treatment is complete, and make sure partners are tested and treated too.

title: Congenital syphilis
answer: Congenital syphilis happens when a pregnant woman with syphilis passes it to her baby in the womb. It can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, early birth, low birth weight, death of the newborn, or babies born with infections and lifelong health problems. The good news is that it can be prevented: when pregnant women are tested early and treated, the baby is protected. Partners should also be tested and treated.

title: Syphilis test in antenatal care
answer: During antenatal care, pregnant women in Rwanda are offered tests including HIV and syphilis, often with a quick finger-prick test. This is done for every pregnant woman, not because anyone is suspected of anything. If the test is positive, treatment during pregnancy protects both mother and baby, and the partner is invited for testing and treatment too. Starting antenatal visits early in pregnancy gives the best protection.

title: Follow-up after syphilis treatment
answer: After treatment for syphilis, a health worker may ask you to come back for blood tests over the following months to make sure the treatment worked. Some syphilis tests stay positive for a long time, even for life, after the infection is cured, so a positive rapid test does not always mean a new infection. Keep your follow-up visits, avoid sex until told it is safe, and ask the nurse to explain your results.

title: What is genital herpes
answer: Genital herpes is a common infection caused by the herpes simplex virus. It can cause painful blisters or sores on or around the genitals or anus, but many people have very mild signs or none at all. The virus stays in the body for life and can cause sores to come back from time to time. There is no cure yet, but medicine from a health worker can make outbreaks shorter and less frequent.

title: How herpes spreads
answer: Herpes spreads through skin-to-skin contact with the genitals, anus or mouth of someone who has the virus, during vaginal, anal or oral sex or close genital touching. It spreads most easily when sores are present, but can also pass when there are no sores. Oral herpes (cold sores) can be passed to the genitals through oral sex. Condoms lower the risk but do not cover all skin. Avoid sex when sores are present.

title: Signs of genital herpes
answer: Signs of genital herpes can include tingling, itching or burning on the skin, followed by small painful blisters that break into sores, then scab and heal. The sores may be on the penis, vulva, vagina, anus, buttocks or thighs. Some people also feel flu-like, with fever or swollen glands, especially the first time. Many people have mild or no signs. Only a health worker can tell what is causing a sore.

title: First herpes outbreak and repeat outbreaks
answer: The first herpes outbreak is often the worst, with more sores and sometimes fever or body aches. After that, the virus rests in the nerves. Some people get repeat outbreaks, which are usually milder and shorter, and often happen less over time. Stress, illness, tiredness or friction can trigger them. Many people learn the early tingling signs. A health worker can offer medicine to help if outbreaks are frequent or painful.

title: Is herpes curable
answer: There is no cure for herpes yet; the virus stays in the body for life. But herpes is manageable. Medicine from a health worker can shorten outbreaks, ease pain and lower the chance of passing it to a partner. Many people have few or no outbreaks after the first. During an outbreak, keeping the area clean and dry and wearing loose clothes can help. People with herpes can have healthy relationships and lives.

title: Herpes spreading without sores
answer: Yes, herpes can spread even when no sores are visible. Sometimes the virus is active on the skin without causing signs, and it can pass during sex. This is how many people get herpes from a partner who did not know they had it. The risk is highest when sores are present, so avoid sex then. Using condoms and, for some people, medicine from a health worker lowers the risk at other times.

title: Cold sores and genital herpes
answer: Cold sores, the small blisters around the lips, are usually caused by herpes simplex virus type 1. Many people get it in childhood from kisses. The same virus can be passed to the genitals through oral sex, causing genital herpes. Avoid kissing or oral sex when you or a partner has a cold sore, and do not share lip balm or cups during an outbreak. Cold sores are common and not a reason for shame.

title: Herpes in pregnancy and birth
answer: Most women with herpes have healthy babies. The biggest risk to a baby is when a woman gets herpes for the first time late in pregnancy, because the baby can catch it during birth, which can be very serious. If you are pregnant and have ever had genital sores, tell your antenatal nurse or midwife. They can plan care, and sometimes medicine or a different way of giving birth is advised.

title: Telling a partner about herpes
answer: Telling a partner you have herpes before sex can feel scary, but it shows respect and care. Choose a calm, private moment. Explain that herpes is common, often mild, and can be managed, and that you can lower the risk together by avoiding sex during outbreaks, using condoms, and asking a health worker about medicine. Give your partner time to think. A nurse or counsellor at a health center can help you plan what to say.

title: Testing for herpes
answer: Herpes is usually recognised by a health worker looking at the sores, and sometimes by taking a swab from a fresh sore. Blood tests exist but are not used routinely and can be hard to interpret. Testing works best while a sore is present, so go to a health center soon after you notice one. Many other conditions can cause sores, including syphilis, so the health worker may also suggest other tests.

title: What is HPV
answer: HPV (human papillomavirus) is a very common virus passed through skin-to-skin sexual contact. Most sexually active people get it at some point, and most never know because it causes no signs and the body clears it by itself. Some types of HPV cause genital warts. Other types, if they stay for many years, can cause cancer, especially cancer of the cervix. Vaccination and screening protect against these problems.

title: How HPV spreads
answer: HPV spreads through skin-to-skin contact of the genitals, anus or mouth, usually during vaginal, anal or oral sex, and sometimes through close genital touching without penetration. It can pass even when the person has no warts or signs. HPV is so common that most people who have sex will meet it. Condoms lower the risk but do not cover all skin. The HPV vaccine gives strong protection against the most dangerous types.

title: What genital warts look like
answer: Genital warts are small growths on or around the penis, scrotum, vulva, vagina, anus or groin, caused by some types of HPV. They can be flat or raised, single or in groups, skin-coloured, pink or darker, and sometimes look like a small cauliflower. They are usually painless but may itch. They are not dangerous, but they can be upsetting. Other harmless bumps can look similar, so let a health worker check.

title: Treatment for genital warts
answer: Genital warts can be treated by a health worker, for example by freezing them or using special treatments applied at the clinic or at home as instructed. Sometimes warts also go away on their own. Treatment removes the warts but may not remove the virus, so they can come back. Never try to cut, burn or use acid, wart products for hands or other home remedies on your genitals, as this can cause serious injury.

title: Does HPV go away by itself
answer: Yes, most of the time. In most people, the immune system clears HPV naturally within about one to two years, without any treatment and often without the person ever knowing they had it. In a small number of people, high-risk types of HPV stay for many years, and that is when cell changes that can lead to cancer may develop. This is why vaccination and regular cervical screening for women are important.

title: HPV and cervical cancer
answer: Almost all cervical cancer is caused by long-lasting infection with high-risk types of HPV. When these types stay in the cervix (the opening of the womb) for many years, they can slowly change the cells, and these changes can turn into cancer if not found and treated. This process usually takes 10 to 20 years or more. HPV vaccination before sexual activity and regular screening later in life can prevent most cervical cancer.

title: HPV in boys and men
answer: Boys and men get HPV too, and can pass it to partners. Most have no signs and clear the virus naturally. Some get genital warts on the penis, scrotum, anus or groin. Rarely, long-lasting HPV can cause cancers of the penis, anus or throat. There is no routine HPV test for men. Using condoms and having fewer partners lowers the risk. If you notice any growths, see a health worker.

title: HPV testing
answer: An HPV test checks for high-risk types of HPV in cells from the cervix. It is used for cervical cancer screening in adult women, not for teenagers, because HPV in young people usually goes away by itself. The sample can be taken by a health worker or, in some programmes, by the woman herself. There is no routine HPV test for men. Ask at a health center about screening when you reach the recommended age.

title: Condoms and HPV
answer: Condoms lower the chance of getting HPV and genital warts, but they do not give full protection, because HPV can live on skin that a condom does not cover, like the scrotum, vulva or thighs. Using condoms every time is still very worth it, because they also protect against many other STIs, HIV and pregnancy. Combining condoms with the HPV vaccine and fewer partners gives the best protection.

title: HPV vaccine in Rwandan schools
answer: Rwanda offers the HPV vaccine free to girls, usually around age 12, mainly through schools, with health workers coming to give it. It protects against the HPV types that cause most cervical cancer. Girls who are not in school can get it at a health center. If you are unsure whether you were vaccinated or how many doses you need, ask the school nurse, a health center or a community health worker, or call 114.

title: HPV vaccine safety and side effects
answer: The HPV vaccine is very safe. It has been given to hundreds of millions of people around the world and is closely monitored by WHO. Common side effects are mild and short: a sore, red or swollen arm where the injection was given, headache, mild fever or feeling tired. Some young people feel faint after any injection, so sitting down for a few minutes helps. Serious reactions are very rare.

title: Missed the HPV vaccine at school
answer: If you missed the HPV vaccine at school, for example because you were absent or out of school, you may still be able to get it. Talk to your school nurse or teacher, visit your nearest health center, or ask a community health worker. They can check your records and tell you whether you are eligible and when the next vaccination is. You can also call 114 for free information.

title: Why the HPV vaccine is given young
answer: The HPV vaccine works best when given before a person is ever exposed to HPV, which means before they start any sexual activity. Young people's bodies also make a very strong immune response to the vaccine. Getting it at age 9 to 14 does not mean anyone expects the girl to have sex; it simply protects her for the future, like other childhood vaccines.

title: HPV vaccine and boys
answer: Some countries vaccinate boys against HPV too, but in many countries, including Rwanda, programmes focus on girls because cervical cancer causes the most deaths. When most girls are vaccinated, boys are also indirectly protected because less HPV spreads in the community. Boys can protect themselves and partners by using condoms and limiting partners. Ask a health worker if you want to know about vaccine options for boys.

title: HPV vaccine and fertility myth
answer: No, the HPV vaccine does not cause infertility. Large studies of millions of girls and women have found no link between the vaccine and problems getting pregnant later. In fact, by preventing cervical cancer and its treatment, the vaccine helps protect a woman's ability to have children. Rumours like this spread easily, so it is best to ask a trusted health worker if you have worries.

title: Screening after the HPV vaccine
