answer: Yes, women who had the HPV vaccine still need cervical cancer screening when they reach the recommended age. The vaccine protects against the types of HPV that cause most cervical cancer, but not every type. Screening finds early changes in the cervix so they can be treated before they become cancer. Vaccination when young plus screening as an adult gives the strongest protection.

title: What is cervical cancer
answer: Cervical cancer is a cancer that grows in the cervix, the lower part of the womb that opens into the vagina. It is one of the most common cancers in women in Africa, and almost all cases are caused by long-lasting HPV infection. It usually develops slowly over many years, which gives time to find and treat early changes. It can be prevented through HPV vaccination and regular screening, and treated if found early.

title: Signs of cervical cancer
answer: Early cervical cancer usually has no signs, which is why screening is so important. Later signs can include bleeding between periods, after sex or after menopause, unusual or bad-smelling vaginal discharge, pain during sex, and pain in the lower back or belly. These signs are much more often caused by other problems, but they should always be checked by a health worker at a health center.

title: What is cervical cancer screening
answer: Cervical cancer screening is a check for women with no symptoms, to find early changes in the cervix before they become cancer. It may be an HPV test, a visual check with vinegar (VIA), or a Pap smear. It is quick and done in private by a trained health worker. If early changes are found, they can usually be treated simply, often the same day. Ask your health center about screening when you reach the recommended age.

title: VIA screening
answer: VIA means visual inspection with acetic acid. A trained health worker gently opens the vagina with a small instrument, applies a mild vinegar solution to the cervix, and looks for white areas that may show early cell changes. It takes only a few minutes, and the result is known right away. It may feel a little uncomfortable but should not be painful. If changes are found, treatment can often be given at the same visit.

title: Pap smear
answer: A Pap smear (Pap test) is a cervical screening test. A health worker gently opens the vagina with a small instrument and uses a soft brush to collect a few cells from the cervix. The cells are sent to a laboratory to look for changes that could lead to cancer. It takes a few minutes and may feel slightly uncomfortable. Results come back later, and the health worker will explain what they mean.

title: When to start cervical screening
answer: WHO advises that most women start cervical cancer screening from about age 30, and women living with HIV from about age 25, then repeat it regularly as advised. Teenagers usually do not need screening, because HPV in young people often clears by itself. Your health center will tell you the age and timing used in Rwanda. If you have unusual bleeding or pain at any age, see a health worker without waiting.

title: Lowering the risk of cervical cancer
answer: You can lower your risk of cervical cancer by getting the HPV vaccine when it is offered, going for screening when you reach the recommended age, using condoms, delaying sex and having fewer partners, and not smoking. Women living with HIV have a higher risk, so staying on HIV treatment and getting screened regularly is important. Most cervical cancer can be prevented, so these steps make a real difference.

title: Abnormal cervical screening result
answer: An abnormal or positive screening result does not mean you have cancer. Usually it means HPV or early cell changes were found, which can often be treated before they ever become cancer. The health worker may offer treatment, such as freezing or removing the changed area, sometimes the same day, or may ask you to come back for more tests. Keep all follow-up appointments, and ask questions until you understand.

title: What is trichomoniasis
answer: Trichomoniasis, often called trich, is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by a tiny parasite. It mostly infects the vagina in women and the urethra (the tube inside the penis) in men. Many people have no signs, especially men. It can be easily cured with the right medicine from a health worker. Both partners need treatment at the same time to avoid passing it back and forth.

title: How trichomoniasis spreads
answer: Trichomoniasis spreads mainly during vaginal sex without a condom, and through genital-to-genital contact, with someone who has the infection. It can pass from a man to a woman, a woman to a man, or between women. Because many people have no signs, they can pass it without knowing. It does not spread by hugging or sharing food. Using condoms every time lowers the risk.

title: Trichomoniasis signs in girls and women
answer: Many girls and women with trichomoniasis have no signs. When signs appear, they may include a frothy yellow-green or grey vaginal discharge, often with a strong or fishy smell, itching or soreness around the vagina, burning when urinating, and discomfort during sex. These signs can also come from other infections such as bacterial vaginosis or yeast, so only a test at a health center can tell the cause.

title: Trichomoniasis signs in boys and men
answer: Most boys and men with trichomoniasis have no signs at all, which is why they can pass it on without knowing. Some notice itching or irritation inside the penis, a thin discharge, or burning after urinating or ejaculating. Signs may come and go. Because other infections cause similar signs, only a health worker can tell the cause. If your partner is diagnosed with trich, you need treatment too.

title: Testing and cure for trichomoniasis
answer: Trichomoniasis can be found by testing a swab from the vagina or a urine sample, depending on what the health facility has. Sometimes the nurse treats based on signs. Trich is curable with medicine from a health worker. Take all the medicine, avoid alcohol if the nurse tells you to, avoid sex until you and your partner have both finished treatment, and go back if signs return.

title: Trichomoniasis in pregnancy
answer: Trichomoniasis in pregnancy can raise the chance of the baby being born too early or too small. It can be treated safely during pregnancy with medicine chosen by a health worker. If you are pregnant and notice unusual discharge, itching or burning, tell the nurse at your antenatal visit. Your partner should also be treated so you do not get infected again.

title: What is hepatitis B
answer: Hepatitis B is an infection of the liver caused by a virus. It can cause a short illness, or it can stay in the body for life (chronic hepatitis B), slowly damaging the liver and sometimes leading to liver cancer. Many people have no signs for years. Hepatitis B can be prevented with a safe and effective vaccine, and chronic infection can be controlled with treatment from a health worker.

title: How hepatitis B spreads
answer: Hepatitis B spreads through blood, semen and vaginal fluids. This can happen during sex without a condom, sharing razors, toothbrushes or needles, unsterile tattoos or piercing, and from a mother to her baby at birth. It does not spread through hugging, kissing on the cheek, sharing food or cups, coughing or breastfeeding. The vaccine, condoms and not sharing sharp objects protect you.

title: Signs of hepatitis B
answer: Most people with hepatitis B have no signs for a long time. When signs appear, they can include yellow eyes or skin (jaundice), dark urine, very pale stools, extreme tiredness, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting and belly pain. Signs may appear weeks or months after infection. These signs can come from other illnesses too, so a blood test at a health center is the only way to know.

title: Testing for hepatitis B
answer: Hepatitis B is found with a blood test, often a quick finger-prick test. If it is positive, more blood tests show whether the infection is new or long-lasting and how the liver is doing. Testing is a good idea if you were never vaccinated, if a family member or partner has hepatitis B, or if you are pregnant. Ask at your nearest health center or call 114 to find out where testing is offered.

title: Hepatitis B vaccine
answer: The hepatitis B vaccine is safe and very effective, protecting most people for life. In Rwanda, babies receive it as part of routine childhood vaccines. WHO also recommends a first dose soon after birth. Older children and adults who were never vaccinated may be able to get it; ask a health worker. Being vaccinated against hepatitis B does not protect you from other STIs or HIV, so condoms still matter.

title: Is hepatitis B curable
answer: When adults get hepatitis B, most clear the virus on their own within about six months. If it stays longer, it is called chronic hepatitis B. There is no complete cure for chronic hepatitis B yet, but medicine can control the virus, protect the liver and help people live long, healthy lives. Not everyone needs medicine; a health worker decides based on tests. Regular check-ups are important.

title: Long-term hepatitis B
answer: Chronic hepatitis B means the virus stays in the body for more than six months. This is much more likely when a person is infected as a baby or young child than as an adult. Over many years, chronic hepatitis B can scar the liver (cirrhosis) or cause liver cancer, often without signs until late. Regular check-ups and treatment when needed greatly lower these risks.

title: Hepatitis B in pregnancy and newborn
answer: A pregnant woman with hepatitis B can pass it to her baby, mainly at birth. Babies infected this way very often develop lifelong infection. This can be prevented: pregnant women should be tested, some receive medicine during pregnancy, and the baby should get the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, followed by the routine doses. Mothers with hepatitis B can usually still breastfeed. Talk to your antenatal nurse.

title: Living with hepatitis B
answer: People with hepatitis B can live full lives. Go to regular check-ups, take any medicine exactly as advised, and avoid alcohol, which harms the liver. Do not take herbal or other remedies without asking a health worker, as some damage the liver. Protect others by using condoms, not sharing razors or toothbrushes, and covering cuts. Encourage partners and family to get tested and vaccinated. You can still eat, study and play with others.

title: What is hepatitis C
answer: Hepatitis C is a liver infection caused by a virus. Many people have no signs for years, while the virus slowly damages the liver, sometimes leading to scarring or liver cancer. Unlike hepatitis B, there is no vaccine for hepatitis C. The good news is that today's medicines can cure most people in a few months. A blood test at a health center can show whether you have it.

title: How hepatitis C spreads
answer: Hepatitis C spreads mostly through blood, for example by sharing needles or syringes, unsterile medical, tattoo or piercing tools, sharing razors or toothbrushes, and from mother to baby. It can spread through sex, but this is less common, with higher risk during sex that may cause bleeding, such as anal sex. It does not spread by hugging, kissing, sharing food or breastfeeding.

title: Testing for hepatitis C
answer: Hepatitis C is tested with a blood test, often a quick finger-prick test. If it is positive, a second test checks whether the virus is still active, because some people clear it naturally. Testing is a good idea if you ever shared needles, razors or had unsterile tattoos or piercings, or a family member has it. Rwanda has expanded hepatitis testing; ask at a health center or call 114.

title: Is hepatitis C curable
answer: Yes. Modern medicines taken by mouth for about two to three months can cure more than 9 out of 10 people with hepatitis C. Treatment must be prescribed and followed up by a health worker. Rwanda has worked to make hepatitis C testing and treatment widely available. Being cured does not protect you from getting it again, so keep avoiding shared needles, razors and unsterile tools.

title: What are pubic lice
answer: Pubic lice, sometimes called crabs, are tiny insects that live in pubic hair and suck small amounts of blood. They can also live in other coarse body hair, like armpits, chest or eyebrows. They are different from head lice. Pubic lice are annoying and itchy but not dangerous, and they can be treated. Having them is nothing to be ashamed of; see a health worker for help.

title: How pubic lice spread
answer: Pubic lice spread mainly through close body contact, usually during sex or intimate touching, even without penetration. Less often, they can spread through sharing bedding, towels or clothing that someone with lice has just used. Condoms do not prevent pubic lice because the lice live in hair outside the area a condom covers. They do not come from toilet seats or animals.

title: Signs of pubic lice
answer: The main sign of pubic lice is itching in the pubic area, often worse at night. You may see tiny greyish or brownish insects moving in the hair, or small white eggs (nits) stuck to the hair near the skin. Some people notice small blue spots or tiny drops of blood on their underwear from bites. Scratching can make the skin sore. A health worker can confirm it quickly.

title: Getting rid of pubic lice
answer: Pubic lice are treated with a special lotion or shampoo recommended by a health worker or pharmacist, used exactly as instructed and often repeated after a week. Wash bedding, towels and clothes used in the past few days in hot water and dry them well. Sexual partners need treatment at the same time. Shaving alone does not reliably get rid of them. Never use petrol, kerosene or insecticides on your skin.

title: What is scabies
answer: Scabies is a skin condition caused by tiny mites that burrow under the skin, causing very itchy spots. It is not only an STI: it spreads through any long, close skin contact, such as sleeping in the same bed, within families, schools and boarding schools, and also during sex. Anyone can get it, and it has nothing to do with being dirty. Scabies can be treated.

title: How scabies spreads
answer: Scabies spreads through prolonged skin-to-skin contact with a person who has it, such as sharing a bed, caring for family members, or sexual contact. Brief contact like a handshake rarely spreads it. Less often, it spreads through shared bedding, clothes or towels. Because it spreads easily in homes and dormitories, everyone who has close contact should be treated at the same time.

title: Signs of scabies
answer: The main sign of scabies is strong itching, often worse at night. You may see small red bumps, blisters or thin wavy lines on the skin, often between the fingers, on the wrists, elbows, armpits, waist, buttocks and genitals. On the penis, it can cause itchy lumps. Scratching can cause sores that get infected. Many skin problems look similar, so see a health worker to check.

title: Treating scabies
answer: Scabies is treated with a cream, lotion or sometimes tablets recommended by a health worker. Everyone living closely with you or sexual partners should be treated at the same time, even if they do not itch yet. Wash clothes, bedding and towels in hot water and dry them in the sun. Itching may last a few weeks after treatment; if it continues longer, go back to the health center.

title: What is a vaginal yeast infection
answer: A vaginal yeast infection, also called thrush or candida, happens when a yeast that normally lives in the body grows too much in the vagina. It is very common, and most women get it at least once. It is not usually passed through sex and is not a sign of being dirty. It causes itching and discharge but is not dangerous, and it can be treated.

title: Signs of a yeast infection
answer: Signs of a vaginal yeast infection include strong itching around the vulva and vagina, redness and soreness, a burning feeling when urinating or during sex, and a thick, white discharge that can look like curdled milk, usually without a strong smell. These signs can look like other infections, including STIs. If it is your first time, or the signs keep coming back, see a health worker to check.

title: What causes yeast infections
answer: Yeast infections happen when the normal balance in the vagina changes and yeast grows too much. Things that can trigger this include taking antibiotics, pregnancy, uncontrolled diabetes, a weak immune system, hormonal changes, staying in wet or tight clothes, and washing inside the vagina or using scented soaps. Sometimes there is no clear reason. Yeast infections are not caused by poor morals or being unclean.

title: Is a yeast infection an STI
answer: No, a yeast infection is not considered an STI. It can happen to girls who have never had sex. However, sex can sometimes irritate the vagina and trigger it, and a partner may occasionally get mild itching too. Because yeast infection signs can look like those of STIs, if you have had sex and have new discharge or itching, it is wise to see a health worker.

title: Yeast infection in boys
answer: Boys and men can also get yeast infections, usually on the head of the penis or under the foreskin. Signs include redness, itching, soreness, a white substance under the foreskin and sometimes a rash. It is more likely if the area stays moist, if the person has diabetes, or after antibiotics. Washing gently with water and drying well helps. Other infections look similar, so see a health worker.

title: Preventing yeast infections
answer: To lower the chance of yeast infections, wear clean cotton underwear, change out of wet or sweaty clothes soon, and avoid very tight clothes. Wash the outside of the genitals with clean water only and avoid scented soaps, sprays or douching inside the vagina. Wipe from front to back after using the toilet. Only take antibiotics when a health worker prescribes them. If infections keep coming back, get checked.

title: Treating a yeast infection
answer: Yeast infections are treated with antifungal medicine, such as a cream, vaginal tablet or pill, recommended by a health worker or pharmacist. See a health worker if it is your first time, if you are pregnant, if signs keep coming back, or if treatment does not work, because another infection might be the cause. Do not put yogurt, garlic, herbs or other home remedies inside the vagina.

title: What is bacterial vaginosis
answer: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a very common vaginal condition. It happens when the normal balance of bacteria in the vagina changes and some bacteria grow too much. It is not caused by poor hygiene. Many women with BV have no signs, while others notice a fishy smell. BV is usually not dangerous, but it can raise the risk of some infections, so it is worth getting checked.

title: Signs of bacterial vaginosis
answer: Signs of bacterial vaginosis can include a thin white or grey vaginal discharge and a fishy smell, which may be stronger after sex or during your period. It does not usually cause much itching or soreness. Many women have no signs at all. Trichomoniasis and other infections can cause similar signs, so a health worker needs to check to know what is causing them.

title: What causes bacterial vaginosis
answer: The exact cause of bacterial vaginosis is not fully known. It happens when the healthy bacteria in the vagina decrease and other bacteria increase. Things that make it more likely include washing or douching inside the vagina, using scented soaps, having a new sex partner or several partners, and not using condoms. Girls who have never had sex can also get it.

title: Is bacterial vaginosis an STI
answer: Bacterial vaginosis is not counted as a typical STI, and it can happen to girls who have never had sex. But it is linked to sex: it is more common with new or multiple partners, and condoms can lower the risk. Having BV can also make it easier to catch STIs, including HIV. Male partners usually do not need treatment, but a health worker will advise you.

title: Treating bacterial vaginosis
answer: Bacterial vaginosis can be treated with antibiotics given by a health worker, as tablets or a gel. Finish all the medicine, even if the smell goes away quickly, and avoid alcohol if the health worker tells you to. BV sometimes comes back; if it does, go back to the health center. Avoid douching, scented soaps, or putting anything inside the vagina to remove the smell.

title: What is a urinary tract infection
answer: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection of the parts of the body that make and carry urine, most often the bladder. It is usually caused by bacteria from the bowel getting into the urethra, the tube urine comes out of. UTIs are very common in girls and women because their urethra is short. A UTI is not a sexually transmitted infection, and it can be treated.

title: Signs of a UTI
answer: Signs of a urinary tract infection include burning or pain when urinating, needing to urinate often or urgently but passing only a little, cloudy or bad-smelling urine, blood in the urine, and pain or pressure in the lower belly. STIs can cause some of the same signs, so see a health worker, who may test your urine to find the cause.

title: Difference between a UTI and an STI
answer: A UTI is an infection of the urinary system, usually caused by bowel bacteria, and it is not passed between partners. An STI is passed through sexual contact and can affect the genitals, throat or anus. Both can cause burning when urinating, which is why they are easily confused. STIs more often cause discharge, sores or itching. A health worker can test to tell them apart, and treatments are different.

title: Preventing UTIs
answer: To lower your chance of UTIs, drink plenty of clean water, urinate when you feel the need instead of holding it, and wipe from front to back after using the toilet. Urinating soon after sex can help flush out bacteria. Avoid washing inside the vagina or using scented products. If you get UTIs often, see a health worker to look for a reason.

title: UTI danger signs
answer: A UTI can spread to the kidneys if not treated. Go to a health facility today if you have burning urine together with fever or chills, pain in your back or side under the ribs, nausea or vomiting, or feel very unwell. These can be signs of a kidney infection, which needs quick treatment. If someone is very weak or confused, call 112 or 912 for an ambulance.

title: What is PID
answer: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an infection of a woman's upper reproductive organs: the womb, fallopian tubes and ovaries. It usually happens when bacteria from an STI, such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea, move up from the vagina and cervix. PID can be mild or very serious. It needs prompt treatment, because it can damage the tubes and make it harder to get pregnant later.

title: Discharge from the penis
answer: Normally, only urine, semen and a small amount of clear fluid when aroused come out of the penis. A discharge at other times, especially if it is white, yellow, green or cloudy, or comes with burning when urinating, is often a sign of an STI such as gonorrhoea or chlamydia. Only a test at a health center can tell the cause. Go soon, avoid sex until checked, and do not self-treat.

title: Burning when you urinate
answer: Burning or pain when urinating can be caused by a urinary tract infection, an STI such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea or trichomoniasis, a yeast infection, irritation from soaps, or not drinking enough water. Because the causes are different and need different treatment, it is best to see a health worker, who may test your urine. Go quickly if you also have fever, back pain, discharge or sores.

title: Sores on the genitals
answer: Sores, blisters or ulcers on the penis, vulva, vagina or anus can be caused by STIs such as syphilis, herpes or chancroid, but also by injury, friction or skin conditions. Some STI sores are painless and heal on their own even though the infection remains. Genital sores also make HIV easier to pass. Do not squeeze or put anything on them; see a health worker soon and avoid sex until checked.

title: Sudden testicle pain
answer: Sudden, strong pain in a testicle is an emergency. It can be testicular torsion, where the testicle twists and loses its blood supply, which can destroy the testicle within hours. Go to a health facility immediately, or call 112 or 912, especially if there is swelling, nausea or vomiting. Do not wait to see if it goes away. Milder pain can be from an infection and also needs checking soon.

title: Lower belly pain in girls
answer: Lower belly pain in girls has many causes: period pain, constipation, a urinary infection, an STI that has spread to the womb and tubes (PID), or a pregnancy problem. Go to a health facility now if the pain is severe, comes with fever, vomiting, fainting, or heavy bleeding, or if you might be pregnant, because an ectopic pregnancy is an emergency. Otherwise, see a health worker soon.

title: What happens during an STI test
answer: At an STI check, a health worker will ask some private questions about your symptoms and sexual history to decide which tests you need. They may look at your genitals, take a urine sample, a swab, or a small blood sample from your finger or arm. Some results come the same day, others later. You can ask questions at any time, and you can ask for a health worker of the same sex if possible.

title: Privacy of STI testing
answer: Health workers must keep your visit, test results and treatment confidential. This means they should not share your information with your parents, school, friends or partner without your permission, except in rare situations such as when a child is in danger, which they should explain to you. If you have worries about privacy, ask the health worker how your information is protected before testing.

title: When to test after unprotected sex
answer: If you have symptoms, get checked right away. Without symptoms, tests for chlamydia and gonorrhoea are most accurate about two weeks after sex, while blood tests for syphilis and HIV may need several weeks and sometimes up to three months. Do not wait if a condom broke or sex was forced: go to a health facility as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours, for medicines that can prevent HIV and pregnancy.

title: Testing when you have no symptoms
answer: Yes, it is worth getting tested even without symptoms. Many STIs, like chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and HIV, often cause no signs for a long time, while still harming the body and passing to partners. Consider testing if you have had sex without a condom, have a new partner or more than one partner, or a partner has an STI. A health worker can advise which tests suit you.

title: Finishing all STI medicine
answer: Always take all the STI medicine exactly as the health worker tells you, even if you feel better or the signs go away after a day or two. Stopping early can leave some bacteria alive, so the infection may come back, keep harming your body, or become harder to treat. If you have side effects or forget a dose, talk to the health worker instead of stopping on your own.

title: No sex until treatment is finished
answer: Avoid all sex, including oral and anal sex, until you and your partner have finished treatment and the health worker says it is safe, usually about a week after treatment ends and once symptoms have gone. Having sex before this can pass the infection to your partner or bring it back to you. If you cannot avoid sex, use a condom every time, and talk to the health worker.

title: Partner treatment
answer: When you are treated for an STI, your sexual partners from the past few months also need testing and treatment, even if they feel fine. Otherwise, they can keep the infection, suffer complications, pass it to others, or give it back to you. The health worker can explain which partners need treatment and may give you a referral card or medicine for your partner. Treating everyone protects everyone.

title: Worry after unprotected sex
answer: Feeling scared after sex without a condom is very common, and worrying will not change what happened, but acting quickly can help. Within a few days, a health center can talk with you about emergency contraception, testing for HIV and other infections, and medicine that can prevent HIV if you go very soon. Try to slow your breathing and talk to someone you trust. You are not a bad person. You can also call 114 for free, private advice about what to do next.

title: Waiting for a pregnancy test result
answer: Waiting to find out if you are pregnant can feel very stressful. Remember that a test is most accurate from the day your period is late, so testing too early can give a wrong answer. While you wait, keep busy, sleep and eat well, and talk to someone you trust. Stress itself can also delay a period. A nurse at the health center can do a test and explain your choices kindly and privately. Whatever the result, you do not have to face it alone.

title: Anxiety while waiting for HIV test results
answer: Feeling anxious before or after an HIV test is normal. Many health centers give results the same day, and a counsellor will explain what they mean and support you whatever the result. If the result is positive, treatment today lets people live long, healthy lives. While you wait, breathe slowly, stay with a trusted friend or family member, and avoid alcohol. You can call 114 for free to talk about your worries and ask questions.

title: Constant fear of having an STI
answer: Some young people worry again and again that they have a sexually transmitted infection, even after a negative test. The best step is to get checked once at a health center and believe a clear result from a health worker. Searching symptoms online often makes worry worse. If fear keeps coming back and affects your sleep, school or mood, it may be anxiety, and talking to a counsellor or nurse can really help. You can also call 114.

title: What a panic attack feels like
answer: A panic attack is a sudden wave of strong fear. Your heart may race, you may shake, sweat, feel short of breath, dizzy, or feel that something terrible is happening. It is very frightening but usually passes within minutes and is not dangerous by itself. Breathing slowly and reminding yourself it will pass can help. If attacks keep happening, talk to a health worker or counsellor. If you have chest pain or cannot breathe, get urgent care or call 112.

title: Calm breathing exercise
answer: Slow breathing tells your body it is safe. Sit comfortably and put a hand on your belly. Breathe in gently through your nose while you count to four, feeling your belly rise. Hold for a moment, then breathe out slowly through your mouth while you count to six. Repeat for a few minutes. You can do this before an exam, a test result or whenever you feel tense. Practising every day makes it work better.

title: Grounding when worry feels overwhelming
answer: Grounding brings your mind back to the present when worries feel too big. Try the 5-4-3-2-1 game: name 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell and 1 you can taste. You can also press your feet into the floor, hold something cool, or describe the room out loud. These simple steps help calm racing thoughts. If worry often feels overwhelming, talk to someone you trust or call 114.

title: Stress delaying your period
answer: Yes, strong stress can affect the hormones that control your cycle, so a period may come late or be skipped. Worry, family problems, illness, big changes in weight or poor sleep can all do this. But if you have had sex, a late period can also mean pregnancy, so a pregnancy test is the safest way to know. If periods stay irregular for several months, see a nurse at the health center.

title: Exam stress and changes in periods
answer: During exams, many girls notice changes: a late or early period, more cramps, spotting, or stronger mood changes before the period. Long study nights, little sleep, skipped meals and worry all affect hormones. Usually the cycle settles once exams finish. Try to sleep enough, eat regular meals and take short breaks. If you have had sex and your period is late, take a pregnancy test. If changes continue for months, see a nurse.

title: Coping with exam stress
answer: Some exam stress can help you focus, but too much makes it hard to think. Make a simple study plan, break work into small parts and take short breaks. Sleep well, because the brain stores what you learned during sleep. Eat regular meals, drink water and move your body. Avoid comparing yourself with others. Talk to a teacher, school counsellor or family member if you feel overwhelmed. Your worth is more than one exam result.

title: Stress and low interest in sex
answer: It is very common for stress, worry, tiredness or sadness to lower interest in sex for both young men and women. The body focuses on the problem instead. This usually improves when the stress gets better. Getting enough sleep, exercise and talking about what is bothering you can help. Never feel pushed to have sex when you do not want to. If low interest comes with feeling down for weeks, talk to a health worker.

title: Poor sleep and your body
answer: Not sleeping enough affects your whole body. It can make you moody, worried or irritable, lower your concentration and memory, weaken your immune system, and make you want sugary food. Poor sleep can also upset hormones, which may affect your periods or sexual desire. It makes risky choices more likely because tired brains think less clearly. If you sleep badly for weeks despite good habits, talk to a health worker.

title: Overthinking at night
answer: Many people find that worries feel bigger at night. Try writing your thoughts on paper before bed so your mind can let them go until morning. Keep a calm routine: dim the lights, stop using your phone, and do slow breathing. If you cannot sleep after about 20 minutes, get up, do something quiet, then try again. If night-time worry happens most nights, talk to someone you trust or call 114.

title: Worry about future fertility
answer: Many young people worry they will not be able to have children one day. Most people can. Things that help protect future fertility include using condoms to prevent infections, getting STIs treated early, not smoking, keeping a healthy weight and avoiding unsafe herbs or products in the genitals. Using modern contraception does not cause infertility. If you have specific worries, a health worker can talk with you about them.

title: Stress headaches and body aches
answer: Stress often shows up in the body as headaches, a tight neck or shoulders, stomach aches, or feeling sick. This happens because stress makes muscles tense and changes how the body works. Rest, water, regular meals, gentle movement and slow breathing can ease it. Talking about what worries you also helps. If pain is severe, sudden, or keeps coming back, see a health worker to check for other causes.

title: Always feeling tired
answer: Feeling tired all the time can come from too little sleep, late phone use, skipping meals, not drinking enough water, stress or low mood. In girls, heavy periods can lead to low iron, which also causes tiredness. Try regular sleep, balanced meals with iron-rich foods, and daily activity. If tiredness lasts more than a few weeks, or you feel dizzy, breathless or very pale, see a nurse at the health center.

title: Caffeine, energy drinks and sleep
answer: Coffee, strong tea, cola and energy drinks contain caffeine, which keeps you awake. Energy drinks often contain a lot of caffeine and sugar. Too much can cause a fast heartbeat, shaking, worry, stomach problems and poor sleep. Avoid them in the afternoon and evening, and do not mix energy drinks with alcohol, which can hide how drunk you are. Water and good sleep are better ways to have energy.

title: Bedwetting as a teenager
answer: Some teenagers still wet the bed sometimes. It is more common than people think and it is not your fault or a sign of laziness. It can run in families or be linked to deep sleep, bladder development, constipation, stress or sometimes an illness such as an infection or diabetes. Empty your bladder before bed and avoid lots of drinks late at night. A health worker can check for causes and help, so please do not be ashamed to ask.

title: Feeling guilty after sex
answer: Feeling guilty after sex is common, especially if it went against your values, happened quickly, or you worry what others would think. Guilt is a feeling, not a sign that you are a bad person. Think about what you want for yourself next time, and remember you can decide to wait. Make sure you are safe: if there was no condom, visit a health center soon. Talking to a trusted person or calling 114 can help.

title: Shame about sexual thoughts
answer: Having sexual thoughts, feelings or attractions is a normal part of growing up. Thoughts are not actions, and having them does not make you dirty or bad. You choose what you do with your feelings. If thoughts feel confusing or upsetting, it can help to talk with a trusted adult, counsellor or health worker. Learning accurate information about your body also helps reduce shame.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Regret after first sex
answer: Some young people regret their first sexual experience because it happened too soon, with the wrong person, or not how they imagined. Regret is painful, but it does not define you. Having had sex once does not mean you must continue; you can choose to wait until you feel ready. Look after your health: visit a health center if you had no protection. If it was not your choice, that is not your fault and you deserve support.

title: Religious beliefs and guilt about sexuality
answer: Faith is important to many young people in Rwanda, and it can guide choices about sex. Sometimes young people feel torn between their beliefs and their feelings. Having feelings is human. You can respect your faith and still learn accurate health information to protect yourself. Talking with a trusted faith leader, family member or counsellor can help you make peace with your choices. Feeling guilty for a long time is not healthy, so ask for support.

title: Feeling dirty after sex
answer: Some people feel 'dirty' or uncomfortable after sex. This is usually about emotions, not about your body being unclean. Washing the outside of the genitals with clean water is enough; do not wash inside the vagina. Ask yourself whether you truly wanted the experience. If it felt pressured or forced, it is not your fault and you deserve help: talk to someone you trust, go to a health center or call 114, or 112 if you are in danger.

title: Forgiving yourself after a mistake
answer: Everyone makes mistakes, including about relationships and sex. Being kind to yourself helps you learn and make better choices. Name what happened, think about what you can do differently, and take any health steps you need, like testing. Talk to yourself as you would to a good friend. Holding on to shame makes it harder to move forward. If the feelings stay heavy, talk to a trusted adult, counsellor or call 114.

title: Coping with rumours about your sex life
answer: Rumours and gossip about your sex life can be very hurtful, whether true or not. Try not to reply with anger; it can make gossip spread. Stay close to friends who support you, and tell a trusted adult, teacher or school counsellor. If photos or messages are being shared, keep evidence and report it. What people say does not decide your value. If the stress becomes too much, call 114 to talk.

title: What self-esteem means
answer: Self-esteem is how you see and value yourself. Healthy self-esteem means you believe you are worthy of respect, even with weaknesses. It helps you make good choices, say no to pressure, and expect respectful relationships. Low self-esteem can make people accept unhealthy treatment or take risks to feel liked. Self-esteem is not fixed; it can grow with practice, support and kind thoughts about yourself.

title: Ways to build self-esteem
answer: You can build self-esteem step by step. Notice your strengths and write down things you do well. Set small goals and celebrate reaching them. Spend time with people who respect you, and limit time with those who put you down. Look after your body with sleep, food and activity. Replace harsh self-talk with fair, kind words. Helping others and learning new skills also make you feel capable.

title: Unhappy with how your body looks
answer: Many young people feel unhappy with their body, especially while it is changing. Bodies come in many healthy shapes, sizes and skin tones. Try to focus on what your body can do, like walking, laughing and learning. Avoid people or pages that make you feel worse. Look after your health instead of chasing a 'perfect' look. If body worries take over your thoughts or eating, talk to a health worker or counsellor.

title: Comparing your body to social media
answer: Photos on social media are often edited, filtered or carefully posed, and they show only the best moments. Comparing your real body to these images can make you feel bad. Remember that real bodies have marks, hair, rolls and different shapes. Follow accounts that make you feel good, unfollow ones that make you feel worse, and take breaks from your phone. Your value is not measured by likes.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Wanting to gain weight
answer: If you feel too thin, first know that many teenagers are slim while growing and fill out later. To gain weight healthily, eat regular meals and snacks with energy-rich foods like beans, groundnuts, avocado, milk, eggs, fish, bananas and whole grains. Being active builds strength too. Avoid pills, injections or syrups sold to make you gain weight or get curves; they can be dangerous. A nurse can check if your weight is healthy.

title: Being teased about your body
answer: Being teased about your weight, height, skin, breasts or other body parts hurts, and it is a form of bullying. It says more about the person teasing than about you. Stay with supportive friends, calmly ask them to stop if you feel safe, and tell a teacher, school counsellor or parent. Keep reminding yourself of your strengths. If the teasing makes you feel very low, talk to someone you trust or call 114.

title: Skin-lightening creams dangers
answer: Many skin-lightening or bleaching creams contain harmful substances such as mercury or strong steroids. They can cause rashes, thin and damaged skin, dark patches, infections, and harm to the kidneys and nervous system. Some are sold without clear labels. Your natural skin colour is beautiful and healthy. For skin problems like acne or dark spots, ask a health worker for safe advice instead of using bleaching products.

title: Worries about breast size
answer: Breasts come in many sizes and shapes, and it is normal for one breast to be slightly bigger than the other. Breasts may keep growing until your late teens. Size does not affect your health, femininity or ability to breastfeed. Wearing a comfortable, well-fitting bra can help you feel better. If you notice a lump, pain that does not go away or very fast changes, see a health worker.

title: Breast enlargement creams and pills
answer: Creams, pills, herbs or massages sold to make breasts bigger do not work in a safe or lasting way. Some contain hormones or unknown substances that can harm your health, cause irregular bleeding or skin problems. Breast size is decided mostly by your genes and body fat, and breasts can keep developing until your late teens. Please do not spend money or risk your health on these products.

title: Hip and buttock enhancing products and injections
answer: Pills, creams, syrups and injections sold to make hips and buttocks bigger can be very dangerous. Some contain steroids or unknown chemicals, and injections given outside a proper hospital can cause serious infection, lumps, damage to the body and even death. Body shape is mostly decided by genes. Eating well and exercises like squats can build healthy muscle. Never let anyone inject substances into your body outside a health facility.

title: Positive self-talk
answer: Self-talk is the voice in your head that comments on what you do. If it is always harsh, like 'I am stupid' or 'nobody likes me', it can lower your mood and confidence. Try to notice these thoughts and replace them with fairer ones, such as 'I made a mistake, but I can learn from it'. Speak to yourself as you would to a good friend. With practice, kinder thoughts become a habit.

title: Boys and pressure to be muscular
answer: Many boys feel pressure to have big muscles, a flat stomach or a certain height. Boys grow at different speeds, and muscles often develop more in the late teens and early twenties. Strength comes from regular activity, enough food with protein, and good sleep, not from pills. Being a man is not about muscles. If you feel very unhappy with your body or exercise too much, talk to a health worker or someone you trust.

title: Steroids and muscle-building supplements
answer: Steroid pills or injections taken to build muscle are dangerous for young people. They can shrink the testicles, lower sperm production, cause breast growth in boys, acne, mood swings and aggression, liver and heart damage, and stop growth early. In girls they can cause deep voice, body hair and period problems. Many supplements sold in shops have unclear ingredients. Eating well, training and resting are the safe way to build strength.

title: Perfectionism and pressure to be perfect
answer: Wanting to do well is good, but believing you must always be perfect can cause stress, fear of failure and low mood. Nobody is perfect, and mistakes are how people learn. Set realistic goals, celebrate effort as well as results, and allow yourself rest. If pressure comes from family or school, try talking about how you feel. If stress feels too heavy, talk to a counsellor or call 114.

title: Saying no with confidence
answer: Being assertive means saying what you want or do not want clearly and respectfully. Use a calm voice, look at the person, and keep it short: 'No, I do not want to.' You do not have to give long reasons or apologise. Repeat it if needed and walk away if the person keeps pushing. Practising with a friend can help. Saying no to drinks, drugs or things you are not ready for protects your health.

title: Setting personal goals
answer: Having goals for your studies, work, health or family life gives you direction and helps you make choices that protect your future, such as avoiding early pregnancy, alcohol or drugs. Choose goals that are clear and possible, break them into small steps, and write them down. Share them with someone who supports you. If something goes wrong, adjust your plan instead of giving up. Small progress still counts.

title: Healthy ways to cope with stress
answer: Healthy coping helps you feel better without causing new problems. Ideas include talking to someone you trust, slow breathing, walking or sport, music, dancing, prayer or quiet time, writing your feelings, getting enough sleep, and breaking big problems into small steps. Different things work for different people, so try a few. If stress keeps building or affects school and sleep, talk to a counsellor, health worker or call 114.

title: Unhealthy coping habits
answer: When stressed, some people turn to alcohol, drugs, smoking, overeating or not eating, staying in their room for days, or seeking risky sex to forget their problems. These may feel helpful for a moment but often make things worse and can harm your health and future. If you notice these habits, be gentle with yourself and try a healthier step instead. Talking to a trusted adult, counsellor or calling 114 can help.

title: Talking to a trusted adult about feelings
answer: A trusted adult is someone who listens, respects you and wants you to be safe, such as a parent, aunt, uncle, teacher, school counsellor, faith leader or health worker. Sharing your feelings can make problems feel lighter and help you find solutions. Choose a calm time and a private place. If the first person does not help, try someone else. You can also call 114 for free to talk.

title: How to ask for help when it feels hard
answer: Asking for help can feel scary, but it is a sign of strength. You can start simply: 'Can I talk to you about something that is worrying me?' If speaking feels too hard, write a note or send a message. You do not need to share everything at once. Say what kind of help you want, such as listening or advice. If you prefer to speak to someone outside your circle, call 114.

title: Writing feelings in a journal
answer: Writing down your thoughts and feelings in a notebook can help you understand them and feel calmer. You can write about your day, what worried you, what went well, or things you are thankful for. There are no rules and no one needs to read it. Keep it in a private place. If what you write shows the same sad or scary feelings again and again, share them with a trusted person.

title: Managing anger
answer: Anger is a normal feeling, but how you act on it matters. Notice early signs like a hot face, tight fists or a fast heartbeat. Step away, breathe slowly and count to ten before you speak. Physical activity can release tension. Later, when calm, explain what upset you using 'I feel' words. Never use violence. If anger often gets out of control or you hurt others, talk to a counsellor or health worker.

title: Feeling lonely
answer: Feeling lonely happens to many young people, for example after moving school, a breakup or feeling different. Small steps can help: join a club, sport, choir or youth group, say hello to one new person, or reconnect with an old friend or relative. Online contact can help but is not the same as face-to-face time. If loneliness lasts or makes you feel very low, talk to a trusted adult, counsellor or call 114.

title: Stress from family problems at home
answer: Problems at home, like parents fighting, money worries, illness or separation, can make you feel stressed, sad or angry, and can affect school and sleep. These problems are not your fault. Find a calm place and people outside the home who support you, like a relative, teacher or school counsellor. Keep up healthy routines where you can. If you are being hurt or feel unsafe at home, call 112. To talk, call 114.

title: Signs of depression
answer: Depression is more than a bad day. Signs include feeling sad, empty or irritable most of the time for two weeks or more, losing interest in things you used to enjoy, sleeping or eating much more or less, feeling tired, finding it hard to concentrate, and feeling worthless. Depression is a health condition and it can be treated. If you notice these signs, talk to a trusted person, see a health worker, or call 114.

title: Signs of an anxiety problem
answer: Everyone feels worried sometimes. Anxiety may be a problem when worry is strong, hard to control and lasts for weeks, or when it stops you doing normal things like school or seeing friends. Signs can include restlessness, a racing heart, trouble sleeping, stomach aches, tense muscles and avoiding situations. Anxiety can be treated with support and counselling. Talk to a trusted adult, a health worker, or call 114.

title: Mental health stigma
answer: Mental health is part of health, just like physical health. Anyone can have stress, depression or anxiety, and it is not a weakness, a curse or a punishment. Unfortunately, some people judge or mock those who seek help, which stops others from getting care. You can help by listening without judging, using kind words, and encouraging friends to get support. Getting help early makes recovery easier.

title: Helping a stressed friend
answer: If a friend seems stressed or down, find a quiet moment and ask, 'How are you really doing?' Listen without judging or rushing to give advice. Let them know you care and that their feelings make sense. Encourage them to talk to a trusted adult, counsellor or health worker, or to call 114, and offer to go with them. Look after yourself too. If your friend is in danger, get an adult's help or call 112.

title: A healthy daily routine
answer: A regular routine helps your body and mind feel steady. Try to wake and sleep at similar times, eat breakfast and regular meals, drink water, and move your body every day. Make time for study, rest, family and friends, and something you enjoy. Wash daily and change underwear. Limit screen time, especially before bed. A routine does not need to be perfect; small steady habits make a big difference.

title: Managing time between school and life
answer: Balancing school, chores, friends and rest can be hard. Write a simple weekly plan with study times, chores and free time. Do the hardest tasks when you have the most energy. Break big assignments into small steps and start early. Put your phone away while studying. Remember to plan rest and fun too, because a tired mind learns less. If you have too many responsibilities at home, talk to a teacher or counsellor.

title: Hobbies and fun for wellbeing
answer: Doing things you enjoy is good for your mental health. Hobbies like music, drawing, football, dancing, reading, gardening, crafts or joining a club help you relax, build skills, make friends and feel proud of yourself. They also give you healthy ways to spend free time instead of drinking or other risky activities. Even 20 minutes of something you enjoy each day can lift your mood.

title: Where to get mental health help in Rwanda
answer: In Rwanda you can get support for stress, low mood or worry from several places. You can talk to a nurse at your nearest health center, who can help or refer you to a hospital mental health service. At school, a counsellor or patron/matron can listen. You can call 114 for free, private advice. Community health workers can also guide you. If you or someone else is in danger, call 112.

title: Mental health care at the health center
answer: Yes, you can go to a health center for emotional problems, not only for physical illness. You can tell the nurse you have been feeling stressed, sad, worried or unable to sleep. They will listen, ask some questions, offer support or counselling, and refer you to a hospital or specialist service if needed. You do not need to be 'very sick' to go. Asking for help early is a smart choice.

title: What a school counsellor does
answer: A school counsellor, or a teacher or patron/matron trained to support students, is there to listen and help with problems like stress, exam worries, family difficulties, friendships, bullying and feelings about relationships or your body. They can help you find solutions and connect you with health services if needed. Talking to them is not a punishment. If your school has no counsellor, ask a teacher you trust.

title: Is counselling confidential
answer: Counsellors and health workers are expected to keep what you tell them private. They will not share your story with friends, teachers or family without good reason. The main exception is when they believe you or someone else is in serious danger, such as abuse or a risk to your life; then they may need to involve others to keep you safe. You can ask at the start, 'Who else will know what I say?'

title: What happens at counselling
answer: At a first counselling visit, the counsellor will welcome you, explain that the talk is private, and ask what brings you. You can share as much or as little as you want. They will listen, ask questions to understand, and help you think of ways to cope or solve problems. It may take a few meetings to feel the benefit. Counsellors do not judge you or give you orders; you work together.

title: Fear of being seen as crazy for seeking help
answer: Many young people fear that others will call them 'crazy' if they see a counsellor or mental health worker. Seeking help for your feelings is no different from seeing a nurse for a fever. It shows courage and good sense. Services aim to keep your visit private. Most people who get help for stress, low mood or anxiety feel better. Your health matters more than what others might say.

title: Getting mental health help without telling parents first
answer: Many young people want help but are not ready to tell their parents. You can call 114 for free, or talk to a school counsellor, teacher or nurse at a health center first. They can listen, give support, and help you think about whether and how to involve your family. Parents can often be a great support once you feel ready. If you are in danger, call 112.

title: Community health workers and emotional support
answer: Community health workers (abajyanama b'ubuzima) live in your village or cell and are trained to help with many health issues. You can talk to them if you feel stressed or worried or need information about sexual and reproductive health. They can listen, give basic advice and guide you to the health center when needed. They are expected to treat what you share with respect and privacy.

title: When to call 112 instead of 114
answer: Call 112 when someone is in immediate danger and needs police or emergency help now, for example violence, someone unconscious, an overdose, severe injury or someone at risk of harming themselves. Call 114, the free RBC health line, for health questions, advice and support when it is not an emergency, such as stress, worries about sex or where to find services. If unsure and someone could be hurt, call 112.

title: Alcohol and decisions about sex
answer: Alcohol slows down the part of the brain that helps you think clearly and judge risk. After drinking, people are more likely to have sex they did not plan, forget or misuse condoms, choose partners they would not normally choose, or be taken advantage of. This increases the risk of pregnancy, HIV and other infections, and regret. If you choose to drink as an adult, drink little, stay with trusted friends and plan how to get home safely.

title: What drink spiking is
answer: Drink spiking means someone secretly puts alcohol or drugs into another person's drink without them knowing. It can make the person feel very drunk, dizzy, confused, sleepy or unable to move, and they may not remember what happened. Some people spike drinks to rob or sexually abuse others. It is never the victim's fault. Knowing about it helps you protect yourself and your friends.

title: Protecting your drink
answer: To lower the risk of spiking, open your own drink or watch it being poured, keep it in your hand, and do not leave it unattended. If you leave it, get a new one. Do not accept drinks from people you do not know or trust. Go out with friends, agree to look after each other and leave together. If a drink tastes strange, stop drinking it. Spiking is always the fault of the person who does it.

title: What to do if your drink was spiked
answer: If you suddenly feel very drunk, dizzy, confused or sleepy after only a little drink, tell a trusted friend right away and stay with them. Do not leave with strangers. Get to a safe place and seek medical help at the nearest health facility; call 112 if someone is unconscious, struggling to breathe, or in danger. If you think something sexual happened, go to a health facility quickly for care and protection medicines.

title: Signs of alcohol poisoning in a friend
answer: Drinking a lot of alcohol quickly can be deadly. Danger signs include confusion, not waking up, vomiting while barely awake, slow or irregular breathing, cold or bluish skin, and seizures. Call 112 straight away. While waiting, do not leave the person alone, lay them on their side so they do not choke on vomit, and keep them warm. Do not give coffee, cold showers or more drink; these do not help.

title: Alcohol and the teenage body and brain
answer: The brain keeps developing until about age 25, and alcohol can harm this growth, affecting memory, learning and mood. Young people also get drunk faster and are more likely to have accidents, fights, unplanned sex and alcohol problems later. Drinking can worsen sadness and anxiety. The safest choice for teenagers is not to drink. If you do drink as an adult, drink small amounts and never drive afterwards.

title: Alcohol and men's sexual health
answer: Many people think alcohol improves sex, but it often does the opposite. Drinking can make it harder to get or keep an erection and harder to reach climax. Heavy drinking over time can lower testosterone, reduce sperm quality and lower fertility. It also increases risky choices like sex without a condom. Cutting down usually helps these problems improve. If problems continue, see a health worker.

title: Cannabis and sexual health
answer: Cannabis (marijuana, urumogi) affects judgement and memory, so people who use it are more likely to have unplanned or unprotected sex. Regular use may lower sperm quality in men, upset periods in women, and harm the developing brain, increasing the risk of anxiety, low mood and serious mental illness in some young people. It can also become hard to stop. If you are worried about your use, talk to a health worker or call 114.

title: Drugs and sexual risk
answer: Drugs change how people think and act, which makes unprotected sex, multiple partners and sexual abuse more likely. Some people exchange sex for drugs, which carries high risks. Sharing needles or syringes to inject drugs can spread HIV and hepatitis directly through blood. If you use drugs, never share needles, always use condoms, and seek help. Health workers can test you and support you without judging.

title: Using alcohol or drugs to feel braver about sex
answer: Some young people drink or use drugs to feel less shy before sex. But if you need alcohol to feel ready, it may be a sign you are not ready yet. Being high or drunk makes it harder to choose safely, use a condom, give or understand consent, and remember what happened. Real confidence comes from feeling comfortable and respected. Take your time; there is no rush.

title: Refusing alcohol at parties
answer: You can enjoy a party without drinking. Hold a soft drink or water so fewer people offer you alcohol. Have a simple answer ready, like 'No thanks, I have to wake up early' or just 'No thanks.' Go with friends who respect your choice and plan how you will get home. If people keep pressuring you, it is okay to leave. Real friends accept your decision.

title: Getting help for alcohol or drug use
answer: If you feel you drink or use drugs too often, need more to feel the same effect, or struggle to stop, help is available. You can talk to a nurse at your health center, who can support you or refer you to a hospital service. A school counsellor or trusted adult can also help. Call 114 for free advice. Stopping is easier with support, and asking for help is a strong step.

title: Shisha smoking risks
answer: Shisha (hookah or water pipe) is not a safe alternative to cigarettes. The water does not filter out the harmful chemicals. A single session can expose you to a lot of smoke, carbon monoxide and nicotine, which is addictive. Shisha is linked to lung and heart disease, cancers and lower fertility. Sharing the mouthpiece can also spread infections. The healthiest choice is not to use it.

title: Sniffing glue and solvents
answer: Sniffing glue, fuel, paint thinner or other chemicals to get high is extremely dangerous. These fumes can damage the brain, liver, kidneys and lungs, cause memory problems, and can even cause sudden death the first time someone uses them. People who sniff solvents are also more vulnerable to abuse and risky sex. If you or a friend use them, please get help from a health worker or call 114.

title: Smoking and women's reproductive health
answer: Smoking harms women's reproductive health. It can make it harder to get pregnant, cause more painful periods, and increase the risk of cervical cancer. In pregnancy it raises the risk of miscarriage, early birth and small babies. Smoking also damages the heart and lungs and ages the skin. Women who smoke should tell their health provider when choosing contraception. Quitting at any age brings health benefits.

title: Smoking and men's sexual health
answer: Smoking damages blood vessels, including those that carry blood to the penis, so over time it can cause erection problems. It also lowers sperm quality and number, which can reduce fertility. Smoking increases the risk of heart disease and cancers, including some that affect the genitals. Many of these effects improve after quitting, so stopping early is one of the best things you can do for your sexual health.

title: Is vaping safe
answer: E-cigarettes or vapes are not safe for young people. Most contain nicotine, which is very addictive and can harm the developing brain, affecting attention, learning and mood. Vape liquids and aerosols contain chemicals that can damage the lungs. Some young people who vape later start smoking cigarettes. Sweet flavours are designed to attract youth. The healthiest choice is not to vape at all.

title: Second-hand smoke
answer: Second-hand smoke is the smoke you breathe in when people near you smoke. There is no safe level. It can cause coughing, asthma attacks, chest infections, and over time heart disease and lung cancer. It is especially harmful to babies, children and pregnant women. If family members smoke, kindly ask them to smoke outside and away from others. Open windows do not fully protect you.

title: Quitting smoking or vaping
answer: Quitting nicotine can be hard but many people succeed. Choose a quit date, tell friends and family, and remove cigarettes or vapes from your space. Notice your triggers, like stress or certain friends, and plan other things to do, such as chewing gum, walking or drinking water. Cravings usually pass in a few minutes and get weaker over time. A health worker can support you, or you can call 114.

title: Not getting an erection sometimes
answer: It is normal for young men to sometimes not get an erection or lose it, especially when tired, stressed, nervous, after drinking alcohol, or when not really in the mood. This does not mean something is wrong with your body. Erections come and go naturally. Worrying a lot can make it happen more. If it happens almost every time for several months, it is a good idea to see a health worker.

title: Morning erections
answer: Waking up with an erection is normal and healthy for boys and men. It happens naturally during sleep several times a night and is linked to the sleep cycle, not to sexual thoughts. A full bladder may also play a part. Morning erections are a sign that blood vessels and nerves are working well. There is nothing to be embarrassed about, and they usually go away on their own.

title: Performance anxiety
answer: Performance anxiety is worry about 'doing well' sexually, such as fear of losing an erection, finishing too fast, or disappointing a partner. Stress releases hormones that make erections and arousal harder, so worry can create the very problem you fear. Being with a partner you trust, going slowly, communicating, and not using alcohol help. Remember you never have to have sex to prove anything. If worry continues, a health worker can help.

title: When erection problems need a health worker
answer: If you can rarely or never get or keep an erection for a few months, or it happens suddenly with pain or after an injury, see a health worker. Ongoing erection problems can be linked to stress, depression, alcohol, smoking, drugs, some medicines, or health issues like diabetes or heart problems. A health worker can check you privately. Do not buy sex pills or herbs from markets or online; they can be dangerous.

title: Erection that will not go down
answer: An erection that lasts several hours (about four hours or more) and is painful, without sexual excitement, is called priapism. It is a medical emergency, because it can damage the penis permanently. It is more common in people with sickle cell disease and after some drugs or medicines. Go to the nearest hospital or health facility immediately or call 112. Do not wait for it to pass.

title: Early ejaculation
answer: Ejaculating sooner than you or your partner would like is very common, especially for young men and in new relationships. Nervousness and excitement play a big role, and it often improves with time, experience and feeling relaxed. Slowing down, breathing calmly and talking with your partner can help. It is not a disease and does not affect fertility. If it worries you a lot, a health worker can talk with you. Avoid creams or pills from markets.

title: Low sexual desire
answer: Sexual desire naturally goes up and down. It can be lower because of stress, tiredness, sadness, relationship problems, past bad experiences, illness, alcohol or some medicines, including some hormonal methods for some people. Having lower desire is not a disease, and nobody should pressure you. If a change in desire bothers you or comes with low mood or other symptoms, talk to a health worker.

title: Different desire levels in a couple
answer: It is very common for partners to want sex at different times or amounts. Neither person is wrong. Talk openly and kindly about how you feel, without blame. Respect is key: no one should be pushed, guilted or forced into sex, even in a relationship or marriage. Spending time together in other ways can strengthen closeness. If differences cause a lot of stress, a counsellor or health worker can help.

title: Not feeling interested in sex
answer: Some young people feel little or no interest in sex or sexual attraction, and that is okay. Everyone develops at their own pace, and some people simply feel less sexual attraction throughout life. You do not need to force yourself or follow what friends do. You can still have close, loving relationships. If lack of interest is new and comes with sadness, tiredness or other changes, talk to a health worker.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Pain during sex for women
answer: Sex should not be painful. Pain can happen because of nervousness, not enough arousal or wetness, infection, dryness, injury, or other conditions that need checking. Pain deep in the belly with fever or unusual discharge may be an infection. Do not ignore it or keep going through pain. Stop, talk with your partner, and see a nurse or health worker at the health center so they can find the cause and help.

title: Genital pain during or after sex for men
answer: Pain in the penis, testicles or lower belly during or after sex or ejaculation is not normal if it keeps happening. Causes can include infections, including STIs, problems with the foreskin, injury or prostate inflammation. Burning when urinating or discharge from the penis are signs to get checked soon. See a health worker at the health center; most causes can be treated. Use condoms until you are checked.

title: Vaginal dryness and lubrication
answer: The vagina naturally makes moisture when a woman feels relaxed and aroused. Dryness can happen if she is nervous, not ready, not aroused enough, after childbirth, while breastfeeding, or with some medicines or hormonal changes. Dryness can make sex uncomfortable and cause small tears. Taking time, communicating and using a suitable lubricant can help. If dryness continues or comes with itching or pain, see a health worker.

title: Choosing a lubricant with condoms
answer: If you use a lubricant with latex condoms, choose a water-based or silicone-based lubricant. Oil-based products like petroleum jelly, body lotion, cooking oil, shea butter or baby oil can weaken latex and make condoms break. Saliva is not a good lubricant and can carry infections. Some condoms already come lubricated. You can ask at a health center or pharmacy for a lubricant that is safe with condoms.

title: What an orgasm is
answer: An orgasm, or climax, is the peak of sexual pleasure, when built-up tension is released, often with a pleasant feeling and muscle contractions. Both men and women can have orgasms. In men it usually happens with ejaculation. Orgasms can happen during sex, masturbation or in sleep. Not everyone experiences them the same way, and it is normal to learn about your body over time.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Not having an orgasm
answer: Many people, especially women, do not have an orgasm every time, or have not had one yet. This is common and not a sign that something is wrong. Feeling relaxed, safe, respected and not rushed matters a lot, and talking with a partner can help. Stress, pain, worry or alcohol can make it harder. Sex is not a test. If you have pain or other worries, talk to a health worker.

title: Penis size worries
answer: Many boys and men worry their penis is too small, often because of jokes or pornography, which shows unusual sizes. Penises vary a lot in size when soft, but sizes are much more similar when erect. The penis keeps growing during puberty, often until the late teens. Size does not affect fertility, manhood or the ability to have a satisfying relationship. If you have real concerns, a health worker can check privately.

title: Penis enlargement products
answer: Pills, creams, herbs, oils, pumps or exercises sold to make the penis bigger do not work in a safe, lasting way. Some contain hidden medicines or chemicals that can be dangerous for the heart or skin, and some cause injury, swelling or infection. Sellers profit from people's worries. Penis size is decided by genes. If you are worried, talk to a health worker instead of risking your health.

title: Testicle size worries
answer: Testicles grow during puberty and come in different sizes. It is normal for one testicle to be a little larger than the other. Size does not usually tell you about fertility or manhood. See a health worker if a testicle seems to be shrinking, one is missing from the scrotum, there is a lump or swelling, or there is pain. Steroid use can also shrink testicles.

title: Normal semen colour
answer: Healthy semen is usually whitish, grey or slightly yellowish, and it can be thick or watery. Colour and thickness can change with how often you ejaculate, how much water you drink and what you eat. See a health worker if semen is red, pink or brown (which may mean blood), green or strongly yellow with a bad smell, or if you have pain, burning or discharge, as these may be signs of infection.

title: Blood in semen
answer: Seeing blood in semen, which may look pink, red or brown, can be frightening. In young men it often has a simple cause, such as a small burst blood vessel, and may go away by itself. But it can also be caused by infection or other problems, so it is wise to see a health worker, especially if it happens more than once or comes with pain, fever, burning when urinating or blood in urine.

title: Amount of semen
answer: The amount of semen varies from person to person and from time to time. It is usually less if you ejaculate often and more after several days without ejaculating. Drinking little water can also reduce it. The amount does not show how strong or fertile you are. If you suddenly produce very little or no semen at all, or have pain, see a health worker.

title: Myth that losing semen makes you weak
answer: Some people believe that ejaculating, wet dreams or masturbation drain a man's strength, blood or brain power. This is a myth. The body makes new sperm and semen all the time, and releasing semen does not cause weakness, illness, back pain or infertility. Feeling tired afterwards is normal and passes quickly. If you feel weak all the time, there is another cause, so see a health worker.

title: Blood after first sex
answer: Some girls and women notice a little bleeding the first time they have vaginal sex, and many do not. A small amount of light bleeding that stops within a day or so is usually not serious. Heavy bleeding, bleeding that does not stop, strong pain, fever or bad-smelling discharge need care: go to a health center. If the sex was not your choice, you deserve care and support; please go to a health facility quickly.

title: No bleeding after first sex
answer: Many girls and women do not bleed the first time they have sex. The hymen is a thin, stretchy tissue that differs from person to person, and it can stretch through sport, daily activity or simply be naturally open. No bleeding does not mean someone has had sex before. Bleeding is not a test of virginity, and nobody can tell your sexual history by looking at your body.
source: UNESCO Technical Guidance on Sexuality Education 2018

title: Feeling nervous about first sex
answer: It is normal to feel nervous about having sex for the first time. Ask yourself if you truly feel ready, or if you feel pushed. You can always wait or change your mind, even at the last minute. If you decide to go ahead, talk with your partner first, plan protection against pregnancy and infections, and choose a time and place where you feel safe and respected. Never use alcohol to calm nerves.

title: Bleeding after sex
answer: Bleeding after sex that is not your first time, or that happens again and again, should be checked. It can be caused by dryness, small tears, infections including STIs, changes on the cervix, or bleeding linked to contraception. Most causes can be treated, but some need early care. Please see a nurse or health worker at the health center, especially if you also have pain, unusual discharge or bleeding between periods.

title: Can having sex often harm you
answer: For healthy adults, having sex often is not harmful by itself, as long as both partners want it, it is comfortable, and you protect yourselves against infections and unplanned pregnancy. Soreness, pain, burning, bleeding or unusual discharge are signs to rest and see a health worker. Having many partners increases the risk of infections. Sex should never feel forced or a duty.

title: Testicle ache after arousal
answer: Some boys and men feel a dull ache or heaviness in the testicles after being sexually aroused for a long time without ejaculating. This happens because extra blood flows to the area. It is uncomfortable but harmless and goes away on its own within a short time. It is never a reason to pressure anyone into sex. Severe or sudden pain, swelling or pain that lasts needs a health worker.

title: Medicines that affect sexual function
answer: Some medicines, including some for depression, blood pressure, epilepsy and other long-term conditions, can affect desire, erections, wetness or climax for some people. If you notice changes after starting a medicine, do not stop it on your own, because that can be dangerous. Talk to the health worker who prescribed it. There are often other options or ways to manage the side effect.

title: Vaginal steaming
answer: Vaginal steaming means sitting over hot water, sometimes with herbs, to 'clean' or 'tighten' the vagina. There is no evidence that it cleans, tightens or improves fertility. It can cause painful burns to delicate skin and upset the natural balance of the vagina, leading to infections. The vagina cleans itself. If you have discharge, smell or itching, see a health worker instead.

title: Feminine sprays and perfumes on the genitals
