answer: Perfumes, body sprays, deodorants, scented powders and 'feminine fresheners' are not needed on the genitals. They can irritate the delicate skin, cause itching, burning or allergic rashes, and upset the natural balance of the vagina, making infections more likely. A mild natural smell is normal. Washing the outside daily with clean water is enough. A strong or fishy smell needs a health check, not perfume.

title: Tight and synthetic underwear
answer: Underwear that is very tight or made of synthetic material like nylon traps heat and sweat. This can cause rubbing, rashes, and make yeast and other infections more likely in girls. In boys, tight underwear and trousers keep the testicles warm, which may slightly lower sperm quality. Cotton underwear that fits comfortably lets the skin breathe. Change it daily and when wet with sweat.

title: Wiping front to back
answer: Girls and women should wipe from front to back after using the toilet, from the vagina towards the anus. Wiping the other way can carry germs from the bottom to the urinary opening and vagina, causing urine infections and other infections. Use clean toilet paper or water and wash hands afterwards. Signs of a urine infection include burning when urinating and needing to go often; see a health worker if this happens.

title: Sleeping without underwear
answer: Sleeping without underwear, or in loose cotton clothes, is healthy for most people. It lets the genital area stay dry and breathe, which can help prevent sweat rashes and yeast infections. If you prefer to wear underwear at night, choose clean, loose cotton. During your period, wear underwear with a pad. Clean bedsheets regularly. It is a personal choice; both options are fine.

title: Vaginal tightening herbs and dry sex
answer: Some women are told to put herbs, powders, stones or other products in the vagina to make it tight or dry before sex. These practices are harmful. They irritate and damage the vaginal walls, cause pain, small wounds and infections, and greatly increase the risk of HIV and other STIs. They can also make condoms break. Natural wetness is healthy. If you feel pressured to do this, talk to a health worker.

title: Talcum powder and wet wipes on genitals
answer: Powder is not needed on the genitals. Talc or scented powder can irritate the skin and should not be put on or near the vulva. Scented wet wipes can cause itching and rashes, and flushing them can block toilets. If you need to freshen up, use clean water and dry gently with a clean cloth. For sweating or rubbing in the groin, wear loose cotton clothes.

title: Peeing and washing after sex
answer: Urinating after sex can help flush out germs and may lower the chance of a urine infection, especially for women. Washing the outside of the genitals with clean water is fine. However, peeing or washing after sex does not prevent pregnancy, HIV or other STIs. Do not wash inside the vagina. Condoms remain the best protection against infections, and contraception protects against pregnancy.

title: Heat and sperm health
answer: Testicles hang outside the body because sperm develop best slightly below body temperature. Frequent heat, such as very tight trousers, long hot baths, sitting for many hours, or laptops resting on the lap, can temporarily lower sperm quality. This usually recovers once the heat is reduced. Wearing loose underwear and taking breaks from sitting helps. If you have concerns about fertility, see a health worker.

title: Breast pain not linked to periods
answer: Breast pain at times other than before your period is common and is usually not a sign of cancer. It can come from a poorly fitting bra, exercise, muscle strain in the chest, injury, growth, or some hormonal contraception. A supportive bra and rest may help. See a health worker if pain stays in one spot, lasts more than a few weeks, comes with a lump, redness, warmth, fever or nipple changes.

title: Breast cancer in young women
answer: Breast cancer is rare in teenagers and uncommon in young women, though it can happen. Most breast lumps and pains at a young age are not cancer. Still, it is good to know how your breasts normally look and feel and to report changes, such as a new lump, skin dimpling, a nipple turning inward, bloody discharge or a sore that does not heal. Early checks save lives, so see a health worker if worried.

title: Mother or relative with breast cancer
answer: If your mother, sister or another close relative had breast cancer, especially at a young age, your own risk may be a bit higher, but most people with a relative who had it never get it. Tell a health worker about your family history; they can advise when you should start regular checks. Meanwhile, know your breasts, stay active, keep a healthy weight, avoid alcohol and do not smoke.

title: Testicular self-examination
answer: Checking your testicles once a month helps you know what is normal. The best time is during or after a warm bath when the skin is relaxed. Gently roll each testicle between your thumb and fingers. It should feel smooth and firm. The soft tube at the back (the epididymis) is normal. Look for lumps, swelling, hardness or changes in size. If you notice anything new, see a health worker.

title: A lump on the testicle
answer: A new lump, hard area or swelling on a testicle should always be checked by a health worker, even if it does not hurt. Many lumps are harmless, such as cysts or fluid, but testicular cancer, though rare, is most common in young men and is very treatable when found early. Do not be shy or wait to see if it goes away. The check is quick and private.

title: Swelling in the scrotum
answer: Swelling in the scrotum can have different causes, such as fluid around the testicle, a hernia where part of the bowel pushes down, infection, injury or enlarged veins. Some cause no pain; others hurt. A swelling that gets bigger when you cough or stand may be a hernia. Any new swelling should be checked by a health worker. Sudden pain, redness or fever needs care the same day.

title: Injury to the testicles
answer: Getting hit in the testicles, for example in football, is very painful, and mild pain usually settles within an hour. Rest, lie down and use a cool cloth wrapped around ice for short periods. Seek care quickly if pain is severe or does not improve, there is swelling, bruising, blood in urine, nausea or vomiting, as the testicle may be damaged. Wearing protection in contact sports helps prevent injury.

title: Mother with cervical cancer: am I at risk
answer: Cervical cancer is mostly caused by long-lasting infection with HPV, a virus passed through sexual contact, not by genes passed from mother to child. So having a mother with cervical cancer does not mean you will get it. You can protect yourself by getting the HPV vaccine, delaying sex, using condoms, not smoking, and going for cervical screening when you reach the recommended age. Your mother also needs love and support.

title: What the prostate is
answer: The prostate is a small gland, about the size of a walnut, found only in men. It sits below the bladder and surrounds the tube that carries urine out of the body. It makes some of the fluid in semen that helps sperm move and stay healthy. The prostate often grows bigger as men get older, which can cause problems with urinating in later life.

title: Prostate cancer basics for your father
answer: Prostate cancer is a common cancer in older men, mostly after age 50. Early on it often has no signs. Later signs can include trouble urinating, a weak flow, blood in urine or semen, and pain in the back or hips, though these can also have other causes. Men in their 50s, or earlier if a close relative had it, should talk to a health worker about checks. Treatment works best when found early.

title: Father having trouble urinating
answer: Many older men have trouble urinating because the prostate grows bigger with age and presses on the urine tube. Signs include a weak flow, difficulty starting, needing to go often, especially at night, or feeling the bladder is not empty. This is common and usually not cancer, but it should be checked by a health worker. If he cannot pass urine at all, or has pain or fever, he needs urgent care.

title: Encouraging your father to get a check-up
answer: Many men avoid health centers until problems are serious, sometimes because they feel embarrassed or think being strong means not seeking help. You can gently encourage your father by showing you care, sharing simple information, offering to go with him, or asking a respected relative or community health worker to talk to him. Regular check-ups help find problems like high blood pressure, diabetes or prostate issues early.

title: Skipping breakfast
answer: After a night without food, your body and brain need energy. Skipping breakfast can make you tired, unable to concentrate in class, irritable, and more likely to eat sugary snacks later. A simple breakfast helps, such as porridge (igikoma), sweet potatoes, bread with an egg or groundnut paste, milk, or fruit. If there is little food at home, even a small meal is better than nothing; tell a teacher if you are often hungry.

title: Sugary drinks and junk food
answer: Soda, sweet juices, sweets, chips and fried snacks taste good but contain a lot of sugar, salt and fat and few nutrients. Having them often can lead to tooth decay, unhealthy weight gain and, over time, diabetes and heart disease. Enjoy them only sometimes. Choose water, milk, fruit, groundnuts and home-cooked food more often. Your body needs real food to grow, learn and stay strong.

title: Drinking enough water
answer: Water helps your body control temperature, digest food, keep skin healthy and think clearly. Not drinking enough can cause headaches, tiredness, constipation, dark urine and poor concentration. Drink water regularly through the day, more when it is hot, when you exercise or when you are sick. Light yellow urine is a good sign you are drinking enough. Use clean, safe water, boiled or treated if needed.

title: Protein foods for growth
answer: Protein helps build muscles, bones, skin and blood, which is important while you are growing. Good protein foods include beans, peas, soya, groundnuts, eggs, milk, fish such as isambaza, meat and chicken. Beans and other legumes are affordable and very nutritious. Try to include some protein in most meals. You do not need protein powders or supplements if you eat a variety of these foods.

title: Calcium and strong bones
answer: Your teenage years are when bones become strongest, so calcium matters. Good sources include milk, yoghurt (ikivuguto), small fish eaten with bones like isambaza, beans, and dark green leafy vegetables. Being active, especially running, jumping and dancing, also strengthens bones. Too many fizzy drinks, smoking and alcohol can weaken them. Strong bones now help protect you later in life.

title: Fruits and vegetables every day
answer: Fruits and vegetables give your body vitamins, minerals and fibre that help fight illness, keep skin healthy and help digestion. Try to eat some at every meal, such as dark leafy greens (dodo, isombe), carrots, tomatoes, cabbage, bananas, mangoes, avocados, oranges and passion fruit. Choose different colours. Wash them well with clean water. They are often cheapest when in season.

title: Eating well on a small budget
answer: Healthy food does not have to be expensive. Beans, peas, sorghum, maize, cassava, sweet potatoes, groundnuts, small dried fish, eggs and local leafy greens are affordable and nutritious. Mix a staple with beans and a vegetable to make a balanced meal. Buy fruits and vegetables in season and avoid spending money on soda and snacks. If your family often lacks food, a community health worker may know of support.
